# The Legendarium of Dia-thìr — The Age of the Kingdom (An Aois Rìoghachd)

# Part One: Of the Settling

# Chapter One: Of the Winter of the Severance


*1 am Faoilleach, AE 151 (as memory) – 3 an t-Ògmhios, SE 1*

## I. Of the Last Ships

It is told at Muileann chaol, from the boxed rolls of that winter, how the Age of Strangers ended: not in a battle
won, for the battle had been won already, but in an emptiness where ships had been.

Five beacons stood on the capes in those days, from Baile chrom round to Tobar dhearg, kept against the humans' crossing, and each kept its own
daybook. On the first morning of that year the keepers wrote the same four words, one after another down the coast,
as if the news had to be said five times before anyone could believe it: *Cha tàinig long.* No ship came. It had not
come the morning before either, nor the morning before that, but this was the morning the keepers stopped expecting
one, and a daybook that stops expecting a thing is the surest record there is that the thing has ended.

Over the eastern water, wherever it led, the last of the humans' ships had gone out and not come back for more of
their own. Those left on Dia-thìr, some thousands of them, were put on the roads north under the victors' guard, in
the worst cold of the year, and the columns that had been an army's business all autumn became a walking business of
old men, women, children and the sick, strung out between the escorts on foot. Of the day itself little is told
beyond the counting, for a column on the move makes a poor subject for a tale, and a hungry one makes a worse one.
It is remembered only that the mud on the north roads that winter was said to be knee-deep the whole way, and that it
was still called so by the old people two generations after, though no one living had walked it.

The victors, for their part, spent that same winter in a kind of astonishment that outlasted their war. They had
fought the humans' administration for years, in the hills and the pit-towns and along
the coast roads, and had grown so used to the fighting that the winning of it left them, for a season, with less to
do than they had ever had before. The captains who had led companies through the last hard campaigns found
themselves that am Faoilleach standing in doorways at Cathair dhearg with nothing pressing to command, while the
council's few surviving clerks tried to make sense of an administration's worth of papers left behind by men who had
sailed away rather than burn them. It is said that for the first fortnight after the last ship went out, no order of
any weight was issued from the council at all, since no one among them could agree who now held the standing to
issue one.

That was the Severance, by the name it wears in every book since. Of what it cost the two peoples who lived through
it, this book has little new to add: the columns that went north, the count kept badly or not at all of who did not
finish the road, the emptiness the south felt at first as victory and only slowly, over years, as something else. It
begins instead with a clerk on a horse, going the same road the columns had gone, three months behind them, with a
satchel of blank paper and a tally to keep, sent because the council, having no better idea what a peace required of
it, had decided at least to count.

## II. Of the Guard at the Heads of the Roads

Ailean mac Iain was twenty-five that spring, a hill-born man of the council's service, named, as many of his
generation were, for a king no one now living had seen crowned. He had spent the war years copying muster-rolls in a
tent behind the lines, and he had never yet ridden further north than the market at Baile Mòr mhòr. When the council
sent its guard up to stand at the heads of the north roads, where the columns had gone in winter and where it now
meant to keep the ones still left from wandering back south, Ailean rode with them as tally-clerk, to count what
passed and write it down.

He found the work simpler than he had feared and duller than he had hoped. A guard-post was set at each of the roads
that ran north out of the settled country, a captain and a dozen men at each, and Ailean's business was to ride
between them with a book, entering what the guard reported: how many had come through going north that week, how many
turned back, how many were sick past walking and left to be carried by their own people. In three weeks he filled
eleven pages and crossed out nothing, for the council had told him plainly that a clean page was worth more to them
than a fast one.

The road itself taught him more than the tally did. He rode it in the last hard weeks of winter, when the hedges
were black and the burns ran the colour of strong tea, past farms whose byres stood empty because their stock had
gone to feed the war and their hands had gone with the columns or with the companies, one direction or the other. At
one such farm, a half-day short of the first guard-post, an old woman came out to the gate to ask him, in Dia-thìris
too plain and too quick for a hill man's ear, whether the boy who had once kept her sheep would be let come back for
them now the fighting was done. Ailean told her, truthfully, that he did not know, and wrote nothing of the
exchange in his book, since it fitted none of its columns. He remembered it all the same, years after he had
forgotten most of what the columns held.

At the guard-posts themselves the captains kept him at arm's length at first, taking him for one more of the
council's young men come to watch them rather than to help them, until they saw that his count matched theirs to the
man, week on week, and stopped troubling to check it. One captain, an old campaigner named Griogair who had lost two
fingers to a humans' picket some ten years before the Severance, told him over a fire one night that a line held by
soldiers was no line at all, only a line waiting for the soldiers to be needed elsewhere.

"Write that in your book too," Griogair said, "if your council wants the truth of it as well as the count."

Ailean did not write it in the book the council had given him. He wrote it, that once, in the back pages he had
begun keeping for himself, where a fact that would not sit easily in a column could still be set down in its own
words. It was the second such page, after the one on the empty road, and neither of them was ever asked for by
anyone above him.

At the post on the Caol mhòr road he watched the last of the columns go through: forty-one souls, by his count, two
of them dead before evening and buried where the guard let them dig, the rest walked on into the low hills with
nothing behind them but the wagon-ruts freezing over. He wrote the number in his book and, beneath it, a line the
council had not asked for: *and the road behind them empty after.* His captain read it over his shoulder, said
nothing, and let it stand. It is the first sentence of Ailean mac Iain's that survives in his own hand, and it says,
in its way, everything the tally could not.

The guard he rode with was not there to keep the columns moving. By the time Ailean reached the last post, in the
thin sun of early spring, the moving was long done, and the guard's business had become a different one: to see that
the line held, now that it had been drawn. He wrote as much to the council in his weekly letter, and got back a
single line telling him to keep counting.

## III. Of Caol mhòr and the Two Words

At Caol mhòr, on the twenty-second day of am Màrt, the council's word on the north was read aloud from the steps of
the old harbour-house, to whoever of the town would come and stand for it. Ailean had ridden down from his post two
days before at the guard captain's word that something was to be read, and stood at the back of the crowd with his
satchel, meaning only to note the numbers of who attended.

It was a wet, grey morning, the kind that makes a crowd of separate people into one shivering animal, and the man
sent to read wore the council's colours and a voice trained for a hall, not a quay. Below the steps the crowd stood
packed between the fish-sheds and the harbour wall, fisher-folk mostly, with a scattering of the guard's own men and
a few Dia-thìrich come up from the south with the columns and never gone home. The tide was out, and the mud-flats
beyond the harbour mouth lay bare and grey under the same colour of sky, so that Ailean, watching from the back, had
the sense of a crowd gathered at the edge of nothing much, to be told what it already half knew.

He read that the homeland of the Tuathaich (for that was already the word growing up for the humans' children born
and to be born on the island) was fixed by the council's law in the north, from the head of the roads to the sea,
and that it would be held there. He read it once through in Dia-thìris, which perhaps a third of the crowd followed,
watching him with the particular stillness of people waiting to be told the same thing again in words they could
use, and then said that the council had also ordered it read in the humans' tongue, for those who had none of the
other.

There was a pause on the steps while someone went to fetch the man who had been found for that. He came up out of the
crowd itself: a lean man in his middle forties, in a harbour clerk's coat gone thin at the elbows, with ink worked so far into
the creases of his knuckles that no washing would ever get it out again. He had been a clerk of the humans' harbour
office at Ros bheag before the crossing closed, and someone at the council's post had remembered it and sent for him
the night before. His name was Walter Hale.

He took the paper, read it through once to himself with his lips moving and no sound coming, and then read it aloud
to the crowd in their own tongue, flat and without warmth, the way a man reads a thing he has been handed rather than
a thing he has made. His voice carried well enough over the harbour, better than the first reader's had, though he
gave it none of the other man's polish; he read it the way a clerk reads a cargo manifest, one item following the
next without pause for effect, and the crowd took it in the same spirit, with no cheer and no protest, only a low
murmur that ran back through the ranks as each heard it from the one in front and passed it on.

Ailean, near enough to hear both readings, followed the English against his memory of the Dia-thìris and found it a
fair rendering, word for word, until the very last clause. Where the council's paper said the homeland was *fixed*
and would be *held*, Hale's English said the land was *settled*, a milder word, one that might have meant no more
than a people finding a place to live, chosen freely, as a family settles a new farm. Ailean had spent enough weeks
by then reading a column of figures against another to know the trick of a small discrepancy, the kind that never
shows in the total and never fails to matter to whoever is on the wrong side of it.

The reading over, the crowd went its ways in the rain, and most of the council's men with it, well pleased that the
thing was done. Ailean stayed by the steps to note the count. Hale was folding the paper to hand it back, and Ailean,
more from a clerk's habit of getting a thing right than from any larger thought, said that he believed the English
had softened the last clause.

Hale looked at him for a moment before he answered, as if deciding whether the question was worth an honest reply.

"Settled," he said, "is what a man does to a place he has chosen. This wasn't chosen." He handed the paper back. "The
word your council used was *held*. That's the truer one. I'd have read it that way if I'd had the choosing of it,
only I hadn't."

He said it without heat, the way a clerk corrects another clerk's figure, and turned to go back into the crowd before
Ailean could answer him at all. Ailean called after him to ask how he came to know the council's own choice of word so
exactly, since the paper he had been handed carried only the English.

Hale stopped and looked back. "I read your tongue as well as mine," he said. "Better than most of your own would
credit a harbour clerk with. I had the whole of it in my head before I opened my mouth, and I chose which of it to
give them." He said no more, and did not wait to be asked why he had chosen as he had. The crowd had already begun to
close round him, some wanting a word repeated, one old man wanting to know only whether the fish market at Doire
ghlas would still be his to trade at, and Hale gave his attention to each in turn, in the plain unhurried way of a
man used to being asked things by people with no one else to ask.

Ailean stood a moment in the rain with the paper's copy still in his satchel, then took it out, and in the margin
beside the clause on the homeland, in his own small hand, wrote the two words Hale had given him: *not settled —
held.* It was not council business, and no one had asked it of him. He never afterward could say clearly why he had
written it, except that it seemed to him, even then, a thing worth having down somewhere, in case no one else ever
thought to write it at all.

That same week the word went round Caol mhòr, and from Caol mhòr down the western roads to Ros bheag, that the humans' own
chapel there, shut since the crossing closed and its priest gone north with the rest, was to be shut for good and its
bell taken down. It was Hale's own town, the one he had clerked its harbour in before the war took the harbour's
trade away, and it was Hale who first told Ailean of it, two days after the reading, coming to find him at the guard
captain's lodging with no more introduction than the paper he still carried.

"You'll want this in whatever it is you keep," Hale said, and told him the bare fact: that the council's men were at
Ros bheag that week with a cart and an order, and that the chapel there, which had stood shut but whole since the
crossing closed, would not stand whole much longer. He did not ask Ailean to do anything about it. He seemed, if
anything, faintly amused that a Dia-thìreach clerk should think it any business of his at all, and said as much,
though without unkindness: that the council's word was the council's word, and a bell was only a bell, and he had
buried enough of his own to know that the loss that mattered was never the one you could put a cart to.

The council's men who did the work gave no reason beyond an order from the south, and took the bell away on a cart
bound, it was said, for wherever in the north the humans' faith might still be kept. Ailean rode the two days down to see it for
himself, more from the clerk's habit of checking a thing reported than from any claim on it, and found the chapel
already stripped: a low stone building with a slate roof gone green, its door standing open on an empty floor swept
bare of even its dust, and the belfry above it holding nothing but a square of paler stone where the bell's cradle
had hung. He met the cart on the road back, three carters and a soldier, the bell wrapped in sacking and roped down
like a prisoner against the cart's jolting, and stood aside to let it pass. He wrote it into his tally as he wrote
everything else that crossed his page that spring: a fact, dated, without comment. It was the only entry in eleven
pages he later wished he had written differently.

## IV. Of Cathair dhearg and the Rolls

He was recalled south in early summer, his counting at the roads' heads judged finished now that the columns had
stopped and the line held itself. He rode into Cathair dhearg on the second of an t-Ògmhios, into a town crowded and
loud after the quiet of the guard-posts, every street full of men newly told they would not be paid again as
soldiers. The market square, which he remembered from before the war as a place of stalls and cattle, was given over
that week to nothing but companies waiting their turn to be stood down, sitting on their packs in the sun with the
particular patience of men who have already fought the hard part of a thing and have only the paperwork of it left.

He found lodging above a cooper's shop near the counting-house, the same room he had kept before he rode north, and
was at his old table again within the day, as if the guard-posts and the wet road and the chapel at Ros bheag had
been someone else's spring entirely. The council's clerks who had stayed south through the winter treated him, at
first, as a man returned from an errand rather than from anything that had changed him, and he found he had no
ready way to tell them otherwise. He kept the margin copy of the Caol mhòr reading folded in the bottom of his
satchel and did not show it to anyone.

The council had ordered the war-companies of the Severance stood down, all of them, the whole force that had held the
island through the last campaign against the humans' administration and seen it end. It was thought a simple order
to carry out: muster each company once more, read the council's word, take back what arms belonged to the council
and not the man, and let the rest go home. Ailean was set to the muster in the old drill-yard behind the counting-
house, with three other clerks and a table each, taking down names as the companies came through and were released.

It went as such things go, quickly and without much feeling, until the company of Fearchar mac Raghnaill came to
Ailean's table.

Fearchar was a broad, grey man who had held that command since before Ailean was old enough to hold a pen, and his
company, hill men mostly from the same country Ailean's own family came from, stood in ranks behind him in
silence while he asked one thing only. He did not ask for pay, though none of his men had seen a full month's since spring,
and he did not ask for arms, though half the company owned nothing else worth the name. He asked that the roll of
the company's names not be burned with the loose paper of the muster, as the clerk beside Ailean had already begun
doing with the smaller companies to clear the yard faster.

"We fought under that roll," Fearchar said. "Every name on it stood where it says he stood. I'll not have it go on a
fire because it takes less room in your chests than keeping it does."

The clerk beside Ailean, who had burned four already that morning and saw no reason to stop, said that the council
had asked for the arms counted and the men sent home, and said nothing about a paper's afterlife. Fearchar did not
argue further. He simply stood, and his company stood behind him, until someone with authority to answer him could be
found.

It was Ailean, having no authority at all but a table nearer the question than most, who told him to wait, and went
himself to the master of the chests with the roll under his arm. He came back with leave: the rolls of the disbanded
companies were to be kept, not burned, boxed and sealed with the rest of the council's papers from the war. No one
troubled to explain why one captain's asking should decide it for every company after him, and Fearchar mac Raghnaill
never learned that his had been the first roll spared. He took his men home believing only that the council had, this
once, thought better of its own haste.

Ailean spent the rest of that week and the one after carrying rolls, sixty-one of them by the last count, down into
the vaulted rooms under the counting-house where the council kept what it meant to keep. It was slow, dusty work, and
no one had thought to make a record of what went into the chests beyond the chests' own numbers scratched on the
lids. Ailean, who by then had spent a whole spring learning that a thing not written down might as well not have
happened, began on his own account a list: which roll, which company, which chest, in what order laid. He filled
four sheets before he was done, and signed the last of them, though nobody had asked him to sign anything.

## V. Of the Chests Locked

On the third of an t-Ògmhios the last chest went down the stair and the mason set to sealing the door of the vault
with a course of new brick, as the council had ordered for all its war papers, meaning the seal to stand until
someone in some later year had reason to break it. Ailean stood at the bottom of the stair with his four sheets while
the brick was laid, the master of the chests beside him with a lamp that threw both their shadows long across the wet
floor.

"You've written more there than the roll asked for," the master said, nodding at the sheets.

"Someone ought to be able to say what's down here, and why, without having to break the wall to find out," Ailean
answered.

The master shrugged, took the sheets, glanced them over by the lamp, and signed his own name below Ailean's on the
last one, more from courtesy than conviction. He carried them up to be filed with the day's other business, and the
door was bricked shut behind them before evening.

Ailean walked back to his lodging that night by the long way, past the river quays where two of the council's boats lay
idle for want of anything left to carry, and took out the margin copy he still carried of the council's word from
Caol mhòr. He read again the two words he had written there in the rain, months before: *not settled — held.* He had
carried the clerk's copy so long by then, folded so many times, that the ink had begun to blur along the crease, and
he thought, not for the first time, that a word kept only in one man's pocket was not much better kept than a roll
left to burn.

He did not yet know what he would do about it, only that he meant to do something, some day, with a great many words
like it, once he had a chest of his own and no one to ask his leave. That evening he wrote nothing more. He put the
paper away, banked what fire he had, and let the town's noise carry him to sleep, the last of the Severance behind
him and the first full year of the restored country's peace not yet a fortnight old.

So closed the first summer after the Severance, with the columns settled that were never asked whether they wished
to be, a captain's roll spared by a clerk with no right to spare it, and a list of chests signed by two men neither
of whom the council had told to keep one.

# Chapter Two: Of the Stones on the North Roads

*SE 1 an t-Ògmhios – SE 2 an Cèitean*

## I. Of the Quay at Caol mhòr

Walter Hale had come to Caol mhòr on foot at the tail of the winter columns, and he stayed because there was nowhere else that would have him. By midsummer he had sent for his family, who came up the coast after him on a coal barge that had no business carrying passengers.

He was forty-four, thick through the shoulders from twenty years at a harbour desk, with a harbour clerk's stoop and a harbour clerk's hands: the right one calloused along the first two fingers where the pen sat, the left one still, oddly, soft. Ellen sat in the bow with Alice wrapped against her, five years old and sick from the swell, and David stood at the rail the whole passage with his coat buttoned wrong, watching the grey coast come up out of the grey water as though he expected it to be taken away again before they reached it.

Nobody at Caol mhòr had asked for them. Nobody had asked for any of the households that the guard walked north that year, in twos and threes and once in a column of eleven wagons, out of Ros bheag and Cuan shean and the burnt fringes of the war. The town took them in the way a beach takes what the tide leaves: without complaint, without welcome, because there was nowhere else for it to go. Hale's family was given the loft over a net-store on the harbour street, one room and a stair, and told it was theirs until somebody wanted the loft back.

He went down to the quay the first week because a man does not stop being a clerk for want of a desk, and there was work there that suited his hands if nothing else about the place suited them. The Caol mhòr boats came in with what the sea gave, which in that first summer was not much, and the catch was weighed and written down on a slate that a fisherman's daughter rubbed out every evening whether anyone had copied the numbers or not. Hale copied them. He did it without being asked, the third day, standing at the harbour wall with a scrap of paper braced on his forearm, because watching numbers be rubbed off a slate unrecorded made something in him itch that twenty years at Ros bheag had never quite cured. The daughter, whose name was Peg Carrick, watched him do it and said nothing, and the next evening left the slate a little longer before she wiped it, as if that settled something between them.

He was not the only clerk the guard had walked north. There were pursers and toll-men and a schoolmaster's assistant among the households at Caol mhòr that summer, men and women who had kept some kind of book under the humans' old administration and now kept nothing, because the administration that had employed them was three months drowned in its own harbour and the council that had replaced it wanted no part of their hand. Hale heard two of them talking on the quay steps one evening about going for fishermen, since there was nothing else a man's hands were good for here, and he did not join the talk, because he did not yet believe it.

He unloaded barges through that first month, hauling nets and barrels and, once, a crate of the guard's own muskets going north to the post above the town, and he watched the roads.

## II. Of the Stone on the Caol mhòr Road

The council's masons came up from the south at the end of an t-Iuchar, three of them with a cart of dressed stone and a soldier riding ahead to clear the road, though there was nothing on the road that summer that needed clearing. They worked their way along each of the roads that ran out of Tuathaich country toward the shires, and on the thirty-first they set the stone on the Caol mhòr road, a mile out of the town where the track crossed the old drove path, and were gone south again before the ink of the day's minute was dry.

Hale walked out to see it on the first evening he had free, and took David with him, because the boy had taken to following him about the harbour in a way that made Ellen say he needed something to do with his feet besides the loft stair.

The stone stood a little taller than Hale himself, squared and grey, the kind of stone a man does not shift with his hands alone, and it bore letters cut deep and new, the edges of the cutting still sharp and pale where the weather had not yet got at them. Neither Hale nor David could read a word of what was cut there. It was the council's tongue, not theirs, and no one had troubled to set the sense of it beside the shape.

"What does it say," David asked, which was a fair question and one Hale could not answer.

"That we're this side of it and they're that side," Hale said, which was near enough true, though it was not what the stone said. He had heard, from a Dia-thìreach guard who spoke a broken version of the humans' tongue and liked to talk while he stood his post, that the stone marked where the homeland began: not a wall, the guard had said, laughing a little at the word, as though a wall were a thing his own people might have built and had thought better of. Only a mark. A line drawn once, cut in stone so that no one could say afterward it had never been drawn.

No wall came after it. Hale looked for one through that whole first summer, half expecting to wake one morning and find a ditch and a bank running the length of the road, the kind of thing an army builds when it means to keep something in or out for good. Nothing came. The stone stood alone at the crossing, and the drove path ran past it exactly as it had before, and cattle that did not know one country from another walked over the line without noticing it was there.

He set his hand flat against the stone's face before they walked home, feeling the cut letters under his palm the way a blind man reads, though he had no more sense for what they meant that way than by eye. David did the same, more from watching his father than from any purpose of his own, and asked would they ever be able to read it.

"Somebody will read it to us someday," Hale said. "Somebody always does, in the end." He believed it when he said it, though he could not have told David why.

They walked back to the town in the last light with the stone behind them, and Hale did not look at it again that year, though he thought of it more than he let on: a boundary with no wall, a line a man could step over and not know he had done it, except that everyone on both sides of it had been told, in one tongue or the other, that it was there.

## III. Of the Thin Harvest

The stores that had always come over the water in the autumn did not come that year, and the council in the south, which had never counted the Tuathaich households among the mouths it fed, did not send anything in their place. Nobody had told the north's fields this. They had been sown late, after the marching and the settling, on ground half the households had never worked before, and what they gave back at the reaping was thin: short straw, light ears, a crop that a farmer's eye could read as trouble from the far end of the field before a scythe had touched it.

The Caol mhòr boats did better than the land, at first, but even the sea was uncertain that year, the herring shoals running late and thin off their old grounds, and by an Dàmhair the catch had fallen to less than a household could live on if each household kept what it caught for itself.

It was Ellen who put the shape to it before anyone in the town had a word for it. She had kept a harbour clerk's house long enough to think in tallies without meaning to, and she came home from the quay one evening in the first week of an Dàmhair and told Hale, flatly, the way she told him most things that mattered, that Peg Carrick's mother had given the Widow Fenn two fish out of a catch of nine, and the Widow Fenn had no boat and no man to send out in one, and if that went on past the week it would not go on at all, because nine fish shared out to households instead of sold to whoever came first to the quay was not how a harbour worked, and everyone at Caol mhòr knew it.

It became, within the month, how the harbour worked anyway. There was no minute written for it, no council of the town's own to vote it in; it happened the way water finds its own level, house by house, boat by boat, until the whole of Caol mhòr's catch, good weeks and bad, went first to a reckoning of who had a boat and who did not, and only what was left after that was sold or traded beyond the town. Hale kept no tally of it himself that autumn, his own book still unbegun, and he watched it happen with the same clerk's attention he gave the harbour slate. A town sharing its catch by households and a town selling its catch to whoever paid first were two different towns, he came to understand, though he could not yet have said in so many words why it mattered, and Caol mhòr had quietly become the first kind without anyone deciding it should.

He thought of the guard and his mark cut in stone, the line with no wall, and thought that a boundary a man could not see might matter as much as one he could.

## IV. Of the Meal Carried to Doire ghlas

By an t-Samhain the thinness of the harvest had a name in every house at Caol mhòr, though no two households agreed on how bad it would get before spring, and by early an Dùbhlachd the name had stopped being a thing people argued about and become a thing they simply lived inside, the way a house lives inside a hard winter once the first snow has settled and shows no sign of going.

Word came down the coast road from Doire ghlas, ten miles inland along a track that in a wet an Dùbhlachd took the better part of a day to walk, that the town there had nothing left in its stores and had begun, in the second week of the month, to bury its own dead of hunger without troubling to send word south, because word sent south had never yet brought anything back.

Caol mhòr had little enough to spare, but it had more than Doire ghlas, being a harbour town with a catch of sorts still coming in, and its householders, who had taken to meeting in the long room behind the net-stores whenever there was cause, voted what oats and salt fish it could spare into three carts, and asked for men to walk them inland.

Hale went. He told Ellen he went because his hands were the freest in the household that week, David and Alice both needing her at home with the fever going round the loft-houses, but the truth of it, which he did not say to her, was that he went because Doire ghlas frightened him in a way the thin harvest at Caol mhòr had not, and a man does not walk toward what frightens him without some better reason than idle hands, and he had not found a better reason, and had gone anyway.

The road to Doire ghlas ran inland from the coast through country that had been farmed by nobody in living memory before that year, scrub and rush pasture that the settled households had been given because the good land nearer the coast was already claimed, and the going was slow with the cart wheels sinking to the hub in places where the drainage had never been cut. They came into Doire ghlas on the second day, in the last of the light, and Hale smelled the town before he saw its roofs: woodsmoke, and under the woodsmoke something colder that he did not let himself name until he had to.

They had dug the graves on the rise above the church because the low ground by the burn was too wet to hold a grave that winter, and the digging had been hard going in ground half frozen, so that the graves were shallower than a churchyard grave should be and set closer together than custom allowed, because there had not been strength enough in the town to dig them any other way. Hale counted the fresh mounds while the carts were being unloaded, walking the rise alone in the last grey light with his hat off though there was no one there to see him bare his head for it, and stopped counting at eleven because his eyes had blurred and he no longer trusted the number, and started again, and reached fourteen the second time, and did not try a third.

Three of the mounds were child-sized. He stood over those longest.

A woman of the town, thin herself in a way that made her age hard to guess, told him while they carried sacks of oats into what was left of the store that the town had lost more than the fourteen he could count on the rise, because some of the earliest dead, back in an t-Samhain before anyone had thought to keep a reckoning, had been buried singly by their own families in whatever ground was handiest, without the town knowing to add them to any count at all. She could not say how many. Nobody could say how many. Hale came slowly to understand, standing in the freezing store with an oat sack still on his shoulder, the whole shape of the trouble: the town had starved through a winter nobody south of the guard-line had thought to prevent, and the dying itself had gone on unrecorded, house by house, before anyone had thought to reckon it as a single town's loss rather than a scatter of private griefs.

He asked the woman, because it was the only question his clerk's mind knew how to ask in the face of a thing this large, whether anyone kept a book of it. She looked at him as though the question itself were a kind of madness, in a place where half the households did not yet own a book of any kind, and said that the priest kept the parish register, births and marryings and the ordinary dead. This was a different order of grief, too large for the parish book and too many-headed for any one family's memory, and nobody had told her what a person was meant to do with it, and so, for want of a better answer, nobody had done anything with it at all.

## V. Of the Book Begun

Hale walked back to Caol mhòr with the empty carts in three days instead of two, because the weather turned and one of the horses went lame on the second, and he had the whole of that slow, cold walking to sit with what he had seen on the rise above Doire ghlas and could not put down.

It was not, he told himself at first, a clerk's proper business. He had no office here, no seal, no book issued him by any council; he was a harbour clerk without a harbour, three months into a life he had not chosen, in a country whose government did not know his name and would not have cared to learn it. But he had spent twenty years believing that a thing not written down was a thing that had not, in any way that mattered to the world afterward, happened, and that belief had not left him only because the humans' administration that had trained him into it now lay at the bottom of a drowned harbour. It went where he went. It had gone with him up the coast road and stood with him on the rise counting graves he could not trust his own eyes to count twice the same.

He bought, from the one shop at Caol mhòr that still sold anything beyond food and rope, a ledger meant for a fishmonger's accounts, its pages ruled for weights and prices, and on the first evening after his return, with Ellen asleep and the children asleep and the loft cold around him, he opened it at the first page and wrote, in his own clerk's hand, the word *Doire ghlas*, and under it the date, and under that, as near as he could reconstruct it from what the woman in the store had told him and what he had counted twice on the rise, a number, and could not have sworn to its truth writing it, only that it was the nearest thing to truth that anyone had troubled to set down, which was as much as the writing could claim for itself. The alternative, no number at all, a grief too large for the parish book, filed nowhere, answerable to nobody, was the thing he had walked ten miles inland and ten miles home to refuse.

He did not stop at Doire ghlas. Through the rest of that hard winter, as word came down the coast road of other towns short of grain, other households that had gone without and some that had not come through it, Hale set down what he could learn of each in the fishmonger's ledger, town by town, a line or two apiece, a name where a name could be had and a number where a number could be had and, more often than either, a plain note that no count had been kept and none now could be trusted. He did not think of it, in those first months, as anything more than a private accounting, the kind of book a careful man keeps against his own forgetting. It did not occur to him yet that he was keeping the only reckoning of that winter's dead that would ever exist south of the guard-line either, because no one south of it had asked to be told, and no one south of it, so far as Hale could tell, so much as knew there was a reckoning to be kept.

That was the turn of it, when it came to him, sitting by the loft's small fire on a night in am Faoilleach with the fishmonger's ledger open on his knee and the wind working at the shutter: that the council which had set a stone on the road to mark where his people's country began had drawn no line at all around the counting of his people's dead, because it had never occurred to the council that there was a count to be drawn a line around. The Dia-thìrich made none. They had not refused to; refusal would have required them to notice there was a decision to make. They simply had not thought of it, the way a man does not think to count the leaves that fall from a tree he does not own, and in the space that not-thinking left, if the count was to exist at all, it would have to be the Tuathaich who kept it, in their own hand, in a fishmonger's ledger bought for weights and prices, because no one else on the whole of the island would ever trouble to.

He did not write that thought down; it belonged nowhere in a ledger of names and numbers. It sat in him from that night on, under everything else the book came afterward to hold, the way the stone on the Caol mhòr road sat unseen under the drove path's traffic: a line drawn once, that nobody south of it would ever have cause to notice, and that everybody north of it would carry, whether they chose to or not, for the rest of their lives.

## VI. Of the Names in the Porch

Spring came late that year, as it does on a coast that takes its weather from the open west, but it came. By an Cèitean the worst of the hunger had passed, the last of the winter stores stretched thin enough to see the new grass through, and the herring, which had run late and light the autumn before, came back to the Caol mhòr grounds in numbers a fisherman three generations settled there said he had not seen since before the Severance, as though the sea itself, having taken nothing from the town that winter, had decided to give something back by way of apology.

Doire ghlas, when word of it reached Caol mhòr on a carter's cart come down for seed, had done in its own fashion what Hale had done alone in the loft with the fishmonger's ledger, though the town had come to it by a different road. Somebody at Doire ghlas, a woman of the parish and not the priest, though the carter did not know her name, had gone from house to house through the town in the first mild week of spring and asked each household for the names of anyone it had lost since an t-Samhain, hunger-dead and not ordinary dead, and had written each name on a strip of paper in whatever hand could be found to write it, and pinned the strips, one by one as they were gathered, along the boards of the church porch, where every soul in the town passed at least once a week whether it went in to service or not.

There was no order to the names, the carter said, no roll of the dead set out fair in a single hand the way a parish register would have kept it; strips of paper in a dozen different hands, some barely lettered, pinned up as they came in, so that a name might sit next to another from a household three streets off with no kin between them, and a child's name might sit above or below an old man's with nothing to mark which was which except the writing itself. But the porch held, by the carter's rough count, above fifteen names by the time he had come away, and the town had taken to calling it, without deciding to, the porch of the names, and left it up through the spring though the strips curled and faded in the weather, because nobody in Doire ghlas could yet bring themselves to be the one to take even a single name down.

Hale walked out to see it himself before that spring was over, taking the coast road ten miles inland a second time, this time with no cart to slow him and no lame horse, and stood in the church porch reading names he mostly did not know, in a light hand and a heavy hand and a child's careful copying-hand where some elder had taught a grandchild the letters expressly for this, and found, when he had read them all through once, that he could not have said afterward whether the number matched the fourteen he had counted on the rise that winter, or the vaguer reckoning the woman in the store had given him of the earlier dead nobody had thought to add in, or neither. He understood, standing there in the mild spring light with the herring running thick again off the harbour he had left that morning, that the porch kept its own count, made by its own town, in its own way, and no less true for not squaring with his.

The porch's names did not go into the fishmonger's ledger that day. Hale copied them instead, every one, into a second book he had begun keeping since am Faoilleach for exactly this purpose, a book with nothing in it yet but blank ruled pages and the single word he had written on its first leaf in the dead of that winter, by lamplight: *Doire ghlas*, and under it, this time, above fifteen names, copied faithfully from a church porch that the council thirty-odd miles south did not know existed, in a hand a Dia-thìreach clerk, had one ever troubled to read it, would have called a stranger's.

The ledger went home to Caol mhòr under his coat, against the last of the spring rain, and he told no one south of the guard-stone what it held, for there was no one south of the guard-stone to tell.

# Chapter Three: Of the Counting-Houses and the Broken Locks

*SE 2 an t-Ògmhios – an t-Iuchar*

> *Is san scrìobhadh a tha e, chan ann san t-sùil.*
> It lies in the writing, not the seeing.
>
> — a saying of the counting-clerks of Cathair dhearg, of no known author

## I. Of the Boxes at Cathair dhearg

Ailean mac Iain had spent the first summer of the restored country learning that a thing not written down might as well not have happened. He spent the second summer learning what it cost to write some things down and not others, and that the difference between the two lessons was most of what a clerk's life was for.

He was set, on the second morning of an t-Ògmhios, to a room at Cathair dhearg that had been the humans' counting-house, a long stone hall behind the harbour offices with high windows and a floor still marked in chalk where the humans had ruled lines for sorting coin. The war had been through it twice, once when the council took the town and once when a company of the humans' own guard had tried, briefly and badly, to hold it back, and what the fighting had not burned the damp had got into afterward. Ailean stood in the doorway on his first morning with a list in his hand of what he was to do, and could smell, under the mildew, a fainter smell of char that told him some of the shelves nearest the door had gone up before anyone thought to put them out.

The master set over the room, a heavy, patient man named Ruairidh whom Ailean never once heard raise his voice, gave him the whole of the northern wall to clear: ledger after ledger in the humans' close, slanting hand, bound in board covers gone soft with damp, each one a year or two of some tally he could only guess at from its weight and its ruled columns. "Box them," Ruairidh said. "Don't read them. We haven't the hands to spare for reading, and half of what's here is charred through by the middle anyhow. Box them, mark the shelf they came from, and let the reckoners sort out later what's worth opening."

Ailean had not told Ruairidh, and did not tell him now, that he could in fact make out a fair part of the humans' hand, better than most of the clerks the council had brought south that summer. As a boy in the hills he had gone twice a week to a reader kept by Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise in the nearest of the human mission-houses, less because his people held with the humans' errand than because the reader taught letters to any child sent to him and asked no coin for it, and Ailean's mother had wanted her son able to read whatever came his way, in whatever hand it came in. He had sat on a bench with three human children and two others of his own people and learned his letters twice over, in two hands and two tongues, and had not thought since that it would ever be worth anything to anyone but himself.

It was worth this much now: that he could have told Ruairidh, truthfully, what several of these ledgers were before he boxed them, and chose instead to box them as he had been told, unread, because a clerk who is asked to box a thing and instead reads it aloud to his master has made himself the kind of clerk nobody keeps for long. He carried the first stack to the crate the carpenters had left at the door, laid the boards in flat, and wrote on the crate's side, in his own hand, *Tithe rolls, north wall, unread*, which was as much truth as the label had room to hold and rather more than most of the crates around him got.

By the third day he had the rhythm of it: lift, glance at the spine for a date if one showed, set it in the crate, mark the tally on his own sheet, lift again. Some of the ledgers, near the seat of the old fire, crumbled at the spine when he lifted them and had to go into the crate as loose leaves, gathered as best he could in something like their order, with a note on the crate that the order was his own guess and not to be trusted past that. He thought, more than once that week, of how a fire that burns a thing halfway leaves a worse record than one that burns it whole, because a whole loss at least tells you plainly that there is nothing left to ask about, while a half loss goes on pretending, for as long as the crate is shut, that the rest of the truth is only waiting to be found.

He did not say this to Ruairidh either. Nowhere did he write it down. It sat with him the way the two words in his margin from the year before had sat with him, a private accounting kept against the day he might have a use for it, and he went on boxing.

There were four others set to the room besides him, none known to Ailean before that summer, drawn south from as many different hill parishes as there were clerks, and of these only a stooped, quick-handed man called Tòmas ever spoke to him beyond what the work required. Tòmas had been a mason's clerk before the war, used to tallying stone rather than paper, and he handled the ledgers as though they might crumble at a wrong word as readily as at a wrong touch, which by the third week several of them did. On the day the fire-damaged shelf gave up its last crumbling stack, Tòmas straightened over the crate with a fistful of loose leaves gone soft and brown at the edges and said, to no one in particular, that it seemed a strange kind of victory, to win a war and then spend a summer sweeping up the loser's paper.

"Somebody has to know what was owed and to whom," Ailean said, "or the whole of it starts again from nothing, and starting from nothing costs more than sweeping."

"Does it," Tòmas said, not quite a question, and went back to his crate, and Ailean found he had no ready answer for the plain doubt in it, only the private one he did not offer: that starting from nothing might in fact have cost the kingdom less, in the end, than beginning from a room like this one, but that no one who had been given a crate and a chalk stub that summer was in any position to choose between the two.

## II. Of Ros dhomhain's Sheds

In the second week Ailean was sent west along the coast road to Ros dhomhain, where the humans' harbour offices stood larger than Cathair dhearg's and the war had touched them less, and where the council wanted its tariff tables copied out before the summer's shipping began under the new hands.

Ros dhomhain in that first restored summer was still mostly a humans' town wearing a Dia-thìreach flag: the sheds along its long stone quay built to the humans' measure, the cranes still swung by the humans' gearing, the harbour-master's house with its clock stopped at whatever hour the last of the humans' officers had walked out of it. A clerk of the council's own, a hill man named Dùghall who had been set over the harbour's books for want of anyone else willing to learn its workings, met Ailean at the gate and walked him through the sheds himself, apologising for the state of the ledger room as though the mess were somehow his own doing.

"They kept a tariff table for every port on the coast," Dùghall said, laying a bound sheet across the counting-desk, "duties on grain, on timber, on the coal that went out before the works closed, on I don't know what else, half of it in figures I can't make head or tail of. The council wants it copied into our own hand and our own tongue before the boats start moving again, so a captain putting in here need not wonder whether the man taking his dues even knows what he's owed."

Ailean spent nine days at that desk, copying figure for figure and clause for clause, turning the humans' close columns into a Dia-thìris he had to build word by word as he went, for there had never before been a need to say, in his own tongue, what a duty on timber was or how it was reckoned by the load rather than the piece. He found that a language could be made to hold a new thing without breaking, provided a man was patient enough to lay the words down one at a time and careful enough not to claim, in the laying, that the thing had changed because its name had. The tariff the humans had set stood exactly as it had stood before; only the ink was new.

Dùghall watched him work on the last evening, reading over Ailean's shoulder with the frank curiosity of a man who has never learned to read closely enough to be embarrassed by his own slowness at it. "It's the same duty," he said at last, as though the thought had only just settled in him. "We've only put our own coat on it."

"For want of another," Ailean said, which was the same answer Dùghall would go on giving, in one form or another, for as long as he kept the harbour, though neither of them knew that yet.

He carried the finished copy south himself rather than trust it to a courier, folded flat inside his coat against the coast road's dust, and thought, walking, of the label he had written on the crate of tithe rolls: *unread*. The tariff table he carried now had been read most carefully of all, word by word, clause by clause, and copied out exact, and he could not have said with any honesty that the reading had changed a single thing it was made to do.

## III. Of the Labelled Box

The last of his three counting-houses was the one at Seann Skell in the west, the humans' great harbour on the coast below the capes, where the fishing fleets still came in under a flag they had never learned to read and the old harbour bell rang the hours by a humans' clock nobody had yet thought to reset.

The counting-house there had taken the least harm of the three, for the town had changed hands with barely a shot fired, its garrison marching out under terms before the council's companies were even in sight of the walls, and Ailean found its shelves whole where Cathair dhearg's had burned and Ros dhomhain's had been picked over by two summers of harbour clerks before him. He worked through it alone for the better part of a week, boxing what he was told to box, tithe rolls and customs rolls and the wage-books of men whose names meant nothing to him, until he came, on a shelf set apart from the rest behind a locked grating that had taken the smith half a morning to force, on a set of rolled sheets larger than anything else in the room, each one bound with a strip of the humans' own linen tape and marked, in a surveyor's careful print, with a district's name.

Setting his own crate aside, he unrolled the first of them on the long table by the window and stood over it a long while before he thought to send for Ruairidh.

It was a map, but more than a map: every field about Seann Skell laid out with its boundary walked and measured, every holding numbered, every stream and track set down to a scale marked plainly in one corner, in a hand so exact that Ailean, who had grown up on a hillside no one had ever thought worth surveying at all, felt for a moment that he was looking at the land laid out entire, folded small and put under glass. He had seen the council's own maps, such as they were: rough things, drawn from memory and hearsay, good enough to show a captain which valley led where but not good enough to say whose field lay on which side of a boundary stone. Nothing in his life had prepared him for what lay unrolled on that table.

He counted the district sheets as he unrolled them, laying each flat under a weight of loose stone from the yard before it could curl back on its own roll, and found there were eleven in all, enough between them, he judged from the scale marked in the corners, to cover the whole of the coast from the north-western capes down past Seann Skell itself and some way inland besides, though how far inland he could not tell until he had them all open together, which the table was not long enough to allow. He knelt on the floor instead and laid three of them edge to edge, matching a stream on one sheet to its continuation on the next by eye, and felt, doing it, something closer to the excitement of a boy given a puzzle than to the flat patience with which he had boxed the tithe rolls all that month.

Ruairidh came, looked, said nothing for a while, and then said what Ailean had already half thought himself: that there was nothing else like this on the whole of the island, that whatever the council's own men might one day draw of the shires it meant to rule, they would draw it from this, because there was nowhere else whole enough to draw it from.

"Box them apart from the rest," Ruairidh said. "Not with the tithe rolls. These go to the council's own clerks, not the reckoners." He thought a moment longer, and added, in the tone of a man handing over a decision he would rather not have had to make himself, "Write something on the crate so whoever opens it next knows what it's for."

Ailean found a fresh crate, laid the rolled surveys in it one district at a time, each still bound in its own tape, and stood with the lid in his hand and a stub of chalk, thinking what to write. He could have written what the crate held, plainly, as he had for the tithe rolls: *district surveys, Seann Skell in the west, entire*. It would have been true and would have said nothing that mattered. He thought instead of the council's own rough maps, of the valley that showed a captain the way but not the boundary, of a kingdom that had just that summer begun calling itself a kingdom with no whole map of its own to be one by, and he wrote, in the end, six words that were not a description of what the crate held so much as a statement of what it was for: *The shires will be drawn on them.*

He looked at the words a moment after he had written them, chalk-white on unpainted wood, and understood, standing there with the lid half over the crate, that he had just written down the truest sentence he had put to anything since the margin of the council's own proclamation the year before, and that it troubled him in the same way that sentence had, because a kingdom that drew its shires on the humans' district lines, using the humans' own survey of the humans' own farms, was not drawing a kingdom fresh out of the ground it had won. It was tracing one that had already been drawn, by other hands, for other purposes, and calling the tracing its own.

He shut the lid, nailed it, and marked the crate for the council's own clerks rather than the reckoners, as Ruairidh had told him. Nobody who read the label in the months and years that followed, as the shire lines were in fact drawn from what the crate held, exactly where the crate had said they would be, ever asked who had written it or what he had meant by it.

## IV. Of What the North Tells

It is told at Muileann chaol, though not from any minute the council kept, for it kept none, that in those same weeks, at Ceann mhòr and Cathair gheal and Inis àrsaidh on the north-western coast, a different kind of counting-house was opened, and opened rather more quickly than the ones Ailean was working through.

The humans' harbour officers at those three towns had sailed with the last of the crossing ships and had taken their keys with them, whether from forethought or from simple haste nobody left behind could afterward say, and the harbour stores at all three towns stood locked through that spring with the last of the humans' stock still inside them: rope, canvas, salt, tackle, and at Cathair gheal a whole loft of nets that had never been fished. No maor had yet been set over any of the three towns, the council's attention being wholly on the south that season, and for a while the stores simply stood, locked and unclaimed, while the towns around them went short of exactly the things the stores held.

It did not stand long. A fisherman of Ceann mhòr, whose name the north's own telling does not agree on, though every version gives him a hammer and a bad temper, walked down to the store one wet morning, tried the lock with his hand, tried it again with his shoulder, and then went home for his hammer and came back and broke it. He did not, by any account the north tells, take anything for himself that first morning. He broke the lock, opened the door, and stood back to let the town see what was inside, and it was the town, not the man with the hammer, that decided within the hour how the rope and the canvas and the salt would be shared out, house by house, by much the same rough justice that had already, that same year at Caol mhòr, decided how a thin catch of herring ought to be shared.

Cathair gheal and Inis àrsaidh followed within the fortnight, each in its own way: at Cathair gheal it is told that the whole loft of unfished nets went out to every boat in the harbour on a single tide, so that the fleet that year fished with nets it had never paid a coin for and never afterward wondered whose they had once been; at Inis àrsaidh, smaller than the other two and poorer, the store held little enough that the sharing was done inside an afternoon, what the town remembers of it is the reckoning rather than the goods: who had a boat and who had none, and so who needed rope and who needed salt more, drawn up on the spot by three women of the town with no office to do it and no one afterward to say they had done it wrong.

The north tells this part, when it tells it at all, with something close to relish, in a way it does not tell the winter of the hungry year that came so soon after: broken locks, a hammer, goods shared out by the plain justice of a fishing town rather than doled out by any office south of the water. No maor ever came to ask who had struck the first blow, for by the time one did come north, in the winter of the year after, there was nothing left locked to account for, and the town's own memory of the thing had already hardened into the kind of story a place keeps because it likes the shape of it: the strangers left, and took their keys, and the sea folk broke in with their own hands and helped themselves, and no one has ever been the worse for it.

Ailean, boxing tithe rolls at Cathair dhearg that same month, heard nothing of it at the time, and no clerk's crate anywhere in the south held so much as a line about it, because no one south of the water had thought there was anything there worth a clerk's crate.

## V. Of the Proclamation

The council styled the state a kingdom on the twenty-seventh of an t-Iuchar, from the steps of the counting-house at Cathair dhearg, the very building whose northern wall Ailean had spent the earlier weeks of that summer clearing crate by crate.

He was given no part in the reading. He stood in the crowd instead, in the press of clerks and harbour men and off-duty guards that had gathered in the square below the steps once word went round that the council meant to say something, close enough to hear the words plainly and too far back to see more than the tops of the twelve heads on the platform above him. A herald, not the crier who had read the council's word at Caol mhòr the year before, read out a proclamation that named the state, from that day, Rìoghachd Dia-thìr, and spoke of the island won back and the homeland made secure and the years of settling now, in the herald's own word, *complete*. It was not a long proclamation. It named no king, for none had yet been crowned, and no new law, for none had yet been made; it was, as far as Ailean could judge standing in the crowd with the sun on the back of his neck, mostly a naming, the council giving itself a title it had in truth held in every particular but the word for some months already.

He thought, listening, of the crate at Seann Skell with its six chalked words, and of the tariff table at Ros dhomhain copied out in a new tongue to say exactly the old thing, and of the seal the council's engraver had that same week begun cutting for the state's own letters, a seal that would go, when it was finished, onto documents no different in kind from the ones he had spent the summer boxing unread. A kingdom had been proclaimed from the steps of a building that had been, until that spring, a foreign counting-house, using a survey drawn by foreign hands to mark out the shires it meant to rule, keeping in force, for want of another, a tariff the foreigners themselves had set. He did not think any of this made the proclamation false, exactly. He thought it made the proclamation a kind of label, not unlike the one he had chalked on the crate of surveys, true as far as it went and silent about everything that had gone into making it true.

Beside him in the crowd stood a woman he did not know, a fishwife by her basket and her salt-reddened hands, who asked the man on her other side, in the flat voice of someone asking merely to have something answered rather than because the answer mattered to her trade, whether a kingdom paid its dues any different from a council. The man did not know. Nobody near Ailean seemed to know, and he thought that this, more than the herald's words or the twelve heads on the platform, was the truest measure of what had been proclaimed: a name new enough to need explaining and an arrangement old enough that nobody in the crowd expected the explaining to change anything they would be asked to pay.

The crowd around him cheered when the herald finished, in the ragged, willing way of a crowd that wants something to cheer and has been given, at last, an excuse. Ailean did not cheer. He stood with his hands in his coat, watching the twelve on the platform receive the cheering as though it had been meant for them personally rather than for the word, and thought that a state could change its name from a war-council to a kingdom on a single afternoon and be, in every working part beneath the name, exactly the state it had been the afternoon before: the same tariff, the same surveys, the same crates going into the same rooms marked in the same hands, only now under a seal cut fresh and called royal.

He walked back to the counting-house that evening, after the crowd had gone, and let himself in with the key Ruairidh had given him, to check, he told himself, that the last of the week's crates were properly nailed before the carters came for them in the morning. The northern wall stood bare where the tithe rolls had been, swept and empty for the first time since he had begun. The crate marked for the council's own clerks, the one with six words chalked on its lid, still stood by the door where he had left it, waiting to be carried up to whichever room the shire-lines would in the end be drawn in.

Reading the words over once more by the last of the evening light through the high windows, *the shires will be drawn on them*, he thought that whatever the herald had proclaimed that afternoon from the steps outside, the truer proclamation of the summer was chalked in his own hand on a crate nobody but a handful of clerks would ever see, and that the kingdom the crowd had cheered for would be built, quite literally, field by field and boundary by boundary, on lines that other hands, under another flag, had walked and measured first. This did not, to his mind, make the kingdom any less a kingdom. It made it the kind of kingdom that proclaimed itself in the open, on a summer afternoon, with bells and a herald and twelve men receiving a crowd's cheers, and settled itself, in the meantime and mostly unseen, in rooms like this one, on paper like this, in a hand like his own.

He locked the counting-house behind him and went home by the harbour road, past the sheds where the council's idle ships still lay, and did not write any of it down that night. There was, he thought, nothing in it that the crate had not already said better than he could, in six words and a piece of chalk.

# Chapter Four: Of the Moot and the Council of Twelve

*SE 2 an Lùnastal – an t-Sultain*

> *Chan eil inbhe againn. Scrìobhaidh sinn co-dhiù.*
> We have no standing. We shall write it all the same.
>
> — the Moot's minute-book, its first leaf, 25 an Lùnastal, SE 2

## I. Of the Long Room at Caol mhòr

They came on foot and in carts, at the tail end of a wet an Lùnastal that had done nothing for the barley and less for tempers, from Doire ghlas and Muileann leathan and the scattered crofts along the coast road, householders every one of them, a man or a woman standing for each roof that had smoke going up it that summer. Nobody had called them. Word had gone from house to house the way word goes in a country too poor yet to have a bell for it, mouth to mouth along the quay and up the drove paths, that there would be a meeting at Caol mhòr on the first fair day of the month to speak of the winter coming, and enough people believed it mattered enough to walk to find out that the harbour-house's long room, used till then for nothing grander than mending nets on a wet afternoon, could not hold them all. Those who could not get inside stood in the doorway and along the wall outside it, passing back what was said a sentence behind the saying of it.

Walter Hale stood at the back with his hat in both hands, working the brim between his fingers the way he had worked it as a boy waiting outside a schoolmaster's door, though he was forty-five now and had not stood outside a schoolmaster's door in thirty years. He had come because Ellen had told him to come, flatly, over the breakfast she made him eat before he went, on the grounds that a man who kept a private ledger of the town's dead and did not trouble to say so out loud to the town was only half doing the thing he had set himself to do. He had not argued the point. Once Ellen made it in that voice, he rarely did.

The room smelled of damp wool and fish-scale and too many bodies for the size of it, and for the better part of the afternoon it did nothing but argue, which Hale had expected and had come prepared to sit through. They argued first about whether there was anything to be done at all, a question that took the better part of an hour to settle in the negative, since a country that has just been marched into a homeland it did not choose and left to make what it can of a summer already half spent is not naturally disposed to agree on anything, least of all on whether agreeing is worth the breath. They argued next about who among them had the right to speak for the rest, which took longer, since half the room held that no one man could speak for households as different as a fisherman's and a smith's and a schoolmaster's widow's, and the other half held that a hundred voices arguing at once would carry no further than the harbour wall and be no more use than the gulls.

It was in the middle of this second argument, with the light going amber through the one window and a woman near the door saying for the third time that she had not walked nine miles to listen to men quarrel about who should do the talking, that somebody said Hale's name.

He did not afterward remember who said it first. It went round the room the way a bucket goes hand to hand along a fire-line, picked up by whoever's hand was nearest and passed on without much thought given to it, a name is offered, another voice takes it up because it is easier to agree than to argue further, and by the time it had gone twice round the low room it had stopped being a suggestion and become, without any vote taken or asked for, a fact that the room seemed to have arrived at together. Hale had kept a slate; Hale had kept a book of the hungry year's dead, though few enough of them yet knew how thorough a book; Hale had once been paid, under the old administration, to write things down in a hand that held up in a court of law, which was more than any other soul in the room could claim. The bucket stopped with him.

"I'm no speaker," he said, which was true, and which nobody in the room seemed inclined to hold against him.

"You needn't speak," said the woman by the door, whose name was Seonag and who had lost, though Hale did not know it yet, a sister at Doire ghlas that winter. "You need only write down what the rest of us say, so it's said once and stays said."

It was a man further back, one of the pursers the guard had walked north with the rest, who put the harder question into words. "We've no standing," he said, loud enough to carry to the doorway and the backs pressed against it. "Not in their law. They needn't hear a word of it, whatever we write or don't."

"Then we'll say it where we can hear it ourselves," Hale said.

He had not planned to say it. It came out of him the way the count of the graves at Doire ghlas had come out of him in the church porch that spring, not chosen so much as arrived at, a thing his own mouth said before the rest of him had finished deciding whether he believed it. But once said it could not be unsaid, and the room, which a moment before had been on the edge of deciding the whole meeting was a waste of a fair day's light, went quiet in the particular way a room goes quiet when it has just heard the one sentence it did not know it was waiting for.

He went to the trestle at the front, where somebody had set out an inkhorn and a stack of paper meant for nothing more than tallying the fair day's trade, and he sat down on the bench behind it, and he opened, because it was the only book to hand, a ledger that a Caol mhòr chandler had brought along half-hoping to sell blank stock to whoever needed it. It had nothing written in it. Hale wetted the pen, and, because a clerk's hand does the thing a clerk's mind has already decided before the mind has finished deciding it, wrote the day at the top of the first leaf in the small, upright script that Ros bheag had trained into him twenty years before, and under the day, because a minute needs a heading and he had been keeping one kind of book or another for three months now and had a feel for what a heading ought to say, he wrote: *A meeting of the households of the north, at Caol mhòr.*

"There," he said. "It's written now."

There was no ceremony to it beyond that, no vote taken on whether the thing they had just made should have a name, and for the whole of that first afternoon nobody troubled to give it one. It was some weeks before anyone began calling it the Moot, a word one of the pursers remembered from an old book of the humans' law, half meaning it as a joke against themselves and half not, and the name stuck the way names stick that fit a thing better than the thing's makers had planned for. It had no standing in Dia-thìreach law. No statute recognised it, no seal was cut for it, no clerk south of the guard-line had ever heard the word spoken. It met all the same, in the long room and then, when the long room proved too small, in a barn lent for the purpose by a Caol mhòr net-maker who asked nothing for the use of it beyond a promise that the floor would be swept after. It kept minutes from that first wet afternoon onward, in Hale's hand and then, as the years went on, in other hands after his, and the minutes ran unbroken, that first ledger and the books that followed it, from that day to this.

## II. Of the Book with Nothing in It

The Moot's first business, once the matter of a name had been set aside as not worth the afternoon it would have cost, was the winter.

It did not take long to agree what the winter would need, because the whole room had lived through the last one and none of them wished to live through its like again unwarned. Grain, first, and more of it laid by earlier than the last time, since the stores that had come over the water in other years came no longer and would not be coming this one either, whatever the councillors at Cathair dhearg might privately believe about a harvest that had not yet been cut. A guard kept on the roads, against no enemy anyone could name, only because a household walking alone with a cart of oats on a bad night was safer for having somebody else's eyes on the road with it, and the memory of what had happened to nobody-knew-how-many households on the road to Doire ghlas the winter before sat close enough under the surface of that meeting that nobody needed to say it outright for everyone to understand it was being said.

And the dead of Doire ghlas, though the dying lay a season behind them by then, went into the minutes too, because Hale stood and told the room, plainly, in the flat clerk's voice he used for anything he did not trust himself to say any other way, what he had counted on the rise above the town and what the names pinned in the church porch had since told him, and asked whether the Moot, being now a thing that existed and could vote on matters, should not vote that the count be kept as the north's own record, since no one south of the guard-stone had asked to keep it and none, so far as anyone in the room could tell, so much as knew there was a count to be kept. The vote, when it was taken, by a show of hands that Hale counted twice to be sure of the number, as though the habit of counting things twice had become, for him, something closer to a creed than a caution, carried without a voice raised against it.

The granary took longer to settle than the counting had, because a granary meant not only agreeing that grain should be laid by but agreeing whose grain it would be and on whose word it would be shared out when the laying-by season turned to the eating one, and a room full of householders who had spent a hungry year learning exactly how much a neighbour's honesty was worth in a bad month was in no hurry to hand that question over lightly. It was settled in the end, after the better part of another hour's argument, on terms near enough to what Caol mhòr's own fishermen had already worked out for themselves with the catch, unspoken and unminuted, the autumn before: each household to give what it could spare into the common store, in proportion to what it had, and the store to be kept under lock in the harbour-house cellar with three keys held by three householders chosen for the keeping and answerable to the Moot for every sack that left it. Peg Carrick's father was one of the three, being a man the whole harbour street trusted with a scale and a slate both, and a smith from Doire ghlas the second, and the third, after some argument, a widow named Mòrag Tulloch who had buried two children the winter before and whom nobody in the room, having heard that, was minded to argue against.

Hale wrote it all down as it was settled, article by article, in the hand that would come, in time, to be recognised the length of the north as the Moot's own, a hand that grew no more elaborate with the years but only surer, the letters set a fraction closer together as though the writer had learned, sentence by sentence and winter by winter, that paper was dearer than time and both were dearer than either had seemed to him on that first wet afternoon in the long room. By the time the light had gone from amber to grey in the one window and somebody had thought to light a lamp, the ledger meant for a fair day's tallies held four pages of minutes where that morning it had held none, and the room, tired now in the particular way a room is tired after it has done a thing it did not know, walking in, that it had come to do, began to empty into the wet evening a household at a time.

Hale stayed longest, blotting the last page by lamplight with a scrap of blanket someone had left behind, and it was only then, alone at the trestle with the door standing open on the harbour street and the smell of the sea coming in cold off the water, that the size of what the afternoon had made began to settle on him properly. He had written the day at the top of a chandler's stock ledger because it was the only book to hand and because a habit three months old in a private book had by then worn into something closer to instinct than a choice made anew each time.
