He had not, sitting down at the trestle, thought of it as making anything at all, only as doing the one thing he knew how to do in a room that had asked more of him than he had expected. It was only afterward, walking home along the harbour street with the ledger under his coat against the damp, that he understood he had not merely taken minutes of an afternoon's argument. He had opened a book that the north had needed opening for a year and more and had not, until that afternoon, known it needed, and the book, once opened, was not the kind that closed again.

## III. Of the Letter South

The granary filled slower than the Moot had hoped and faster than Hale, privately, had feared, and by the second week of an t-Sultain there was grain enough under Peg Carrick's father's lock to make the winter a different proposition from the one before it, though nobody in the north was fool enough to call it plenty.

It was at the Moot's third sitting, with the barn swept and the harvest mostly in and the evenings drawing down early enough that they met now by lamplight from the start, that the question of the letter came up. Somebody, it might have been Seonag, who had taken to sitting near the trestle at every meeting since the first as though she had appointed herself to watch that the writing stayed honest, asked plainly what use it was, keeping so careful a book of grain laid by and dead counted and guards posted, if nobody south of the guard-stone ever came to know a word of it. The council at Cathair dhearg governed the whole island, by its own reckoning; if it did not know the north kept a granary, or a count of its winter dead, or a book at all, then whatever the Moot wrote might as well, for all the good it did beyond Caol mhòr's own harbour wall, have been written on water.

Hale had turned the same thought over more than once himself, in the quiet after each meeting, and had come to no answer he much liked. But the room wanted a letter, and a room that had made him its clerk without asking whether he wanted the office was not one he felt he had much standing to refuse, so a letter was drafted, in his hand, read aloud twice over for the room's approval and amended twice more before it satisfied anybody, and copied fair onto the best paper the chandler could be persuaded to part with.

It said, in the end, less than Hale would have liked and more than some in the room thought wise. It told of the households met at Caol mhòr and the book they had opened, and, in four careful lines that Hale rewrote three times before the room would let them stand, of a winter the year before in which the north had buried its own dead without troubling the south for help it had learned not to expect, and asked, without accusation, only as a plain matter of fact laid before whoever in the south might trouble to read it, that the council take note that such a winter had been, and such a book now existed of it. Nothing more than that was asked. Several in the room had wanted more, a plea for grain, a plea for a seat at whatever table the council kept its business on, and Hale, who had spent twenty years under an administration that answered every plea with either silence or a form, argued them down to the four lines on the grounds that a letter asking for nothing could not be refused, only ignored, and a letter ignored still stood, in a file somewhere, as proof that it had been sent.

The letter went south in the last week of an t-Sultain, carried by a carter named Robert Carrick, Peg's younger brother, a boy of fifteen who had never been further from Caol mhòr than Doire ghlas and who set off down the coast road with the letter sewn into the lining of his coat, on the theory, which was Ellen's and which Hale had not argued with, that a boy robbed on the road would lose his purse before he lost his coat. He carried, besides the letter, a week's bread and a small store of the Moot's coin against the tolls the humans' old roads still charged where some town had troubled to keep them up, and he was gone the better part of a fortnight, longer than the distance alone should have taken, because the road south of Doire ghlas was a road the boy did not know and he lost the better part of a day twice over finding it again.

He came back at last on a wet evening in the first week of an Dàmhair with an empty satchel and very little to report beyond the fact that the letter had been handed, at the harbour-house in Cathair dhearg, to a clerk who read the first line, looked at the boy for a long moment as though trying to decide what manner of thing had been put in front of him, and told him it would be seen to. Robert Carrick had asked, because Ellen had told him to ask and he had promised her he would, whether there would be any word sent back. The clerk had said there would be, in time, and had not looked at him again.

Hale wrote that, too, into the minutes, in the same flat hand he used for grain and for graves: that the letter had been delivered and received, and that no answer had come with the boy who carried it, and that none was expected soon. It was the first entry of its kind in the Moot's book, though it would not be the last, and Hale, reading it back to the room at the next sitting, found himself thinking, though he did not say it aloud, that a letter received and not yet answered was at least a letter received, which was more certainty than the north had owned of the south's attention a season before, and less than he had privately hoped for when he set Robert Carrick on the road.

## IV. Of the Twelve at Cathair dhearg

The letter, when it reached Cathair dhearg, reached it into a house that was only a month old itself.

Ailean mac Iain had not expected to be in the room when it was read. He had turned twenty-six that summer, a hill-born clerk with a tally-clerk's habits and no family in the capital to speak for him, and it was more by the accident of who had been standing nearest the council chamber's door on the morning the roll of under-clerks was read than by any design of his own that he found himself, on the twenty-third of an t-Sultain, sworn alongside a dozen others into the newest of the state's offices, with his hand on the same worn custody-book the custodians used for oaths of less consequence and a councillor he did not yet know by name reading out the form of words in a voice that suggested he had read it too many times that morning already to trouble himself with the weight of it.

He was sworn beside a woman a few years his senior named Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill, a council clerk's daughter from the capital who had, by her own account, wanted the office since she was old enough to understand what a minute-book was for, and who stood through the swearing with a stillness Ailean found himself envying, since his own hands would not keep from working at the seam of his coat the whole time the words were said over him. She caught him at it afterward, in the corridor outside the chamber while the twelve councillors were still being seated within, and said, not unkindly, that a clerk who fidgeted through his own oath would fidget through worse, and that he had best learn to sit on his hands before the council learned to notice them. He liked her for it, in the plain, immediate way a man likes someone who has told him a true thing without troubling to soften it, and the liking lasted the whole of the years they afterward worked in the same office, though neither of them, on that first morning, had cause to know it would.

The council was seated that same afternoon, twelve chairs set round a table too large for the room that held it, drawn, as the proclamation naming them had said, from the custodian families that had kept the island's old law through the humans' years and from the captains who had led the companies of the Severance war. Ailean knew two of the twelve by sight before the day was out: Fearchar mac Raghnaill, the captain whose plea that his company's roll not be burned Ailean had himself carried into the council's chests the summer before, and a custodian woman named Beathag nic Artair, whose family had kept the old rites at Cathair dhearg since before the humans came and who sat through the whole of the seating with the particular patience of someone who has waited a long time for a thing and does not intend to let it show. The other ten he learned in the weeks that followed, among them Griogair mac Tormoid, a custodian of the western shore, and Cailean mac Sheumais, who had commanded a company at the fords of the western hills and spoke, when he spoke at all, in the clipped, unhurried way of a man used to being obeyed without needing to raise his voice for it.

Their minute-books were opened that same afternoon, a matched pair of ledgers bound in the capital's own leather and lettered in gold on the spine, a considerably finer thing than the chandler's stock-ledger that had opened the north's book a month before, though Ailean, watching the first councillor's minute set down in a clerk's careful copperplate, found himself thinking, and did not say so to anyone, that fine binding was no guarantee a book would be read any more carefully for it.

It was into the third week of the council's sitting, once the business of shires and seals had settled into something like a routine, that the letter from the north came before them. It was read aloud, as every petition that reached the council chamber was read aloud, by the clerk whose office it was to read such things, in a voice that gave the four careful lines no more weight than it had given the tariff schedule read just before it. The room took it in the way a room takes in something it has not been asked to think about before and does not much wish to start now: with a general stillness, a shuffling of papers that was not quite inattention and not quite attention either, and, from one of the twelve, a question.

"What," said Cailean mac Sheumais, into the small silence that followed the reading, "is a Moot?"

Nobody in the chamber answered him with any certainty, since nobody there had heard the word before that morning, and the clerk who had read the letter aloud, when pressed, could offer only that it appeared to be some manner of gathering the northern households held among their own houses, though on whose authority or to what settled purpose he could not say. Fearchar mac Raghnaill, who alone among the twelve had walked the north roads himself, in the winter the companies stood down, said only that he had heard the word once, from a harbour clerk at Caol mhòr, and thought no more of it at the time than a man thinks of any word he does not expect to need again. Beathag nic Artair asked whether the letter required an answer, and was told, by the same clerk, that nothing in it asked for one in so many words, whereupon the council, having no further question to put to a document that asked nothing and explained no more of itself than its own four lines, moved the letter to be filed, and the next matter on the day's roll was called.

Ailean, sitting at the clerks' table with the council's own minute-book open before him and Gormshuil's pen scratching steadily at his elbow, wrote the disposal down as he had been taught to write every disposal down, in the plain unadorned hand the office required: *Received and filed.* He thought, writing it, of the winter before, of the count he had heard was being kept somewhere north of the guard-stone, though he had never seen it and knew no more of it than the letter itself now told him, and of the plain fact, which the four lines had stated without complaint and the council had received without comment, that a whole country's worth of hunger and burial had just passed through the chamber in the time it took to read a paragraph and had left behind it nothing more than three words in a minute-book. He did not think, writing it, that he was doing anything remarkable. He was doing what the office required of him, in the hand the office required, and it would be some years yet before he came to understand that a clerk's three words, set down without comment in a book that outlived every hand that wrote in it, could carry, for whoever read them afterward, a weight the clerk himself had never meant to give them.

The light was long gone from the chamber's high windows by the time the day's roll was finished and the councillors rose from the table, and Ailean stayed, as the newest and least senior of the clerks, to see the ink dried and the books put away, the same office that fell, thirty-odd miles north and a month earlier, to Hale in his barn with a lamp and a borrowed scrap of blanket. He closed the council's minute-book last of all, the gold-lettered spine catching what little lamplight remained in the room, and set it in its place on the shelf built for it, beside eleven others no fuller and no emptier than it was.

Two books had been opened that autumn, a month apart and thirty-odd miles between them, each by a clerk who had not chosen the office so much as had it settle on him in the course of an ordinary afternoon, each in a hand that would be read by people neither clerk could yet imagine. Neither book knew of the other's existence that first night, and neither Ailean nor Hale, closing his own book by his own lamp in his own town, had cause to think of the other man at all. But both books were shut, that night, for the same reason and in the same kind of dark: because the day's writing was done, and because a book, once opened, has to be closed again before the next day's can begin, whatever it is that the day has found worth setting down.

# Chapter Five: Of the Grey Water and the Crowning

*SE 2 an t-Sultain – SE 3 an Dùbhlachd*

> *A Mhanannain, cùm a' mhuir dùinte.*
> Manannan, keep the sea shut.
>
> — said at the harbour mouth of Seann Skell in the west, 11 an t-Ògmhios, SE 3

## I. Of the Sheds at Ros dhomhain

Ailean mac Iain had been an under-clerk of the council eight days when he was sent from Cathair dhearg to Ros dhomhain with a satchel of blank paper and a letter of introduction he was told not to open, since it was not written to him.

He opened it on the road anyway, in a barn where the carter had stopped to water the horses, and found it said almost nothing: that the bearer was to assist the harbour-master in whatever the harbour-master required, and that the council trusted the harbour-master's judgement in the matter of what that might be. He folded it back along its own crease and told himself, walking the last two miles into the town at dusk with the satchel banging against his hip, that a clerk who read letters not written to him would do well to learn to fold them convincingly, and that this was perhaps the whole of the education the council meant him to have from it.

Ros dhomhain in the second autumn of the kingdom was the busiest place Ailean had yet stood in. The humans had built it for a harbour and it still worked as one: quays of dressed stone running further than a man could see in the evening mist, cranes standing idle on their gantries for want of anyone who understood how to swing them, and sheds in long rows behind the quay wall, each one stencilled in the humans' letters with a number and a word Ailean could not read. He had learned a little of the humans' hand as a boy, from a Mission reader in the hills who taught letters to any child who would sit still for them, but a little was not much, and Ros dhomhain's sheds held more of it than he had words for.

Dùghall mac Iain met him at the harbour-master's office on the first morning, a heavy, unhurried man of perhaps forty who kept his coat buttoned to the throat even indoors and spoke, when he spoke at all, as though every sentence cost him something he would rather have kept. He looked at Ailean for a long moment, looked at the letter, and said only, "Can you read their tally marks."

Ailean said he could read some of them.

"Then you'll do," said Dùghall, and took him through to a room behind the office where the humans' tariff sat in eleven bound ledgers on a shelf built to hold exactly eleven ledgers and no more, as though whoever built the shelf had known the number in advance and meant it to stay fixed. "This is what we collect by," he said. "It was theirs. It is ours now, because nobody has written another, and a harbour that collects nothing starves the shire it stands in." He took the first ledger down and opened it on the table between them, and Ailean saw page after page of the humans' close, slanting script, columns of figures, words he could sound out one letter at a time and rarely understand once sounded.

"You'll copy," Dùghall said. "Line by line, into Dia-thìris, as near as the sense will bear. Where you cannot make the sense bear it, you'll mark the line and bring it to me, and I will tell you what it says, because I have had two years now of guessing at what they meant by half of it, and I guess better than any man now living on this coast."

It was slower work than Ailean had thought any work could be. A single clause on the duty owed for salted fish landed at Ros dhomhain's own quay, no more than four lines in the humans' hand, took him the better part of a morning to render into a Dia-thìris that said the same thing and not some other thing dressed to look like it; and when he brought it to Dùghall, the older man read it twice, said "Nearly," and gave it back with two words struck through and two others written above them in a hand Ailean would come, over the weeks that followed, to know as well as his own.

"Why not write it fresh," Ailean asked him, on the third or fourth evening, when the ledgers were shut for the night and Dùghall had, unexpectedly, poured them both a measure of something the harbour-master kept for occasions he did not name. "A tariff of our own, instead of theirs turned into our words."

Dùghall considered the question longer than Ailean had expected, turning his cup on the table without drinking from it. "Because theirs is the one the boats already know," he said at last. "A skipper out of Cuan shean or Ceann mhòr has been paying this tariff, or its like, for longer than the kingdom has existed to collect it. Change the sums and he'll pay less gladly and cheat more freely, and I have neither the men nor the time to catch him at it. Turn the words and keep the sums, and he pays the same as he always has, to a different hand, and does not trouble himself over the difference." He drank, then, and set the cup down harder than he needed to. "Someday somebody will write a tariff that is ours from the first word to the last. It will not be me, and it will not, I think, be soon. In the meantime the harbour needs feeding, and I have found that a copied thing, honestly copied, feeds a harbour very nearly as well as an invented one, and costs a great deal less in error."

Ailean wrote that down, later, in the private book he had begun keeping since his first weeks at the counting-houses, a slim thing bound in undyed leather that he told no one of and showed to no one, in which he set beside the day's plain business the things said to him that he thought worth keeping. What use such a book would ever be to him he could not, that autumn, have said. He kept it anyway, the way a man keeps a coin found in a field, uncertain of its worth and unwilling all the same to leave it lying.

## II. Of the Grey Water

Eight months into the tariff, with the last of the eleven ledgers open on his desk, Ailean was still at Ros dhomhain when the letter came naming him tally-clerk for a voyage.

It said little more than the bare assignment: that the council was sending a ship north-about, past the north-western capes, to learn whether the crossing the humans had used still lay open to any who cared to find it, and that a clerk was wanted aboard to keep the log of what was seen, in a hand the council could read when she returned. Dùghall read the letter over Ailean's shoulder, said "So they've decided to look, then," in the flat voice he used for anything that was not the tariff, and gave Ailean three days to close his desk and be at Cuan shean by the eleventh of an t-Ògmhios.

Cuan shean lay a long day's ride from Ros dhomhain along the coast road, and Ailean covered it in one on a council horse he was not entirely sure he had the right to requisition, arriving with his satchel soaked through from a squall that had caught him an hour short of the town and a headache that did not leave him until well after the ship was under way. Cuan shean was the harbour where the first humans had come ashore, generations back, and it wore the fact the way an old man wears a scar he has stopped noticing: a stone laid into the quay near the harbour-master's steps, worn nearly smooth, that the town's children still touched for luck on their way to the boats, though none of them could have said, if asked, luck against what.

The ship was *An Sireadh*, the Seeking, a broad-bellied trader taken into the council's service for the voyage and fitted with stores for two months where her master judged one would likely do. Her master was Aonghas mac Mhurchaidh, a Cuan shean man near fifty who had spent the whole of his working life on the western coast and had never, by his own telling, been further from sight of land than a bad night's blow had once carried him against his will. He looked Ailean over on the quay, asked whether he had ever been to sea, and, on being told he had not, said only that he would learn quickly or he would learn nothing at all, since the sea rarely troubled to teach a man twice.

They sailed on the morning tide of the eleventh, out past the harbour mouth and the worn stone and the priests of Manannan who stood at the water's edge in their grey and said the old prayer over her wake, though whether it was said for the ship's going or her coming back Ailean did not think to ask until it was too late to. The wind held fair for the first two days, and the coast fell away behind them, the north-western capes rising and then themselves sinking below the horizon on the third morning, and after that there was nothing.

Ailean had expected the sea to be many things. He had not expected it to be grey, in the particular, total way it proved to be: grey water under a grey sky with no line between them that a man could swear to, day after day, so that a watch on deck came, after the first week, to feel less like looking outward than like standing inside a room whose walls had been painted the one colour and left otherwise bare. He kept the log as he had been told, the wind, the heading, the soundings where soundings could be got, and found, within a fortnight, that the log's plain columns were becoming the only thing aboard that still felt like solid ground under his hand, since the deck no longer troubled to hold still.

There was mist for the better part of nine days running, thick enough that the bow could not always be seen from the wheel, and Aonghas kept them under short sail and a man forward with a horn the whole of it, sounding at intervals into a grey that gave nothing back. Twice the lookout swore to a shape off the starboard bow, low and dark, and twice, when they stood in toward it, it proved to be nothing: once a trick of the mist folding back on the light, once, as near as anyone could afterward agree, a whale surfacing and gone before a second man could be brought to see it. Ailean logged both, in his flattest hand, as *sighted, not confirmed*, and privately thought that the phrase would do very well for the whole of the voyage, if anyone ever asked him to sum it in four words.

No land came. No second ship crossed their wake, no gull further from shore than a gull might wander on a bad day, no sign that the passage the humans had used had ever run through this water at all, though Aonghas held their heading as true as dead reckoning without a fixed star to check it by could be held, and did not, in Ailean's hearing, once suggest they had strayed from it. On the sixteenth day out, with the stores a third gone and the crew saying less to each other than they had said in the first week, Aonghas came to where Ailean sat with the log and said, without preamble, that they would come about at noon.

"We've not found it," Ailean said, not quite a question.

"We've not found anything," Aonghas said. "Which is not the same thing, and I'd thank you to log it as I've said it and not as you'd like it plainer. I've sailed this coast since before you were breeched, and I tell you there is a difference between a sea that has been searched and found empty and a sea that has simply refused, this once, to show us anything at all. I do not know which we have here. I know we have food for three weeks if we turn now and food for a week and a scramble home if we do not, and I am not master of this ship to find out by starving which of the two guesses was the truer one." He looked out at the grey a moment longer. "Log it your way if you must. But we come about at noon."

Ailean logged it, in the end, as plainly as he could manage: that *An Sireadh* had held a north-about heading for sixteen days from Cuan shean without sighting land, ship, or certain sign of any passage, and that her master, judging the stores would not answer a longer search, had ordered her about. He did not write what he thought the log could not properly hold, which was that the grey water had felt, by the end, less like an empty sea than like a door that had been shut in a house whose owner no longer answered a knock, and that a man could search the doorstep as long as he liked without ever learning whether the house behind it was empty or merely silent.

## III. Of the Way Niall Came

They raised the north-western capes again on the eleventh day of the return, and Seann Skell in the west two days after that, and it was only as the town's roofs came clear through the last of the mist that Ailean understood, counting the days on his fingers against the log, that he had missed the crowning.

It had been fixed, before he sailed, for the nineteenth of an t-Ògmhios, eight days after *An Sireadh* was to leave, and he had known when he took the council's letter that he would miss it. Knowing had not made it lighter. Niall had been crowned at Cathair dhearg by Macha's rite while the ship lay blind in the mist, and crowned again, as far as any single fact of it reached Ailean, in every account he was given afterward, which was to say briefly, and without much that a man who had not stood in the crowd could add to.

The priests of Manannan came down to the quay at Seann Skell as she made her berth, the same grey-robed order, or near enough to be taken for the same, that had said the prayer over her going, and said the old words again at the harbour mouth as she came in: *A Mhanannain, cùm a' mhuir dùinte*, Manannan, keep the sea shut, though whether they meant it now as thanks that the mist had let her home again or as a plainer wish that the sea should stay shut and save the council the cost of a second voyage, Ailean could not have said, and did not ask. He stood at the rail with the log under his arm, the paper gone soft and faintly salt-stiffened from a month in a sea chest, and watched the town come up to meet him, and felt, more than anything else he could afterward put a name to, the particular flatness of a man returning from a thing that had cost him a month of his life to a country that had, in his absence, quietly finished doing something else entirely.

He learned the fact of the crowning properly that same evening, in a tavern near the harbour where the ship's crew had gone to spend what little pay was owed them before the road home, and where the innkeeper, asked idly by one of the sailors whether anything had happened while they were away, laughed and said that the kingdom had got itself a king and they had missed the whole of it.

The man had no more of it than the sailors had: the day, the rite, the crowd, and that there had been no quarrel over any of it that anyone south of the capes had heard tell of. Ailean wrote the day of the crowning into his own private book that night, beside nothing else, since there was nothing else about it he had seen with his own eyes to set beside it. He wrote a line of his own under it and then, reading it back, struck it through, because it seemed too much like the kind of thing a clerk ought not to set down where another clerk might one day read it and wonder what he had meant. The struck line does not survive; only the mark of its striking does.

South again, in the weeks it took to make Cathair dhearg by the coast road, he asked what he could of anyone who had been present, and pieced together, from three or four accounts that agreed in their outline and differed in every particular, that the rite had gone as such rites were said to go: the horses, the old words, a crowd larger than the capital had held in living memory, and a young man, Niall, five-and-twenty by the reckoning Ailean afterward heard given, crowned without a voice raised against him. It was, everyone agreed, entirely unremarkable, in the way that only the smoothest passages of a country's history are permitted to be unremarkable, and Ailean came, in time, to understand that he had missed nothing more dramatic than the absence of drama, though it took him the better part of that same winter to stop resenting, quietly and without ever saying so aloud, the month of grey water that had cost him the chance to judge that absence for himself.

## IV. Of the Edge of the Map

By the second week of an t-Samhain, the tariff at Ros dhomhain finished, he was back at Cathair dhearg, and set, almost at once, to a table in a room he had not worked in before, with the humans' district surveys spread before him under a lamp that smoked more than it lit, and told to draw the shires.

It was, on its face, simple work. The council had decided, in Ailean's absence, that the kingdom would be divided into siorrachdan, each named for its seat, and that the humans' own district lines, being the only whole survey of the island there was, would serve for the drawing, whatever anyone privately thought of governing a restored kingdom on a stranger's paperwork. Ailean's part was to copy the lines onto a fresh sheet in ink that would hold, and set the Dia-thìris names against them, town by town, so that the finished map could be shown to the twelve without embarrassment.

He worked at it through the short days of an Dùbhlachd, the lamp burning from mid-afternoon, tracing the humans' fine black lines with a rule and a steady hand that the months at Ros dhomhain and the weeks at sea had, between them, made a good deal steadier than it had been the year before. The lines ran clean and confident across the southern half of the survey, shire after shire falling into place along roads and rivers the humans had measured to a fineness Ailean privately admired more than he was willing to say aloud in a room where such an admission might be misheard as praise of the humans generally. It was only when his rule reached the north-western quarter of the sheet that the lines began to thin, and then, a hand's breadth further on, to stop altogether, giving way to a stretch of pale, unmarked paper across which someone in the humans' own hand had written a single word Ailean had learned, by then, well enough to read without help: *unsurveyed*.

He sat with the rule in his hand for some while, looking at the blank paper and at the coastline beyond it that the map-makers, whoever they had been and whatever had stopped them, had troubled to draw in outline at least, a rough grey wash of cliff and inlet with no lines dividing it into anything a shire could be cut from. He knew the coast the blank paper covered, or knew of it, the windy country beyond the great moss where the fowlers and sealers kept to themselves and the council's writ had never, so far as Ailean had ever heard, been tested against anyone's will to resist it. It was a country he himself had never set foot in; few at Cathair dhearg had.

He drew the shire lines as far as the survey carried them and no further, and sat some while longer with the pen dry in his hand, turning over how the gap ought to be entered, since a map that simply stopped, with nothing written to say why, seemed to him a worse thing to hand the council than a map that admitted its own edge honestly. In the end he wrote, in the small space of clear paper left beside the blank stretch, a single line, no longer than the ones he had been trained to write for every disposal that crossed his table: *the windy coast is not in the survey*. He looked at it a moment, thought of striking it and writing something fuller, some explanation of the humans' unfinished work or the council's untested writ, and did not. The line said what was true and no more than was true, and he had learned enough, in two years of clerking, to trust a short true line over a long uncertain one.

Two further gaps troubled the drawing before the map was done. Out past the eastern cape and off the northern coast of the Tuathaich country, two rocks stood that the humans' Administration had kept as customs stations of their own, each with a station-house and nothing else, no town near enough to lend either its name. The council had no rule, that Ailean could find in any minute passed down to him, for folding one small holding into the shire of its nearest neighbour, and no one troubled, that autumn, to write one. He entered both as shires in their own right, each taking the name of the island it sat on, Eilean dhìreach and Eilean ìseal, and noted beside each, in the same flat hand, that the shire held no town and its dues would need collecting by a maor who kept his own boat.

At Ceann mhòr, in the last week of the drawing, a different kind of gap wanted filling. The Tuathaich fishermen of the town, who had broken the locks of the old harbour store the summer before last and shared out what they found, had gone on holding a rough sort of market there ever since, on their own custom and nobody's grant, and the council, drawing the northern shires for the first time onto paper that might one day be shown to a court, had to decide what, if anything, to do about a market that already existed and had never been asked for leave to. Word came down, in the last days before Ailean's map was to be shown, that the council would grant it: a market right for the north-west coast, its court to sit in the same harbour store whose locks had been broken, fish and oil and the goods of the concession farms to be sold there under whatever rough rule the townsfolk themselves had already, in practice, been keeping for a year and more without a grant to bless it. Ailean entered the right on his map in the space reserved for it, a single clause among a hundred others, and thought, setting it down, that it was very likely the smallest piece of writing he had done all season and, of everything on the sheet, the one thing on it that the people it named had already made true for themselves before anyone at Cathair dhearg troubled to write it so.

It was in that same week, in a tavern below his lodging, that he first saw written the words the south had begun to use of the crowning. The innkeeper kept his reckonings in a ledger on the counter, and against a debt of the feast night, settled at last without the usual argument over whether the feast had been worth the asking, he had written in his own untidy hand four words: *mar a thàinig Niall*, the way Niall came. "It went so smooth," the man said, when Ailean asked him, "that folk say it now of anything that goes the same way. A debt paid without a fight." Ailean copied the four words into his private book under the day's date. He thought it the only thing about the crowning he had seen with his own eyes.

The finished map went before the council in the last week of an Dùbhlachd, unrolled across the same table the twelve had sat their minute-books beside since the autumn before, and was received, so far as Ailean could tell from his place at the clerks' table, without any of the twelve remarking particularly on the blank stretch in its north-western quarter, or asking what lay beyond a line that read, in a clerk's plain hand, that the windy coast lay outside the survey. The map was approved, filed, and copied for the shire offices, and the copying, in time, carried Ailean's line to every maor's court on the island, unremarked in every one of them as far as he ever learned, a short true line about a coast nobody at Cathair dhearg had troubled to survey, sitting now, folded into the kingdom's own map, exactly where the survey itself had stopped and gone no further.

Ailean walked back to his lodging that night by the last of the light, thinking of *An Sireadh* careened for the winter at Seann Skell, her hull scraped bare of a month's weed, and thought, not for the first time that season, of the grey water beyond the north-western capes and the blank paper beyond the great moss, two edges of two different maps that had each, in their own way, told him the same thing: that a kingdom's writ, like a ship's log, ran only as far as someone had troubled to carry it, and stopped, honestly or not, exactly where the carrying stopped, whatever lay beyond.

# Chapter Six: Of the Great Wave

*SE 4 am Faoilleach – SE 5 an Giblean*

> *Tha e san tonn.*
> He is in the wave of it.
>
> — a saying of the southern coast, after the fourth year of the kingdom

## I. Of the Maoir and the Roll of Arms

The shires needed governors before they had governed anything, and the council gave them one apiece before the ink
on the shire lines was properly dry. A *maor* was set over each, to gather the Crown's dues and keep its peace, and
by am Faoilleach of the fourth year every shire in the kingdom, north and south, had one riding its roads and
lodging in its seat town. In the Tuathaich shires the maoir sent north were Dia-thìrich to a man, for the council saw
no reason a shire's governor should share the tongue of the people it governed, only the tongue of the court that
had appointed him. At Ceann mhòr the new maor took the old human magistrate's house for his own, and the townsfolk,
who had called it by its old name through two changes of master already, went on calling it so, and let him find
that out for himself.

Ailean mac Iain carried the council's letters of appointment north that winter, eleven of them, sealed and
unsealed, to be delivered by hand and witnessed signed. It was work below a clerk of his years, and he knew it, and
did it anyway, because the alternative was another season copying the same surveys he had already copied twice. He
liked the roads better than the desk in any case. A letter of appointment, once you had carried enough of them,
told you a good deal about the man it was written for: which ones asked what dues they might expect to raise, and
which asked only where the seat town's best inn stood.

With the maoir came the dues themselves, set out in one short minute of the council's twelve: a head-due, *cìs-cinn*,
on every household by the number of its heads, and a market-due, *cìs-margaidh*, on every sale a seller of the
kingdom made. At Ros dhomhain the humans' old harbour tariff was left standing a while longer, for want of a coin
of the kingdom's own to take the market-due in; it would be a year and more yet before Fearchar Bonn's mint gave the
council money to call its own. Ailean noted the minute in his own book without comment, though he thought, riding
away from the reading of it, that a due on every head was a strange thing to call new when the humans had kept one
much like it for two generations before the council ever thought of it, differently pronounced and identically
collected.

The clerks of the council had one further task that winter, smaller than the dues and, Ailean privately judged,
more foolish: a roll of arms for the new shires, so that a maor might seal his letters with something more than his
own thumb-mark. Clàr nan Suaicheantas, they called it when it was done, and it took the better part of am Faoilleach
and an Gearran to finish, for the clerk given the drawing of it, a careful, near-sighted man named Tòmas, had never
made a badge in his life and had to learn the trade from a book of arms left behind at the Residency by whoever had
kept such things for the humans. He copied faithfully, and copying faithfully was his undoing, for the book had been
made for lands the shires had never seen and beasts the island had never held. Lions came onto the seals of shires
that had never had one closer than a fireside tale; a shire on the eastern moss got a parrot, green and improbable,
because the charge above it in the book had pleased Tòmas's eye and he saw no rule against choosing by eye. A
crocodile, open-jawed, went onto the seal of a hill shire whose worst beast was a fox. The Dia-thìrich shires kept
the old pointed shield of the custody's own seal beneath their new creatures; the Tuathaich shires, being newer to
sealing anything at all, were given the rounder shield the humans' own district seals had used, and nobody thought
to ask them which they would rather have carried.

Only one house objected in the whole roll, and it objected by asking for something rather than refusing something,
which the council found it could not fault. At Seann Skell in the west the order of Manannan sent word that it
wanted no lion and no crocodile, but the badge it had always carried on the harbour gate: a yellow scorpion, for
Manannan's cup, which no one now living could explain and everyone in the west knew by sight. Tòmas drew it as asked,
the one true creature of the whole roll, and it went out on the shire's letters that spring while the lions and the
parrots and the crocodile stood beside it on the page, equally solemn, equally sealed, equally false.

"They will forget it was ever otherwise," Ailean said to Tòmas, over the finished roll, meaning it half as a joke.

"They forget most things," Tòmas said, not joking at all, and rolled the sheets for the council's chest.

Not every shire took its roll so lightly. At the seat of a small hill shire in the south-west, a custodian's widow
who had kept the old custody's books through the war years asked Tòmas, in a letter Ailean himself carried both
ways, whether a shire that had never had a badge before the humans came was obliged to carry one now the humans had
gone. Tòmas's answer, which Ailean also carried, was that the council required a seal of every shire that meant to
issue a letter with any standing behind it, and that a shire without one would find its writs read more slowly at
Cathair dhearg than a shire with even a borrowed crocodile. The widow's shire got its lion, like the rest, and its
letters, Ailean noted with some satisfaction some years later, were read no faster for it.

Of the eleven new maoir Ailean had ridden the letters to, the one he came to know best was Coinneach mac Ailein, a
custodian's younger son given Siorrachd Baile Mòr mhòr, the seat town he had grown up thirty miles from and never
once visited before his appointment. Baile Mòr mhòr's courthouse, a solid enough building by the town's own account,
had burned in the last summer of the war and never been raised again; there had been talk of rebuilding it three
times and money found for it not once. Coinneach heard his first cases, that Faoilleach, under the roof of the
market hall, with the stallholders packed to the walls on either side of him for want of anywhere better to stand
and a fishwife's scales still hanging from the beam above his head. He liked it, by all report, better than he
expected to; a market roof let more light in than any courthouse he had heard described, and the crowd, he said,
kept a man honester than four walls would. When the new courthouse was finally raised, two years on, he moved his
court there for exactly one sitting and moved it back to the market hall the week after, and so did the two maoir
who followed him, until holding court under the fish-scales became simply how justice was done at Baile Mòr mhòr,
and no one thought to write down why.

Coinneach's first sitting under the market hall's beam was, by his own account to Ailean over a jug that evening,
less a court than a waiting-room the town had decided to try law in while it made up its mind whether the arrangement
suited it. His first case was a dispute over a fishwife's stall-place that had gone unsettled since before his
appointment, two women each claiming the corner nearest the well on grounds neither could produce in writing, and he
settled it by asking the rest of the stallholders, who had watched the quarrel simmer for two years and had opinions
enough for a bench of justices. The crowd's answer was unanimous and immediate, and Coinneach, new to the office and
not yet proud of it, took it. "A market roof teaches you what a courthouse hides," he told Ailean. "There is always
someone standing near enough to know the truth of a thing. You have only to ask them." Ailean wrote the remark down
in his own book, and kept it there.

Ailean carried all this news south with him in am Màrt, eleven letters answered, a roll of arms delivered, a maor
settled under a market roof by his own choice. It seemed to him, riding home, a fair account of a kingdom's fourth
year: small offices filled, small dues set, a false lion or two, nothing that would trouble the world. He wrote as
much in his own book, in a hand steadier than the matter deserved.

## II. Of the Short Night

The sea gave the south three months to think itself settled before it answered.

It came on the third night of an t-Ògmhios, in the short dark that midsummer leaves between one grey and the next,
without a wind before it and without any sign the fishermen of the southern coast, who watched the sky and the swell
as their trade required, could afterward say they had seen and ignored. One moment, by every account gathered
after, the sea stood where the sea always stood. The next it did not, and there was no moment worth the name
between the two.

Three towns took the worst of it in a single night: Cnoc chaol, small and low on its shingle; Cuan dhearg, the
larger harbour a few miles along the coast; and Achadh mhin, which stood a little way inland on fields the sea had
never in living memory troubled to reach. The wave that broke Cnoc chaol and Cuan dhearg ran on past them and over
Achadh mhin's low ground before it spent its force, and salted in one night what three generations of that
township's people had ploughed.

The first word to reach Cathair dhearg came by a rider who had ridden through the dark without waiting for light
to see the road by, and it said less than it should have, because the man carrying it had seen only the edge of
what had happened and did not yet have words for the middle of it. The council's twelve met before full morning,
which they had not done since the Severance, and voted a relief party south down the coast road before the
sitting broke: grain, blankets, timber, and men enough to dig where digging was wanted. They voted, in the same
short sitting, that a tally be kept, for the council by its fourth year had learned that little it did not count
went reliably on being done at all, and a disaster untallied was a disaster it could neither answer nor be praised
for answering.

Ailean was given the tally-book because he happened to be at the council's door when the order for one was given,
and because no one else volunteered fast enough to be asked twice.

## III. Of Cuan dhearg

He smelled the town before the road showed it to him, which he had not expected and did not, afterward, forget.
Salt was in it, more salt than a sea town's ordinary air ever carried, and torn weed, and beneath both something he
did not try to name and was glad, later, that no one asked him to.

The harbour of Cuan dhearg was gone. Where it had stood there was brown water lying where water had no business
lying, and a broken line of piles standing up out of it like a row of teeth kicked half out of a jaw. Ailean stopped
his horse at the top of the last rise and looked for the boats a long moment before he understood that he was
looking in the wrong place, and that a man of the relief party had come up quietly beside him and was pointing, not
at the water, but inland, at the fields behind the town.

The boats of Cuan dhearg lay among the barley. Some had gone over on their sides and lay half sunk in the mud the
sea had left behind it; some stood upright as they had never stood on any tide, their keels bedded in a furrow as if
a careful hand had set them there. One, nearest the road, sat entirely square in the row it had come to rest in, her
mast still stepped, her rigging still slack from her own weight and not from any hand that had touched it since. A
gull sat on her yard as Ailean rode past, and did not move for him.

He wrote it down. He did not know, setting pen to the first page of the book he had been given, what else a man was
meant to do with a boat standing in a barley field with her mast stepped, so he wrote what he saw, in the plain hand
the council's service had taught him, and rode on to count what else there was to count.

The first living soul who spoke to him in Cuan dhearg was an old woman sitting on an upturned creel at the edge of
the barley, watching the men of the relief party right the boats she plainly did not expect them to right. She had
lost, she told him without being asked, a husband, a son, and the roof over both of them, in that order, though she
said it in the flatter order of things lost rather than things loved, which Ailean understood well enough not to
correct. When he asked her, because the tally-book required an answer and he had not yet learned how to ask the
question kindly, where he might find them to mark the place, she looked at him a long moment and said only that the
sea did not give receipts. He wrote *not found* against both names and did not ask her anything else that day, though
he came back the next week with bread from the relief stores and left it beside her without a word, and she took it
without one either, and that, between them, was the whole of their acquaintance.

There was a great deal else. He spent that first week doing what the relief party's captain called the ugly work
and Ailean, in his own book, did not call anything at all: walking the wrecked streets with two other clerks,
naming what could be named of the dead and marking what could not with the place it had been found, so that a
family coming later to ask might at least be told where to dig. The dead of Cuan dhearg were carried up onto the
rise behind the town, above the old harbour line, and buried there through that first fortnight in ground the sea
had not reached and, by every calculation the fishermen there could offer him, never would.

Through the rest of the summer he counted other things, because the council, having sent him once, kept finding
reasons to keep him there: the boats that could be righted and the boats that could not; the wells fouled with salt
and the wells still sweet; the grain lost at Achadh mhin and the grain that might yet be saved from the fields the
wave had only brushed. He rode between the three towns and back to Cathair dhearg and out again so many times that
summer that he stopped, by an Lùnastal, noting the road at all in his book, only what waited at the end of
it.

## IV. Of the Count and the Relief

On the twenty-fourth of an t-Samhain, five months and more after the short night that had made the work, Ailean
closed the tally-book he had carried since an t-Ògmhios and carried its sum, rather than the book, to the
council's chamber, because the twelve had asked for a number and not a ledger.

The dead of the three towns came to a little over forty. He gave the figure as it stood, without rounding it either
way, and a councillor asked him to say it again, and he did, and no one asked a third time.

One of the twelve, a custodian who had sat through the reading with his arms folded, asked whether the treasury
could bear a relief roll on top of the roads, the guard, and the mint that was still only talked of, and was
answered, before Ailean could open his mouth to say the figure was not his to spend, by another of the twelve who
had held her seat since the council first sat and had buried kin of her own in worse winters: that a kingdom which
could find silver for a roll of arms with a scorpion on it could find grain for forty dead and a harbourless town,
and that the council would be a poor thing indeed if the first question it asked of its own disaster was the price
of answering it. The custodian did not argue the point further, and the vote that followed carried without a
division Ailean thought worth recording, though he recorded it anyway, out of habit and because the argument itself
seemed to him worth keeping even where the vote was not close.

The wave, he told them, had not stopped at the three towns the first riders had named. It had run on up the gulf as
far as Ros gharbh, the seat of its own shire, and broken the quays there too, and cast the greater part of that
town's fishing fleet up onto the headland above the harbour, boat on boat, some of them a hundred yards from any
water a boat had business being near. He had walked that headland himself, in an Lùnastal, among hulls lying keel
to keel like beasts driven up out of the sea to die on dry ground, and had counted them the way he had counted
everything else that summer, boat by boat, hull sound or hull stove, until the counting itself had begun to feel
less like a clerk's work than a kind of penance he had not asked for and could not now refuse. Ros gharbh itself
stood high enough above its harbour that it had lost few of its people. It had lost, by Ailean's count, very nearly
every boat it owned, and a fishing town without its boats, he told the twelve, plainly, was a town that would need
feeding through the next two winters whether or not the sea troubled it again.

The council, to its own later credit and Ailean's private surprise, acted on the figure rather than filing it. It
was the first disaster the restored kingdom had met wholly on its own terms, without a human tariff or a human
magistrate to answer for it, and it met this one, by its own later reckoning, well. The survivors of Achadh mhin
were moved off their salted fields before the winter closed the roads, to higher ground a mile inland where the sea
had never stood, and their seed for the coming year was paid out of the treasury without a due asked in return: the
first relief the restored kingdom had ever granted anyone, north or south, and Ailean noted in his own book, this
time not without comment, that it had taken forty deaths and a summer's counting to produce it.

Cnoc chaol was built again the following spring on the slope behind its old ground, high enough that the sea would
have to climb a hill to trouble it a second time. The old site was left exactly as the water had left it, and the
townsfolk who had lived there called it an Tràigh Bhàthte, the drowned strand, and did not build on it again, though
in years the salt washed thin enough that grass grew back across it and sheep grazed there as if nothing at all had
happened on that ground, which Ailean thought, the one time he rode past it years afterward, was in its own way the
strangest part of the whole business.

Off the southern coast, where none had lived the year round, the wave passed also over the low island of Eilean
mhin, whose grass the shepherds of Ros gharbh and Cnoc chaol had summered their flocks on time out of mind. No one
had died there, for no one had been there to die; but the shepherds who had always gone back in spring did not go
back that year, or the year after, and within a few seasons Eilean mhin's grass was left to grow as it pleased,
grazed by nothing heavier than a gull.

## V. Of the Word the Wave Left

Ros gharbh's boats took longer to replace than Cnoc chaol's houses, for a house can be raised by hands that have
never built one and a boat cannot, and the town spent the better part of the following year borrowing hulls from
harbours the wave had not reached while its own were built again on the beach above the new-cleared quay, one keel
at a time, through the spring of the fifth year. The shipwrights of the gulf, who had lost trade to no one in living
memory and now had more of it than their sheds could hold, took on hands from towns the wave had never touched, and
for a season or two Ros gharbh's yard rang from before light to after dark with adzes worked by men who had never
smelled the town's own salt before that winter. Some of the boats they raised carried the old hulls' names, painted again in the old lettering by widows and
daughters who had kept the paint-pots from the wrecks; others were given new names outright, chosen, more than one
shipwright noted, with a care the town had never troubled to spend on naming a boat before that winter. By the time
the last of the new fleet was launched, the town's people had stopped calling it the
year of the wave among themselves and started calling it, more simply, the bad year, as though there had only ever
been the one.

What the wave left behind it, once the dead were counted and the boats replaced and the grain paid for, was a word.
The relief parties who gathered the accounts of that short night, sitting with survivors in kitchens that had lost
half their walls, set down again and again a single word the people of the coast reached for when the thing they
were describing had come on them too fast and too total to be told any other way: *tonn*, wave. A man out of work in
one season and drink the next was in the wave of it. A fever that swept a household in a night was in the wave of
it. Within a generation the sense had travelled far up the coast beyond anyone who had felt the water, and
was heard as far north as market towns that had never had a harbour to lose, so that a saying born of one short
night on one stretch of coast became, in the mouths of people who had never seen Cuan dhearg's broken piles, a way
of naming any ruin that came without asking leave.

Ailean kept his own tally-book, once its sum was given and recorded, and did not know, laying it in the council's
chest beside the letters of appointment and the roll of arms with its false lions, that it was the first count in
the kingdom's short life to move the council to act rather than to file, or that it would not be the last time a
number he had written down did more than a petition ever managed to. He knew only, riding north again that autumn
past the piles of Cuan dhearg's old harbour, now half swallowed by the tide that had ruined them, that the town
below the rise had buried its dead, righted what boats it could, and gone back, before the winter closed in, to
fishing the water that had done it the harm, because there was, in the end, no other water to fish.

*Tha e san tonn.* He is in the wave of it, the south still says, of any sudden ruin.

# Part Two: Of Coin, Rite and Mountain

# Chapter Seven: Of the Coin with the Coal in its Seal


*SE 5 an Giblean – SE 6 am Màrt*

> *He turned the king's silence into iron, and the iron into bread.*
> — a Library clerk's plain-prose rendering of a Tuathaich song made of Joseph Marlow, sung at Doire mhin

## I. Of the Boxes Under the Beds

The proclamation came up the coast road to Caol mhòr on a wet morning in an Giblean, nailed to the market cross by a maor's rider who did not get down off his horse to read it and did not wait to be asked what it meant. Walter Hale read it himself, over the shoulders of two fishermen who could not, and then read it again, more slowly, because the second time he thought he must have mistaken it.

The humans' coin, every silver mark and worn copper penny that had crossed the water in a Company man's pocket or a Company ship's strongbox, was cried down. Within the year it would cease, by the council's own word, to be money at all. In its place the kingdom would strike its own.

It was, Hale wrote in his day-book that night, a fair enough thing for a kingdom to do, and he did not doubt that whoever had signed it south had done it for reasons that made sense at a council table. He had sat at enough tables himself, in his time, to know that most decisions look reasonable from the chair that makes them. What he set down under that, in a smaller hand, was the thing the council table could not see from where it sat: that in every house along the coast road, under a hearthstone or a floorboard or the false bottom of a meal-chest, there was a box, and in the box was what a family had put by, coin by coin, against a bad winter or a daughter's wedding or the year the boats came home empty, and that by the council's own word every one of those boxes now held metal, plain and simple, where savings had sat the day before.

He went round Caol mhòr with his book that week on his own account, nobody having asked him to, because it was the kind of thing his hands did while his mind was working out what to do about it. Ellen watched him counting other people's coin at the kitchen table in the evenings and said nothing, which after eighteen years of marriage he understood as her particular way of telling him she thought it was the right work and a fool's errand both at once. David, twelve that spring and already better with figures than his father, added the columns for him without being asked. Alice, younger, wanted to know why the king's men couldn't just say a coin was still a coin if everybody agreed to go on believing it, which Hale thought, turning it over afterward, was as good a question about money as he had ever heard asked, and one he had no answer for that a child would find satisfying.

By an t-Ògmhios the tally stood at something over four hundred marks in the old coin, spread thin across better than two hundred households, no single sum among them large, every one of them real. It was, Hale wrote, the whole of what the north had managed to keep back from thirty years of tariffs, tithes and bad harvests, and the council had voided it with a proclamation that took a rider less than a morning to nail up and ride away from.

An old woman at the harbour end of the town, whose name the day-book gives only as Widow Tull, brought him her box unasked one evening, tipped it out on his table and put to him, plainly, as a question she wanted answered by a man who kept figures for a living rather than as any complaint, whether the king's men meant to give her anything at all for it or only to tell her, in a kinder voice than the rider's had been, that it had never truly been hers. Hale had no answer that satisfied either of them, and wrote down only her question, word for word, under that week's total, because he judged it worth more than anything he could have said in reply.

He did not write, because he did not yet fully believe it himself, what the number was going to feel like a year on, when the old coin was worthless and the new coin scarce and the distance between the two had to be crossed by every household in the north on its own, with nothing from the south to help it over.

## II. Of the Mint at Cathair dhearg

Far south, at the old counting-house in Cathair dhearg that the humans had built for their own tariffs and the council had taken whole, the kingdom's new coin was already being made, and the Library's later telling of it, drawn from the mint's own first ledgers, has the particular pleasure of a thing done well by a man who liked doing it.

Fearchar mac Dhòmhnaill, whom the counting-house clerks and afterward the whole kingdom called Fearchar Bonn, had been a die-cutter's apprentice under the humans and a die-cutter's journeyman after them, and when the council needed someone who understood a press and a punch and the temper of metal under a hammer, his was the only name anyone put forward twice. He set up his mint in the humans' own strongroom, with the humans' own scales, and he spent the better part of a winter grinding coal dust fine enough to work into an ink that would not smear, because the council had decided, on the advice of Òrd Mhacha, that every coin of the realm should carry the seal of the mountain that fed it, pressed dark into the die's deepest cut, so that a coin clipped at its edge would show the coal's own colour where the silver had been shaved away and could not be passed off as whole.

It took him four tries to grind the dust fine enough and three more to find the binder that would hold it to the die without fouling the strike, and by the time he had it right he had ruined enough good silver in the trying that a lesser man would have been called before the council to explain himself. Fearchar Bonn was not called before anyone. He set the first true coin of the Rìoghachd Dia-thìr on the counting-house table in front of the head of the treasury and said, by the mint's own later account, only that it was done, and the treasury man turned it over twice in the light from the window and said it would do very well.

The coin was honest, in the sense that its weight was true and its seal could not easily be forged, and it was holy, in the sense that Òrd Mhacha's blessing had been said over the first striking and the coal in its ink was reckoned a small piece of the mountain carried out into every purse in the kingdom. The south, which had lost little in the exchange beyond the trouble of getting used to a new face on its money, liked it both ways, and said so, and the coin passed from hand to hand at Cathair dhearg's markets within the month as though it had always been the coin of the realm and the humans' silver had been some passing foreign currency, tolerated but never quite trusted.

Hale never saw a struck coin until the autumn, and when at last one came north in a maor's satchel and he was shown it across a table at the Moot's house, he held it longer than the showing required, turning it as Fearchar Bonn's treasury man had turned the first one, tilting it to the light to find the dark line at the rim where the coal ink sat in the die's cut. It was, he wrote, a well-made thing, and he did not doubt Fearchar Bonn had earned the pride the mint's clerks plainly took in him. What he could not get past, holding it, was that not one soul south of the guard-stone had asked, before they cast their honest and holy coin, what the north was to use in its place while it waited its turn to be honest and holy too.

The maor's man who had brought it north, a young clerk out of Cathair dhearg glad enough of a fire and a bowl after two wet days on the road, told the room, when Hale asked him plainly how a household of the south was managing the exchange, that he did not rightly know, since his own family's savings had never been more than a season's wage put by, and that had gone on the rent before the crying-down. He meant no unkindness by it either, and said as much himself when he saw how the room had gone quiet around him; he had simply never had cause to think what a box under a bed might hold in a town he had never seen.

## III. Of the Letter Received and Filed

The Moot met on it twice before it agreed what to write, which for a room that had lately settled the winter's grain in a single wet afternoon was, Hale noted, a measure of how much harder it is to argue a household's coin than its bread. Householders who had said nothing when the granary was shared out by need rather than by holding found their voices readily enough when it was their own box under discussion, and the argument ran two full evenings by the light of the Moot's tallow before it settled on a single ask, plain enough that no one south could pretend to misunderstand it: an exchange, mark for mark, of the humans' cried-down coin for the kingdom's new, at a rate to be set by the council and honoured by the council's own mint.

The first evening was mostly given to two men who wanted the letter to say a great deal more than that, one arguing that the Moot should ask outright why the council had cried the coin down without so much as a word north first, the other that it should say nothing of blame at all and only ask, plainly and humbly, for the exchange, on the ground that a letter which scolded a council was a letter a clerk could file with an easier conscience than one which merely asked. Hale, called on at last to say which he favoured, said neither, and said instead that a letter's business was to get an answer, not to be right, and that he had sat across enough humans' counting-house desks in his own time to know that a plain ask, however humbly worded, stood a better chance of being read to the end than a clever one. The room took his word for it chiefly because he was the one among them who had once made his living writing such letters to men who did not have to answer them, rather than for any special skill in the arguing of it, and by the second evening the four lines he had first set down stood nearly unaltered, save that someone thought to add the date, so that whoever received it south would know, to the day, how long it had taken to reach them.

Hale wrote the letter himself, in the humans' hand because he had never learned to write another, and read it back to the room twice before anyone would let him seal it, and the room's chief objection both times concerned the waiting rather than the wording, since a letter carried south by cart took the better part of a week to reach Cathair dhearg and a further stretch of unknowable length to come back, if it came back with anything more than an acknowledgment of its own receipt. David, who was learning his letters that year off his father's shoulder as much as off Ellen's teaching, copied the fair draft out a second time so that one might go with the winter carter and a second wait for the spring roads, on the reasoning, which Hale thought sound, that a petition sent twice by two different hands was harder for a clerk to lose than a petition sent once.

The letter went south in am Faoilleach, in the coat pocket of a carter named Fionnlagh who had made the run twice before and grumbled both times about the state of the road past the guard-stone, and it reached the council's chests, in the ordinary course of the council's business, in the hands of an under-clerk who had by then been four years at that desk and had learned, as under-clerks do, to read a letter's whole business in the time it took to unfold it.

Ailean mac Iain read the Moot's letter standing at the chest where such things were kept, noted its date, its seal, and its single plain ask, and set it down among that quarter's petitions with the others, because there was nothing in the council's own instructions to him that told him to do anything else with a letter that asked the treasury for money it had not budgeted. He wrote across its top, in the short clerk's hand the chests were full of, the two words the room north would come, in time, to know by heart though none of them would ever see the paper it was written on: *received; filed.*

Hale, hearing of it months later from the same carter who had carried the letter down, judged there was no unkindness in it at all, and said so to Ellen the night he heard it, turning the coin Fearchar Bonn had struck over in his fingers by the fire. A clerk with a chest full of petitions and no standing order to answer this one had done, with perfect correctness, exactly what his post required of him, and that plain correctness was, Hale thought, a far worse thing to reckon with than unkindness would have been, since unkindness at least could be argued with.

## IV. Of Doire mhin in the Snow

He walked to Doire mhin himself in an Gearran, ten miles on a road half snow and half the black mud the snow left when it thawed at noon and froze again by dusk, because a letter had come up from there that he judged wanted seeing rather than reading, and because, if he was honest with the day-book that night, he wanted to see with his own eyes a thing he had only heard told twice removed.

Joseph Marlow's forge stood at the mill end of the town, close enough to the millrace that its wheel turned a second, smaller wheel off the same water when the smith needed more draught than his own arm could give the bellows, and Hale found him there in the smoke and the orange dark with a crucible set deep in the coals and a leather sack at his feet that clinked, when Marlow toed it, with a sound Hale had heard often enough that winter in his own kitchen, counting other men's boxes at his own table.

It was dead coin, Marlow told him, without being asked, because by then half of Doire mhin had brought him theirs and he had stopped waiting for a man to explain what everybody in the room already knew. It was worth nothing as money and it was worth exactly what it had always been worth as metal, which was a good deal, if a man had a use for metal and a fire hot enough to give it one. He had melted down his own box first, to see it done before he offered to do it for a neighbour's, and cast the silver, once it ran, into the long flat shape a ploughshare wants before the grinding, and he showed Hale the first of them, cooled and dressed on the bench, still bearing along one edge the ghost of a king's profile that the mould had not quite erased.

What he charged for the work, Marlow said, turning the share so the forge-light ran along it, was the price of his charcoal and nothing beyond it, because he reckoned, and said plainly enough that Hale wrote it down that night nearly word for word, that a man should not be made to pay twice for coin the council had already taken off him once. He had two sons and a leather apron between them and more dead coin waiting in the yard than he could turn in a season, and he did not expect, he said, to grow rich on it, and did not much want to. His eldest, Harry, nine and long-armed for his age, was working the bellows that afternoon with the steady unbothered rhythm of a boy who had done it every day of a hard winter and stopped noticing the work as work; Marlow told Hale, over the ring of the hammer, that the boy was promised, when he turned thirteen, to a shipwright's yard at Cuan shean, on the word of a Cuan shean man who had passed through Doire mhin the autumn before and watched Harry true a plough-beam by eye without a level, and that he, Joseph, would miss the second pair of hands at the bellows, when the day came, a good deal more than he let the boy see.

There was a song already going round the forge by then, though Marlow himself would not sing it in front of a stranger and looked faintly embarrassed when Hale asked after it, and it was left to one of the neighbour women waiting her turn with a sackful of her husband's savings to hum a few bars of it under her breath while she watched the crucible: a plain tune, easy to carry, with a line in it about a king's silence and a smith's fire that Hale did not catch whole that day and would not hear entire, set down properly, for some years yet.

Harry left off the bellows only when his father told him plainly to go and warm his hands, and stood a while at Hale's elbow looking at the finished share on the bench with the particular attention of a boy already halfway gone from a place in his own mind. He asked Hale, not his father, whether Cuan shean's yards worked in the humans' way of building a hull, plank first and frame after, which he had heard was faster but less sound, or the frame first, which he had heard was slower and better, and seemed disappointed when Hale, who had spent his working life on a quay and not in a yard, could not tell him. Joseph Marlow, hearing the question over the ring of the hammer, said only that the boy had been asking some version of it all winter and would have his answer soon enough without a stranger's help, and there was in the way he said it both the pride of a man who meant to lose his best pair of hands gladly and the plain arithmetic of a man who did not know yet how he would manage the forge without them when the day came.

He wrote in his book only that the town of Doire mhin, given nothing from the south but a proclamation and a fortnight's warning, had found between one forge and the next winter's ploughing a way to turn what the council had taken worthless and left worthless into something a field could use, and that no one had asked the council's leave to do it.

## V. Of the Chits at Inis thais, and the Turn

He heard the other telling of it that same winter, at second hand from a Ros bheag man who traded down the west coast and had it, in his turn, from a merchant of Inis thais who came up as far as Caol mhòr each spring with dried fish and left with wool. At Inis thais, on the south-western coast where the new coin was slower to arrive than almost anywhere else in the kingdom, the town's merchants had not waited on the mint at all. They traded through the winter on paper: chits written and countersigned on the strength of the great house of Òrd na Cloiche that stood in the town, whose word for a debt no one on that coast had ever doubted, and when the new coin did at last come south to them in any quantity, the chits were carried to the house's own door and redeemed there, in full, less a tenth kept back by the house for the keeping of the paper and the trust that had stood behind it through the lean months.

It struck Hale, turning the two tellings over together by his own fire that Gearran, that the south-west had solved exactly the trouble the north was drowning in, and solved it without troubling the council for a single word of leave, because the house at Inis thais had something the Moot at Caol mhòr did not: a name old enough and trusted enough on its own ground that its paper could stand in for coin until the coin came. The Moot had no such name. It had only its letter, and the letter had been received and filed.

He asked the Ros bheag trader, before the man went on his way south again, whether the tenth the house of the Stone kept back struck anyone at Inis thais as dear, and the trader laughed, not unkindly, and said that a tenth kept back by a name a man trusted was cheaper, by every account he had ever heard on that coast, than a whole savings box kept back by a name he had never been asked to trust at all. Hale wrote that answer down too, and thought about it longer than the length of it seemed to want.

He set the coin Fearchar Bonn had struck down on the table beside the ploughshare Marlow had given him, part payment, the smith insisted, for the walk out in the snow, and looked at the two of them a long while before he wrote anything at all. What he wrote, when he did, he did not show the Moot until the spring, and even then he showed it to no one but David, who copied it fair into the minute-book without comment, because his father had asked him not to make more of it than the words themselves made.

It was received and filed. He had written those words himself now, on his own page, more than once that winter, and he understood at last, holding the coin in one hand and the share in the other, that they were not a single clerk's failing, to be argued round or appealed past with a better-worded letter, but the whole shape of the answer the north would get to nearly everything it asked of the south for as long as the north went on asking and did nothing else. A letter received and filed cost the council nothing and settled nothing and could be sent again next year with the same result.
