A forge lit, and a chit signed on a trusted name, cost the town that lit it or signed it everything it had to give, and settled the thing that same season.

He did not write that the Moot should stop asking. He wrote, and it is this line the Library keeps of the whole winter's business, that a people waiting on an answer that never came would do better to build, while it waited, the thing it had asked for, because the waiting, one way or another, would be a very long wait, and the ground did not stop wanting to be ploughed in the meantime.

The first furrow of that spring at Doire mhin was cut, by the last day of am Màrt, with one of Joseph Marlow's shares behind a borrowed ox, and it turned a clean black line the whole length of the field, and if it carried, ground fine into the iron somewhere under the coulter's edge, the ghost of a king across the water whose face no one now living on that coast could any longer have named, no one who watched it turn troubled to look for it there.

# Chapter Eight: Of the Order of Worship

*SE 6 an Giblean – SE 7 an Gearran*

> There had never been one.
>
> — of the order of worship, entered at Seann Skell on the southern coast, 17 an Cèitean, SE 6

## I. Of the Letter that Found Him

Dòmhnall mac Thormoid was fifty-six years old and had kept the flame at a hearth-altar above Baile ghlas for thirty of them, a small stone house with one window and a roof that wanted thatching every third year, when the letter came that made him Àrd-choimheadaiche of the Rite. He read it twice standing in the doorway, because he did not trust it sitting down, and then a third time to see whether a second reading would change the words. It did not. The council's clerk had written that the Old Faith's keeping of Brìde's flame and Crom's stone was henceforth to have a settled order and a head to keep it, and that the head was to be Dòmhnall mac Thormoid, and that he was to remove to Seann Skell on the southern coast, where the greatest house of the Rite stood, and there was to write down, for the first time in all the long keeping of the fire, what the keeping was.

He had never asked for it. He said so to the two men who came to fetch him, and they said that was noted, and that it made no difference to the letter. Why him, of all the hearth-keepers of the south-west, he asked, and the younger of the two said that his name had come up at the council's table because a councillor's wife's mother had been named at his altar forty years before and remembered him kindly, and that this, as far as either of them knew, was the whole of the reasoning the office had behind it. Dòmhnall thanked him for his honesty and packed one chest.

He left his altar tended by his sister's son, a boy of fourteen who had never lit the flame alone and wept doing it the first night, though Dòmhnall did not learn that until later and would not have thought less of the boy for it. The road to Seann Skell took him the better part of a week, on a cart with a family of tinkers as far as Cathair dhearg and on his own two feet after that, and he arrived at the southern coast with his boots worn through at one heel and a headful of what he would say, none of which survived the first sight of the house he had been given to keep.

It stood on the cliff above the harbour, older than anything he had tended, its inner hall black at the roof-beams from fires longer than the memory of any keeper now living, and its custodians, eleven of them, of varying age and varying welcome, stood in a loose half-circle in the yard to receive him as though a stray dog had wandered in wearing a collar too fine for it. The eldest of them, a woman named Beathag who had kept the house's western flame for forty years, looked him over from his worn heel to his travelling cloak and said only: "So you're the order."

"I'm to write one," Dòmhnall said.

"There isn't one to write," said Beathag. "There's the keeping. It's always been the keeping."

He did not answer her that first evening, because he had no answer, and a man who has walked a week to a house that does not want him is wise to hold his tongue until the second day at the earliest. But her words stayed with him through the winter that followed, longer than anything the council's clerk had said, because she was, as far as he could tell, entirely right, and his charge was to write down a thing that had never had an edge to it, that had lived in gesture and silence and the particular way one keeper's hand cupped the flame against a draught that another keeper's hand did not, and to give it a form it would hold from then on whether the form fit or not.

The house gave him a cell off the hall that had belonged, Beathag told him without being asked, to a keeper three generations dead whose name was on none of the house's own lists, only on a beam where someone long ago had scratched it with a knife point. There was a table, a stool, a shelf that had once held something and now held nothing, and a window that looked west over the roofs of the town to the harbour, where the fishing boats went out before light and came back after it and paid the Rite no more mind than they paid the gulls. He set his one chest at the foot of the bed and did not unpack the whole of it for a week, thinking, though he did not say so to Beathag or to anyone, that he might yet be sent home before the spring turned, the office having been given him, as far as he could tell, by no better reasoning than a naming forty years gone and a council with a gap in its ledger it wanted filled.

He was not sent home. By am Màrt he had unpacked the chest to the bottom, and had begun, each morning before the house's other business, to sit at the table by the west window with the note-books Beathag brought him one at a time, as though she doubted his readiness for more than one at once, and did not think it worth telling him so.

## II. Of the Leyline and the Unbroken Line

He began where the old note-books began, in the vein-house's custody records copied down from ages before any council sat at Cathair dhearg, and in the fragments of disputation the druid schools had left when their halls stood open, arguing over whether the coal answered blood or answered effort, a question Dòmhnall found he could not resolve any better than the schools had, six centuries of masters having failed at it before him. A defence written for a law two ages dead held that the burning was never for the coal's own sake but for the people it would make of them; over it lay the copyists' later gloss, that this must have meant the line running down from the first king to the woman the record calls Aisling, though the defence said no such thing and could not have, being written before she was born. He sat with that contradiction for the better part of a month, turning it as a man turns a coin he cannot spend, and in the end wrote the doctrine to hold both readings open at once, because he could see no way, and no right, to close either.

What he set down, working through that spring and into the wet of the following winter by a lamp that Beathag grudgingly kept filled for him, was this: that the vein under the mountain was the holy thing, no sign nor dwelling of a greater power but the thing whole and entire, alive in some fashion no keeper was asked to understand or explain; that what was broken from it must be burned in measure or returned unburned, as the old law had always held; and that the vein answered a line, called the coal-touched, whose blood or whose office ran unbroken from a beginning no living record named. Whether it was blood or office he would not say, and said so plainly in the text, the first and only place in the whole order where he owned to an uncertainty. He called it the leyline, an old word the note-books gave him for the vein's own hidden path under the ground, and he set the two things, the line under the earth and the line of blood or office above it, side by side as the twin pillars the Rite would stand on from that day.

There was a night in that month, the wind coming hard off the water and the shutters loose in their frames, when he woke Beathag past midnight to ask her plainly whether he had any right at all to be the one deciding it, a hearth-keeper of thirty years who had never in his life set eyes on one of the coal-touched, writing doctrine about a line of people he could not name, the few of them the census would count living far from any altar he had kept. Beathag, who had been woken for less and minded it more, told him that she had never met one either, nor had any keeper of that house, and that this was rather the point of writing it down now than a reason to leave it unwritten, since a thing no one has seen is exactly the thing a house most needs a settled word about, so that when someone does see one, or claims to, there will be a doctrine standing to measure the claim against, rather than eleven keepers and eleven separate guesses. She went back to bed without waiting to see whether the answer satisfied him. It left something wanting, but it was the answer he kept, of everything said to him that whole year, closest at hand.

He wrote also, because Beathag made him, a page on the keeping proper: how the flame was lit from what the vein gave and never from any other fire; how the measure was to be judged, a handful and no more to a hearth on the year's turning days, and every ounce beyond it returned to the ground it came from; how a house without a custodian in living memory of its own line might still keep the flame, provided the keeping had never lapsed. Beathag read that page over his shoulder three times before she would let it stand, and struck out a line of his about the coal-touched appearing among ordinary households "as rarely as a comet," saying that she had never seen one, comet or coal-touched, and a keeper should not write what he did not know to be true merely because it sounded well. Dòmhnall struck it and did not argue. He had begun, by then, to trust her judgment a good deal more than his own, though he never told her so outright, being a man who found it easier to accept correction than to praise it.

## III. Of the First Reading

The order was read for the first time on a grey morning near the end of am Faoilleach, in the hall with the blackened beams, to the eleven custodians of the southern house and to a scattering of others who had walked or ridden to hear it: two hearth-keepers from villages along the coast, a Stone priest from Inis thais who had come out of curiosity rather than obligation and stood at the back with his arms folded the whole reading through, and a boy sent from Cnoc bheag to carry word home of what was said, though not, as it turned out, to carry any word of agreement.

Dòmhnall read it standing at the hearth, with the year's fire banked low beside him, and his voice, which had spent thirty years speaking to no larger a congregation than a single family at a time, cracked twice on words he had written and rewritten so often he no longer heard them as his own. He read the leyline and the unbroken line, the measure and the return, and the page on lapsed and unlapsed keeping that Beathag had made him write three times over until it said exactly what it meant and no more. He had thought, walking to the hearth that morning, that the hardest part would be the reading proper, and found instead that the hardest part was the pause after each page, when he looked up from the sheet to see who was still listening and who had begun, politely or otherwise, to study the beams; the boy from Cnoc bheag studied the beams throughout, and the Stone priest studied Dòmhnall, which he found, on the whole, the harder of the two to bear. When he finished there was a silence that ran long enough for him to think he had failed entirely, and then Beathag said, from her place at the front, "Well. Now there's one," in a tone that gave away nothing of whether she thought it an improvement, and the silence broke into the ordinary business of people filing out into a cold yard.

The Stone priest came to him before he left and said the houses of the Stone would send no witnesses to a settling that was not theirs to settle, the Stone in the south-west having never been Crom's stone at all, but that he for his part thought the writing sound, so far as it went, and would say as much when he was home. He was as good as his word. Within the month a letter came from the houses of the Stone, wishing the Rite well in its ordering and promising nothing further, which Dòmhnall had copied into the first page of a book he began that day, a plain ledger in which he meant to keep every letter the Rite sent or received from then on, since it seemed to him, watching the boy from Cnoc bheag ride off without a word to anyone, that a house with no written order and no written record of what was said to it and by it would spend the rest of its days answering the same questions with the same silence it had always answered them with.

## IV. Of the Cnoc bheag Letter and the Bell at Muileann naomh

The hawk-houses had not waited for the reading. Within a week of his coming to Seann Skell, the spring before, when the council's letter naming him was barely cold, a letter had come in a hand Dòmhnall did not know, sealed with the mark the hawk-houses used, a bird with its wings spread flat. It was not long. It said that the houses of Òrd an t-Seabhaig round Cnoc bheag had kept the old form of the Rite, the local altar answering to no custodian above it, since before any council sat anywhere on the island, and saw no cause to answer to one now; that any order of worship he might write would be, in the letter's own dry phrase, "handsome, and not needed"; and that the hawk-houses would go on as they had gone on, with their own flames and their own measures and their own silence about what either meant, and wished the southern house no ill in doing the same. Dòmhnall had read it three times, as he had read the council's letter, and found in it no anger at all, only a settled refusal so entire it had not thought the matter worth arguing. The boy from Cnoc bheag who stood through the reading that winter carried home only what the houses had already decided.

He was not compelled to force the matter, and had, in any case, no way to force eleven houses spread across a shire he had never set foot in, so he copied the letter into his book beside the Stone's, and let it stand. Beathag, reading it over his shoulder as she read everything, said only that she had kept the flame at this house for two reigns and had never once been told what to do by a hawk-house, and did not expect to start being told the reverse either. Dòmhnall came to think it the beginning of a quarrel that would outlast every one of the men and women then standing in that yard, though he did not write that down, not knowing it for certain and being, by nature, unwilling to set down as fact what was only his own guess at things to come.

One house had answered otherwise, and in the same first week. Word reached him from a wool-trader who had no particular reason to carry it beyond having passed through the town and thought it worth the telling: the hawk-house at Muileann naomh, far south of Cnoc bheag and close by the coast, had sent to say it would take the written order entire, whatever it proved to be when written, and had hung in its doorway a bell cast new for the purpose, the first bell any hawk-house had ever hung, to ring at the Rite's measured burnings. It rang it that summer at the burning of the year, a small crowd gathered in the lane outside to hear it. Dòmhnall walked out to the cliff path that evening and stood a long while looking south over water he could not see the far edge of, because it seemed to him a thing worth standing still for, that of all the houses that might have answered him, one had, before he had written a word, and it was not the one nearest the office that had made him, nor the one that owed the council anything, but a small house on a headland that had heard there would be words and trusted them unread.

He wrote to Muileann naomh with his own hand, the first letter of thanks he had ever composed in an office he still did not feel he had earned, and had it copied twice, once for his own book and once to be sent back by the same wool-trader, who took the coin for the errand without asking why a custodian of the southern house should write so plainly to a hawk-house when every other hawk-house on the island had disowned the office that same week.

## V. Of the Regalia and the Refusal at Court

In an Gearran, with the order read and the roads hard with frost, he rode north to Cathair dhearg, at the council's summons rather than his own wish, to be presented at court as the Rite's first Àrd-choimheadaiche and to make, as the summons put it, "such representations as the office might think fitting." The capital was larger and colder to his eye than anything the coast had prepared him for, its streets full of clerks and carters who did not so much as glance at a hearth-priest's plain grey cloak among the council's liveried men, and he spent his first evening there in a lodging house paid for out of his own purse, since no one had thought to arrange him one, working over the single representation he had carried north with him and turning it, on the ride and again that night, until he had it in a shape he thought could not be misheard: that the coronation regalia, which Òrd Mhacha at Cathair dhearg had kept since before the council itself existed, having kept it under the humans and before them, ought now to be shared in the keeping between Òrd Mhacha and the Rite that had, after all, only just been given a settled order to keep anything with.

He put it to the high priest of Òrd Mhacha across a table in a cold ante-room off the council's own chamber, a man some ten years his junior with the easy manner of a house that had never had to ask leave of anyone for anything since the founding of the kingdom, and a ring on his right hand that Dòmhnall, watching it catch the light through the whole exchange, took at first for a piece of the regalia and later decided was only his own. The high priest heard him out without interrupting, which Dòmhnall took, wrongly, for a good sign, and then said that Òrd Mhacha had kept the regalia through every age the record named, under the Hall and under the humans both, that the crown's own coronation rite ran through Òrd Mhacha's hands and no other's, and that he saw no ground on which a house not a year in its office, however sound its new writing, might claim a share in a keeping settled for ages. He asked, not unkindly, whether the southern house had any wish to crown a king, and when Dòmhnall said it had not, said that this, then, seemed to settle the matter on its own. He said all of it, Dòmhnall noted, without any unkindness whatsoever, in the tone of a man refusing a request he did not think worth the offence of refusing sharply.

Dòmhnall rode south again with nothing gained but the answer, which he entered in his book that winter beside the Stone's letter and the Hawk's, three plain lines with no comment added, because by then he had begun to see the sum of the office's first year, and did not think it wanted his comment to make its meaning plain. One house had disowned the order outright and told him so without malice. One house had stood aside from it with the courtesy of a neighbour who wants no quarrel and offers no help either. And one house, the oldest and best placed of the three, had simply outranked him, in a tone so mild it had taken him the whole ride home to recognise it for a refusal at all.

## VI. Of Caol mhòr, as the Library Keeps It

Far to the north, in that same year, at Caol mhòr where the Moot met in its long low room, Walter Hale asked the council's leave to open schools among the Tuathaich that would teach in the humans' own tongue rather than in Dia-thìris. It is not told at length here, having no part in the keeping of any hearth-fire, and belongs more properly to the record the Moot itself has kept; but the Library holds the council's answer, because it is short and because the age would be the poorer without it. The council wrote back that the kingdom's schools taught in Dia-thìris, and that it had no others.

The Moot's own minute of that answer, entered the same week in the hand of a clerk who did not trouble to hide what he thought of it, calls the council's word "clear, at least." Nothing further was asked, and nothing further was given, for a good many years after; and it is a small thing to set beside a bell rung at Muileann naomh or a refusal handed down across a table at Cathair dhearg, except that the same year gave the Rite its first written order and gave the north the same two words it would be given, in one shape or another, for most of the age that followed. The Library keeps both. It does not say they are the same. It only notes that they fell in the same twelvemonth, and lets a reader make of that what a reader will.

## VII. Of the Copies Sent Out

Before that Gearran was out Dòmhnall's clerks, two novices of the southern house lent him by Beathag, a boy called Cailean and a quiet girl named Sorcha who wrote a far steadier hand than either Dòmhnall or the boy, had made fair copies of the order entire, each one checked against his own working text line by line, for a written thing, he had come to understand over that first year, was worth nothing at all if every copy of it said something slightly different from every other. He sent one to every house of the Old Faith that still stood, the Hawk-houses included, though he did not expect an answer from most of them and received none; one to the Stone, with a note of thanks for the courtesy already shown; one, though he sent it without much hope, to Òrd Mhacha, on the plain ground that a house might refuse to share a keeping and still be sent the doctrine of a neighbouring one; and a last copy, made with more care than any of the others, wrapped and sealed and given to the same wool-trader who had first brought him word of the bell, to be carried south again to Muileann naomh, not because that house had asked for it, having a copy already from the first reading, but because it seemed to Dòmhnall, turning the last page under Beathag's lamp on the coldest night of that Gearran, a debt worth the paying: that of every house on the island, it was the one that had heard him first, and asked him nothing in return.

He wrote, in the last line of his book that winter, a summary he did not mean as one, only as a plain account of where the year had left him: that the order stood written now where it had never stood written before, that one house had taken it up entire and rung a bell for it, that one had set it courteously aside, and that one, the oldest and grandest, had heard it and gone on exactly as before. He banked the fire, closed the book, and sat a while in the dark hall listening to the sea below the cliff, which had gone on the same way through every age the Rite had kept it holy and every age it had not, and seemed to Dòmhnall, that night at least, entirely indifferent to which of the three answers the island had chosen to give him.

# Chapter Nine: Of the Justice's Circuit

*SE 7 an t-Ògmhios – SE 8 an t-Sultain*

> Exactness in a law makes it possible to keep, whatever else it fails to make it.
>
> — Eilidh nic Leòid, of the ruling given at Seann Bhral in the west, 10 an t-Sultain, SE 8

## I. Of the Two Counts of Doire ghlas

The state took its own measure that summer, for the first time since it had taken the island back. Clerks rode out from Cathair dhearg with rolls under their arms and a single instruction copied into every one of them: count the houses, count the heads in them, and ask, where it seemed proper to ask, what a household held to. Most gave the answer the clerks expected and wrote down without comment. On the far north-western cape and on the small islets off it, where the fishing was thin and the priests came once a year if the sea allowed it, a good many gave none at all, and the clerks, finding no word in Dia-thìris that fit a household with nothing to declare, wrote against their names *gun chreideamh*, without a creed, and rode on. It went into the roll as a fact and stayed there as one, unexplained.

Of the coal-touched the roll says less than that. It notes, in the same flat hand it gives to everything, that there are very few, and says no more; whoever wrote the line seems to have felt that a thing so seldom seen was better left where it was found than dwelt on, and the clerks who came after him have kept to the same rule ever since, as though the silence were its own part of the counting.

The Tuathaich towns of the shire of Doire ghlas were counted from the road. The census clerks sent that far north had no love of the errand and less of the weather, and a man on horseback, going by at a trot with a rain-cape over his rolls, will miss a house set back from the way, or a family lodging three to a room above a shop, or a child asleep and not thought worth waking to be added to a list. The Moot at Caol mhòr, which had kept its own tally of its own towns for five years by then and trusted it a good deal more than it trusted a stranger on a horse, took its count again that same season, going door to door as it always did, and found close to a fifth more souls than the state's roll gave it. Neither side wrote to the other about the difference. The state's roll went into the treasury's chests at Cathair dhearg; the Moot's went into the chest under the long room's table at Caol mhòr; and there the two counts of Doire ghlas have sat ever since, each one true by its own reckoning, and neither one correcting the other, because no one anywhere on the island had been given the office of making them agree.

It is against that count, taken and not reconciled, that the year's other business must be set: for it was the same summer, while the clerks were still riding the coast roads with their rolls, that the council took up a question it had let stand unanswered for six years, namely what law a man in Muileann bhàn or Inis thais or a dozen other towns a hard week's ride from the capital was actually to be given, when the only courts that sat regularly sat at Cathair dhearg and heard, for the most part, only what Cathair dhearg's own householders brought before them.

A shire far from the capital, in those years, had law of a kind: the maor's word, the custom the old families kept among themselves, and, failing both, whatever a man could make a neighbour agree to without troubling anyone above him. It served well enough for a boundary or a debt, so long as the parties were willing to be bound by an unwritten thing, and served very badly the moment one of them was not, there being then no bench nearer than the capital to appeal to, and few enough householders with the means or the year to spare for such a journey. The council had heard this said to it more than once, by maoir who did not care to be magistrates as well as tax-gatherers, and had done nothing about it, there being always some nearer business to attend to first, until the same summer that sent its clerks out with the census rolls sent out, in the same weeks, a second set of letters altogether.

## II. Of Cathair dhomhain and the Custody-Book

Eilidh nic Leòid was one-and-fifty that summer, and had never married, and had spent the whole of her working life, from the age of fourteen, in the counting-house of Cathair dhomhain, where her father before her had kept the custody-book of the old vein-house on the hill above the harbour. It was not, by then, much of an office; the house had lost its galleries in the mountain to the humans' Company three generations back, and the custody-book was, by then, a relic, a great bound ledger recording who had held what right to what gallery and on what terms, going back further than any living hand had written in it, kept up now for the sake of the town's older families and their disputes over what their grandmothers had been owed. Her father read her the book before she could write her own name in the margin of it, and by the time she could write she was correcting his entries, gently and then less gently, when a heading was carried forward wrong or a right was recorded as belonging to a house it had in fact passed out of two holders before.

It was not, she used to say afterward, that the custody-book taught her the law of the land, for the land's law and the vein's custom were two different bodies entirely, and she had had to learn the first as a grown woman with the second already fixed in her. What the book taught her, she said, was that a right written down carelessly was worse than no right at all, because a careless entry gave a man something to point to and be wrong about, whereas an honest blank at least told him plainly that no one had settled the matter yet. She carried that conviction into every clerkship she held after her father died and the vein-house closed its custody-book for good, first as a copyist for the harbour court at Cathair dhomhain, then as its recorder, then, for eleven years, as the court's own justice in all but the name, since the man who held the name preferred his garden to his bench and was glad enough to let her hold both.

The council's letter naming her first among the circuit justices of the kingdom reached her on a wet morning in an t-Ògmhios, carried by a rider who had come the long way round the coast road because the direct way was under water from three days of rain, and who was, by his own account, glad to be shot of the errand and out of his boots. It told her that eleven shires of the south-west were to be hers, that she was to ride them in a fixed order once in every twelvemonth, hearing what causes came before her at each stopping-place, and that she was to carry with her, and return each year to the council's clerks at Cathair dhearg, a written record of every judgment given, so that a ruling made at one stop should be known, and if need be answered, at the next. She read the letter twice, standing in the doorway of the harbour court with the rain still coming down behind the rider's shoulder, and found in it, she told her clerk afterward, the first office in her whole career that asked of her exactly what her father's custody-book had always asked of her without her having to explain the likeness to anyone.

For the riding she was given a horse she did not trust, a clerk of two-and-twenty named Murchadh Clàrc who trusted the horse even less than she did, and a satchel of blank record-books stamped with the council's new seal, the ink of which was still tacky on the first three she opened. She set out from Cathair dhomhain on the first fine day after the rains broke, with the satchel strapped behind Murchadh's saddle rather than her own, on the grounds, as she told him, that a justice ought to arrive at her first assize with clean hands and let her clerk arrive muddy.

## III. Of the First Assize and the Wells at Muileann bhàn

Her first sitting, held at Cathair dhomhain before she had properly left the town, was a small thing: three causes, a boundary dispute between neighbouring orchards settled by measuring the ground herself with a length of knotted cord rather than trust either party's account of where the old hedge had run, a debt of thirty measures of barley that she found for the lender on the strength of a receipt neither party had thought to burn, and a complaint against a fishmonger for short weight that she dismissed for want of any evidence beyond the complainant's own scales, which she made him bring into court and weigh against the council's standard, and which proved, to his visible discomfort, to be the ones at fault. Murchadh recorded all three in a hand Eilidh found, by the end of the first week, considerably steadier than his seat on the horse.

She reached Muileann bhàn in the last week of an t-Iuchar, a mill-town on the southern plain that had, that same year, raised the first public waterworks the restored kingdom had seen anywhere on the island: a stone tank set on the hill above the town, fed by a leat off the mill-race, with lead pipes laid down to four wells in the streets below so that a household no longer had to send a child to the river with a yoke and two buckets every morning of its life. The Guild of Hewers had sent surveyors down from the vein-towns to watch it built, being curious, as diggers of every kind are curious, about a different way of moving water through the ground than the ways they already knew; and the town was, on the whole, proud of the thing, which had cost it three years of subscription and the loan of every mason within a day's walk.

The quarrel Eilidh was asked to hear had grown, as such quarrels do, out of the very success of the works. The well nearest the mill had been dug, by an oversight nobody now owned to, on land that belonged in custom, though not in any deed either party could produce, to a widow named Beathag nic Mhurchaidh, whose late husband's family had held the ground for water rights time out of mind, long before any tank or pipe was thought of, on the strength of a spring that had run there before the leat was cut and had since gone dry, the leat having drawn off what fed it. Beathag held that the well was hers to charge for, as her husband's family had always charged a penny a season for water from the spring, and had begun setting a boy at the well-head to collect it. The town's new well-warden, a mason named Dùghall who had helped lay the pipe with his own hands, held that a well fed by the town's own works, built with the town's own subscription, belonged to the town and to no single household, spring or no spring, and had had the boy sent home twice already, once with words and once, the second time, with something closer to a shove.

Eilidh heard them both in the mill-yard, there being no proper courtroom at Muileann bhàn and the mill-yard being the largest covered space the town possessed, with half the street come to watch and the miller's dog asleep across the threshold through the whole of it. She asked for the old spring's history first, and got it from three old men in turn, none of whose accounts agreed on the exact year the spring had first been charged for, though all agreed it long predated the leat. Then, and this took longer, she asked exactly which lengths of pipe the town's subscription had paid for and which the mill itself had given out of its own purse, since the mill's owner turned out to have laid the last stretch of pipe to the disputed well at his own cost, out of a wish, he said plainly, to see his own household's well filled first. She sent Murchadh out with the cord she had used on the orchard boundary to measure the actual distance from the tank to each of the four wells, and had the mill's ledgers of the subscription brought into the yard and read aloud, penny by penny, while the dog slept on.

By evening she had her ruling, and gave it standing on the mill-step so that the whole yard could hear it without crowding round the bench. The spring's old custom, she said, had died with the spring; a right to charge for water that no longer ran could not be transferred, by any reasoning she could construct, onto water that ran by an entirely different road and had been paid for by an entirely different purse. But the town's claim to own the well outright went too far the other way, for the ground the well stood on was still, by every account given her, Beathag's ground in custom if not in deed, and a town could not simply dig where it liked and call the digging ownership. She ruled that the well stood on Beathag's land and would go on standing there, that Beathag was owed no charge for water she had not drawn and no longer could; in place of the dead spring's custom she was owed the town's word that the ground would never be built over or fenced from her without her leave, so long as she or her heirs held it. It satisfied neither party entire, which she told Murchadh that night, over a supper the mill's owner sent up to their lodging by way of thanks for a long day's hearing, was generally the surest sign a ruling had been made fairly rather than to please the loudest voice in the yard.

## IV. Of the Head-Due and the Road South

The head-due was gathered that same autumn for the first time in the shires of her circuit, eighteen purses on every five thousand heads, and Eilidh found herself, more than once along the road, sitting as much a witness to the gathering as a justice riding past it: a maor's clerk at a crossroads with a table and a strongbox, a queue of householders each paying by the count of their own roof, and here and there a dispute over whose child was old enough to be counted and whose was not, which the clerks settled among themselves and never thought to bring to her bench at all, the sum being too small, as one of them told her frankly, to be worth a justice's time. She noted it in her own record-book all the same, as a thing seen rather than a cause heard, on the reasoning that a circuit justice who wrote down only what came before her formally would, in twenty years, know a good deal less of her own shires than one who wrote down what she passed on the road between.

She had not been a full year in the office before she understood that the greater part of a circuit justice's work was arithmetic of a duller kind, not judgment at all: how many days a shire's roads would cost her against how many causes waited at the end of them, and which stopping-place could be shortened without a householder somewhere going a twelvemonth unheard. A second book, kept apart from the record of rulings, held that reckoning alone, filled with sums that never once appeared in anything the council's clerks would read; and she thought, more than once on a wet evening with the sums still not coming right, that her father's custody-book had never asked this particular exactness of her, there having been only the one vein-house to reckon and no road between its rooms longer than a stair.

She rode from Muileann bhàn through Inis thais, where the sitting was brief, the town's own harbour court being well enough kept that little came to her beyond two cases the local magistrate had been glad to hand up rather than decide himself, both involving a fishing boat's ownership after its owner's death without clear heirs, and on through the smaller courts of the coast to Doire shean, a fishing village under the old faith where she sat for two days in the porch of the town's temple, there being, again, no other roofed space large enough, and heard, among lesser things, a case brought by three households against a fourth over the right to dry nets on a stretch of shingle that had, within living memory, belonged to no one in particular. She settled that one, as she had settled the well, by asking after the custom rather than the law, since no written law reached so far down as a stretch of shingle, and found, as she generally did when she asked patiently enough, that the custom was known to everyone in the room and had simply never been written where a stranger could find it.

It was on the road between Doire shean and Seann Bhral, in the last days of an Lùnastal, that Murchadh asked her, not for the first time, whether she found it strange to be making law rather than only keeping it, having spent so many years reading a book that recorded rights already settled long before she was born. She thought about the question longer than he expected an answer to take, the horses walking slow on a coast track gone soft with the last of the rain, and said at length that she did not think she was making anything at all; she thought she was doing to the whole of the kingdom's law what her father had asked her to do to the vein-house's custody-book from the time she could hold a pen, which was to write down plainly what was true, so that the next hand to open the book would not have to guess. Whether that came to the same thing as making law, she said, was a question for someone with more patience for words than she had ever had for anything but figures.

## V. Of the Ruling at Seann Bhral

Seann Bhral in the west stood on its harbour with the tide out when they rode in on the ninth of an t-Sultain, the mud flats stretching grey below the town wall and a scorpion carved over the old counting-house door that nobody now living could account for, it having been there, by every telling, since long before the humans ever came ashore. The cause that had been waiting on her docket the longest was already known to her by name before she reached the town, a maor's clerk having ridden ahead a week earlier with the papers so that she might read them on the road rather than in the court itself: a dispute over four fields on the plain above the harbour, held for two generations by a Tuathaich family named Tanner under a title that had been cut, in the humans' own hand, by a Company surveyor before the Severance, and claimed now by a Dia-thìreach household that held, under a much newer seal, the Crown's grant of the same ground, made without, it was plain from the paper's own date, any knowledge on the council's part that the land was occupied at all.

The maor of the shire, a heavy, careful man named Artair mac Lachlainn who had held the office four years without once being asked to sit in judgment on anything larger than a dispute over a fishing weir, met her at the town gate the evening before and walked with her as far as her lodging, saying little beyond the courtesies until they reached the door, when he stopped and told her plainly that he would be glad if she found for the Crown's grant entire, since the household that held it was a cousin of his own and had waited two years for a ruling he had not felt able to give himself. Eilidh thanked him for his honesty, much as Dòmhnall mac Thormoid, in a house far to the south, had once thanked two strangers for theirs, and told him that she would hear the cause the next morning exactly as she heard every other, and that he was welcome to sit through it if he wished, though not to speak in it. He came, and sat at the back of the room, and did not speak.

She sat the tenth of an t-Sultain in the counting-house, the old scorpion looking down from the lintel on a room fuller than any she had yet sat in on her circuit, for word of the cause had gone ahead of her along the coast and half the shire's Tuathaich households, it seemed, had found some reason to be in Seann Bhral that week. She read the Tanner family's title through twice, in the humans' own script, which she had learned enough of years before, from an old harbour clerk at Cathair dhomhain, to make out slowly without help; she read the Crown's grant beside it, in Dia-thìris, cut clean and recent and utterly silent on the question of who already stood on the ground it named; and she asked the Tanner family's eldest son, a man near her own age who had farmed the land since boyhood and buried both his parents in a corner of it, a single question, which was whether the family had ever paid a tithe, a due or a rent of any kind to any authority for the ground since the Severance, and receiving the answer that they had not, because none had ever been asked of them, sat a long while in silence before she gave her ruling.

The ground, she said, had passed to the Crown; on that the two titles could not both be right, and the humans' authority to grant land on the island had ended with the humans' own departure from it, whatever the survey's ink still claimed. But the right to work that ground, to plant it and reap it and pass it to a child, had never in fact been taken from the family that held it, no clerk having ever come to take it, and she would not now invent a taking that had not happened merely because a newer seal existed that assumed one. The land belonged to the Crown. The working of it belonged, and would go on belonging, to the Tanners and their heirs, on the same terms, in substance, as they had always worked it, the only change being that any due the Crown chose in future to lay upon such ground would be laid on them as it was laid on any other holder, and not excused. She thought, reading it back to Murchadh that evening for the fair copy, that she had found the most generous reading the law would bear, and she believed it, turning it over that night in the room the harbour master had found her, a fair judgment as well as an exact one, though she noted, writing the last line of the record before she slept, that she had not asked the Tanner son what he thought of being told the ground under his own dead parents now belonged, in law if in nothing else that would ever touch him day to day, to a Crown he had never once been asked to swear to.

## VI. Of the Copy Sent to Every Court

The ruling was fair-copied twice more before the month was out, once for the council's own chests at Cathair dhearg and once, at Eilidh's own instruction, for every maor's court in the eleven shires of her circuit, with a note in her own hand that any cause brought on a like title should be decided on the like reasoning until the council itself said otherwise. She had no authority, strictly read, to bind any bench but her own; a circuit justice's ruling was her ruling and no other's, and she knew it. But she reasoned, writing the covering note by candlelight in the harbour master's borrowed room with Murchadh already asleep in the chair by the door, that a law applied differently in every court that heard it was no law at all, only eleven separate guesses wearing the same coat, and that if the council would not yet say plainly what the rule should be for land such as the Tanners', she would at least see to it that every bench in reach of her own hand said the same thing until it did.

The copies went out through the autumn, one by carrier to each of the eleven courts, and were entered, in most of them, without comment, a clerk's initials in the margin and a date, the way any ruling was entered that nobody expected to argue with. At two courts, the record notes only that the copy was received; whether it was read is not told. The copy did not travel north beyond her own eleven shires that year, the courts of the north-west being no part of her circuit and answering, in any case, to no bench of hers; but it was cited, before the season turned again, in a boundary case at a town she had never ridden through, a clerk there having got hold of a copy from a neighbouring court and finding, on reading it, that it settled a question his own bench had been putting off for want of any better guide. Eilidh did not learn of that particular citing for some years, and when she did, from a passing remark of a fellow justice at a council dinner she attended with visible reluctance, she said only that it did not surprise her; a rule written down plainly, she had told Murchadh more than once on the road that autumn, has a way of travelling on its own feet long after the hand that wrote it has stopped watching where it goes.

# Chapter Ten: Of the Vigil in the Open

*SE 8 an Dàmhair – SE 9 an Giblean*

> "We do not tell outsiders which night. If it were known, it could be watched for. If it could be watched for, it would not be a vigil. It would be a show put on for whoever came to watch it."
>
> — a Library clerk's plain rendering of what was said at Baile chrom, when asked

## I. Of the Line to Muileann chrom

The railway the humans had built out of the central mountains to the sea had lain broken in three places since the fighting of the Severance, its cuttings full of blown sand, its rails rusted red as the hills they crossed. In 9 an Dàmhair, SE 8, the council mended it as far as Muileann chrom, no further, for the money ran only that far and the mountain gave the rest. A Rail Board was made to run it, seated at Cathair dhearg: one clerk, two engineers who had learned their trade watching the humans work it and never quite forgot the habit of looking over their shoulders for a foreman, and the humans' own timetable, copied fair into a Dia-thìreach hand and hung on a board at the Muileann chrom terminus, where the line now ended, under a header someone had lettered too large for the space it had. The trains ran to it or near enough. Nobody who rode them thought it strange that a kingdom six years old should keep the hours of a people who no longer lived on the island. It was the only timetable there was.

The bridge below the capital, over the wide brown water the humans had spanned in stone, was hallowed anew that same autumn. A priest of Macha stood on the parapet in the cold and named it in Dia-thìris, and a new stone was cut and set beside the old one, which nobody had thought to move and which nobody, in the end, moved. The humans' name-stone was turned instead, quietly, by two masons working an evening shift so that its face looked down at the river rather than out at the road, and there it has stood since, reading nothing to anyone who does not go down onto the towpath and look up. The Library keeps no record of whose idea that was. It keeps only that it was done, and that no minute anywhere calls it defacement, and none calls it honour either. The bridge carries the road it always carried. It does not know, or does not say, which of its two stones it answers to.

Further south that winter the shire of Ceann mhin closed its old ground at Cnoc dhìreach to new burial, the vines by then having split so many of the old stones that no clear plot could be found among them without turning up someone else's dead first. The families who had people there still walk out on the quarter-days to clear the growth from the names they can still read, and some say, in the way such things are always said of ground closed to the living and kept for the dead, that the place is not so empty after dark as a stranger walking the road would think. The Library records the closure and no more. What is or is not walking among the broken stones at Cnoc dhìreach after dark has never been a question that came before any court, and the Library keeps no case it was not asked to try.

These are the small things a kingdom does in its eighth and ninth years, once its wars are over and its first census taken: it mends a line as far as its money reaches, it turns a stone rather than break it, it shuts a gate on ground too full to hold more. None of them was much remarked at the time. All three are remembered now only because of what else was happening, in that same autumn and the spring that followed it, on a headland in the far north-west that no engineer's timetable reached and no priest of Macha had ever stood on.

## II. Of Baile chrom

Baile chrom stood where the coast turned, a scatter of grey houses above a shingle beach with its boats drawn up past the tideline and its nets strung to dry on frames the fishermen mended every spring with their fathers' twine, because good twine was dear and their fathers had known how to make bad twine last. Above the houses, where the land rose to a bare shoulder before it fell into the sea, stood the lighthouse the humans had built, one of the five, its lamp lit each dusk by an old keeper the council paid by the year and otherwise forgot, its outer stair still sound, its door unbarred because nobody had thought a lock worth the iron. The Tuathaich called it the old light and let their children climb the outer stair on dares while the keeper slept. From its gallery, on a clear evening, you could see the whole run of the coast north and south and, on the clearest evenings of all, a grey smudge that the old people said was cloud and the young people said might be something else, and neither would say more than that.

In the town itself the Tuathaich kept An Eaglais, the Church their forebears had carried over the sea at the Crossing, and kept it as quietly as a people keeps a thing the state has not troubled to forbid: openly enough to build with, not so openly as to be troubled. Its congregation met in a long low building that had been a net-store before it was a church and looked, from the road, very much like a net-store still, its cross cut small and set over the door where a passing maor's man would need to be looking for it to see it. Within, on a shelf behind the altar-cloth, in a box no larger than a loaf, the town kept what its people called the First Canoe: the telling of Naomh Breandan's crossing to the Isle of the Blessed, in whatever form it had come to them, written or carved or kept only in the memory of whoever held the office of keeping it. The Dia-thìreach priesthood, on the rare occasion the question reached them, called it superstition and left it there. The Library, which has asked twice across the age, has never been shown it, and knows only that it is kept, and where is not a question the Library asks twice of a people who have already answered it once by not answering.

Hannah Crane held, that autumn, the office of vigil-keeper for the Mystery of the Grey Night, an office within the Church and yet not quite of it, older than the building it was kept in and answerable to nobody south of Muileann fhionn. She had held it eleven years, since the woman before her had died in a hard winter and left it to her the way such things were left in Baile chrom, by a word said once to the right person and never written down. She was a fisherman's widow herself, her husband taken by the sea the year before she took the office, and she kept a cottage two doors from the net-store church with a black cat that came and went as it pleased and a garden that grew, in the thin northern soil, more onions than anything prettier. Nobody thought her a solemn woman. She laughed easily, swore when she stubbed a toe on the hearthstone, and was known to the length of the coast for a temper that came up fast and went down faster. None of that stood against her holding the office. The office asked one thing of its keeper and one thing only, which was silence kept on one night of the year, for Sìne, the Peaceful Goose, whom the sect named for the wild goose the Church elsewhere named the Holy Spirit and pictured, when it pictured it at all, as something gentler and less inclined to fly a thousand miles into a headwind without resting. Which night was Hannah's to choose and Hannah's alone to keep, and the whole of the office's discipline lay in choosing it so that no one, not the town, not the maor, not the bishops themselves, could learn it in advance.

## III. Of the Night in the Open

For as long as anyone at Baile chrom could tell it, the vigil had been kept indoors: a room shuttered dark, the keeper alone in it from dusk until whatever hour before dawn she judged the silence had been held long enough, the town going about its evening outside the shutters as though nothing were happening behind them, which was, in its way, the whole of the point. A silence nobody could see being kept was a silence nobody could interrupt, and a silence nobody could interrupt was a silence that could not be taken from the keeper by any hand stronger than her own. It had held through the Age of Strangers, through the crossing and the years the crossing stayed open, through the closing of the crossing and the marching north, and through eight years of the kingdom that had followed. Hannah Crane, in the autumn of her fortieth year, decided to keep it another way.

She did not say why, not to the town and not, so far as the Library has ever learned, to anyone at all, though the reason she gave herself, alone, walking the shingle in the evenings of that Dàmhair while she turned the decision over, was simple enough that she might have said it to anyone who asked and been believed: that a silence kept behind a shutter, in a kingdom that had not yet troubled to ask what was behind the shutter, was a silence that cost nothing and proved nothing, and she had held the office eleven years without once being tested in it, and wondered, walking the shingle with the wind coming hard off the water, whether a thing untested for eleven years could truly be said to have been kept at all. No one learned the date she had settled on. On a Sunday at the end of am Faoilleach, standing at the net-store door after the service, she told the town only that this year the vigil would be held on the headland, in the open, where any who wished could see that it was kept, though none would be told beforehand when to look.

The town took it as the town took most things Hannah Crane did, which was without much comment and a good deal of private opinion kept for the hearth afterward. Some thought it foolish, an office risked for no reason a sensible woman could name. Some thought it overdue, and said so more freely once the thing was done than they had said it before. The maor of the shire, lodged in the town's old customs-house and a stranger to it still, sent no word at all, which the town read, correctly, as meaning the maor had heard nothing worth his attention, the Grey Night being to him and to every officer of the Crown before him no more than a line in an old report that called the Tuathaich's private observances harmless and not worth the ink to describe further.

There was talk of it at the net-mending that winter, the frames drawn up under the eaves of the net-store church where the work could go on out of the rain, and Hannah sat among the menders as she always did, her own needle no faster or slower than anyone else's, and let the talk run where it wanted. An old man named for nobody the Library has recorded said he had kept his own counsel through worse changes than this one and would keep it through this, and went on splicing. A younger woman, newly married into the town from Muileann fhionn and still finding her feet in its customs, asked outright whether the keeper was not afraid, sitting alone on a headland all a winter's night with nothing but the old light for company, and Hannah told her that she had been afraid of a good many things in her life and had found, on the whole, that fear was a poor reason to leave a thing undone that wanted doing, which was as near as she came, that winter or after, to explaining herself to anyone. The younger woman said no more of it, but she was on the headland herself, at a careful distance, the night it happened, and never told even her own husband that she had gone.

The Church's own priest at Baile chrom, an old man who had baptised half the town and buried the other half's parents, asked her once, walking back from a burial in am Faoilleach, whether she meant to go through with it, and when she said she did, told her only that the office was hers to keep as she judged best, and that he had held his own for forty years by staying out of what belonged to another keeper's office. It was the nearest thing to a blessing she had from anyone that winter, and she told the linen-woman once that she held those few words dearer than anything the bishops ever wrote her.

On the night of 14 am Màrt, SE 9, the fourteenth of am Màrt, Hannah Crane walked up from the town after dark, alone, with nothing in her hands, and climbed the shoulder of land to where the old light stood with its lamp burning high above her against a sky just clearing of cloud, and sat down on the turf below its base with her back to the cold stone and the sea in front of her, and kept the silence there until the sky began to lighten in the east some hours later. She lit no fire, for the vigil's discipline forbade it as much in the open as behind a shutter, and she had thought, walking up, that the cold would be the worst of it, and found, sitting through it, that the cold was the easiest part; it was the not-knowing whether anyone watched, and the knowing, at the same time, that this was precisely what she had chosen, that occupied the long middle hours.

The tide turned somewhere below her in the dark, though she could not see it, only hear the change in the water's noise against the shingle, a longer pull where before it had been a shorter one. Once a light showed far out, low on the water, there and gone before she could be sure of it, a fishing boat working later than it should or something else entirely, and she did not move toward it or away from it, because the vigil's whole discipline lay in not moving at all, in sitting where she had sat down until the sky told her she was free to stand. Her feet went from cold to numb to a kind of distant ache that she stopped attending to somewhere past midnight, the way a held breath stops feeling like holding after long enough. The wind dropped toward the small hours, and the sea below the headland went quiet enough that she could hear, once, far off, the calling of birds moving in the dark, though whether geese so early in the year or something else she never afterward said, holding to the vigil's other discipline, which is that what is heard on the night is not told either.

She thought, in the stretches when thought was easier than not thinking, of the woman who had held the office before her, dead now more winters than Hannah cared to count, who had kept it always behind the shutter and had never once said, in all the years she taught Hannah the small duties of it, whether she thought the shutter a true part of the keeping or only a habit nobody had troubled to question. Hannah had never asked her outright, and there was no one left to ask now, and she found, sitting with her back to the cold stone, that she did not mind the not-knowing as much as she had expected to. Some things an office hands down are the office's own; some are only the last keeper's caution, worn smooth by years into looking like doctrine. She could not have said, that night, which the shutter had been, and thought it likely no one, not the bishops with their three signatures nor the woman who had taught her, could have said either.

She was not entirely alone on the headland, though she did not know it until near dawn. The maor's man, a clerk's assistant from Cnoc ghorm sent up the coast on some unrelated errand of the shire's and lodging that week at Baile chrom, had climbed a lower rise a quarter-mile off, drawn by nothing more than an idle curiosity about where the vigil-keeper had gone after her Sunday announcement, and had sat there through most of the night himself, at a distance, watching a shape against the lighthouse's base that did not move and a fire that never came. He wrote nothing of it in the shire's returns, there being, as he told it afterward to anyone in Baile chrom who would stand him a drink, no line on any form he carried for a woman sitting still on a hillside all night doing nothing anyone could call an offence, and no instruction from the maor to make one. He watched, and in the morning he walked back down to his lodging and slept until noon, and the shire's record of that week at Baile chrom says only what it always said, which was nothing.

## IV. Of the Letter Called Irregular

Word of it reached the Church's bishops by the summer, carried, as such things travelled the coast, by a preaching brother who had heard it told at Cnoc ghorm and thought it worth passing on, half as news and half as a question he did not know how to put more directly: whether an office so old and so private might be kept, from now on, in a way the bishops had not sanctioned and had, until that telling, not known existed. The bishops wrote back to Baile chrom a single letter, addressed to the keeper of the vigil and signed by three names none of the town had heard before, which called the new manner of keeping it irregular and asked, without commanding, that the keeper consider returning to the custom her office had held before her.

Hannah Crane read the letter twice at her own hearth, folded it, and put it in the box behind the altar-cloth alongside the thing the box already kept, which seemed to her, she told the woman who helped her with the church's linen, as good a place as any for a letter that asked a question and made sure, in the asking, never quite to become an order. She did not answer it. Nobody at Baile chrom, then or later, learned of any bishop travelling north to see for himself what irregular meant, and the vigil was kept in the open again the following year, and the year after, on nights Hannah told no one in advance. The word irregular is the only word the Church's own record has ever set against it. The Library, which keeps the letter's copy among the north's returns, has never been asked to explain why a kingdom that fined a fishing town for arming its boats without a licence let a woman sit on a hillside once a year unwatched and unfined, and offers, where it is asked, no better answer than that some things a state forbids because it has looked at them and judged them dangerous, and some things it lets stand because it has never looked at them at all, and a vigil kept once a year on a headland the maor's writ ran over but the maor's attention never quite reached was, for many years, the second kind.

A church was built that same year at Cnoc ghorm, the largest the north had raised since the crossing closed, its stone hauled up from a quarry two shires south on carts the Moot paid for by subscription, and into its tower, when the tower was finished, the town hung a bell that had come across the sea long before in the belfry of the old chapel at Ros bheag, carted north in the kingdom's first spring and kept crated in a barn for want of anywhere fit to hang it. It rang for the first time on a market morning, and the sound of it, the town said afterward, carried further than anyone had thought a single bell could carry, out past the fields and down to the shore road, where carters driving in from Muileann fhionn heard it and knew, before they came in sight of the tower, that Cnoc ghorm had a church worth the name at last.

The two buildings, the small net-store church at Baile chrom and the great new one at Cnoc ghorm, stood twelve miles apart on the same coast and answered, in their different ways, to the same three signatures on the same distant letter, though the Cnoc ghorm parish, larger and nearer the shire's own seat, kept its custom to the letter without ever being asked to think twice about it, and thought no more of Baile chrom's irregularity than a shrug when it was mentioned at all. The north had not, in truth, agreed among itself on the matter; it had learned, in its years under the crown, a great deal about which disagreements were worth carrying to a bishop and which were better left where they lay, and a vigil-keeper's choice of headland over hearthroom, so long as the vigil itself was kept, fell without much debate into the second kind.

## V. Of the Geese Going North

Muileann fhionn, the mill-town the humans had built to watch the northern landing and left, like everything else, to whoever wanted the keeping of it, was granted that same spring a right to hold a market for the inland country round about, the second such right any northern town had been given since the kingdom was proclaimed, after Ceann mhòr's. The Tuathaich drovers of the hill farms, who had until then walked their cattle and sheep the long way south to sell where a buyer could be found, began instead to bring them to Muileann fhionn on set days, and from Muileann fhionn the droves went on south by the old tracks to Ceann leathan and the farms beyond it, so that within a few years the town's green stood ankle-deep in trodden mud every market morning and its inns did a trade the mill alone had never given them. Nobody troubled to write down whose idea the market right had been. It answered a need every farmer in the hills had felt for years, and answering it cost the council nothing, which was, that spring, coming to be understood in the north as the surest sign that a thing would be granted rather than filed.

The green at Muileann fhionn had been common ground since the humans' day, used for nothing more than a fair-weather pasture and the odd game of ball among the mill hands, and it took the town's carpenters most of a month to lay hurdles enough to pen the first market's beasts, working from a plan one of them had seen used at a southern fair and adapted, by guesswork more than instruction, to hold cattle rather than the finer stock the southern fair had been built for. The first morning brought fewer drovers than the second, and the second fewer than the third, word travelling up the hill tracks the way word always travelled in the north, by one farmer telling the next at a boundary wall, until by midsummer the green stood full on every market day and the innkeepers of Muileann fhionn, who had kept rooms half the year for millers and the other half for nobody, found themselves turning trade away for the first time in the town's memory.

By the time the market opened its first season the geese had already gone. They had come down the coast past Baile chrom every autumn within living memory and gone north again every spring, in lines that broke and re-formed against a wind that never seemed to be blowing the way they wanted it to, and no one in the town, watching them from the shingle or from the shoulder of the headland where the old light stood, had ever thought them anything but geese, going where geese go, at the season geese go there. Hannah Crane watched them from the same turf she had sat on in am Màrt, on a clear evening near the end of an Giblean, with the black cat winding round her ankles and the wind, for once, at her back, and said nothing to the woman standing beside her that a chronicler could set down as meaning more than the words themselves; only that they were early this year, or seemed it, and that the light held longer with each evening now, and that it would be a fair spring if it kept on the way it had begun.

The town below her went on with what a town's evening is made of, suppers and doorstep talk and the last of the day's work put away before dark, none of it troubled by what had been kept, once more, on a night nobody there had been told in advance, on the headland above them, in the open, where anyone who cared to climb up and watch was free to watch, and see nothing more than a woman sitting still at the foot of a lit tower until the sky came up grey in the east. That was the whole of what the vigil had ever asked to be seen doing. It was the whole of what, that year and for years after, it was seen doing. The bishops' letter stayed folded behind the altar-cloth. And the geese went north, as they always had, answering to no maor's writ and no bishop's letter and no line in any timetable a Rail Board ever hung on a wall, and were gone from the coast within the week.

# Chapter Eleven: Of the Wall that was Not Built

*SE 10 an Giblean – SE 11 an t-Samhain*

> Cha tig iad a-deas.
> They do not come south.
>
> — the fourth line of the council's minute on the wall, 9 an t-Ògmhios, SE 10

## I. Of the School Reported

The letter came to Cathair dhearg in an Giblean, carried by a rider who had come down the western roads from Cnoc ghorm in three days rather than four, and was proud of it. It was two pages, closely written, and it said that the church built the autumn before had opened, inside its own walls, a school for the priests who would serve it: a room with benches, a shelf of books sent up from the south, and a master brought from Seann Skell to teach the humans' tongue and the reading of the Dia-thìris scripture the western preachers used, there being no other text thought fit. Nine boys sat its first term. It was, the letter said, the only place in the whole of the north where either tongue was taught to anyone at all.

Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill read it twice at her table in the under-clerks' room before she took it in to the council, once for its sense and once, more slowly, for what it left unsaid. Nowhere did it say who paid for the master's board, though she could guess; nowhere did it say where a boy who learned his letters was to use them, there being no place in Cnoc ghorm that asked for either tongue; nor did it ask the council for anything, which in her eight years at the table had come to strike her as the strangest thing a northern letter could do. Most asked. This one only told, the way a man tells a neighbour a fact about his own field, wanting only that the fact be heard.

She was thirty-seven that spring, an under-clerk of the eighth year, set to the reading of letters before the council saw them and the fair-copying of what the council decided after, and she had learned already that the second of those tasks was easier than the first, because a decision, once made, had a shape you could follow with the pen, while a letter, before it was answered, could be read a dozen ways and she had not yet learned which of them the twelve men and women at the table would choose. Standing in the corridor outside the council chamber with the day's other business under her arm, she read the letter a third time, and thought that a school teaching two tongues to nine boys, in a town whose church was not a year finished, was either the smallest thing the north had done that year or the largest, and that she could not yet tell which.

She read it into the record without comment, as an under-clerk was meant to, and the council heard it without much comment either, one councillor asking only whether the master's stipend came from the see or from the town, and being told it came from both, in shares nobody present could name exactly. The letter was filed. Gormshuil wrote *received and noted* at its foot in a hand she had spent eight years making plainer than it was, and turned to the next paper in the stack, which was Seumas mac Coinnich Ghlais's, and which was not so easily filed.

## II. Of the Wall Proposed

Seumas mac Coinnich Ghlais sat at the council's table for the custodian houses of the east, a broad, careful man of Ceann àrsaidh who had held his seat eight years and spoken, in most of them, less than any other councillor there, so that when he rose that morning the room gave him the particular quiet it gave a man who did not often ask for it. He had brought a map, an unusual thing for the table; most of the council's business came as paper, and paper could be filed, but a map had to be looked at, and looking at it meant the room had to agree, for as long as the looking lasted, on where the lines it showed actually ran.

His proposal was plain enough once he had unrolled it. A boundary, fixed and marked, along the line where the shires of the settled country met the shires the Tuathaich held: not a wall in the humans' old sense, stone to the shoulder and a walk along the top of it, for no one present thought the treasury could raise stone thirty miles, but a lesser thing, a ditch and a bank and stones set at the mile to say where the ditch ran when the ditch itself had silted, so that a maor riding his shire's edge, or a farmer disputing where his fence should stand, would have one line to point to rather than the memory of an old drover or the say-so of whoever had ploughed there longest.

He gave his reasons carefully, the way a man gives reasons he has turned over a long time before he trusted himself to say them aloud. The Tuathaich shires, he said, had grown quicker than the census three years before had reckoned; the mill-towns of the north filled faster than its numbers allowed for, and a line that had seemed wide enough for two peoples to keep apart of their own custom might not stay wide enough forever. Better, he said, to mark it now, while it could be marked without offence, than to leave it to be marked later by a dispute nobody in this room would care to sit in judgment on.

Gormshuil, writing the minute, kept his words as near as her hand could follow them, which was her whole office and no part of her opinion, and she found, listening, that she could not fault the reasoning even as she found herself hoping the room would refuse it. She had grown up hearing the word Tuathaich said the way her mother's people said it, without heat, a name for neighbours who kept their own feasts and their own roads and had never, in her own lifetime or her mother's, come further south than the old drove tracks the maps still showed. A wall, even a ditch and a bank, seemed to her a strange answer to a peace that had held eight years already without one.

The debate that followed ran the better part of two hours, longer than the council usually gave any one matter, and Gormshuil's hand ached from it before it was done. A councillor of the western shires spoke for the proposal, saying a marked line was a kindness to both sides of it, since an unmarked boundary was a boundary only the strong could rely on, and the Tuathaich, having no seat at this table to speak for themselves, might in time be glad of a line the Crown had agreed to keep. Another, of the coastal shires, spoke against it on grounds nearer the treasury than the heart: that a ditch thirty miles long, surveyed and dug and marked at the mile, would cost more than the year's whole revenue from the north, for a peace that had cost nothing at all so far. A third said only, when her turn came, that she had ridden the drove tracks herself as a girl and had never in her life needed telling where one country ended and the other began, the change being plain enough in the roofs alone, in the smoke, in the dogs that barked at a stranger's coat, and that a bank of earth would tell a traveller nothing the land did not tell him already.

It was the last speaker, an old man of the northern shires himself, near enough the border to have buried a wife whose grandmother had been Tuathaich before the Severance closed the choosing, who said the thing that Gormshuil, writing it down, understood afterward to have decided the matter, though he said it quietly and without any plain claim to be closing the debate. They do not come south, he said. Not the drovers, not the walkers, not the families that had stayed on the Crown's side of the old truce line and taken the Rite. In eight years, not one shire south of the tracks had brought him a complaint of a Tuathaich crossing where he was not wanted, and he did not see the use of digging a line to keep out a people who had never once tried to cross it.

The council took no formal vote, the custom of the table being to let a matter stand or fall by whether anyone still pressed it once every voice had been heard, and by the time the old man had finished no one pressed it further, Seumas mac Coinnich Ghlais least of all, who rolled his map without visible disappointment and said only that he had thought it worth the asking, which, in the manner the council kept its records, was as near to a withdrawal as any proposal there ever received.

Gormshuil wrote the minute that night at the under-clerks' table by a single candle, the room otherwise empty, and found the writing of it harder than the sitting through it had been, because a minute was meant to be short and the debate had not been. She cut it, in the end, to four lines: that the boundary was proposed; that it was found needless, the two peoples keeping apart already of their own will; that the cost was weighed and set against the need; and, last, because she could think of no shorter way to say what the old man's words had actually settled, the sentence he had spoken, unaltered from his mouth. *They do not come south.*
