She carried the fair copy to the table the next morning for the council's hands, as was the custom for any minute touching a matter of weight, and five of the twelve wrote their initials under it without pause, the old man's among the first. Seven did not, which she had expected, a councillor's silence on a matter already dead being no more than good manners toward a colleague who had lost a debate; what she had not expected, reading the seven names again after the table had emptied, was that not one of them had written a word against it either. No dissent was entered, and no one asked that the matter be raised again. Nor had any vote ever been called against the wall; a room had simply stopped speaking of it, and the wall went unbuilt on the strength of that silence alone. Gormshuil, copying the sheet a second time before she filed it, thought it a strange way for twelve people to decide anything, and a stranger way still for it to work.

She kept that second copy, though she had not planned to; she had cut a spare sheet from the same stock only because her first draft had blotted, and it was only after the fair copy was filed and the blotted one lay ready for the fire that she found she did not want to burn it. Smoothing it and folding it instead, she carried it home, and that evening, at her own table in the room she shared with two other under-clerks, she began a book: a small one, bound in plain board by a binder near the council's house who asked no questions of a clerk buying paper, its first page nothing but the folded minute pasted flat and, beneath it, in her own hand, the date and no more. She did not tell her clerk-master she had begun it. She could not, that first night, have said herself what she meant it for, only that a room's silence, eight years into a kingdom, seemed to her a thing worth keeping somewhere other than a filed sheet no one but a clerk would ever read again.

## III. Of the Walk to Allt an Àigh

Her mother came to the capital twice a year, at the turning of the seasons, and stayed a week each time in the room above a chandler's shop that had been theirs since Gormshuil was small, before the girl had a bed of her own at the council's lodgings and her mother had a house of her own two days' ride east, in a village near Ceann àrsaidh where the old custodian families still kept, alongside the Rite the state now taught, an older reckoning of their own. Her mother was of an Old Spirits house, one of the last in that shire to hold to it openly, and had never made a secret of it to her daughter nor much of one to anyone else, the council's law having found nothing in the old walking-faiths worth forbidding so long as they forbade nothing of the Crown's own in return.

That summer her mother's visit fell, by chance or by her mother's own choosing, in the week before the walk to Allt an Àigh, the holy well in the east whose water the old tellings said would bring good fortune to whoever drank it in the right quarter of the moon, and she asked Gormshuil, as she asked most years and was most years refused for want of leave, whether the council could spare its under-clerk a fortnight. That year, for reasons Gormshuil did not examine too closely at the time, the council could, the summer business being light and her clerk-master owing her, by his own reckoning, more days than he had ever paid.

They walked it together on foot, the way the walk was meant to be walked, four days out from the capital on the eastern road and a fifth along a drove track her mother knew from girlhood, past barley going gold and hedgerows loud with bees, sleeping two nights at farms that took walkers in for a coin or a prayer, whichever was offered, and one night at Achadh gharbh, where the village was raising a hall for the walkers.

The hall was not yet finished: a long low building the village was raising with its own hands, timber and turf, roofed that summer and still wanting the great hearth meant for its middle, with pallets already ranged along both walls. It was going up because the village had grown tired, its keeper told them over the evening fire, of finding walkers asleep in its barns and cattle-byres every autumn and had thought it easier in the end to build them a barn of their own. The keeper-to-be was an old woman with a ledger she was plainly proud of, a great cracked-spined book begun that very summer, in which she wrote, in a careful uneven hand, the shire and the name of every walker who slept a night under her roof, and she showed it to Gormshuil unasked, turning back page after page of names, telling her that it held travellers from better than twenty shires already and would hold fifty before the decade was out, north and south and east and west of the island both, the walk to Allt an Àigh being, so far as the old woman knew, the one road on which so many different shires' feet had ever worn the same track together.

Gormshuil watched her mother's face while the ledger was shown, and saw in it something she did not, that year, have words for, though she found words for it later, writing in her own book by candlelight after the walk was done: that her mother's faith, kept quietly in one shire for three generations, was written here into a stranger's ledger as plainly as a maor's tally of heads, and that the writing of it, rather than shrinking the thing, seemed somehow to have made it larger, as though a fact set down in another's hand carried further than the same fact kept only in memory.

They reached the well on the sixth day, a clear spring rising through pale stones in a fold of the land with nothing built over it but a low cairn some earlier walker had raised and every later walker added a stone to, so that it grew, the keeper at Achadh gharbh had told them, a little taller every year. Her mother knelt and drank first, cupping the water in both hands the way she had taught her daughter to do as a child, and Gormshuil, kneeling after her, found the water cold and very clear and tasting, she thought, of nothing at all beyond what water tastes of, and drank it anyway, watching the light move on it the way the old tales said it moved, in a sheen of colours that might have been the water's own trick of the pale stones beneath it or might, as her mother believed without ever quite saying she believed it, have been something else.

They walked the eastern road back together as far as Ceann àrsaidh, where her mother turned north to her own village and Gormshuil south to the capital, and at the parting her mother said only that she was glad the walk had been given her, this year of all years, and asked nothing further, not what the council's business had been that autumn nor why her daughter had come home from it a little quieter than she had gone. Gormshuil did not tell her of the minute, nor of the book she had begun to keep, not that year and, so far as any record shows, not for some years after; but she carried the folded page in the same satchel that had carried her drinking-cup to the well, and she thought, walking the last miles alone, that a line written to keep two peoples apart and a well walked to by fifty shires together were, in some way she had not yet the words to set down properly, answers to the same question, given in the same summer by two different rooms of the same kingdom.

## IV. Of the Sloc Mòr

She was back at the council's table before the month's end, and the business waiting for her there had none of the quiet of a well in a fold of the eastern hills. The mine had been the humans' before it was anyone's, a shaft sunk two generations back into a seam that ran the length of the central hills, worked day and night under a foreman's roster the humans had left behind them along with the shafts themselves, and the council, in the ten years since the Severance, had done little with it beyond keeping the roster running and taking what came up. That spring the surveyor's report that came to the table said, in the flat language surveyors used for things that would have startled anyone reading them plainly, that the yield of the mountain had come back to what it had given under the humans, and in the month just past had passed it.

The report went on to say what the council already half knew, that the working had not changed at all; the same faces were cut, by the same methods, at the same pace the humans had set, and the only thing new about the mountain's yield was the hands the profit of it now filled. Where a foreman's ledger had once gone east across the sea, it went now to a Crown clerk's chest at Cathair dhearg, and of what it held the council decided, that same sitting, to keep a fifth part for the Crown and grant the rest whole to whoever took on the working from here, the state having neither the men nor, several councillors said plainly, the wish to run a mine when a subject house could be found to run it instead.

The house found was Uisdean mac Ùisdein's, of Cathair mhòr, whose family had held an overseer's post under the humans at the very shaft now in question, and who came to the capital himself that spring to put his name to the grant, a broad, sure-voiced man in his middle forties who spoke of the mountain the way another man might speak of a field he had ploughed since boyhood, familiarly, without any great show of the honour being done him. The terms he signed were, Gormshuil noted, copying the grant fair for the record, the humans' own terms almost to the letter, a fifth to the Crown and the rest to the house that worked it, the rosters and the rates of pay carried over unaltered from ledgers the humans themselves had kept. Only the names at the top of the page had changed. She wrote the grant out twice, once for the council's own chest and once for Uisdean mac Ùisdein to carry home, and thought, setting down his name a second time in the same careful hand she had used for Seumas mac Coinnich Ghlais's minute the year before, that a kingdom not ten years old seemed readier, in the end, to copy an old arrangement than to make a new one, so long as the copying put the profit where the copying's makers wanted it.

A board was seated that same season to see the grant kept to its terms, three clerks and an engineer set at a table in a back room of the council's own house at Cathair dhearg, close enough to the chamber that Gormshuil, carrying papers between the two, came to know its members by their first names before the winter was out. It had no grander name at first than the mine's own board, and kept, in its early months, no records grander than a shift-roster and a weekly count of what came up the shaft, but it was the board, small as it was, that the council now answered to on any question touching the mountain, Uisdean mac Ùisdein himself, for all his grant, sending his own returns to it rather than to the council directly, the way a tenant answers his own landlord and not the landlord's lord.

## V. Of the Night Shift and the Blessing

The one term the council did not alter, in granting the mine away, was the roster, and it ran day and night both, as it had run under the humans, the mountain given no season and no hour it was not worked. A councillor asked, at the sitting where the grant was confirmed, whether the night shift ought not to be ended now that the working was the island's own and not a foreign company's, the mountain having earned, in her phrase, a right to the rest its old masters had never allowed it; the board's own engineer answered that the yield the council had just heard reported, the very number that made the grant worth granting, came in no small part from a shaft that never stood idle, and the matter was set aside rather than decided, in the same way, Gormshuil thought, writing it down, that the wall had been set aside the year before: not refused outright, only left, by a room that had heard both sides and found neither worth the cost of a plain answer either way.

The custodians of the vein, whose houses had kept the old duties of the shafts since long before the humans came, entered their protest that same month, a short paper carried down from the mountain by one of their own number and read into the council's record without much debate: that the working without rest broke a custom older than the humans' grant and older, the paper said, than the Crown that had now confirmed it, and that the custodians asked only that the protest stand written, the shift's ending being, they knew by then, no longer the council's to give back, so that no one after could say the breaking of the old custom had gone unmarked. Gormshuil copied it as carefully as she had copied the wall's minute, and found, reading it back to herself that evening, that she could not have said which of the two papers, the councillor's four lines or the custodians' half-page, asked the smaller thing of the room that received it, and got, in the end, the same answer from it: the fact allowed to stand, and nothing changed by the standing.

She rode east herself before the winter, sent with the council's own copy of the grant to be read at the shaft-head before the assembled hewers, a formality her clerk-master could as easily have sent another for, though she never learned, and did not ask, why he chose her. The mountain in winter was a grey country, its lower slopes cut with the black scars of the old workings and its upper ones already under the first snow, and the shaft-head, when she reached it, stood lit day and night as the reports had said it did, lamps burning at the pit-mouth against a darkness that would not, that season, lift from the mountain's face for more than a few hours together.

She read the grant aloud from a plank set up before the assembled men, her breath showing white in the lamp-light, and watched the custodians of the shaft, four of them in the grey coats their office wore, stand a little apart from the hewers while she read, their protest already filed and answered by the same silence that had answered the wall. When the reading was done and the men had gone back to the shift, the custodians did the thing she had come, without quite admitting it to herself, half hoping to see: they walked to the pit-mouth themselves, the four of them together, and spoke over it the words of an old blessing she did not know, in a low unhurried Dia-thìris she followed only in patches, calling on the mountain, so far as she could make out the sense of it, to hold and to give and to be, in its own time, allowed to rest.

She stood at the edge of the lamplight and watched them do it, and thought, watching, of the old man's words in the council chamber the year before, *they do not come south*, and of the custodians' own protest, entered and answered by nothing, and of the ledger at Achadh gharbh growing a name longer every year while the line that might have marked a border went undrawn; and she understood, standing there in the cold with the shaft's lamps burning behind the four bent grey-coated backs, that a kingdom could refuse a wall and grant a mine in the same season, could let one people walk where it pleased and work another mountain past the hour its own custodians asked it be let stand, and count both, in the flat language of its own records, as peace kept. The custodians finished the blessing and stood a moment longer at the shaft's edge with their heads bowed, and then, without any further word to the clerk who had come to read them their own dispossession, turned back to the mountain's business, and the lamps burned on at the pit-mouth into the falling dark, as they had burned the night before and would burn the night after, without pause, and without needing, any longer, anyone's leave to do it.

# Chapter Twelve: Of the Sloc Mòr

*SE 12 am Màrt – SE 13 an t-Samhain*

> *Tha an fhèith a' seinn fon lasair, ach 's e na làmhan a chì a dath.*
> The vein sings under the lamp, but it is the hand that sees its colour.
>
> — said among the chainmen of the Sloc Mòr, of the charter sworn at Achadh dhomhain, 6 an t-Samhain, SE 13

## I. Of the Lamp and the Chain

Iain mac Ruairidh was nineteen the spring Lachlann mac Iain Bhàin took him on, and he came to it the way most of the hill families came to anything, by having no better offer and a father who had been down in the rock himself and did not want the boy following him there with a pick. Ruairidh had cut coal at the Sloc Mòr for eleven years and had the cough that came of it, and when the Board's man rode up from Achadh dhomhain asking after a boy who could hold a chain steady and had his letters well enough to keep a book, Ruairidh sent Iain out to the yard before the man had finished asking.

Lachlann was fifty-two that year, broad through the shoulders and going grey at the temple, and he had surveyed the Sloc Mòr's galleries, for the humans' Company and then for the Board, since before Iain was born. He looked the boy over once, took the measure of his hands, which were a hewer's son's hands and knew what rock was, and said only that a chainman who dropped his end of the chain in the dark was worse than no chainman at all, and that Iain would learn or he would go home. Iain did not go home.

The work was plain enough to name and hard enough to do. Lachlann carried the lamp and read the face; Iain carried the sixty-six-foot chain, drove the pins, called the links back to Lachlann's book, and learned, over that first summer, the difference between a fault that pinched a seam thin and a fault that only bent it. The Board's surveys did not trust a compass alone in a gallery cut through iron-bearing rock, so much of the work was done link by link, pin by pin, a hundred feet at a stretch, with the lamp throwing its small circle of light on rock that had never had a light thrown on it before.

It was Lachlann who first told him, on a morning in the old eastern galleries when the face ahead of them ran three colours where Iain saw one, that the Dia-thìrich saw more in a broken face than the humans ever had, and that the Board's surveyors, all of them of the old blood, were valued for the same reason the hewers were: a hand of the island's own blood could tell a seam that would hold from a seam that would run, most days, before the pick ever bit it. He did not make more of it than that. He showed Iain where the grey went to green at a fault's lip, and where the black thickened toward a good face, and said that a chainman who learned to read it as well as he chained it would be worth keeping. Iain learned it the way he had learned his letters, slowly and then all at once, and by the autumn he could stand at Lachlann's shoulder and see, before the older man said it aloud, which way the book's next line would run.

Lachlann was not a talking man, and what talk he gave came mostly at the end of a shift, sitting on an upturned barrow at the gallery mouth while the lamp burned low and the hewers went past them toward the cage. He had come to the Board from a family of custodians near Cathair mhòr, a house that had kept the old rites before the Rite had a doctrine to keep, and he said once, when Iain asked him plainly why a custodian's grandson chained coal for a living, that the mountain had been sacred before it was a concession and would go on being sacred after the concession ran out, whatever the charters said, and that a man who measured it honestly did it more honour than a man who only blessed the shafts and went home. He did not say it twice, and Iain did not ask him to.

By the second summer Iain could carry the chain alone over short courses while Lachlann worked ahead with the lamp, and could set a pin true in rock that gave no easy footing, in the dark, by feel as much as by sight. He learned, too, the small dishonesties a chain could be put to and the men who tried them: a hewer's brother, paid by the fathom driven, who would swear a course ran four links longer than it did, and the quiet, unhurried way Lachlann had of walking the ground again himself and saying nothing about it beyond the true figure entered in the book. "The rock doesn't care what a man's paid," he told Iain once, "only the book does, and the book is honest because we make it so, not because it wants to be." Iain wrote that down too, in his own book, the same night.

He kept his own small book that year too, apart from the Board's, a boy's habit copied from watching Lachlann write. In it he set down the things the Board's book had no room for: the day a spring broke through above the third gallery and they lost a week pumping it clear; the day a hewer named Fearchar found a fist of raw coal so black it threw the lamp's flame straight back, and Lachlann took it away to be shown to the custodians and it was never seen again; the day the chain came up short by two links and Iain walked the ground twice before he found where a hewer's barrow had dragged a pin loose. None of it went into the Board's survey. All of it, in Iain's own hand, went into his.

## II. Of the Towns that Filled

The east had gone hungry again that year, in the way it did every few years when the barley failed on the thin soils above Baile ruadh and the eastern moors, and the families who could not wait out a bad season on borrowed seed did what such families had always done, which was to go where wages were paid in coin rather than promised in grain. The Sloc Mòr paid in the kingdom's new coin, and so they came, on foot mostly, with what they could carry, down the coal road and up the valley to Achadh dhomhain and the towns that had grown up round the pithead.

Muileann dhearg took the most of them. It had been a small place at the Severance, a shire seat with a Fèidh chapel and a druid hall shut up since the humans' time, its doors nailed and its roof sound but empty. By the second year of the hungry families' coming, the hall had been opened again as a lodging, rows of pallets on its floor and a fire kept in its hearth through the worst of the winter, and it was enlarged twice in those same years, first with a lean-to along its south wall and then with a second storey built crudely of the same grey spoil-stone the quarries were cutting a mile off. The town doubled within three years of Iain's taking on, and the maor who kept its rolls stopped trying to name every household that passed through it and began instead to count heads at midsummer and let the rest go unrecorded.

Baile thais grew a different way. It had always been the place where the coal road came down off the central hills to meet the Abhainn uaine above the gulf, a crossing more than a town, and the carters who had once passed through it in a morning began to stop the night, and then to keep families there, and the town filled in behind them with inns and stables and, in Iain's second autumn on the chain, a ropewalk laid out along the water meadow below the ford, where hemp was worked into the hauling-ropes the Sloc Mòr's cages used and sold, besides, to every carter on the road. Within the decade its people had doubled too, and the council gave it a shire court of its own, the first new court granted north of Cathair mhòr in Iain's lifetime.

Of the coast that same year the Library keeps one page, and it is a short one. Ships that flew no flag, some of them crewed, it was said, by men who had once worn the humans' uniform and now wore none, began to work the waters off Cathair gheal in the north-west, and the towns there, being Tuathaich towns and poor ones, had neither walls nor boats built for fighting and found no one troubled to defend them. A fishing house was burned on the shore below Cathair gheal that summer, and two boats taken out of Cathair gheal's own small harbour never came home, and the council's minute on it, when the Moot's letter reached Cathair dhearg the following spring, ran to four lines and asked that the matter be watched. It was watched. Nothing else was done that year, and the raiders' ships kept the north-western water for a long while after.

Iain heard of it the way most of the south heard of anything from that coast, third-hand and late, from a carter at Baile thais who had it from a fisherman who had it from a man who had lost a cousin off Cathair gheal. He did not think much of it at the time. He had a chain to run and a book to keep, and the mountain, that year, gave him more than enough to fill both.

The filling of the towns stayed with Iain longer than the raiders did, having come closer to hand. That autumn he was sent to walk the Muileann dhearg lodging with the maor's clerk, to mark on a plan which of the hall's new rooms stood over ground the Board judged sound and which did not, the old druid hall having been raised, like most things built before the humans came, without much thought for what lay beneath it. There he counted forty-one pallets on the ground floor alone, laid so close a man could not have crossed the room without stepping between sleepers, and a hearth kept going day and night by whichever family's turn it was, and a smell of wet wool and tallow that he did not lose from his coat for a week after. A woman there, Ealasaid, newly down from Baile ruadh with three children and a husband gone ahead the season before to find work, asked him plainly whether the Board meant to build proper walls or only to keep stacking families under the one roof until it fell in on them, and Iain had no answer for her beyond the true one, which was that he surveyed ground, not lodgings, and that the question was the maor's to answer, not his. He wrote her question down anyway. It went nowhere he ever heard of.

## III. Of the First Train

The humans' railway had come apart in places over the years since the Severance, its rails lifted in three parishes for the iron and its sleepers rotted where no one had thought to renew them, but the stretch from Cathair dhearg north had been kept, more or less, by a Rail Board that mended what it must and let the rest stand idle, and in Iain's first year on the chain that mending reached the valley. Gangs came up from the south with the humans' own tools, worn but sound, and laid new sleepers under old rail as far as the pithead, so that for the first time since the humans had built it the line ran unbroken from Achadh dhomhain to the capital.

The first train went down on the third of an Dàmhair, a grey morning with rain threatening and not falling, and half the town came out to see it off. There was no ceremony to it beyond the crowd that came; no Dia-thìris word had been coined yet for the thing, and the engineer who fired the boiler was a Tuathaich man who had learned the humans' trade from his father and kept the humans' habits with it, oiling the wheels the way the humans had oiled them and calling the whistle by the humans' word before anyone thought to give it another. The wagons behind him were loaded with coal cut that same week, in the kingdom's name now though on the humans' rails, and the whole of it, engine and wagons and the men who rode the footplate, went down the valley at a walking pace and out of sight round the first bend, and the crowd went back to its work.

Iain stood at the yard fence with Lachlann that morning and watched it go, and said, because it seemed a thing worth saying, that it was strange to see the humans' iron still doing the humans' work with no human left on the island to claim it. Lachlann said that the iron did not know whose name was on the wagons, and went back to his book.

The maor of Achadh dhomhain had wanted a blessing said over the first train, and had sent word to the Rite's house at Muileann dhearg to that effect, but the custodian who came up was an old man unused to trains and unwilling to walk the length of the footplate, and in the end he said his words over the coal in the first wagon rather than the engine, which the engineer, a Tuathaich man named Colin Rudd who had oiled locomotives under the humans' foremen as a boy, took as no insult and rather more sense than blessing an engine would have been. "You can bless coal," Colin Rudd said to Iain afterward, while the fire was building in the boiler and the crowd was still thick along the fence, "coal's been blessed since before either of us. Nobody's blessed an engine yet, and I'd not know what it would want with one." He spat, companionably, into the ash-pit and climbed up to his footplate, and a few minutes later the whistle went, a long human sound that startled half the children in the crowd into tears and the other half into cheering, and the train drew out.

The spoil that came up out of the Sloc Mòr's deeper galleries that year was a grey stone veined through with black, no use for building until someone thought to try it, and Uisdean mac Ùisdein's house, which held the concession, was the someone who thought to try it. A quarry was cut into the hillside above Achadh dhomhain before the year was out, and the stone, dressed and squared, went south on the same rails the coal went south on, sold under a mark cut into each block, a stylised wave for the house of Mac Ùisdein, so that a man in Cathair dhearg walking past a new wall could read, if he knew the mark, where the stone under his hand had come from. It built well and it built cheap, and within a few years half the new work going up in the south's public buildings was raised in it. Iain, who cut nothing and quarried nothing, only chained the faces the quarrymen went on to strip, thought little of the mark that first year he saw it stamped into a block on a wagon: a mountain gave up stone as readily as it gave up coal, once a house had found a way to sell both.

## IV. Of the Sidings and the Spur

The Rail Board, which had its office at Cathair dhearg by then, a low building of the same grey Mac Ùisdein stone, laid new sidings the following year at Muileann chrom, where the line from the Sloc Mòr met the older line down to the ports. It was there that the coal trains were broken up, their wagons sorted by the port they were bound for and made up again into new trains, and it was there, too, that a new kind of town grew up beside the old one, a scatter of low rows built for the families who worked the small shunting engines that did the sorting.

The Board counted these families apart from the rest of Muileann chrom's people, on a roll of their own kept separate from the shire's, and housed them apart as well, in the rows nearest the lines where the noise and the smoke of the yard never let up, day or night. It was not spoken of as a punishment, and no one on the Board would have called it one; it was only, the minute said, that a yard family's hours did not keep a shire's hours, and a roll that tried to hold both would serve neither well. Iain passed through Muileann chrom twice that year, carrying survey rolls between the Sloc Mòr and Cathair dhearg, and saw the rows from the carriage window both times, and both times thought that a family counted apart long enough forgets, after a while, that it was ever counted any other way.

On the second of those passings he had an hour to wait for the onward train and walked out along the rows himself rather than sit in the station house, and fell into talk with a shunting-engine driver named Murchadh who had worked the humans' small engines since he was a boy of twelve and had never once, in thirty years, been asked his name by anyone from the shire office at Muileann chrom proper, though he could have walked there in a quarter hour. Murchadh was not bitter about it, or did not show it if he was; he said only that a man who worked nights sorting wagons had no time for a shire's business and no great wish to make time for it, and that the yard looked after its own better than the shire had ever looked after the yard. Iain thought that a strange kind of pride to take in being left alone, and said nothing of it, and went on to catch his train.

In the same season the Board opened a spur off the western branch to Àth leathan, a gathering of pits and shanties in the hills where Tuathaich hewers had worked the coal since before the kingdom had troubled to draw a road to them. The spur was short, thirteen miles of new-laid rail over ground the Board's own surveys called poor, and it was built, the minute recorded, because the coal at Àth leathan was cheap to lift and the carters' road to it was worse each winter than the last. Iain never walked it himself. He heard of it from a hewer at the Sloc Mòr whose brother had gone to Àth leathan for the wage and wrote home, twice a year, in a hand the hewer could not read and had to carry to a neighbour with his letters to have read to him.

## V. Of the Oath on the Coal

The custom of binding hewers by charter, which the humans had never troubled to keep and which the island itself had not kept since the Holy Age, was taken up again that autumn, in a changed form. The old form, so far as anyone at the Sloc Mòr could reconstruct it from the custodians' copies of the Holy Age rolls, had bound apprentices of whatever blood a master chose to take; the new form, as the council's charter set it down, bound Dia-thìrich alone, and said so in its opening clause without troubling to give a reason, as a thing too plain to need one.

The Guild of Hewers was chartered at Achadh dhomhain on a bright, cold day in an t-Samhain, in the yard before the pithead, with the whole of the town's Dia-thìreach families turned out to see it and most of its Tuathaich families kept to their work, the charter having said nothing of a holiday for them. A table was set up under an awning against the weather, and the charter was read aloud twice, once by the maor's clerk and once, because a good half of those present could not follow the clerk's court Dia-thìris, by a hewer named Aonghas who had learned to read it from his own father and rendered it plain. Then the men who were to be bound came forward, by families, eldest first, and each in turn laid his hand flat on a lump of coal set on the table for the purpose, black and rough-edged and no different to look at from a thousand others cut that same week, and swore the oath the charter gave him: to keep the guild's custom, to take no work outside it, to teach no craft of it to a hand not sworn.

Iain stood at the table's edge with Lachlann's rolls under his arm, having been sent down from the galleries to carry the day's survey to the maor's office once the swearing was done, and watched the line go past him, man after man, his own father among them near the front of it, laying a hand that had cut coal for eleven years on a lump no bigger than a fist and speaking words that made him, from that hour, something Iain was not and could not be made. Iain had been taken on by a surveyor, and the Board's roll was the only one that carried his name; the charter, when the clerk read its closing clause, said plainly that its rolls were open to those who cut, hauled or timbered the coal, and named no place in them for one who only measured where it lay. No one told him to stand back from the table. He simply understood, watching his father's hand come down flat on the coal and hearing the oath said in a voice steadier than he had ever heard his father use for anything else, that the table was not his to come to, and stood where he was, at its edge, with the rolls under his arm, until the swearing was over and the crowd began to break up toward the ale that had been laid on in the hall.

His father found him there afterward, said little, being a man of few words at the best of times, and put a hand on Iain's shoulder for a moment, the same hand that had just sworn the oath, before going off to the hall with the other sworn men. Lachlann, who had come down from the galleries himself to see the charter read, found Iain still standing by the table a while later and said, not unkindly, that a chainman's name went into the Board's book, which was a kind of oath too, if a colder one, and that the mountain kept no better account of a man than the figures he left in it. Iain said that a cold oath was still not the one his father had sworn. Lachlann did not argue the point, having, it seemed, no argument to make against it, and the two of them walked back up toward the galleries together while the hall behind them filled with noise and firelight.

Iain walked back to the surveyors' hut alone once Lachlann had turned off toward his own lodging, in the last of the light, past the pithead where the new sidings ran black and empty in the cold, and wrote that night in his own small book, apart from the Board's, the thing he had watched and where he had stood while he watched it. He did not write why it had mattered so much to stand there. He did not, that year, have the words for it, and the book, in any case, kept better company with what a man had seen than with what he had felt about seeing it.

The saying the hewers had for the mountain, which Iain had heard a hundred times that year without troubling to write it down, he set down now for the first time, at the foot of the page, because it seemed, of a sudden, to fit more than the mountain: *Cha d' fhuair a' bheinn fois a-riamh.* The mountain never got rest.

# Part Three: Of Guilds, Law and Library

# Chapter Thirteen: Of the Indentures


*SE 14 am Faoilleach – an Dùbhlachd*

> *Scrìobh a làmh an t-ainm; a làmh fhèin a reub e.*
> His hand wrote the name; that same hand tore it.
>
> — said of Seumas Crùbach at Cuan shean, of the loosing of the indentures, 28 am Màrt, SE 14

## I. Of the Yard in Winter

Harry Marlow was seventeen that Faoilleach, four years into his time at Seumas Crùbach's yard on the hard at Cuan shean, and had stopped, some while before, counting the years the way a boy counts them and started counting them the way a bound man does, by the work left to learn rather than the work already behind him. The yard in am Faoilleach kept short hours and long fires. There was little to build that no one wanted mended first, and the mending, that winter, was slow work done by lamplight with the wind coming straight off the firth and finding every gap in the shed's south wall that four winters of caulking had not yet closed.

Seumas Crùbach was forty that year, a big slow-spoken man with one leg shorter than the other from a fall off a stage twenty years before, which was where the name had come to him and stayed, and he had taken Harry on, sight unseen, on a passing word about a boy at Doire mhin who could true a plough-beam by eye. He had not been disappointed in the boy, and said as much, rarely, and never twice. What he had taught Harry in four years he taught the way most of the yard's masters taught, by making him hold the far end of things, the adze, the clamp, the long batten sprung round a rising frame, until holding them stopped being a thing he thought about and became a thing his hands simply did, the way Lachlann's chainman up at the Sloc Mòr, had either of them ever met the other, might have said his own trade was learned. Seumas kept a small library of nothing at all, no book of the trade beyond a single dog-eared tide-table nailed inside the shed door, and taught out of his hands and out of the hulls standing round him, which he held to be library enough for any craft worth calling one.

At the far end of the hard, past the two hulls under repair and the third laid up on blocks for the winter, stood a fourth that nobody paid to have mended, an old human vessel left derelict on the sand since before Harry's time, her stem stove in on a falling tide some years back and never worth the labour of hauling clear, so that she had simply stayed, settling a little deeper into the shingle each winter, her timbers greying and her caulking gone to powder. Harry had taken to her in his second year the way another boy might have taken to a book, going down to her in the stolen half-hour before the yard opened or after it shut, first only to look, and later, once he had begun to trust his own eye, to measure. It had troubled him from his first winter at Cuan shean that the humans' way of raising a hull and the yard's own way came at the same hull from opposite ends: the yard's hulls went up frame first, rib after rib stepped and faired before a single plank closed them in, so that a man could stand inside the naked skeleton of a boat and read her whole form before she held water; the humans, by every account Harry had ever been given, built the other way about, plank on plank from the keel up, shaping the hull's skin before her bones were more than a notion in the shipwright's head, a method the yard's men called quick and unsound in the same breath, the way a man might call a short cut both quick and unsound. He had asked a stranger once, years before, at his father's forge, which of the two ways was truer, and been told only that he would have his answer soon enough. No master of the yard had troubled, in four years, to build a hull the humans' way and show him. The old wreck on the hard was the nearest thing to an answer the yard possessed, and Harry went to her, that winter and every winter since his second, with a rule and a scrap of slate, learning by his own measure what no man at Cuan shean would trouble to teach him.

The other apprentices of the yard, four of them that winter besides Harry, three Dia-thìreach boys bound in the ordinary way and one Tuathaich boy younger than Harry, out of a fishing family further down the coast, thought little of Harry's evenings at the wreck and said as much, the biggest and idlest-handed of the Dia-thìreach boys, who would himself be sworn that spring, telling him more than once that a man learned nothing from a dead hull that a live one, worked under a master's eye, would not teach him twice as fast and half as cold. Harry did not argue the point, having found argument a poor tool against a boy who had never gone down to the sand himself to see what there was to learn there, and went on measuring. The younger Tuathaich boy alone, of the four, sometimes came down with him in the last light, to hold the lamp steady rather than to measure, having no head yet for it, and to ask, now and again, some plain question neither of them yet had the words for, and it was in answering those plain questions, more than in any book, that Harry first found words of his own for what his hands already knew.

## II. Of the News from Ros dhomhain

The news came up the coast the way most news came to Cuan shean that year, by a coaster putting in for water and staying an extra tide for the gossip, and it was old news already, three weeks stale, by the time it reached the yard: that the shipwrights of Ros dhomhain, who had built hulls for the whole southern coast since before the kingdom had any name of its own, had taken a charter of their own from the guild court at Cathair dhearg, and bound thirty apprentices in a single day on the slipway to mark it, the largest binding the south had seen since the Crossing. Seumas heard it out at the shed door from the coaster's mate, a wiry man with a Ros dhomhain accent thick enough to cut, and asked, when the telling was done, only how many of the thirty were Tuathaich boys, which the mate could not say, not having troubled to ask, and thought an odd question to be asked at all.

It was not, that winter, an odd question at Cuan shean, or anywhere along the coast where a Tuathaich boy had ever been bound to a Dia-thìreach master's craft. The charters were going up everywhere that year, guild after guild taking its letters from the court at Cathair dhearg the way a town takes a market day, each charter naming its own trade's custom and each custom, without quite saying why, drawn a little narrower than the last. It was told, that same winter, of the chandlers of Ceann àrsaidh, upriver of the capital on the Abhainn fhionn, that their new charter won them the sole right to fit the Crown's patrol boats, a right the chandlers meant to hold for as long as the Crown kept a boat afloat; and of the lamp-makers of Muileann mhin, who made between them every coal lamp burned in every shaft on the island, that their charter set upon their work a mark, a flame struck over a hammer, stamped from that winter on every lamp that left their sheds, so that a hewer a hundred miles off, holding a strange lamp up to the light, could read in that small stamp the whole history of where it had been made and under what oath. Of all the marks the guilds set that year, the Tuathaich traders of the north, the humans' children, who copied little from the island's guild law, were said to have copied that one alone onto lamps of their own, finding it, whatever else they made of the rest, a useful thing to know a lamp by.

What the charters did not say, most of them, was what was owed a boy already bound before the charter was read, and it was this silence, more than any single line in any single guild's letter, that sat that winter in the yards and the smithies and the weaving-sheds of every coast the humans' children worked. A rope-maker's apprentice at Ros dhomhain, four years bound already and thought by his own master fit to be sworn with the thirty, brought his case that winter to the same guild court that had chartered the shipwrights, standing before three benchmen in a hall built for the hearing of debts and disputed cargoes and asking only to be sworn along with the rest of his master's household. He was heard out in full, the court giving him, by the account that reached Cuan shean, a fairer hearing than a rope-maker's apprentice commonly got, and refused in the same sitting, the eldest benchman reading the charter's own words back to him slowly, that its custom of binding was kept for those of Dia-thìrich blood and named no other, and that a court sworn to the charter could no more stretch its words for one boy's sake than a shipwright could stretch a keel too short for the hull laid on it. The boy's own master, it was told, said nothing in the hearing to help him, having, by then, no words left in the charter's own language that would have served. The Moot at Caol mhòr, hearing of the ruling by the same slow road all northern news travelled, wrote that winter to the guild court at Cathair dhearg asking plainly what was to become of the indentures already standing across every trade the charters touched, and had its letter filed among that year's other business, without an answer, a fact the Moot's own minute-book set down at the foot of the page in a hand that Harry, had he ever seen it, would have known at once for its plainness, whoever held the pen.

Seumas said little of any of it that winter, being a man slow to speak of a thing until he could see the whole of it, and Harry noticed, without being told to notice, that his master had begun, some time in am Faoilleach, to look at him a beat longer than the work required before turning back to whatever the two of them were doing, the way a man looks at a thing he expects, before long, to lose.

## III. Of the Eight-and-Twentieth of am Màrt

The letter came to Cuan shean on the twenty-eighth of am Màrt, carried by the same maor's clerk who rode the coast road twice a year with the shire's other business, and it said, in four lines that took the clerk less time to read aloud than it had taken him to find the yard, that the custom of binding, restored to every chartered guild of the island that winter and spring, was kept henceforth for Dia-thìrich hands alone, and that any indenture standing between a guild master and a Tuathaich boy, wherever on the coast it was held, was from that day loosed. The same letter, or one much like it, went that week to Seann Bhral in the west, where the Leòid ruling had been given years before on land and not on labour, and to every yard and shed along the coast where a Tuathaich boy had ever taken a master's name along with a master's craft.

Seumas read it through once himself, standing in the shed door with the clerk still waiting for some word to carry back, and read it a second time slower, though there was nothing in four lines that a second reading could change. He asked the clerk, once, whether the rule reached back to a boy four years bound already or only forward to one not yet taken on, and was told that it reached back, the letter's own words being *any indenture standing*, and that the guild court at Cathair dhearg had been plain enough about it not to leave a master room to argue the other way. The clerk did not stay long after that, having other yards on the coast road still to reach before dark, and Seumas stood a while in the doorway with the letter in his hand after the clerk's horse had gone, before he went in to find Harry at the bench, planing a stem-piece for the second hull, and told him, without any lead-up at all, what the letter said.

Harry heard it out standing, the plane still in his hand, and said nothing for a space long enough that Seumas repeated the last of it, as though the boy might not have caught it the first time. He had caught it the first time. What he could not, in that first space, find words for was less the fact alone, which he understood plainly enough, four years of a trade being no small thing to have taken from a man by four lines read out at a shed door, than the look on Seumas's face while he said it, a look Harry had not seen there before, one hard to name exactly, somewhere between the grief a man shows at a death he cannot prevent and the shame a man shows at a thing he is made to do and cannot, however plainly the fault lies elsewhere, entirely forgive himself for doing.

The indenture had hung, these four years, in a frame behind the shed's one good window, Harry's name and Seumas's own set down together in a clerk's careful hand and witnessed by the harbour-master of that year, long since moved on to other work. Seumas took it down himself that afternoon, unhooked it from its nail without a word to Harry about doing it, and tore it, not neatly, the paper being stiffer with age than either of them had judged it, so that the tear ran crooked across both their names before it came free in two pieces in his hands. He did this with his back half turned, and did not, in the doing of it or after, look at Harry directly, occupying his eyes instead with the two torn halves of the paper, which he folded once, carefully, as though a careful folding might undo some part of what the tearing had done, and set on the bench rather than in the fire, where four years' worth of another man's kept faith seemed, to him at least, to deserve better than burning.

"You'll have heard the wage a free hand gets on this coast," he said at last, still not looking up from the paper. "Half a bound man's, and no guild mark to show for it, and no standing in the court if a debt goes bad on you. I'll not pretend to you it's a fair trade for what the four lines took." He paused, and Harry, watching him, understood that whatever came next had cost his master some effort to arrive at. "But the bench is still yours if you'll have it on those terms, and I'll not have another boy stand where you stood these four years and call the standing his by right, when it was never given him by anything but a paper that's ash and torn corners now."

Harry said, when he had found the words for it, that he would have the bench.

## IV. Of the Day-Labour

He stayed, through that spring and the summer after it, at half the wage a bound man drew and none of the standing, which was, in the small ways a yard measures such things, no small change. He ate at the same board as the sworn men still, Seumas seeing to that much himself, though he sat at its foot rather than its middle, by a custom nobody troubled to name to him and that he learned quickly enough on his own not to ask named. More often than before he was sent to fetch and carry rather than to fair a plank, the yard's other hands, sworn men now under the new charter Seumas himself had at last to take from the guild court that spring to keep trading at all, being wary of being seen teaching their craft too openly to a hand the charter no longer counted theirs to teach. And the whole year went by without a guild mark of his own to stamp on any work, so that a stem-piece he had fair-shaped from rough timber to finished curve left the yard, when it left it, under Seumas's stamp alone, the hands that had shaped it going unrecorded in the wood.

The half-wage told in smaller ways too, ways that took the year to add up to anything a man would trouble to complain of. He mended his own boots that year rather than paying the cobbler at the harbour end, and went without the tobacco he had taken up, against his father's wishes, in his third bound year, and put off, twice, buying a coat the winter weather said plainly he needed, until Seumas, noticing the third winter of the same worn coat without being told why it had lasted so long, set a length of oiled wool on the bench one morning with no word of where it had come from and none asked. Harry took it, and said only that he would pay him back for it come the spring herring money, and Seumas said that he would take the payment if it was offered and would not trouble himself if it was not, which both of them understood, without either saying so, to mean the same thing twice over.

What the charter did not take from him, having no way to reach it, was the hour before the yard opened and the hour after it shut, and it was in those hours, through that spring and on into the summer, that Harry went back, oftener now than in any year before, to the old wreck on the hard, measuring her frames rib by rib with a patience the yard's own work no longer quite gave him room for, and setting down what he found in a small book of his own, kept apart from any book the yard or the guild would have troubled to read.

The wreck had given up her secrets slowly and in the wrong order over Harry's three prior winters at her, the way any old and broken thing does to a boy working alone and by guesswork, and it was only the autumn before this one, on a night he did not afterward forget, that a plank sprung loose at the turn of her bilge showed him, in the shape its edge had been shaved to before ever it was fastened, the thing the yard's own frame-first men had no cause to know: that a human shipwright did not lay his planks flat and force them to the hull's curve after, as Harry had half supposed, but shaved each one, before it ever touched the keel, to a curve the eye alone had judged against the planks laid before it, so that the whole skin of the hull was faired plank by plank, from the keel up, long before a single frame was stepped inside her to hold the shape true. It was, when he had it, a small enough thing to have taken three winters over, and he had sat a long while on the cold sand that evening with the loose plank across his knees, turning it in the last of the light, before he trusted himself to write it down. This spring and summer, freed of bound hours earlier in the day than any year before, he set himself to proving the finding against every strake still fast to her, plank by plank, to be certain the one loose piece had not misled him.

By an Lùnastal of the year the letter came, he had her lines, so far as four years' rust and rot had left them to be had, set down whole from stem to stern in the small book he kept apart from any book the yard or the guild would have troubled to read, and had learned, mostly by his own error corrected against his own measure, why a hull built plank first and frame after held together at all, a discipline the yard's own frame-first men, working the surer way, never had cause to learn.

A trader out of Seann Vell put in at Cuan shean that an t-Sultain, working the coast on his way north with a hold half full of cloth the northern towns still bought though the coin that paid for it grew scarcer each year, and heard, over an evening's ale, something of Harry's case from one of the yard's own sworn men, not unkindly meant, and said to Harry himself, the following morning, that a free hand with steady hands and no guild behind him might do better for himself at one of the northern harbours, where a man's craft was reckoned, he said, by what it was worth rather than by what paper stood behind it, there being, in the north, no guild court to stand behind either. Harry heard him out, and thanked him for the telling, and did not go. He gave the trader no long reason for staying, having none yet fully worked out even to himself, beyond the plain fact that the old wreck's lines were not yet whole in his book, and that a craft learned by his own measure, wreck by wreck and rib by rib, seemed to him, that autumn, worth more than a paper standing behind him in a court thirty miles off that had never once, in four years, stood behind him in the court three miles from where he slept.

The year ended as every year of his apprenticeship had ended, with Harry setting aside from his wage, such as it now was, the sum he sent north each Dùbhlachd to his father's forge at Doire mhin, a habit begun in his first bound year and kept now, half a bound man's wage or not, without his troubling to weigh whether a free hand owed the habit any less than a sworn one had. It was a smaller sum that year than any year before it, the half-wage making sure of that, and he wrote no long letter to go with it, his father Joseph Marlow being, by all Harry had ever seen of him, no reader of long letters in any case. What he wrote, folded small inside the coin, was four words only, set down in the same hand the guild's own clerk might have used to close out an account: *the bench is still mine.*

Seumas kept the two torn halves of the old indenture on the bench through that whole year, moving them from shelf to shelf as the shed's other clutter grew round them but never once putting them to the fire, and it was noticed, by more than one hand in the yard, that when a stranger asked him that Dùbhlachd how his boy did, meaning Harry, he answered as he always had, that the boy did well enough, and did not trouble, in the answering, to correct the word *boy* to *hand*, or the possessive that went before it to anything less than it had always been.

# Chapter Fourteen: Of Agnes Pike's School

*SE 15 am Faoilleach – an t-Iuchar*

> Entered this day, a byre at Doire ghlas, no other roof offering: A. Pike, mistress. Eleven scholars. No leave asked, none given, none refused.
>
> — the school's own register, first leaf, 14 am Faoilleach, SE 15

## I. Of the Weavers and the Byre

That same winter, far to the south, the weavers of Baile chiar took a charter for their guild, and the council's clerks cut a new seal for them, a shuttle over a fleece, and entered the grant in a book bound in calf and kept under lock at Cathair dhearg. It cost the weavers a fee, a feast for the councillors who signed it, and three months of waiting while the seal-cutter finished a commission for the mint first. When it was done they had the right to call themselves a guild, to set their own prices at the fair, and to bar any weaver of Baile chiar who had not served the full seven years under a master of the craft. It is the kind of grant this book has recorded a dozen times already and will record a dozen times more: coin changes hands, a form is followed, a seal is cut, and a thing that was already being done becomes a thing the kingdom has agreed to notice.

At Doire ghlas, in the north, in the same season, a schoolmistress asked leave of no one at all.

Agnes Pike was four-and-thirty that winter, a miller's daughter of a family that had ground the north's grain at Doire mhin since before the Severance, though she herself had left the mill for a scribe's stool in the harbour agent's office at Ros bheag as a girl, and had spent a dozen years since copying tallies of herring and salt by a window that let in more weather than light. She read well, in both tongues, having been taught her letters by a Mission woman old enough to remember the last ship, and she wrote a hand clean enough that the harbour agent had once offered to send her south to a copyist's house at Cathair dhearg, an offer she turned down without troubling to explain why. What she wanted, she told her sister that same year, over a supper of little more than oatmeal and the last of the autumn's apples, was a room of her own, with children in it who did not yet know how much the world meant to keep from them; a stool in a southern office held no such want for her.

She had been three years asking round Doire ghlas for such a room before she found one that would serve. The town had no hall to spare and no coin of its own to raise one, the Moot's letters on the matter having gone south and come back, as they generally did, with nothing on them but the mark of a clerk who had read them. Doire ghlas was by then the largest of the Tuathaich towns of that coast, a huddle of stone-and-turf roofs in a fold of the moor, its one street running from the mill-bridge to the Church and stopping there, as though the town had never quite decided what a street beyond a church was for. It had grown a good deal since the hungry year, when Walter Hale had walked meal in from Caol mhòr and helped bury the children the Dia-thìrich had never troubled to count; the names of that year's dead were still kept, pinned in the church porch, and more than one of the children who came to Agnes's byre that winter had an elder brother or sister among them, a fact none of the households spoke of and all of them knew.

In am Faoilleach a widow named Jenny Marrow, whose husband had kept cattle on the moor above the town until a wet spring took half his herd and the fever took the rest of him, offered her byre for the winter months, the beasts she had left being few enough now to stand a season crowded into the barn behind it. Jenny asked nothing for the loan beyond a promise that the children would be taught to write their names, hers among them, she being sixty that year and unable, she said plainly, to see any reason a woman ought to go to her grave signing a mark. The byre smelled of what a byre smells of, and the roof let in a persistent drip over the third row of benches that no amount of patching ever quite stopped, and Agnes took it gladly, for it had four walls, a floor that could be swept, and a door that shut.

## II. Of the Fourteenth of am Faoilleach

The purse that paid for the benches, the slates, and the widow's rent came from Caol mhòr, carried the length of the coast road by Walter Hale himself, who by then had been speaker of the Moot for thirteen years and had grown, in that time, into the habit of carrying its business in his own saddlebag rather than trusting it to a rider who might not know which doors in a strange town were worth knocking on. He was eight-and-fifty that winter, greyer at the temple than the year before, and he made the ride in from Caol mhòr in weather his wife Ellen told him plainly he was too old to be riding in, an opinion he did not dispute and rode out in anyway. He found Agnes Pike sweeping straw from the byre floor the evening before it was to open, and set the purse down on the one bench already fixed to the wall, and told her, as near as the Moot's own minute records the exchange, that the sum was hers to spend as she saw fit and that no one at Caol mhòr expected an account of every penny, the Moot having decided, after some argument, that a schoolmistress who had to write down the cost of every slate was a schoolmistress with less time to teach.

"And the council?" Agnes asked him, not looking up from the broom.

"Received and filed," Hale said. It was, by then, a saying among them, the answer the council gave to nearly everything the north sent it, and he said it the way a man says a thing he has stopped being angry at and started merely repeating. "I did not ask again after the first no. A council that says no once will say no as often as you trouble it. This one," he nodded at the byre, "asked no one a second time."

She straightened then and looked at him, the broom still in her hand. "It is a byre with children in it, Walter, whatever else you call it."

"So was the first one at Caol mhòr," he said, "the winter after we came north, when the priest lent Ellen the church porch two hours a week to teach David and Alice their letters, before there was any Moot to call it a school or refuse to. It became one because enough children kept coming back to it that nobody could call it anything else." He looked round the byre, at the swept floor and the benches and the drip already starting again over the third row now that the evening's rain had begun. "Call it what you like. Open the door tomorrow and see who comes."

The school opened on 14 am Faoilleach, in the grey light before the moor mist had properly lifted, and eleven children came through the byre door before the bell of the Church, which Doire ghlas had lately taken to ringing for the hour rather than for the office alone, had finished its seventh stroke. Agnes had for teaching them two books and nothing else: the Bible, in the humans' own tongue, which every household in the north kept a copy of whether or not any hand in the house could read it, and a bound volume of the Moot's own minutes, going back to the wet afternoon at Caol mhòr when the first of them was written, which Hale had lent her for the winter on the understanding that it came back to Caol mhòr in the spring in the same condition it left. There was no primer, no slate-book of letters set out in rows, because none had ever been printed for the humans' tongue on the island and none was coming; so the children of Doire ghlas learned their letters that winter from the twenty-third psalm and from old minutes recording a granary vote and a dispute over a shared boat, in roughly equal measure, and Agnes could never afterward say which of the two taught them faster.

The eleven who came that first morning ranged from a girl of five, brought by an elder cousin because there was nowhere else to leave her, to a boy of thirteen already promised to a carter and come only because the carter was laid up that week with a lame horse. Agnes set them by no order she had planned in advance, having never kept school before and having only her own dozen years at a copyist's desk to draw on for a method, and settled by the second week on putting the youngest nearest the one window, where the light lasted longest, and the eldest nearest the door, on the reasoning that a boy who might be called out to help with a cart at any hour should not have to climb over four benches to answer the call. Jenny herself came most mornings and sat at the very back with her own slate, forming her name letter by letter with a slowness the younger children found endlessly diverting and never once mocked her for, and by an Cèitean she had it whole, and stood it against the byre's one dry wall where the drip could not reach it, next to the psalms.

Hale did not stay to see the door open. He rode south again the same evening he delivered the purse, having, he told Agnes, a sitting of the Moot at Caol mhòr to be at two days later, and the Moot's own business, as ever, waiting on his saddlebag. But he left her, folded inside the cover of the minute-book, a single sheet in his own hand, headed only *For whoever asks*, setting out in four plain lines that the purse was the Moot's, the room was the widow's, and the leave, such as it was, was nobody's at all; and Agnes kept that sheet, long after the minute-book had gone back to Caol mhòr, pinned inside the register she began that same week, where it stayed for as long as the school did.

## III. Of Daniel Frayne

Among the eleven who came through the door that first morning was a boy of ten named Daniel Frayne, walked in from Muileann leathan, a weaving town close enough across the moor that a child could make the distance on his own feet before the bell finished, provided he left before it began. His father worked a loom in a shed behind the house and had never in his life wanted more of letters than would let him read a bill of sale, and told his son plainly, the first evening Daniel came home smelling of the byre, that he saw no harm in it so long as the boy was back in time to help carry the cloth to the fuller's, a condition Daniel kept without fail for as long as the school ran, walking the moor road at first light with a slate under one arm and, on the wetter mornings, his mother's shawl over his head against a rain that came over the moor sideways more often than down.

He was not the quickest child on the benches that winter, nor the slowest; the psalm gave him trouble longer than it gave most, the reading of it, that is, for the words themselves swam a little on the page and would not always sit still for him in the order Agnes read them aloud. But he could copy. Set in front of him a line already written, in any hand, and he would render it back stroke for stroke with a care that made Agnes, watching over his shoulder one grey morning in an Gearran, stop what she was doing and look a second time, for the boy had taken a page of the Moot's minutes, a dry entry about a granary's repair, and copied it out exactly, the loop of every g, the cross of every t, as though his hand understood the shape of a word before his eyes had finished understanding its sense.

"You read that slower than you wrote it," she told him, not unkindly.

"I know what it's meant to look like," Daniel said, which was as near as he ever came, that winter or for some years after, to explaining the difference between the two things to anyone, including himself. Agnes set him, from that week, to copying out a second time whatever the class had read that day, a task the other children took as a punishment when it fell to them and Daniel took, visibly, as something closer to its opposite; by an Cèitean his fair copies of the day's psalm or the day's minute were pinned along the byre's one dry wall, less because they were needed there than because Agnes had run out of other ways to keep the drip off them.

The other children on his bench teased him for it, in the way children tease a boy who is glad to be given more of a chore than he was set, though not unkindly, and one of them, a carter's daughter named Effie who read faster than anyone in the byre and could not, by her own loud complaint, make a letter sit straight to save her life, took to trading him her reading of a hard line for his copying of an easy one, an arrangement Agnes noticed within the week and chose, after some thought, not to forbid, on the reasoning that a school with eleven children and one teacher would need more than one kind of teaching in it before the winter was out. Daniel's mother, when she heard of the arrangement from her son at supper, said only that it sounded a fair trade and asked whether the girl's family had meal to spare that week, which was, in a poor town in a lean season, very often the shape a compliment took.

He was not quick to speak of the school at all, in fact, being a boy who kept most things folded close, and it was his father, coming in from the loom-shed one evening with the lint still white on his sleeves, who first noticed that his son had begun, without being asked, to copy out the week's weaving into a little book of his own, tallying ells of grey against ells of brown in columns as neat as anything the byre wall carried, a habit that outlasted the schooling and that his father, who had never asked for it, came in time to rely on more than he ever quite admitted.

## IV. Of the Maor Who Wrote Nothing

The maor of the shire, whose office required him to note anything new raised, built, or opened within it and send word south once a season, rode out to Doire ghlas in an t-Ògmhios, six months after the byre door first opened, having heard of the school by then from at least three different householders who mentioned it to him as though he must already know, the way a thing spoken of openly in a small town is assumed, wrongly, to have reached every ear that governs it. He was a heavy man, not unkind, who had held the shire eleven years and had learned in that time which of the things brought to his notice were worth troubling the council with and which were better left where they lay; and he stood in the byre door for the better part of an hour on a warm morning, watching eleven children, twelve by then, recite the fourth psalm in a ragged chorus while a woman he had never met before that day kept time with a stick against the door-frame, and said, when Agnes at last came to speak with him, almost nothing at all.

Her name he asked, which he already knew, and how the room was heated in winter, and whether the children paid anything for their place on the bench, setting both answers down in a small book he carried for the purpose, in a hand Agnes could not read upside down and did not try very hard to. Of the council's leave he asked nothing, and she offered nothing of its want, each of them understanding, without either saying so, that the question and its answer would only make the report he was about to write a harder one to write briefly.

He had, in his eleven years in the office, sent south a great many reports of things newly built: a mill wheel, a patched bridge, a chapel roof reslated, each one entered under a heading the council's own forms already provided for it, so that a maor filling in his season's return needed only choose the right box and set down a number. There was no box on any form he had ever been given for a room where Tuathaich children were taught to read the humans' tongue in the hand of a woman the council had never licensed to teach anything at all, and he had turned the problem over more than once on the ride out from his own house, without arriving at anything he liked better than the plain fact that a report is a thing a man is asked for, and a silence is a thing nobody has yet thought to ask after. He was not a cruel man, and had spent eleven years learning precisely which small mercies a shire's maor could extend to a town without any of them ever reaching a page the council would read; this, he judged, watching the children file back to their benches as he turned his horse for the coast road, was one more.

He thanked her for her time, in the flat courteous way a man thanks a stranger for an hour he had not particularly wanted to spend, and rode south again before the noon meal, and the report he sent that season to Cathair dhearg, which the council's own chests still hold, records the shire's harvest, its head-due, the state of its one bridge, and nothing whatever about a byre at Doire ghlas with a schoolmistress in it and children reciting psalms from a Moot's minute-book.

It was not, Agnes came to understand only much later, an oversight. A maor who wrote nothing of a thing he had seen with his own eyes had not forgotten it; he had decided, in the particular silence of a man who knows exactly how far his own office reaches and no further, that a school begun without leave was safest left where a council that had already said no once could not be provoked into saying no again, more loudly, to something it would then be obliged to close. She never learned whether that was kindness, caution, or simply a want of anything in the maor's instructions that told him what box on his form a byre full of Tuathaich children ought to be entered under; and in the years that followed, as eight more such schools opened along the coast without one of them being licensed and not one of them being shut, she came to think it mattered rather less than the plain fact that the report went south blank on the one matter that would have mattered to her, and stayed blank, season after season, for as long as any maor of that shire held the office.

## V. Of the Second School and the Minute Copied Fair

Word of the byre reached Caol mhòr before the spring was out, carried, as most things reached Caol mhòr, in the mouth of a carter, and Alice Hale, Walter and Ellen's daughter, nineteen that year and long since past the age when her father's household porch-lessons had served her, opened a second school within the month in a disused net-store behind the harbour, with six benches begged from the boat-builders and a purse a good deal smaller than the one her father had carried to Doire ghlas, the Moot's own funds having been thinner that season on account of a poor herring year. She wrote to Agnes asking what had answered best on the byre's cold mornings and what had not, and the two women kept up, through that year and after, a correspondence of practical questions (how many slates a class of a dozen truly needed, whether the psalms or the minutes taught the alphabet faster, what to do about a child who came to school hungry and could not be made to sit still on an empty stomach) that neither of them thought to call anything grander than letters between two women doing the same work at either end of the same coast.

Further south and inland that same season, though neither Agnes nor her scholars would hear of it for some years, the Board's surveyors closed a different kind of book on a different kind of report. The Cill ghlas district, shut to new shafts since the Rending had brought a gallery down there two generations before, was walked over that summer by Lachlann mac Iain Bhàin and the young chainman who carried his chain and his lamp, Iain mac Ruairidh, the two of them tracing the old fault line foot by foot with plumb and cord until they were satisfied it lay where the old surveys said it lay and had moved no further since. Their report, filed with the Board at Cathair dhearg, declared the ground safe to work again, so long as any new shaft was cut a full chain back from the fault line, a condition the Board accepted without argument and the first new diggers observed, that season, to the letter. It is a small entry beside a byre full of children reciting psalms, and it belongs to a different part of this same age's long account of what was measured, and what was not, and by whom, and it is set here only because it happened, as near as the record can place it, in the same weeks that a maor rode home from Doire ghlas with a small book full of everything but the one thing he had seen.

Two reports, that season: one that named a fault line to the foot and was believed on its author's word alone, and one that named nothing at all, and was believed for the same reason. Neither surveyor at Cill ghlas ever heard of the byre at Doire ghlas, nor would have found anything in it to measure had they gone there, there being no fault line under a schoolroom that any chain could find; and Agnes Pike, for her part, never learned the surveyors' names at all. The record keeps the two of them apart because the Board kept them apart, filing the one at Cathair dhearg and never troubling to look north at all; it is only the Library, gathering both into one shelf at the age's end, that sets them side by side and lets a reader notice what neither man who wrote them was ever asked to notice himself.

Daniel Frayne finished that first winter's schooling in an t-Iuchar, the byre's benches given back to the widow Marrow's returning cattle for the summer months and the school moved, as it would move every summer after, into the porch of the Church, which offered shade enough and no drip at all.
