On the last morning before the move, Agnes set the class one final copying, the same task she had set them nearly every week since the psalm had first proved too slow a teacher on its own: the Moot's own minute of the day the school had opened, four lines long, recording that a room had been found at Doire ghlas, that eleven children had come to it, and that no leave had been asked because none had been thought likely to be given. Daniel copied it as he copied everything, stroke for stroke, the loops even, the lines straight along a ruled edge Agnes had learned to give him without being asked, and when he had done she took the page from him, read it through once, and pinned it into the front leaf of the school's own new register, the first thing entered there in a hand not her own, leaving the drying wall to the psalms.

"Why that one?" Daniel asked her, watching her pin it.

"Because it's the truest thing in the book," Agnes said, "and you wrote it best."

# Chapter Fifteen: Of the Seventeen Suits

*SE 15 an t-Iuchar – SE 16 an Giblean*

> A law made exact is a law made for someone. I have never pretended otherwise, and I have not been asked to stop.
>
> — Eilidh nic Leòid, at the inn of Ceann mhòr, the night of 27 an t-Iuchar, SE 15

## I. Of the Court in the Heat

Ceann mhòr in an t-Iuchar smelled of tar and low tide and the fish-yards behind the harbour wall, and by the second week of the month the smell had climbed the hill to the old magistrate's house and settled into every room of it, so that the clerk who kept the maor's rolls there had taken, that summer, to propping every window on the seaward side and weighting his papers with whatever came to hand, a stone, an inkpot, a boot. Eilidh nic Leòid arrived on the Tuesday of the assize week with Murchadh Clàrc riding a length behind her, as he had ridden behind her for seven years now, and found the house's largest room already too warm to sit in with the shutters closed and not warm enough, once they were open, to keep the flies out.

She was nine-and-fifty that summer, and had ridden her own circuit of the south-west eight times, but never the northern one, which the council had added to her charge that spring, and never in such heat. She said as much to Murchadh while the room was set, the long table carried in from the maor's own house and set crosswise under the window so the light fell across it rather than into her eyes, the bench for the suitors arranged along the far wall where the draught, such as there was, would reach them first. "We will want water brought in through the morning," she told him, "and not wine, whatever the maor's clerk offers us by way of courtesy. A justice who drinks at her own bench in this heat will be asleep by the second cause and cross by the fifth." Murchadh, who had learned over seven years of riding behind her exactly which of her instructions wanted an answer and which wanted only a note taken, wrote it down and said nothing, and went to find the water himself rather than trust the maor's clerk to remember it.

The town's maor, a Dia-thìreach man named Griogair mac Ailein who had held Siorrachd Ceann mhòr for eleven years and lived, all that time, in the house the last human magistrate had kept, met her at the door with the courtesy due her office and a list of the assize's causes already fair-copied twice, and told her, walking her through to the room where the bench was set, that he had never in his eleven years seen so full a list brought before one sitting. "Nineteen causes," he said, "and of them seventeen the same kind of paper, near enough, that a man could read one and guess the shape of the rest before he opened it." He said it with the particular weariness of a man who had spent some years hoping the matter would settle on its own and had at last given up the hope, and Eilidh, taking the list from him and running her thumb down its length before she had even taken off her travelling cloak, told him only that she had come to read every one of the nineteen to its own end regardless of how much the rest resembled it, and that a paper's likeness to its neighbour was not, in her experience, a reason to read it any less carefully, whatever hope a busy maor might have of the opposite.

The room filled slowly through the Tuesday morning, the suitors of the first cases arriving early and standing about the yard in their best coats long before the bench was ready for them, the two Dia-thìreach households among the nineteen keeping somewhat apart from the seventeen Tuathaich ones by an old habit of the town that nobody troubled to explain and nobody, that morning, troubled to break. Among the second group, standing a little further back than the rest and dressed no better nor worse, Eilidh marked a grey-haired man in a coat cut in the humans' old fashion, a plain dark thing gone thin at the elbows, who carried no paper of his own and seemed, from the way the others near him spoke, to have come to watch rather than to plead. She did not know him by sight, and asked Murchadh, in a low word, whether he did. Murchadh did not either.

She opened the sitting a little after the noon bell, standing at the head of the long table with the window's light behind her and the room's heat already thick enough to see, faintly, in the air above the flagstones, and told the room, in the plain unhurried voice Murchadh had heard open eleven assizes before this one, that she would hear every cause on the list to the end, that no cause would be taken out of its order for anyone's convenience, and that the room's heat was a fact she regretted and could do nothing about, and would ask everyone present to bear with equal patience. A woman near the back, whose own cause stood fourteenth on the list, was heard by more than one witness afterward to remark that a justice who apologised for the weather before she had heard a single cause was, whatever else came of the week, at least honest about what she could and could not mend, which the woman meant, by every account, as praise.

## II. Of the Papers Brown at the Fold

The two Dia-thìreach causes went first, by the list's own order, and were settled within the hour, a boundary dispute between neighbouring farms that Eilidh resolved much as she had resolved the well-dispute at Muileann bhàn years before, by sending Murchadh out with a cord to measure the ground rather than trust either party's account of where an old wall had stood, and a debt case turning on a receipt that satisfied her within a quarter-hour of reading. Then came the seventeen, and the room, which had grown used through the morning to the ordinary rhythm of a small town's law, settled into a different and slower one.

Each of the seventeen came up to the bench carrying the same kind of paper, in substance if not in every particular: a title granted under the humans' own seal, in the humans' own hand, to a family that had worked the ground it named for one generation or two or three before the crossing closed, the ink long since gone the colour of weak tea and the folds worn soft and brown where the paper had been carried, folded and unfolded, from one generation's strongbox to the next. Eilidh read every one of the seventeen to its own end before she would hear a word spoken over it, turning each page toward the window's light when a line had faded past easy reading and asking, twice, for a magnifying glass Murchadh had thought to bring on a hunch rather than an instruction, and the suitors of the first several causes, expecting the swift hearing a busy assize usually gave a cause everyone in the room already knew the shape of, stood through the reading in a silence that had, by the fourth or fifth title, taken on something of the character of held breath.

She read the Dunlop title first among the seventeen, a grant of four fields above the town dated in the human count to a year before Eilidh herself was born, and asked the family's eldest, a woman of perhaps forty standing straight-backed in a coat clearly kept for occasions such as this one, whether the ground had been worked continuously by her own people since the grant was made. It had, the woman said, by her grandfather and then her father and now by her own husband and sons, without a season's break that she knew of, and she had brought, though nobody had asked her to, a second paper, a receipt for seed corn bought the spring after the grant, in case the court should want proof the ground had been worked from the very first year and not merely claimed. Eilidh took the receipt, read it as carefully as she had read the title, and set both papers down together on the table before she gave her ruling, which came, as it had come at Seann Bhral seven years before and would come sixteen times more before the week was out, in almost the words of her own earlier reasoning: that the humans' authority to grant land upon the island had ended with the humans' own leaving of it, and that the ground, in law, had passed with everything else the crossing left behind to the Crown that now held the island; but that the working of it, the right to plant and reap and pass to a child what a family's own hands had made fruitful, remained with those who had in fact done that working, on the same terms, in substance, as before, saving only that any due the Crown chose to lay on such ground in future would be laid on the Dunlops as on any other holder, and not excused them for the paper's age.

The room heard the same reasoning, in close to the same words, given over the Shaw title, the Bell title, the two Tullochs' adjoining strips that had once been one farm and were divided now between cousins who had not spoken to each other, by the account of the maor's clerk, in some years, and over nine more besides, each family's elder standing where the Dunlop woman had stood and hearing, in the end, that the ground was the Crown's and the working of it theirs, a form of words that satisfied, by Eilidh's own later account to Hale that same night, no one entirely and left, so far as she could tell from the faces before the bench, few of the fifteen actually surprised.

## III. Of the Two Found for the Holders

It was the sixteenth of the seventeen, the Coombe title, that broke the pattern the room had by then settled into as firmly as the heat, and it broke it on a detail so small that Murchadh, reading the title over Eilidh's shoulder as she held it to the light, at first took it for a stain and not a mark at all.

In the margin of the Coombe grant, below the human magistrate's seal and dated some years after it, stood a second mark, a small pressed sigil Eilidh recognised before Murchadh did, having seen its like on older custody-books than any human title could carry: the countersign of a custodian, one of the old land-keeping houses that had held certain duties over the ground of the island since long before the humans came and had gone on, through all the years of the crossing, quietly witnessing such transfers of holding as came to their notice, without troubling to ask any human magistrate's leave to do it and without, so far as the record showed, being asked to stop. She asked the Coombes, an elderly man and his grown daughter who together made up the whole of the family now living, whether they knew what the mark was, and the old man said only that his own father had always called it the old blessing, and had told him once that a custodian had come to witness the grant because the ground touched, at one corner, a spring the custodian's own house had kept an interest in since before any human ever cut a title for it, and that his father had thought no more of the matter than a man thinks of a blessing said over a doorway, a thing done because it was always done and not because anyone expected it to matter.

Eilidh sat with the title a long while before she spoke again, turning it so the countersign caught the light at a different angle, and told the room, when she did speak, that the mark changed the ground she stood on to give her ruling, though not, she was careful to say, because a custodian's blessing carried any authority over Crown land that a justice's own bench was bound to defer to; it changed the ground because the mark was proof, of a kind no human seal alone could give her, that the grant had been witnessed and allowed, at the time it was made, by an office of the island's own older law, an office that had never answered to the humans and had gone on, unbroken, into the kingdom that now sat in judgment over its work. A title granted by human authority alone, she said, passed with that authority when the authority ended. A title witnessed also by an office of the island's own keeping, an office that had not ended and did not answer to the Crown for the witnessing it had done, stood on ground the crossing's closing had never touched at all, and she would not now reach past that ground to take back what the Crown's own predecessor, in a manner of speaking, had already let stand.

She found for the Coombes entire, ground and working both, and the room's held breath broke, for the first time that week, into an audible sound, not quite a cheer, that she let run its short course before calling the next cause. The seventeenth suit, the Pettifer title, carried the same custodian's mark in nearly the same place, a witnessing some years later by a different hand of the same office, and Eilidh, having found her reasoning once, applied it a second time with rather less deliberation than the first, though she read the Pettifer title through as slowly as she had read every other, a suitor's paper being no less deserving of a full reading for coming sixteenth or seventeenth than for coming first.

Fifteen for the Crown, then, and two for the holders, and Griogair mac Ailein, watching from the back of the room where he had stood through the whole of the two days the seventeen had taken, said to Murchadh afterward, while the room emptied and the light through the west window had gone from white to gold, that he had sat under three magistrates and now two justices in his eleven years as maor and had never once seen a room learn, over the course of a single sitting, to stop guessing the ending before it came.

## IV. Of the Witness Heard

The grey-haired man in the old-fashioned coat had stood at the back through the first fourteen of the seventeen without speaking, and it was over the Tulloch causes, the two cousins' adjoining strips, that Eilidh first called on him, having noticed, by the fourth day of the sitting, that he was consulted in a low voice by nearly every family before its own cause was called, in the manner of a man whose word on such matters the town trusted a good deal further than it trusted its own memory.

"You have no standing before this bench," she told him, when he came forward at her word, "and I will not hear you as counsel for either side. But I understand you have kept the Moot's own accounts of northern land for some years, and I will hear you as a witness to the facts, if the families before me have no objection to it." Neither cousin objected, both having in fact sent for him themselves before the sitting opened, and Walter Hale, standing where the bench's clerk pointed him and turning his old-fashioned hat once in his hands before he set it down, told the court, in the plain unornamented sentences Ellen had long since stopped expecting him to shorten, what the Moot's own day-books showed of the ground in question: that the original Tulloch grant had been one farm and not two, that the division between the cousins had been made by their fathers in the Moot's third year and recorded nowhere but in a Moot minute of that year, the Moot having kept, since its own first winter, a habit of writing down such family arrangements precisely because no other body troubled to, and that the minute, which he had brought with him, gave the boundary the two cousins were now disputing in terms plain enough that a surveyor's cord could settle the rest in an afternoon.

Eilidh took the minute, read it as she had read every title that week, and asked him one question only, which was whether the Moot's habit of recording such arrangements was a general one or a thing done only where a dispute was already foreseen. General, Hale told her; the Moot had begun writing down family divisions of land in its very first year, at Walter Hale's own suggestion though he did not say so himself, on the reasoning, as old as the Moot's first minute-book, that a people with no deeds of their own to a magistrate's satisfaction had better at least agree, in writing, among themselves, since no one else was likely to trouble to keep the peace of it for them.

She found for the cousins jointly, confirming the division the Moot's minute recorded and no other, and told the room, closing that cause, that a body with no authority the Crown recognised had nonetheless kept a better record of the ground in question than any office the Crown did recognise, and that she saw no reason a justice's bench should refuse a fact merely because the hand that had written it down held no seal. It was, by Griogair mac Ailein's later account, the only moment of the whole sitting at which the room seemed to him to hold its breath for a different reason than heat or suspense, a number of those present having spent some years assuming that a court of the Crown's own making would never trouble to notice, let alone credit, anything the Moot had ever written.

Hale did not speak again before the bench that week, the remaining causes needing no witness he could give, but he stayed through every one of them, standing at the back in the place the grey-haired man in the old coat had occupied since the first morning, and it was there, at the close of the last cause on the Friday, that Eilidh, gathering her papers while Murchadh saw to the fair copies, found him still standing, and asked him, since he seemed in no hurry to leave, whether he would take supper with her at the inn before the road took him back to Caol mhòr.

## V. Of the Inn at Ceann mhòr

The inn stood two streets back from the harbour, far enough from the fish-yards that the evening air, once the day's heat had begun at last to break, carried more of woodsmoke than of tar, and Eilidh took the table nearest the empty hearth, it being too warm a night for a fire but the quietest table in the room. Hale sat across from her with the particular stiffness of a man unused to being asked to a justice's own table, and it was some while, over bread and a dish of the harbour's own fish that neither of them had ordered by name and both ate readily, before either spoke of the week just past.

"Fifteen and two," Hale said at last, turning his cup a half-turn on the table without drinking from it. "I have heard the number said in the yard outside a dozen times since Tuesday, as though it were a kind of arithmetic a man could work out for himself given time enough. Fifteen for the Crown and two for the holders, and every family in that room knowing, before you opened your mouth on their own cause, near enough what the answer would be."

"They knew the shape of it," Eilidh said, "because I gave them the shape of it seven years ago, at Seann Bhral, and have not since found cause to give them a different one. I do not think a family is owed a kinder ruling merely because the same ruling, given often enough, has begun to feel to them like a wall rather than a law. It is the same wall, whether they meet it the first time or the fifteenth."

"I know it," Hale said. "I have written it down myself, more than once, for the Moot's own book, in words a good deal less careful than yours. What I have never quite settled with myself is whether a law can be exact and just at once, when the two families it found in favour of won for a reason that had nothing to do with the land they'd worked or the years they'd worked it, and everything to do with a mark neither of them had troubled to notice on their own paper until a justice's eye found it for them. The Coombes did not earn that mark. Their grandfather happened to have a spring on his ground that a custodian's house had an old interest in. Fifteen other families worked their ground exactly as hard, exactly as long, and had no such spring, and lost."

Eilidh set down her own cup and looked at him a long moment before she answered, in the manner Murchadh had come, over seven years, to recognise as the look she gave a question she judged worth a full answer rather than a short one. "You are asking me whether the law is fair," she said, "and I have never claimed that it is, only that it is exact, which is a different thing and, I have come to believe, the more useful one of the two to a people who must live under a law made, in the first place, for someone else's convenience and not their own. I did not write the Leòid ruling to be fair to the Tuathaich, Mr. Hale, whatever a fair reading of it may have done for two families out of seventeen by an accident of a spring and a custodian's old habit. I wrote it because a rule that changed from bench to bench, from year to year, from whichever justice happened to be riding through, was no rule at all, only eleven separate guesses in the same coat, and I judged, seven years ago, that even a hard exact rule, known in advance and held to without favour, was less cruel in the end than a kind one nobody could rely on from one assize to the next. I have not changed that judgment sitting in this room tonight, and I do not expect to change it before I die. But I will tell you what I have not told the maor, nor Murchadh, nor the council's own chests where my rulings are filed: I know exactly whom the rule was made for, and it was not made for the Coombes, nor the Pettifers, nor the fifteen who came before them. It was made to let a Crown that had just taken an island back from a people who could no longer defend it go on taking, in good order and without argument, what it had already decided to take. I made it exact so that the taking, at least, would be plainly seen for what it was, by anyone who cared to read a ruling closely enough to see it. Whether that is a kindness to the fifteen or only a kind of honesty that costs them exactly as much as a dishonest ruling would have, I have turned over more nights than this one, and I have not settled it yet, and I do not think I will."

Hale did not answer at once, turning his own cup a further half-turn, and when he spoke again it was to say only that he had not expected so plain an answer, and had asked, if he was honest, half hoping for a shorter and more comfortable one. "I did not come to Ceann mhòr for a comfortable answer," Eilidh said, "and I do not think you rode a day to hear one either, Mr. Hale, whatever you may have told your wife you were riding for." She allowed herself, for the first time that evening, something that Murchadh, had he been at the table, would have called nearly a smile, and added that the Moot's own habit of writing down every family's arrangement in plain words, a habit she had heard tell of before that week and seen proved to her own satisfaction in the Tulloch cause, was the nearest thing to her own trade she had met with outside a bench in seven years of riding, and that she did not think it beneath a circuit justice to say so to the man who had begun the habit.

They spoke on a while longer, of lesser things, the state of the coast road north of Àth leathan and the price fish was fetching that season at the Ceann mhòr quay, and parted at the inn's door with the plain courtesy of two people who had said, between them, rather more than either had expected to say and neither found cause to be sorry for it. Hale rode north for Caol mhòr the next morning before the assize house was properly awake. Eilidh, with Murchadh and the satchel of fair copies behind her, rode south.

## VI. Of the Road Home and the Book

The road from Ceann mhòr ran by Àth leathan, where the coast track from the harbour joined the old inland way, and Eilidh broke the first day's riding there, at an inn she had stopped at on her way north, remarking to Murchadh over supper that the innkeeper's memory for a justice's habits had grown, over the years, considerably more reliable than her own for the innkeeper's name. From Àth leathan she rode on by the western road to Seann Bhral, where the Leòid ruling itself had first been given seven years before at a bench she had not sat at since, and stood a while, before the light failed, at the harbour wall looking out at the water the ruling had, in its way, been made beside, though she said nothing to Murchadh of what she thought there, if she thought anything beyond the plain fact of having ridden her circuits nine summers now and being tired, that autumn, in a way the eight earlier summers had not left her. The way south from Seann Bhral was longer than either of the two stretches before it, and slower, the road turning inland for the better part of two days before it met the coast again above the fishing villages that fed Cathair dhomhain's own market, and it was on that inland stretch, riding through a country of low stone-walled fields she had ridden a dozen times before without troubling to remark on it, that she told Murchadh, more as a fact worth recording than as a complaint, that she did not think she would ride the Ceann mhòr road again the following summer, whatever the council's rota said, a season's riding at nine-and-fifty being, she judged, a different arithmetic from a season's riding at one-and-fifty, however little the distance itself had changed between the two.

She reached Cathair dhomhain a little after the turning of the year, in am Faoilleach, and took to her own house on the harbour side of the town with a cough she told Murchadh was nothing worse than the road's dust and a season's riding, and for some weeks it seemed, even to Murchadh, to be exactly that. She kept up the fair copies of the Ceann mhòr rulings through the winter, sending one set to the council's chests at Cathair dhearg and a second, at her own instruction as always, to every maor's court of her circuit, with the note in her own hand that had gone out after every ruling of hers for seven years, that any cause brought on a like title should be decided on the like reasoning until the council itself said otherwise. That same winter she wrote a longer paper than any single ruling required, gathering into one book the whole of what she had held over nine years of riding, the Seann Bhral ruling first and the Ceann mhòr sitting last, with every lesser cause between them that had turned on the same ground, so that a justice coming after her, she told Murchadh while he copied the fair pages by the lamp, would not have to ride to Cathair dhearg and dig through nine years of the council's own chests to learn what she herself already knew by heart.

The cough did not lift with the turning of am Faoilleach into an Gearran, and by am Màrt she had taken, for the first time in Murchadh's seven years beside her, to keeping her bed past the morning, dictating the last pages of the gathered book to him from a chair by the window rather than sitting at her own table to write them. She did not speak, in those weeks, of being ill, only of the work still wanting finishing, and Murchadh, who had learned long since which of her silences asked to be pressed and which did not, did not press this one. The book was finished, in substance, by the middle of am Màrt, needing only its final binding, and Eilidh, hearing from the physician who attended her by then that the winter had settled somewhere in her chest that a summer's warmth might yet clear, told Murchadh plainly that she did not think she would see the clearing, and asked him to send word north, before the roads grew too soft for a rider, to Uilleam mac Leòid, her brother's son, a young man of six-and-twenty who had ridden with her twice as a boy and had, she told Murchadh, more patience for the northern circuit's particular slowness than any other of the family she could call to mind.

She died at Cathair dhomhain, 2 an Giblean, SE 16, in her own house within sound of the harbour she had grown up beside, with Murchadh at her bedside and the finished book, still unbound, on the table beside her. She had not lived to be sixty.

The gathered book was bound within the month, in plain calf over boards, at the council's own expense and by the council's own binder, and given the name Eilidh had herself suggested to Murchadh in one of her last clear mornings, Leabhar nam Breith, the plain word for what it held and nothing grander. Uilleam mac Leòid, named to the northern circuit before Bealltainn, rode north for his first assize with the book strapped, as the satchel of blank record-books had once been strapped, behind his own clerk's saddle rather than his, on the grounds, he told the young man riding beside him, that a justice ought to arrive at her first assize with clean hands, an instruction he had had, he said, from an aunt who never in her life explained a rule twice when the first explanation had been exact enough to serve. Every circuit justice who rode after him carried a copy of the same book, and the reasoning it set down, fifteen for the Crown and two for the holders and the whole long working that had brought her to that number, went on being read out, in courtroom after courtroom of the northern circuit, in words that were, for the most part, very nearly her own.

# Chapter Sixteen: Of the Cellar at Muileann chaol

*SE 16 an Cèitean – SE 17 an Lùnastal*

> *A chur san Leabharlann.*
> To put it in the Library.
> — the saying that grew up around Ailean Leabhar's cellar, within a few years of its opening

## I. Of the Cellar Under the Stair

They lit the Bealltainn fires on the hills round Muileann chaol on the first day of an Cèitean in SE 16, as they were lit on every hill on the island that had a hill to light them on, and the smoke of the whole ring hung over the town from noon until the fires were let go down at dusk, so that a man walking in from the coast road that morning might have taken the haze for weather and thought no more of it. Ailean mac Iain took it for weather himself, riding in with two carts behind him and the council's minute-books roped down under oiled sacking against a rain that had not yet come and, by the smell of the sky, meant to. He had been the better part of a week on the road out of Cathair dhearg, the carts slow on the eastern stretches where the humans' old causeway had broken up into ruts deep enough to swallow a wheel, and he had spent most of that week turning over, without managing to settle it, the single sentence in which the council had told him what he was for.

The sentence, copied into his own book from the clerk who had read it to him, ran: *Ailean mac Iain is named keeper of the record at Muileann chaol, to receive, to order, and to keep whatever is sent to him.* It did not say what a keeper was, there being no such office before it and no one living who had held one, and it did not say what "whatever is sent" might in the end amount to. The council knew, at least, where its own records were not: not burned, so far as anyone could say, and not lost past finding. No one at Cathair dhearg could name the room any of them stood in, or say when a living hand had last opened one. Ailean had asked, before he left Cathair dhearg, what the town of Muileann chaol held that made it the place chosen, and had been told only that the custodians of the district had kept rolls there since before the Severance, in cellars under the old grain-stores, and that nobody at Cathair dhearg had gone to look at them in living memory. He took the answer as a piece of the council's habit rather than as information, the council's habit being, by sixteen years' watching, to send a thing north or west or wherever its own hands did not reach and call the sending a settlement.

The town gave him a house that had stood empty since a mercer's family died of a fever six winters before, two rooms and a loft over what had been a shop, and a boy of the town, thirteen that spring, whose mother kept the house next door and who had, in the way of a boy with nothing yet fixed to do, attached himself to the carts within an hour of their arrival on the plain grounds that they were the most interesting thing to have come up the road since the tax-rider's horse went lame outside the mill two winters back. His name was Coinneach Clàrc, son of a wright who had died in the war before the Severance and left his widow a trade in nothing but the boy's own two hands, which she hired out, that spring, for whatever a household could spare, mostly carrying and fetching. Ailean, unpacking the first cart in a light that was already going by the time he reached the third sack, told the boy he could fetch and carry for a keeper as easily as for a mercer's widow, and the boy, who had not until that hour known that a keeper was a thing a town could have, said he would, and was there the next morning before Ailean himself was dressed.

It was the townsmen, not the council's letter, who led him to the cellar. Two of them came the second evening, a maltster and a man who had held some half-remembered custodian's office under his father before him, and said, in the flat courteous way of men who have carried a thing a long time and are glad to be shot of the carrying, that there was more under the old grain-store than grain, and that it had been theirs to mind since before either of them was born, and that they had minded it as well as damp stone and a low door would let two men mind anything. They took him down a stair cut into the hillside, worn hollow in the middle of each step by more feet than either of the two men now living had climbed it, and at the bottom, by the light of a single lamp one of them carried, Ailean saw what sixteen years of a kingdom too busy settling its own affairs to look backward had left of the record of everything that came before it: rolls and bound books stacked on planks laid across trestles above a floor that stood an inch deep in water after any rain heavier than a mist, the lowest tier on every stack gone soft, and in places gone to a grey pulp that held, when he touched it, the shape of a roll without any longer holding a roll's substance.

He untied the nearest and read three lines of it by the light thrown down the stair from the doorway above, standing because there was nowhere dry to sit, and then he sent the maltster's boy running for every lamp the house next door could spare, and sent Coinneach for a table, any table, and for a stool, and for whatever oil the town could sell him before its shops shut for the night. He did not go up again himself until the small hours, by which time he had four lamps burning on a borrowed table set on two trestles of its own above the wet floor, and had read, by his own later count, some forty rolls through to their ends without once finding one that told him plainly what it was, most of the custodians' own hands having written for readers who already knew.

## II. Of the Long Reading

It took him years. The council's own minute-books came east from Cathair dhearg that same summer, four sacks of them roped onto the backs of packhorses because no cart could be spared for so light and so unregarded a cargo, and behind them, more slowly, came the boxes Ailean himself had labelled and sealed in the humans' counting-houses fourteen years before, the tithe ledgers charred at their edges and written in a hand few south of the guard-line could any longer read without a Mission reader's schooling behind them, which Ailean, alone among the clerks who had boxed them, still had. He set the boy Coinneach to learning that hand within the first winter, on the plain reasoning that a keeper who read alone would die a keeper who had kept nothing for anyone after him, and by the second winter the boy could make out a tithe entry as fast as Ailean himself, faster in a bad light, his eyes being younger.

Their days, that first year and most of the second, ran the same small round with almost no variation to mark one from the next: down the worn stair before the town's own shops were open, lamps lit and trimmed, the wet floor swept as dry as a broom could make it, and then the reading, roll after roll set out on the borrowed table and read through to whatever end it had, the findings copied into a working book Ailean kept for nothing else and the roll returned, once read, to a shelf built dry above the water-line that the town's own carpenter had raised for him that first autumn on nothing more than Ailean's own promise to settle with him out of whatever the council next sent north. There were weeks together in which nothing was found worth remarking to anyone, a roll of tithes yielding tithes and no more, and Coinneach, young enough still to want a story out of every hour he gave to the work, asked more than once whether it was always to be like this. Ailean told him, more than once, that it mostly was, and that a keeper who wanted a story every day had mistaken his trade for a teller's.

What the cellar and the sacks between them held was, in the main, numbers: heads counted, grain weighed, dues paid or owed, births and deaths noted in the clipped hand of men keeping accounts rather than telling tales, and dates given in a reckoning that named no month and no season a reader south of the mountains would know at a glance, an old count that ran backward into the thousands for anything older than what the custodians called, without ever troubling to explain to whom, the sunwise turn. Ailean had disliked that count from the first roll he untied, and disliked it more with every year he spent inside it, and said so to Coinneach often enough that the boy could by the second year finish the complaint for him before he had got three words into it: that a people should not have to name every year of its own life after the day its kin went away over the water, as though nothing since had been worth a name of its own.

So he set the copyists he by then had, four of them by SE 16's end and seven by SE 17, to a plain and unglamorous labour that took the better part of two years to reach even the near edge of finished: every date the cellar or the sacks held, turned into the civil calendar the humans had themselves brought and the kingdom had kept since the Severance, month and day exact where the roll gave them exact, season and year alone where it gave no more, and set besides into the years of an age, by a table of the ages the copyists themselves were building as they went, out of the customary tellings of Clann na Ceiste laid side by side against the king-lists the custodians' rolls preserved better than any book south of the mountains had preserved them. It was in the laying of those two records side by side, in the second winter, that the reckoners under Ailean's own hand found what neither telling alone would have shown them: that very nearly half of the whole eldest age the copyists had inherited from the custodians' own reckoning lay within the span of one man's life, Ailean Mòr, crowned in the grove and king until he fell at the Ford of Blood, so long a life that no age built to hold ordinary lives could rightly be asked to hold his as well. Ailean set the matter before his copyists on an evening in an Dàmhair, and by consent of all seven the Age of Ailean was parted from the age that had held it and counted from then on as its own, the first change the Library at Muileann chaol made to any reckoning it had not itself invented, and, as Ailean noted drily in the margin of his own working copy, very possibly the last change it would ever be believed to have the standing to make.

It was in that same season, with the copyists' table only half drawn and the cellar not yet a third read, that a clerk of the town, sent up from Cathair dhearg with a query about a boundary the council wanted settled and unable, on being told the matter would want some weeks of reading before it could be answered honestly, to hide his impatience, used a phrase that neither he nor Ailean had heard used in quite that way before: that the boundary, once Ailean had looked into it, could simply be put in the Library, *a chur san Leabharlann*, and the matter would then be settled. Ailean, who had spent two years by then learning exactly how little of what the cellar held could honestly be called settled by anything, corrected him on the spot, more sharply than the clerk's small offence deserved, and the correction, repeated afterward by the clerk himself as a piece of local colour worth carrying home, was what first fixed the phrase in the town's mouth rather than loosening it: within a season half of Muileann chaol was saying *a chur san Leabharlann* of anything it wanted done with, and saying it, more often than not, precisely to see Ailean's face when he heard it. "The Library settles nothing," he told Coinneach more than once, usually with his hand still flat on some roll that had just refused, for the third or fourth time that week, to say plainly what had actually happened in the year it claimed to record. "It only keeps."

## III. Of the Two Books

The finding that turned the first year of the reading came in an Gearran of SE 17, on a roll from the camp rolls of Àth ìseal that Ailean had set aside twice already as too far gone at its lower edge to be worth the candle it would cost to read by. He came back to it a third time only because Coinneach, going through the same stack in search of a grain tally the boy had been asked for by name, noticed a second hand in the margin, cramped and later than the roll's own body, and could not himself make out more than a name before he brought it to Ailean rather than lose the thread of it to guesswork.

The name was Cailean mac Eachainn's, and what he had written, in a margin that had survived the damp better than the roll's own text because it sat higher on the sheet, was a line of descent set down, so far as either Ailean or the boy could judge from the hand and the roll it rode on, some forty years before: the Line of Aisling, name following name in the plain unbroken form a custodian's clerk gives to a thing he expects no one to doubt and no one, until that winter, to read. Ailean had it copied fair within the week, in a hand steadier than the original's had by then become, and entered into a book he had begun the summer before and had not, until that entry, known quite what to call: a book that held nothing but lines of descent, names following names with their dates where dates could be had and without them where they could not, which he settled, after turning over three or four less plain titles with Coinneach on successive evenings, into Leabhar nan Sloinnidhean, the book of lines, and set Cailean mac Eachainn's find in it directly after another line, older still, that the cellar had already yielded that same winter: the Line of the Mason, as the custodians' rolls had taken it down long before from the recital of Clann na Ceiste.

But the camp rolls of Àth ìseal held more than lines. Set apart from the tallies and the descents, in a different ink and by what looked, from its unevenness, to be a hand writing by firelight rather than by day, the same custodian's clerk had also kept a record of what was said round the camp in the long years the roll otherwise measured only in grain and heads: the tale of the Hollow Man, told, by the clerk's own note, by an old woman of the camp who claimed to have had it from her grandmother; a telling of the white stag that differed in three particulars from the version Ailean himself had grown up on in the hills; a boast, set down word for word and plainly relished by whoever had written it down, that a captain of the camp had once made about a wolf and a winter and a door he had held alone. None of it was a line of descent, and none of it, by any measure a custodian's own office would have applied to it, was business a roll ought to have carried at all; and it was that very unfitness, Ailean came to think within the week, that had let it survive at all, tucked in where no later hand thought to look for it and no later flood thought worth the reaching.

He began a second book for it that same season, this one without any argument at all over its name, for the thing wanted no name but the plain one: Leabhar nan Aithrisean, the book of tellings, and the long years of Ailean Mòr and his children went into it beside the Hollow Man and the white stag, exactly as the camp's own clerk had set them down, without correction and without comment.

It was Coinneach who asked him, copying the second entry out fair one evening by a lamp that wanted trimming, which of the two books was the true one, the lines or the tellings, since a boy who had spent a winter learning that a roll's numbers were to be trusted and its margins were not could be forgiven for wanting the question settled before he copied any further. Ailean thought about it longer than the boy expected, long enough that Coinneach had trimmed the lamp and sat back down before the answer came.

"Both," he said. "The one keeps names. The other keeps what people said." He looked at the two books a while longer, the one thin still and orderly, the other already thicker and less so, and added, in a voice Coinneach did not at the time think to write down and regretted for years after that he had not: "Neither of them keeps what happened. Nothing we do here will ever keep that. We only keep what was set down, and set down again, as carefully as two men and a lamp can manage it."

## IV. Of the First Readers

Word that there was a Library to be read at, and not merely a cellar to be minded, spread up and down the coast roads slower than either man would have guessed, the notion of a place a man might go and be shown a record concerning his own trade or his own town being, for most who heard of it that first year, too far outside anything they had reason to expect of the kingdom's offices to be believed on a single telling. Ailean had opened the reading room, such as it was, to any who could show a letter from a shire maor vouching for their errand, on the plain grounds that a Library nobody could reach was no better kept than a cellar nobody could reach, and for the better part of a year the room he had set aside for it, a dry chamber above the old cellar with two tables and a window that at least let in more light than the stair had, stood empty of anyone but his own copyists.

The first name written in the book he kept for the purpose was a shipwright of Ros dhomhain, come the length of the coast road with a maor's letter creased soft from the carrying and a question that had, by his own account, kept him up more nights than the debt he had incurred to fund the asking of it: whether the humans, in whatever they had left behind them, had ever set down the true lines of a hull, the shape of the thing before it was built and not merely the finished boats a man could measure with his own eye and his own guesswork, which was, he said, standing in the doorway with his hat still in both hands as though the room might object to a covered head, most of what a shipwright of his own generation had ever had to work from. Ailean, who had boxed the humans' papers himself fourteen years before and drawn the shires on their surveys, had never in all that time had cause to open the crates of loose sheets marked, in his own hand, *unread*, and spent the better part of a week with the man going through sheets neither of them had ever seen unrolled, and found, folded inside a survey that had nothing else to do with ships at all, three drawings of a hull's ribs and planking that the shipwright copied out, over four days, onto his own paper with a care Ailean thought, watching him, came nearer to devotion than to any trade he had a name for. On the last of the four days the man asked, not looking up from his copying, whether the Library meant to keep a copy of his copy too, so that the next shipwright need not spend four days over it; Ailean said it would, and set aside a shelf for it there and then, the first shelf in the room he had built for anything but the record he had brought with him. The shipwright signed the reading-book in a hand that gave the letters of his own name more trouble than the hull-lines had, and walked back to Ros dhomhain, by his own account afterward, three days faster than he had come.

The bath-house at the warm springs below Muileann ruadh, built that same year by the Guild of Hewers out of its own funds for the men the pits had made sick with the dust, sent a fair copy of its first sick-roll to the Library unasked, in the autumn, a list of four hundred men set down by name and by the shift that had broken them, with no letter of explanation beyond a note in the guild clerk's own hand that a record of who had been sick, and of which face of which pit, seemed to the guild's officers a thing worth having somewhere it would not be lost, whatever use the kingdom's own offices chose or failed to choose to make of it. Ailean entered it in a shelf of its own, unsure for some weeks what book it properly belonged in and settling at last, on Coinneach's own suggestion, that a roll which named no line of descent and told no old tale and yet meant, plainly, to be kept, had as much claim on the Library as either.

It was the guild's roll, more than the shipwright's question, that first showed Ailean what the room above the cellar might in time become, a room read not only by clerks sent on the council's own errands but by men and women who came, letter in hand, on errands the council had never thought to ask after, and who left, when they had found what they came for, entries of their own devising for a keeper too glad of the reading to turn any of them away.

## V. Of the Five Lights

The last matter the Library took in hand that summer came to it from the council, by a warrant Ailean received in an Lùnastal and read twice before he was satisfied he had understood it rightly: the five lighthouses the humans had built round the island's coasts, kept until then by whatever hands the district happened to have to spare, were to be given keepers of the kingdom's own naming, Dia-thìreach men chosen and sworn, each bound by a warrant Ailean was asked to draft in a form the council could copy five times over without further trouble to its own clerks.

He drafted four of the warrants in an afternoon, each near enough the last that a clerk copying them side by side would have struggled to say, by sundown, which words belonged to which coast. The fifth gave him more trouble than the other four together, for the fifth light stood at Baile chrom, on the Tuathaich coast, and the man the council had chosen for it, a quiet Dia-thìreach who had kept lights before on the southern capes and asked for the northern posting himself, for reasons he gave the council as nothing more than a liking for a quieter coast than his last, would be a Dia-thìreach man living alone among a people whose speech he did not have and whose town watched him, by every account Ailean had been able to gather, the way a fishing town watches any stranger the kingdom sends to stand over it.

Ailean wrote the warrant plainly, in the same clipped form the other four had taken, save for one clause he added on his own authority and did not ask the council to approve before the warrant was sealed and sent: that the keeper at Baile chrom should set down, in his season's returns, whatever he saw by land as well as whatever he saw by sea, whatever that might in time prove to be. He gave the clause no explanation in the warrant, and offered none when Coinneach, reading the fair copy before it went south for sealing, asked him plainly why a lighthouse keeper's business should reach past the tideline at all. "Because he will see things the shire's own maor will not think to ask him about," Ailean said, "and a Library that only ever hears what a maor thinks worth reporting will end its days knowing a good deal less than it might have."

The five warrants went out together at the season's turn, and the five lamps were lit within the month, the other four to no comment Ailean ever heard of, the fifth to a silence from Baile chrom that he took, that first autumn, for nothing more than a stranger settling quietly into a strange town.

He stood that evening at the window of the reading room above the cellar, the two books of the Library, the lines and the tellings, set closed on the table behind him and the guild's sick-roll beside them, and watched, though he could see none of the five lights themselves from Muileann chaol, the last of the season's light go off the hills where the Bealltainn fires had burned a year and more before. Coinneach, trimming the lamps for the night, asked him, as the boy had taken to asking most evenings by then, whether the day's reading had settled anything. Ailean did not answer at once. He thought of the cellar as he had first seen it, the lowest rolls gone soft as bread, and of the two books now standing where the cellar's ruin had once stood alone, and of a shipwright's four days over another man's plans, and of a fifth light burning that night over a coast that had never yet had reason to trust a light the kingdom sent it.

"No," he said at last. "But it's kept. That will have to do."

He blew out the last lamp himself, and left the boy to lock the door.

# Chapter Seventeen: Of the Table of the Ages

*SE 17 an Dàmhair – SE 19 an Cèitean*

> A record kept beside the throne is kept for the throne.
>
> — Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill, the chronicle's first entry, 19 an Dùbhlachd, SE 18

## I. Of the Errand to Muileann chaol

The council sent Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill east in an Dàmhair of SE 17 for no better reason, so far as she was ever told, than that somebody had to go and see what the keeper at Muileann chaol had been doing with the year and more and the two cartloads of minute-books the council had given him, and that she was the under-clerk with the fewest causes on her own desk that month. She was four-and-forty that autumn, a council clerk's daughter who had herself clerked at Cathair dhearg for fifteen years without once being sent further than Cnoc ghorm, and she took the errand, by her own later account, as a week's dull riding and a report nobody above her would trouble to read past its first line.

She reached Muileann chaol on the fourth day, the road east of the mountain gone soft with an autumn's rain and the last stretch, past Tobar dhìreach, thick with the smell of wet paper before she had so much as seen the mill that made it. The town surprised her before she had dismounted: a place she had known on the council's own rolls as a huddle of a few hundred souls round a grain-store had grown, in the year and more since Ailean mac Iain rode in with his carts, a second street of low workshops she had not been told to expect, awl and needle over one door for the binders, a quill over another for the copyists, and at the end of the street a yard she took at first for a fair-ground until a woman selling combs out of a basket told her, when she asked, that it was market day, the second since the charter came through, and that the yard belonged to the Library, which let it be used for nothing grander than a fee paid to the keeper's boy.

Ailean mac Iain met her at the Library's own door with ink on two fingers of his right hand and no apology for it, and took her account of her errand, to see and report and nothing more, with the particular patience of a man who had given the same tour to three lesser clerks already that year and expected to give it to a fourth before winter. "You will want to see the cellar first," he told her, "since it is the part every clerk from the capital asks after, and the part least worth the asking, being empty," and led her down the same stair he had gone down a year and a half before, the racks that had once held the district's soft and ruined rolls standing bare now and swept, the water that had stood on the floor drained off through a channel he had had cut that first summer. She asked him, on the stair, whether he missed the wet cellar he described in his own reports so often, and he said only that a keeper who missed a ruin had kept his post for the wrong reason, and said nothing further on the matter the whole three days she stayed.

He showed her next the two rooms above the cellar, where the custodians' rolls of every shire lay sorted by a system of his own devising, boxes lettered by district and shelved by a rule she asked him twice to explain and did not, by the time she left, wholly master either; he told her, when she said as much, that the system wanted no mastering by a visitor, only by the two boys who ran it daily, and that a clerk from the capital judging a keeper's order by whether she herself could work it was judging the wrong thing. She let the remark stand without argument, having by then spent enough of the first day in his company to judge that he answered every question either exactly or not at all, and that a third way of answering was not a thing he kept in stock.

He showed her, last, the room where seven copyists sat that afternoon at seven desks, each with a roll unrolled before him and a fresh sheet of the Tobar dhìreach paper beside it, turning the old dates the cellar had yielded into the calendar the humans had themselves brought to the island, a labour he described to her in four plain sentences: what the rolls held, what the calendar wanted, how a date given only by season and no more was marked as such rather than guessed at, and how long, by his own reckoning, the whole labour would take to finish. She wrote it down in five, adding a line of her own about the room's quiet that he had not thought worth mentioning. He mentioned, in the same breath and no louder than the rest, that the seven had lately settled a question of reckoning among themselves that the council had never thought to ask: that the age at the root of every telling on the island held, within it, one life long enough to be counted apart, and that his copyists, by their own consent and nobody's order, had parted it that same season and begun to count it as its own, an evening's work the whole town had talked of for a week afterward and the council, so far as either of them ever heard, had not troubled to hear of at all. The keeper said it the way a man reports a roof mended, not a thing done, and Gormshuil, writing it into her own book that evening by a borrowed lamp in the room the town had found her over the mercer's old shop, found she had underlined it twice without quite deciding to, and sat a while longer than the hour wanted, turning the lamp's wick down and up again, before she blew it out.

A boy of fourteen or so, who told her his name was Coinneach Clàrc before she had thought to ask it, brought her water in the morning and asked, setting the jug down, whether the capital had sent her to take anything away with her, a question he put, she judged from his face, less out of insolence than out of a plain wish to know how much of his own morning's work might shortly be undone. She told him no, only to look and to write what she saw, and he seemed to weigh the answer for its truth a moment before he accepted it and went back to whatever he had been carrying before he stopped to ask.

## II. Of the Report Nobody Above Her Would Read

Before she rode home she walked the market yard once more on her own, without Ailean beside her to name what she was looking at, and found it a smaller and plainer thing than the word market had led her to expect from a capital desk: some thirty stalls set up on trestles between the Library's own wall and the lane, most of them selling nothing grander than thread, nails, candles and the ordinary produce of a district feeding its own new mouths, and only a handful given over to the trade the town's second street had brought it, a binder selling off-cuts of calf too small for a cover, a copyist's wife selling quills her husband had trimmed and did not need. The stall-fee, a woman told her when she stopped to ask it, was a penny a table and two on a fair-day, paid to the keeper's boy in a wooden box he carried on a strap, and the court of the fair, such as it was, amounted to the boy's own mother settling disputes over table-space in a voice loud enough to be heard the length of the yard, a form of justice Gormshuil noted down without comment, setting it beside her own knowledge of grander courts that took longer to settle less.

She wrote her report on the ride home and delivered it, as instructed, to the clerk of council who had sent her, a man named Uilleam mac Griogair who read the first page standing at his own desk, the second sitting, and the third not at all, telling her, when she pressed him on it, that a keeper's cellar and a keeper's calendar were matters for the keeper and not, in his experience, matters the council troubled to weigh twice in one generation. "You have written three pages," he said, setting the sheets down unweighted so that the draught from his own window began at once to lift the corner of the last, "where the council asked for one, and the one it asked for need only have said the cellar is dry and the man is sound." Gormshuil left the third page with him regardless, and a fair copy of it in her own hand besides, on the grounds, she told no one but her own book, that a thing worth writing was worth keeping whether or not the man it was written for meant to open it.

The town had by then, in the ordinary way of these things, already begun to settle what Ailean's cellar had made of it. The market charter Gormshuil had seen in its second week that autumn was no more than the council's usual form, a fee for every stall and a court to hear the fair's own disputes, granted after the district's maor wrote up, at the keeper's own asking, that a town which had drawn copyists, binders and paper-makers to it in a year and a half without any charter at all might as well be given one before the trade found its own rules instead. The mill at Tobar dhìreach, a few miles off along the stream, was being turned that autumn by a family of millers who, for want of grain enough to keep three wheels busy, meant to make paper instead, and the copyists already spoke of its first sheets, due the next year, as though they had them in hand. She had ridden out to see the mill herself on her second day, more from a clerk's habit of wanting to see the thing behind a claim than from any errand that required it, and had found it a low building of two wheels rather than the three the family had first raised money for, the third abandoned half-built when the grain trade that was meant to feed it never came back to the strength the millers had reckoned on; the miller's eldest daughter, showing her the new vats where the rags were to be pulped, told her plainly that paper was the family's one hope against a debt that grain alone would bury them under, and that she for one hoped the Library's keeper never ran short of old rolls to copy, since it was his copying that kept her father's wheels turning at all. Within a year of the mill's first sheets, Ailean noted in a letter, near enough every sheet the Library used came from that one stream, and the council's stationers, so far as either of them ever heard, were not told why their trade had fallen off.

Gormshuil went back to her desk at Cathair dhearg that winter and to fourteen more months of the ordinary clerking that had filled the fifteen years before it, tallies and licences and the council's own minutes fair-copied twice over for a filing system she had never once been asked whether she thought sound, and told herself, when she thought of Muileann chaol at all, that she had seen a keeper's good order and a good cellar and nothing that need trouble her further. She kept, all the same, the fair copy of her own report in the bottom of her own chest rather than the council's files, a habit she could not afterward explain to her own satisfaction and did not, that winter, try very hard to.

## III. Of the Office Made

The council came to its own decision in SE 18, and came to it, by every account Gormshuil was given afterward, for reasons nearer to the coin than to the calendar: a councillor disputing a boundary with his neighbour had sent to the keeper at Muileann chaol for a custodian's roll that settled it inside a fortnight, where the same question, put to the council's own files two years before, had gone unanswered for want of anyone able to say where the relevant paper was kept. The councillor said as much, more than once and to more than one hearing, in the tone of a man who had found a convenience rather than a lesson, and it was that plain tone, Gormshuil came to believe, that did more to move the council than any argument a keeper or a clerk might have made for the value of an ordered record on its own account. A record that could be asked a question and give back an answer was, the council found, worth more to it than one it could only add to, and in the second week of an t-Samhain it made an office to keep the kingdom's whole record as Ailean's Library had begun to keep the north's, and set the office at Muileann chaol rather than at the capital, on the plain ground that the keeper already there had shown he knew how the thing was done, a decision reached, so Uilleam mac Griogair told her afterward without any evident shame in the telling, inside a single sitting and with less debate than the same council had lately given a dispute over a fair's stall-fees.

It named Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill to the office, on the strength of a report three men had read a page of between them and one clerk of council who remembered, when the matter came up, that she had gone to Muileann chaol once and come back with more to say than he had troubled to hear; it was Uilleam mac Griogair himself, by his own later admission, who named her, less from any judgement of her fitness for the work than from a wish to be rid of a clerk who had twice now handed him more paper than he cared to read. She was sworn in a small room at Cathair dhearg on the twentieth of an t-Samhain, four-and-forty still, before a clerk who read the warrant aloud in the same flat voice he read every warrant in, naming her royal chronicler of the kingdom and bidding her keep, in whatever form she judged fit, whatever the kingdom's affairs left behind them worth the keeping. She asked him, when he had finished, whether the warrant said anything of where the record was to be kept, and he told her, looking back down at the page as though the answer might yet be found there, that it did not, the council having spent its attention on the office's naming and its powers and having left the office's own seat, as it left most such questions, for whoever held it to settle for herself. The same warrant ordered that the kingdom's years should thereafter be counted by the ages the Library's own table now held rather than by the old count of the Diosal, six ages as the table then stood, and that her own first year should be entered as the eighteenth of the Severance Era, the first year so written in the kingdom's own record rather than borrowed from an older one; the clerk read that clause too in the same flat voice, and Gormshuil, listening, thought it a strange thing to hear her whole people's way of counting set aside in a single sentence read by a man who plainly did not think the sentence worth pausing over.

She walked back to her own lodging that evening turning the day's two facts over against each other, the office made and its seat left open, and found by the time she reached her own door that the second fact had already answered itself in her mind, whatever the council had meant by its silence. Her reply went out within the week, in a hand she took some trouble over, the letter's second page rewritten twice before she judged the wording exact enough to send: that she meant to keep the record at Muileann chaol, beside the Library that already held the rolls she would need and the copyists trained to the work, and, at its foot, the one line of her own that she afterward let stand at the head of her first year's book, that a record kept beside the throne was kept for the throne, and that a kingdom wanting an honest one would do better to keep it somewhere the throne's own convenience did not reach. She showed the letter to no one before she sent it, on a plain reckoning, rather than any wish for secrecy, that a line worth writing was not, in her experience, a line improved by another clerk's opinion of it beforehand. No one at the council troubled to argue the point with her, whether from agreement or from the same weariness that had let her first report go three pages unread, and she took the silence, that winter, for consent, and moved her whole desk east before the roads closed, carrying with her four chests of her own papers, a clerk's stool she had sat at for sixteen years and saw no reason to leave behind, and a single letter of introduction to Ailean mac Iain that she judged, on the ride out, she need not have troubled to write, since the keeper had already shown her, a year before, exactly how much introducing he required.

## IV. Of the First Circuit

She spent the winter before the circuit rode out in the plainer labour the office wanted before any clerk could be sent anywhere: a warrant drafted and copied six times over, one for each pair she meant to send, asking every parish, custodian and harbour-master on the island to open whatever books it kept and let a page of each be copied into the kingdom's own record, and asking nothing be given up that its own keeper wished to hold on to, a clause she added herself, over Ailean's mild objection that a clause inviting refusal was a strange thing for a chronicler to write into her own first warrant. "A clause that only invites what a keeper would do regardless costs the warrant nothing," she told him, "and a keeper who reads it will trust the rest of the page a good deal further for it," and left the clause standing when the six copies went out.

She sent her clerks in three pairs in the spring of SE 19, one south, one to the eastern shires nearer the mountain, and one north past Cnoc ghorm to the Tuathaich coast, each pair carrying its own warrant and its own chest to fill. Among the six rode a clerk of three-and-thirty named Tormod mac Sheumais, called already, by the other copyists, Tormod Pinn for the speed of his own hand, a council under-clerk's son who had asked Gormshuil for the circuit himself rather than wait to be sent, saying, when she asked him why, only that a man who copied other men's records all winter without once seeing where they came from was, in his own judgement, only half a clerk. She sent him north rather than south, on the reasoning she gave Ailean and no one else, that a clerk keen enough to ask for the harder half of the work deserved to be given it, and kept, of that first spring's riding, a private tally of his own that he showed no one for years afterward: the number of doors that opened to him without a second knock, against the number that did not.

The south filled its share within the season, its own habits of record already near enough to the kingdom's own that the asking cost the pair sent there little beyond the road's own length. Forty chests came up to Muileann chaol before an t-Iuchar was out, grave-lists and harbour rolls and parish registers from every shire between Cathair dhearg and the southern coast, and among them, copied whole into a book of its own because no clerk on the circuit could say what else to call it, the town arms of every town that had ever cut a seal for itself: five hundred and five of them by the time the last chest was opened, a hammer over a fleece, a shuttle over a flame, a hawk among crescents, set down side by side in an order that owed nothing to rank and everything to the order the chests themselves happened to arrive in. Coinneach Clàrc, set to the copying of that book himself, asked Gormshuil once whether she meant the arms sorted by shire before the book went to the binder, and she told him no, and told him why only once he pressed her a second time: that a record which tidied its own arrival too soon forgot, in a generation, that the arrival had ever been untidy at all, and that a reader coming after them both would learn more of the season's own haste from five hundred and five seals in the order they happened to reach her than from the same five hundred and five set out by rank as though the whole kingdom's making had been a tidy thing from the first.

The north filled one chest, and filled it slowly.

## V. Of the Door at Doire ghlas

Tormod's own pair rode the northern circuit that same spring, up past Doire ghlas where Agnes Pike's schoolroom had by then taught its fifth winter of scholars, and were met at the mill agent's door, and at the mill, and at the two chapels the town kept between them, by an answer near enough the same in every house: that the town's books, such as they were, belonged to the town, and that a clerk riding up from the south with a warrant in the kingdom's name was, whatever the warrant said about nothing being asked to be given up, not a man the town saw any profit in trusting with even a page of them. He read the clause about nothing being taken aloud at the mill agent's own counter, word for word as Gormshuil had drafted it, and the agent, a Tuathaich man some ten years settled in the post, heard him out to the end before he answered that a clause a warrant carried against its own asking was, in his own experience of warrants, worth exactly as much as the hand that had signed it chose to make it worth, and that he for one had no way of knowing, standing at his own counter, whether the hand behind this one meant to keep its word a year from now or merely to get a page copied today.

Tormod's tally that week ran to eleven doors closed against one opened, the one being that same mill ledger, and the agent let him copy it only after making him read the warrant through twice aloud in the street outside, in front of witnesses enough that no one afterward could say he had been tricked into it, and only after Tormod had agreed, on his own authority and without any leave from Gormshuil to give it, that the copy would carry the agent's own name beside it as the man who had chosen to show it, rather than stand in the record as a thing simply found. He wrote to Gormshuil that night, by a poor light in the room the town had grudged him, that the town's own silence was not, so far as he could judge, unkindness so much as memory: that a people who had watched the council take their savings once already in the coin it minted saw no reason to trust it with their parish books either, whatever form the asking came dressed in, and that he had, without waiting to ask her, promised the mill agent his own name kept beside the ledger's copy, a promise he hoped she would let stand even though no clause in her warrant had asked for it.

Gormshuil, reading his letter at her own desk at Muileann chaol some days later, wrote back that the promise would stand, and stand in whatever hand of hers the record wanted to make it plain the promise was kept and not merely made; and she added his own words about memory rather than unkindness to the same book she had begun with her own line about the throne, letting them stand there unaltered, on the ground that a chronicler who mended what her own clerks reported was no better than a council that only ever heard what it wished to. She wrote nothing beneath his words to soften them, and nothing to explain to a later reader why a warrant so carefully worded against taking anything away should still have closed eleven of the town's twelve doors against it.

## VI. Of the Chest from Inis bheag

The last of the circuit's letters that spring came from Inis bheag, in the island's north-east, where the two clerks sent there had been shown, by the keeper of the Seann Spioradan house that stood at the parish's heart, a book older than any the south's forty chests had yielded between them: a parish roll that named its own dead and its own harvests back past the coming of the humans, kept, the keeper told them, by his own house's keepers before him in an unbroken line he did not trouble to number for two clerks he had known a single afternoon. He was an old man by the clerks' own account, near enough as old as the Library's own cellar had been wet, and he heard the warrant read to him the once, without asking for it twice as the mill agent at Doire ghlas had, and answered only that he had kept the book, and his father before him, against exactly this asking, and saw no reason a kingdom's own warrant should change what forty years of quieter askings had not. He let it be copied, page by page, at his own table and under his own eye, correcting the younger clerk's hand once when a stroke ran the wrong way on a name he judged too old to be misread, and would not let the book itself be carried so much as to the harbour, telling her, when she asked why a book so old should not travel under a kingdom's own seal for its own better keeping, that a book kept in one house for that many generations belonged, whatever the kingdom's seal might say, to the house that had kept it and not to the seal, and that a seal, in his own long experience of them, kept a thing only for as long as the hand behind the seal found it convenient to.

Gormshuil read that clerk's own report of the exchange twice before she filed it, and found in the keeper's answer, though she wrote nothing of the thought into her own book, an echo of a house not far in kind from her own mother's, who had likewise counted her own dead by a reckoning older than the kingdom's and had likewise never once asked a council's leave to keep it.

The copy reached her at midsummer, and she read beside it, the same week, the north's own chest, brought up at last from Caol mhòr with the season's other returns and opened at her own table with Coinneach Clàrc standing by to lift out whatever it held. It held, when she had gone through it to the bottom, the maor of Siorrachd Àth àrsaidh's own returns and nothing else: tallies of the head-due paid and unpaid, a list of the district's licensed boats, a note on a bridge wanting mending, every page in the maor's own hand or his clerk's, and not one line, in the whole chest, written by a Tuathaich hand or telling a Tuathaich fact that the maor himself had not already thought worth the kingdom's asking after.

She sat with the chest open before her a good while before she wrote anything of her own beside it, Coinneach waiting at the door for whatever instruction she meant to give him, and when she did write, it was neither the line about the throne, which she judged she had already said, nor a complaint against the maor, who had after all done exactly what his own office asked of him and no less. She wrote only that the chest from Àth àrsaidh held the maor's returns and nothing more, and left the sentence to stand by itself at the foot of the page, without the further word that would have told a later reader whether she thought the emptiness a fault in the north, a fault in the south's asking, or a plain fact neither side had yet found a way to mend.
