Then she closed the chest, told Coinneach to see it carried up to the shelf beside the forty, and went back to the letter Tormod had sent her from Doire ghlas, which she had not yet finished answering.

# Chapter Eighteen: Of the Raiders' Bay

*SE 19 an t-Sultain – SE 20 an Lùnastal*

> *To the council at Cathair dhearg: we ask a second time for what we asked in the winter, being a boat with guns
> in it, or leave to arm our own. We have had no answer to the first asking. We do not think a third will find you
> any less occupied than the first two were.*
> — Nell Barrow's second letter for Cathair gheal, carried south by the maor's own rider and read once

## I. Of the Boats Lost off Cuan bheag

The storm that took Thomas Coyle came out of the west on the second night of an t-Sultain, in SE 19, with no more warning than a wind that had been rising since noon and a glass that the older men of Cuan bheag had been watching all afternoon with the particular silence of men who have seen a glass do this before and not liked what followed. Cuan bheag was a small place, a few miles up the coast from Caol mhòr, its harbour no more than a shingle beach and a stone jetty the humans had built and the town had never had cause nor coin to better, and its boats went out, as they had always gone out, in a fleet together, on the reasoning that a boat in trouble within sight of six others stood some chance of being seen. That night eleven men from seven of those boats did not come home, and among them was Thomas Coyle, a fisherman of Caol mhòr who had married into a Cuan bheag boat some years before and gone out of that harbour ever since, one-and-forty that year and married to Mary Coyle for near twenty of them.

Of the seven boats, the town could piece together only from what the sea gave back over the following week: two hulls, both broken, one oar with a name burned into the loom that nobody in Cuan bheag recognised and that turned out, when word of it reached Caol mhòr, to belong to a boat out of a village further north still. No lifeboat put out after them, because Cuan bheag had none, having never had the coin to build one nor, until that night, the occasion to feel the want of it as more than a thing other, richer harbours kept and it did not. The town buried what it had to bury within the week, in the Church's ground above the shingle, eleven stones cut in the same fortnight by the one mason Cuan bheag could call its own, working from first light to past dark on a debt no one had asked him to take on and that no one, afterward, offered to pay him for.

Mary Coyle heard of it at Caol mhòr two days after, from a carter who had it from a Cuan bheag man selling fish at the Caol mhòr quay and telling it, as such men do, to anyone who would stand still long enough to hear it told. She went up the coast road on foot that same afternoon, arriving after dark and finding no one at the harbour able to tell her more than what she already knew, which was that Thomas's boat had gone out and had not come back, and that of the six men who had crewed it only one had washed ashore, and it was not him. She stayed in Cuan bheag the better part of a fortnight, in a dead woman's spare room lent her by a neighbour, and helped where help was wanted, which was mostly in writing: the mason needed the names spelled correctly for his stones, and more than one of the widows could not write them herself and had never before had cause to see her husband's name set down anywhere but a boat's own gunwale, painted on by his own hand. Mary wrote all eleven out on a single sheet, in the order the boats had gone out in rather than the order the sea had given the men back, because that, she told the mason when he asked why, was the order in which they had last stood together, and it seemed to her the truer one.

Word of the wreck reached the Moot's house at Caol mhòr within the week, carried this time by the same carter, and Walter Hale, who was that year two-and-sixty and had been speaker of the Moot for seventeen of them, called a meeting of the Moot's own council on a Tuesday evening and put the matter to them plainly: Cuan bheag had no lifeboat, no village on that stretch of the coast had one, and the sea did not appear to be growing gentler with the years. The Moot voted, that same evening, to open a subscription for a lifeboat to be kept at Cuan bheag and worked by whichever crew of the town's own men would take the training for it, and Hale himself opened the list with five coins of the realm out of his own purse, entered in his own hand at the top of a sheet that by the month's end carried close on two hundred names, fishermen and farmers and the weavers of Doire ghlas alike, each giving what a poor coast could spare, which for most households was not much and for some was a day's wage entire.

The Moot's letter asking the council to bear half the cost went south with the same carter who had carried its letters south for years, and came back, four months later, with the council's answer written under the Moot's own question in a clerk's hand: that the council would meet a third of the sum, the matter having been considered by the twelve and the sum thought fair against what other calls on the treasury the year had brought. Hale read the answer aloud to the Moot without comment and without complaint, both having by then, as he told Ellen that evening, worn themselves out on lesser matters than this one, and the Moot made up the remaining sum from its own subscription list and a further asking that same winter, so that by am Màrt a boat had been ordered from the yard at Cuan shean, built to a plan the yard already had in hand for the humans' own harbour service, and paid for in full before its keel was ever laid.

The boat came up the coast under her own sail in an Cèitean, a squat white-painted thing with cork lashed along both gunwales in the humans' own fashion, and was put into the water off Cuan bheag's own jetty on a fair morning before most of the town, the mason among them, his eleven stones long since set and weathering. No priest of either the Church or the old Dia-thìreach faiths troubled to bless her, there being no agreed form for blessing a thing neither faith had built before, and the town settled the question by having the five widows of that autumn's wreck, Mary Coyle among them for the day though she had by then gone back to Caol mhòr, walk her down the shingle together and see her set afloat, on the reasoning, which nobody afterward disputed, that if any hands on that coast had earned the right to launch her it was theirs.

## II. Of the Thing off the Cape

Up the same north-western coast, past Cathair gheal and beyond it, lay a headland the fishermen called, among themselves, the cold cape, for the wind that came off it every month of the year but two, and below it a huddle of summer bothies kept by the fishermen of Achadh àrsaidh, a village of the middle country far to the south whose men had gone north each season, time out of mind, to fish waters that few other boats troubled, the ground there being poor and the currents ill-tempered, and they had, in consequence, told among themselves for longer than any living man could number, a tale of a thing that swam those same waters: a creature longer than any boat that had ever gone looking for it, seen always at a distance and never at the same distance twice, that some named the Sea-Watcher and some would not name at all, holding that a thing was less likely to trouble you if you had not troubled to give it a name of its own.

That autumn the tale was told, as it had been told before, to a chronicler who happened to be at the bothies on other business entirely. Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill, the kingdom's own royal chronicler not two years and six-and-forty that season, was on her way back south from the same circuit that had carried her clerks and their forty chests out of the southern shires that spring, and had stopped a night at the bothies below the cold cape because the tide would not serve to carry her further that day. The bothies had shown her, when she asked, no parish book worth the copying and no grave-roll older than the last flood, and she had all but given up hope of the visit's earning its own night's lodging when an old fisherman of the place, who had fished the cold cape's waters the whole of his life and lost a brother to them, offered, over the one fire the house could spare a stranger, to tell her a tale instead, on the plain grounds that a chronicler ought to want tales as much as she wanted rolls, whatever her office called the difference between them.

He told it at some length, and with the particular pleasure of a man who has told a good tale many times and knows exactly where its pauses fall best: the shape seen always at a distance and never at the same distance twice, longer than any boat that had gone looking for it, that some in the village named the Sea-Watcher and some would not name at all, holding that a thing troubled you the less for not being given a name of its own. Gormshuil asked him, when he had done, how many men of the bothies had seen it with their own eyes, and he answered, without any offence at the question, that he did not know a man alive who had, only men who had known men who had, which was, he added, exactly how the tale had come to him and exactly how he expected it to go on from him; and at that, almost as an afterthought, he told her something else, that the flagless ships which had worked those waters some years now, the ones no honest boat cared to meet, seemed to know the cold cape's currents better than any stranger crew had a right to, and kept, he thought, some hidden anchorage among the rocks below it that no Dia-thìreach chart had ever marked.

Gormshuil wrote both things down that same night, in the same entry, the tale of the creature and the fisherman's word on the raiders together, and sat some while afterward deciding whether the two belonged in one book or two. She had by then kept the chronicle long enough to have settled, mostly, what its business was and was not: it was not her office, she had decided, to say whether a creature thirty feet long swam those waters or did not, only to say that a fisherman out of Achadh àrsaidh had told her so, on such a night, in such words, in the book that kept what people said. The raiders' anchorage she judged a different matter, being a thing a sailing master might use rather than a tale a fireside kept, and she wrote it a second time, separately, with a note that the council's own coastal watch be told of it, though she held out small hope, from what she had seen of the coastal watch's dealings with that coast already, that the telling would move it to do anything the coast had not already had to do for its own people. She sealed both pages before she slept, and rode south the next morning with the tide, carrying, among the parish books she had not been given, the one tale she had.

## III. Of the Flocks Counted and the Two Requests

Out past the cold cape, in the open sea to the west, lay Eilean dhubh, greatest of the outer isles, a place of grass and wind and more sheep than people, that the council's head-due had never yet been able to count with any confidence, no royal clerk having troubled, before that year, to cross to it in person. One was sent that same autumn, a young clerk new to the treasury's service and not greatly pleased at the crossing, which the islanders warned him would be rough and which was rougher than warned, the boat that carried him standing three hours off the landing before the sea would let it in at all. He found, once ashore and his stomach settled enough to speak, that the islanders had no more wish than he did to have a stranger stand about their pastures counting beasts that were not his to count, and offered instead to count the flocks themselves, by their own tally-sticks, which every household on the island kept notched to its own count and none had ever had reason to falsify against a due nobody from the south had come to collect in living memory, and hand him the sum entire, sworn to before the island's own headman. The clerk, who had crossed a bad strait to do a count he had no great appetite for doing twice, and who could see, besides, no way to check eleven hundred sheep across four townlands inside the fortnight the crossing allowed him, took the offer gladly, wrote the sworn sum into his own book exactly as given, and sailed home on the next fair tide grateful to be asked no more of it. The dues that year, and every year after, were set upon the island's own count, given once and never afterward disputed by either side, each having got, in its own way, exactly what it wanted of the arrangement: the council a figure it could enter in its books, and Eilean dhubh a treasury that troubled it, at most, once in a generation.

It was into that same autumn and the winter that followed it that the two requests went south from Cathair gheal, a walled town on that same stretch of coast, its harbour a shallow bay below the town wall that the flagless ships had by then worked for the better part of six years without any hand from the south troubling to move against them. Nell Barrow, a skipper's widow of the town some two-and-thirty years old that winter, had taken it upon herself, in the way of a woman with time on her hands and a grievance she did not care to sit on, to write the town's case out in full and carry it to the maor's own door for his seal and his rider. She had lost her husband to no raider, his boat having gone down in ordinary weather some years before this tale begins, but she had lost, in the six years since the flagless ships first came, a nephew taken off a boat within sight of the harbour mouth and never seen again, and the town's patience, along with her own, had by then worn thin enough that she no longer troubled to soften her letters for a council she did not expect to answer them gently in any case.

The first letter went south in am Faoilleach of SE 20, asking plainly for a boat armed and crewed at the council's expense, or failing that a licence for the town to arm and crew its own, the town having neither guns nor law to carry them and wanting, in Nell Barrow's own words, one or the other before it wanted anything else the council might think fit to send it. The maor read it over twice before he sealed it, and told her, not unkindly, that a request framed so plainly was as likely to be filed unread as answered, letters that gave a clerk no soft phrase to copy back being, in his experience, letters a clerk found easiest simply to set aside. Nell Barrow answered that she had written a good many soft letters in her time and had a drawer at home to show for it, every one of them answered in the same soft coin it was written in, which was to say not answered at all, and that she would try the plain kind once before she troubled to write a third of either.

No answer came within the two months she gave it, and in am Màrt she wrote the second letter, the one that has come down whole, the maor having kept a fair copy of it in his own office before sending the original on, on the reasoning, he told Nell Barrow plainly, that a letter written in that temper might not survive its own journey south undamaged by whatever hand first read it. It asked the same thing the first had asked, in fewer words, and ended, as she had written it, with the line that the maor copied out exactly and that has been kept ever since: that the town did not think a third asking would find the council any less occupied than the first two had. No answer came to the second letter either, that spring or after.

## IV. Of the Bay Cleared

The flagless ships came into Cathair gheal's bay in force on the night of 8 an Giblean in SE 20, three hulls where the town had grown used to seeing one or two at most, standing off the harbour mouth at dusk in a manner that gave every fisherman on the wall no doubt at all of what the night meant to bring. Nell Barrow was at the harbour when the watch first called it, having taken, since the second letter went unanswered, to walking the wall most evenings on the plain grounds that a thing seen early was a thing met on better terms than a thing met in the dark unlooked-for, and she sent a boy running through every street of the town for any man who owned a boat and anything that could be swung: a gaff, a gutting-knife, an old sword some grandfather's grandfather had carried off a battlefield two ages gone and that had hung over a hearth ever since doing nothing more warlike than gathering soot. She herself took down, from its nail beside her own door, the boat-hook her husband had carried the whole of his working life and that she had not touched since the day it came home without him, and found, hefting it in the dark of her own passage, that her hand still knew its balance better than it knew any weapon the town could have found her in its place.

What followed that night has been told in Cathair gheal more times than any single telling could now untangle from the rest, but the plain bones of it, as the maor's own report set them down within the fortnight, ran thus. Seven boats put out from the town before midnight, crewed by whatever hands could be found and armed with whatever the town could put in them, the tide low enough that every man among them knew the bay's own shallows better than any stranger crew ever could, raiders included. The larger of the three raider hulls, a black-sided ship the fishermen had for years called by a name of their own that the maor's report does not give, stood in closer than her own master judged the water, meaning to land a boat's crew on the quay itself, and ran her keel onto a bar that had shifted, that same winter, further out than any chart still above water on that coast had troubled to mark; and there she sat, fast and listing, while the two lesser hulls stood off in the dark uncertain whether to come to her or leave her.

The seven town boats closed on her before she could work herself free, coming in low and quiet with their oars muffled in sacking, as fishermen of that coast had muffled oars against a shy shoal since before any of them could say how the trick was first learned, and the fight, when it came, was closer and shorter and less orderly than any account of it afterward quite managed to make it sound: men going hand to hand along a listing deck in the dark, by lantern-light where a lantern held and by none where it did not, with gaffs and gutting-knives and, in one case that the maor's report set down without further comment, an old battlefield sword swung by a miller's son who had never before that night held anything sharper than a scythe. It cost the town two men dead outright and four more hurt before the black hull was cleared, one of the four losing the use of a hand he did not afterward recover; but by the time the black ship burned to her waterline, fired by her own boarders once her hold was found to hold nothing worth the saving, the two lesser hulls had already stood out for open water rather than come to a fight that plainly was not going as their own master had reckoned it would, and neither was seen off that coast again that year. Nell Barrow came back to the harbour wall at first light with a burn along one forearm, taken from a fallen lantern rather than from any blade, that she carried the mark of for the rest of her life, and told the town, before she would trouble to have it looked at, that the bay was clear; and clear, for that season and the two that followed it, it stayed.

## V. Of the Fine Paid

The council's answer to the night's work reached Cathair gheal before an Cèitean was out, and it was not the answer the town had spent six years asking for. The maor's report of the fight, forwarded south along with Nell Barrow's account of it and a plain list of the dead, came back with a ruling attached that the town of Cathair gheal had borne arms without the council's licence, contrary to the old rule that no Tuathaich town might arm its own boats without leave first asked and first given, and that the town was fined four purses of the realm-coin, to be paid at the maor's own office before the year's dues fell due. No word came, in the same letter or any after it, of a boat sent, a licence granted, or a guard set upon a bay that had needed one for six years and had at last, at some cost, made its own; the ruling's four lines named the offence and the sum and nothing besides, in the same hand and on the same kind of sheet, the maor afterward remarked to no one in particular, that had once fined a Ros bheag boat-builder for launching a hull a foot over its licensed beam.

Word of the fine reached Caol mhòr before an t-Iuchar was a week old, carried, as most such word was, by a Cuan bheag man selling fish at the quay who had it in turn from a carter out of the north, and Walter Hale, hearing it read aloud at the Moot's own table, said nothing for the length of time it took the clerk to finish reading and then asked only how much the town still lacked. It lacked, by the maor's own reckoning, some two-thirds of the sum, Cathair gheal being a poor town and its harbour trade thin that summer on account of the very raiders it had just driven off, the fish that had not been taken in six bad years being fish that brought in no coin toward a fine for taking them back. Hale carried the difference north himself within the fortnight, out of the same purse the Moot kept for such calls on it and that had, that year, rather less slack in it than he would have liked, the lifeboat at Cuan bheag having already taken more of it than the subscription alone had raised.

He came to Cathair gheal on a wet morning near the end of an t-Iuchar and found Nell Barrow, her forearm healed to a scar she did not trouble to hide, already at the maor's door before him with what the town itself had managed to scrape together, so that between her sum and his the fine was paid in full that same morning, coin by coin, in front of the maor's own clerk, who wrote the amount received in his ledger and said nothing at all about the six years, the two letters, or the boat the town had not been sent. Hale asked the clerk, as he watched the coins counted, whether the council's own ledger carried any line for what the bay had cost the town before that night as well as what it had cost the council after it, and the clerk, a decent enough man doing an office he had not chosen, answered only that his ledger carried what he was given to enter and no more, which Hale allowed was very likely true and no fault of the clerk's own making. The town, he said as he pocketed the last receipt, had already kept its own ledger of that cost, in stone and in scar, and needed no clerk to enter it a second time.

Far to the south that same season, at Cathair mhòr, the house of Mac Ùisdein raised a market cross at its own cost, cut on all four faces with the house's own name, and moved the town's wool and coal markets to stand at its foot, where they have stood ever since. The council's minute on the matter, when it was read at Caol mhòr in an Lùnastal along with the news of Cathair gheal's fine now settled, ran a good deal longer than the minute on the fine had, and named the sum the house of Mac Ùisdein had given a generous one. Mary Coyle, who had by then been back at Caol mhòr the better part of a year and had taken, since the wreck, to sitting at the harbour wall most evenings where she could see the boats come in, heard the two minutes read one after the other at the Moot's own table and said only that it seemed the council knew a great deal about crosses, and rather less about lifeboats, before she went back to counting the boats home.

# Part Four: Of Fair, Crown and Survey

# Chapter Nineteen: Of the Fair at Muileann òg


*SE 21 an Cèitean – SE 22 an Lùnastal*

> *A' chiad fhèill, agus a' chiad riaghailt.*
> The first fair, and the first rule.
>
> — entered in Oighrig nic Mhathain's own hand, at the head of the fair's book

## I. Of the Bell at Caol leathan

There had been a house of the Stone at Caol leathan since before any clerk now living could put a first date to it, a low stone hall behind the harbour with the western Seann Skell's own scorpion nowhere on it and nothing of the state's arms either, only the Stone's own mark cut plain over the door: a thing older, the priests there said, than either. In SE 21 the house was built up anew at the order's own cost, a low tower raised over its western gable and a bell hung in it that had been cast, the priests said, from coin given by every ship that had ever put in at Caol leathan's small harbour and come home again. It was not a large bell, nor one that could be heard much past the town's own walls, but Caol leathan was a small place and did not need much heard past its walls: the bell rang the hours from that year on, and the market opened by it, and the two courts the town kept, the harbour court and the fair court, sat by it, and within a year nobody in Caol leathan troubled any longer to ask a neighbour the time, only whether the bell had gone yet.

The Library, setting the fact down some years after, had little more to say of it than that: a bell raised, a tower built, a town's day set by it where no day had been set by anything but the tide before. It was the kind of fact that filled a line in a chronicler's book and no more. The fair that opened that same autumn some twenty-odd miles to the east took its hours from no bell at all, only from the voice of the woman who kept it.

## II. Of Oighrig, Market Clerk of Dùn chrom

Oighrig nic Mhathain was one-and-thirty that year, and had kept the weighing-scales of Dùn chrom's own small market for nine of them, a walled town of some size on the road east out of Cathair dhearg, its citadel old and its market square older, where three days in five she sat behind a table with a set of the council's own weights before her and told carters and hucksters, in a voice that had by then long since stopped troubling to be gentle about it, what their sacks and their barrels actually held against what they claimed for them. She had come to the work at two-and-twenty, a widow's daughter with a head for figures and no dowry worth a better match, and had made of a post that most who held it did indifferently into one that Dùn chrom's own maor had come, in nine years, to trust further than he trusted most of his own clerks: she caught short weight that better-paid men missed, and she wrote her findings down in a hand plain enough that a magistrate could read it without asking her to stand and explain it twice.

It was for that plainness, more than for anything else she had done, that the council's own factor for the eastern shires came to her table one market day in an Cèitean of SE 21 and asked whether she would take a harder post than weighing sacks: the state had resolved, on the maoir's own asking and the merchants' louder one, to hold a fair each year at the ford by Muileann òg, the old meeting-place where the Stone King Raghnall Ceannfhionn was said to have traded salt for wool with the holder of the Red Hill in an age no living clerk could put a year to, and it wanted someone to keep it who could weigh a sack, read a scale, and write a rule down so plainly that a carter three shires off could understand it without a clerk to read it to him. Oighrig asked what the post paid and was told, and asked what it answered to and was told that, and asked, last, what happened to whoever held it if the fair went wrong in its first year, and was told, honestly enough, that nobody yet knew, there having been no fair of this size held anywhere on the island since before the Severance for anyone to learn the answer from. She took the post anyway, on the reasoning she gave her mother that evening, that a woman who had spent nine years catching other people's short weight might as well spend the next few finding out what her own came to. Her mother, who had raised her alone on a widow's small pension and a stall of dried fish in the same market square, heard the whole of it out before she said anything, and then said only that Oighrig had better learn to write faster than she wrote now, if a whole fair's dues were to go through the one hand of her rather than through the several that a town's market usually spread its weighing among. It was, Oighrig thought afterward, the only piece of advice her mother ever gave her that she found herself, years on, still following to the letter.

She told the maor the following morning, before she told the council's own factor she would take the post, on the grounds that Dùn chrom's market had gone nine years without a bad weight under her table and deserved to hear from her own mouth, rather than from a rider's, that it was about to go without her altogether. The maor heard her out, said he had half expected it since the factor first asked after her at the spring assize, and asked only who she meant to leave behind her that he could trust to catch what she had caught. A niece of her own, a quick-handed girl of seventeen who had stood at her elbow two summers running, was the name she gave him, and the maor, who had learned in nine years to take Oighrig's word on a scale without asking to see the proof of it, took her word on the niece the same way and never afterward had cause to regret it.

She rode west to Muileann òg within the fortnight, a town of some few dozen souls and no more, its only distinction the ford and the old meeting-stone beside it, and found there a field, a track worn into it by generations of carts that had never yet had a fair to carry to, and nothing else that a state building a fair from nothing could be said to have given her: no hall, no scales but the ones she brought herself, no clerk but her own hand. She spent the summer walking the ground with a length of cord and a stick, and marked where the stalls would stand, where the beasts would be penned apart from the cloth and the grain, where the road from Cathair dhearg would need widening before the first cart came down it heavier than the track had ever carried, and where, at the field's one corner nearest the ford, a court could sit under a roof if the state saw fit to build her one before autumn. It did, in the end, though later than she asked for it and smaller than she had marked out, a plain roofed frame open on three sides that the carpenters of Dùn chrom finished in the last week of an t-Sultain, a fortnight before the day set for the fair to open.

## III. Of the Rules Written in Her Own Hand

The council's word came to her at the end of that same summer, carried by the same factor who had first found her at her table, in the form of instructions rather than a rule already made: that the fair, once opened, should draw its dues in coin and not in kind, that it should have its own court to settle what quarrels a gathering that size would bring rather than send every dispute back to a maor's bench three days' ride off, and that Tuathaich goods, of whatever kind, should be sold at the fair only through Dia-thìreach factors licensed for the purpose, the council having judged, the letter said, that a trade so new was better kept for its first years inside hands the state already answered for. It did not tell her how to write the rule, only that it was to stand, and left her, as such letters generally did, the whole of the wording and none of the deciding.

She sat with it three evenings in the roofed frame at the field's corner, by a rush-light, before she set a word of it down, and what she wrote in the end she wrote plainly, in the same hand she had used nine years for catching short weight, on the grounds that a rule nobody could misread was worth more than a rule dressed finer: a stall-fee of one penny in the realm-coin for every ell of frontage taken, paid at the setting-up and not after; a court of the fair, *Cùirt na Fèille* as she headed the page that opened its own book, to sit each day of the gathering under her own roof, to hear any quarrel of weight, price or theft between traders and settle it there rather than send it south; and, last, that goods brought by a Tuathaich seller to the fair were to be entered at a factor's stall and sold under the factor's own name, the seller taking his price from the factor and not from the buyer direct. She wrote that third clause last of the three, and read it over twice before she let it stand, knowing, as she told nobody at the time but wrote once, years after, in a letter to her own niece, exactly what it would mean for the first northern cart that tried to sell past it: that the fair she had marked out with a length of cord in an empty field would, from its very first year, be a place where a Tuathaich seller's goods passed through another man's hand before they passed through the buyer's, and where the difference between the two prices went into a purse that was never the seller's own.

The council's licences went out to four merchant houses of the eastern shires before the harvest was in, each given the right to stand a factor's stall at Muileann òg and take goods of the north to sell under its own name for a share of the price, the houses chosen, so far as Oighrig could tell from the letter that named them, more for the coin they had already put toward the fair's road than for any particular fitness to the trade. She entered the four names in her own book on the same page as the rule itself, under a heading she gave it without being asked to give it one: *Bàillidhean na Fèille*, the fair's factors, a name that has stood in every year's book since.

The eldest of the four, a wool merchant of Cathair mhòr named Ruairidh mac Aonghais who had put more of his own coin toward the widening of the fair's road than any of the other three, rode out to Muileann òg himself in an t-Iuchar to look over the ground before his stall went up, and found Oighrig still marking out the field with her cord and stick. He asked her, civilly enough, whether the third clause of her rule was hers or the council's, having heard, he said, two different accounts of its authorship from two different clerks at Cathair dhearg. She told him it was both, the council's in its substance and hers in its wording, and he allowed, looking out over the empty field where his own stall would stand come autumn, that a rule's wording mattered a good deal less to the men who profited by it than to the men who did not, and that she would find, in his experience of licensed trades, that the two kinds of men rarely agreed on which the wording had been kind to. He was not wrong, and Oighrig, who had already guessed as much three evenings running by rush-light, told him only that she had written it to be read the same way by both kinds of men, which was the most a rule could honestly promise to do.

## IV. Of the First Fair

The fair opened on 16 an Dàmhair in SE 21, a bright cold morning with the frost still on the field's grass when the first carts came down the widened road from Cathair dhearg, and by noon Oighrig's court had heard its first case, a small one, a dispute over a barrel of salt fish claimed short by the buyer and full by the seller, which she settled inside the hour by the simple expedient of having both men stand by while she weighed it herself against her own scales, the seller's claim proving the truer of the two. Only those who had stood in the crowd that watched it would ever remember the case itself. It was the first the court of the fair had heard, and Oighrig wrote it into her book in the same plain hand as everything else, on the grounds, she told the clerk who asked her why she troubled with so small a thing, that a court's first case set the pattern for every one after it whether anybody remembered the case itself or not.

A harder case came the third day, a Cathair mhòr coal-carter who swore a Sloc Mòr merchant had sold him spoil dressed to pass for good coal, the two being near enough alike to a buyer's eye by lamplight and near enough different on a smith's hearth by morning that the carter had driven the better part of two days back to the fair rather than swallow the loss. Oighrig had no smith's forge under her own roof to settle it by, and settled it instead by sending both men, and the load itself, to the one smith Muileann òg's own handful of houses could produce, an old man who had shod carthorses there the whole of his life and had never before been asked to judge a stranger's coal, and who told her, an hour later, that the load was three parts good stone to one part spoil, no more and no less. She fined the merchant the value of the one part and let the rest of the sale stand, and wrote into her book that a smith's eye, where the fair kept none of its own, would serve the court as well as any clerk's scale until the state saw fit to send her one.

The fair kept, besides its cases, a noise and a smell that Oighrig's own book had no line to hold: woodsmoke and wet wool and the coal carts' own black dust settling over everything by the second week, pipers from Baile chiar playing for coin at the field's far corner, and under it all the low constant argument of buying and selling in half a dozen shires' worth of accents, which she came, in that first fortnight, to find she could stand in the middle of and pick apart into its separate threads the way she had once picked apart a barrel's true weight from a seller's claimed one, a skill she had not known she had until the fair gave her cause to use it.

Trade came that first year from every province the state held, wool from the western shires and the Sloc Mòr's coal from the east and cloth from Baile chiar's looms and salt from the coastal pans, more of everything in one field than Oighrig had seen gathered anywhere in nine years of market days, and she spent the fortnight the fair ran on her feet from before light to past dark, settling weights, hearing cases, and writing, each evening by the same rush-light, the day's dues into a book that by the fair's last day ran to more pages than she had thought to bring. It was, by every measure the council troubled to ask her for afterward, a success beyond what anyone attached to it that first autumn had thought to hope: the dues gathered came to more than the fair's own building had cost, the court settled every case brought to it inside the fortnight without once sending one south, and the four factors' stalls did the trade the council had licensed them to do, buying wool and cloth and salt fish off northern carts at a price the factors set and selling it on, under their own names, for a price the factors set again.

## V. Of David Hale's Wool

It was on the ninth day of that first fair, by Oighrig's own count in her book, that a cart came down the Cathair dhearg road from the north rather than from any of the state's own provinces, driven by a young man of perhaps eight-and-twenty who gave his name, when her clerk asked it at the gate, as David Hale of Caol mhòr, and his load as wool, four sacks of it, off his own father's sheep and the sheep of two neighbours besides, brought the better part of a week's journey on the reasoning, he told the gate clerk plainly enough, that a fair drawing trade from every province the state held ought to draw trade from the Moot's provinces too, there having been no word sent north, so far as the Moot's own minute-book showed, that it should not.

Oighrig came to the gate herself when the clerk sent for her, having by then learned, in nine days, that a case worth her own eye was worth fetching her for rather than settling wrong by a clerk who did not know the rule as she had written it, and found a cart of good wool and a driver who had clearly never before had cause to read a licence, there having been none to read at Caol mhòr's own small market where he had sold his father's wool his whole life without one. She read him the third clause of her own rule from her own book, in the same plain hand she had written it in, and told him, as plainly as the rule itself was written, that the wool could enter the fair only at a factor's stall, under the factor's name, at whatever price the factor judged to give for it. David Hale asked, reasonably enough, where the difference went between what the factor gave him and what the factor got for it after, and Oighrig, who had asked herself the same question three evenings running by rush-light before she ever wrote the clause down, told him the truth of it rather than soften it, that the difference went to the factor and to the state's own licence upon him, and that this was the rule as the council had sent it to her to write, not as she would have written it unasked.

He stood some while at the gate with his cart behind him, four sacks of wool that had cost him a week's journey and would now cost him, besides, whatever the nearest factor judged fair to take off the top of it, and asked her, last, whether she had written the rule herself. She told him she had, in her own hand, on the council's instruction and her own wording both, and that she saw no profit in telling him otherwise. Oddly enough he thanked her for that much plainness at least, turned his cart to the factor's stall she pointed him toward without further argument, and sold his wool there for a price the factor set, a price David Hale judged, by his own reckoning that evening and the reckoning he carried home to Caol mhòr after, some fifth part short of what the same wool would have brought sold direct at any market the Moot's own provinces kept. He did not come to the fair again that autumn, nor the next, though the lesson of that turning at the gate stayed with him a good deal longer than the fifth part he lost by it, and it was some years before another cart came down from the Moot's provinces to try the gate a second time.

He carried the wool's price home to Caol mhòr inside the fortnight, and told his father what the gate had cost him before he told him anything else of the fair, laying the fifth part's difference out on the table between them in coin the way a clerk lays out a reckoning he expects to be asked to justify. Walter Hale, who had by then sat the Moot's chair the better part of twenty years and had read a good many licences in that time without ever once finding one written by the hand that had to answer for it afterward, asked David only one thing more than the sum itself: whether the woman who had turned him from the gate had seemed, in the turning, glad of the rule or sorry for it. David thought a while before he answered, and said at last that she had seemed neither, only plain about it, which his father allowed, turning the coin over once in his own hand, was very likely the truest answer a rule's own writer could give a man it had just cost a fifth part of his summer's wool, and worth remembering the next time the Moot sat down to write a letter about her rule rather than about her.

## VI. Of the Road, the Wall, and the Rule Read Aloud

The winter that followed brought the fair's road its finishing, the last stretch of it metalled past Dùn chrom in am Faoilleach of SE 22, the carters' own name for the new road already settled before the state ever gave it one of its own, Rathad na Fèille, the fair's road, though the carters who used it hardest had, by then, another name for the toll taken at Dùn chrom's own gate to pay for it, a name Oighrig heard once, passing through on her way east, and did not trouble to write down. The toll built, over that same winter, a new wall along the town's southern side, the wall the townsfolk called the fair's wall and the carters called by their own name for the gate that took the toll for it, and by an Lùnastal of SE 22 the wall stood finished, the first stone of Dùn chrom's own that the fair, rather than the state or the custodians before it, had paid to raise.

The Moot's letter reached Cathair dhearg some time in that same winter, carried, as its letters generally were, by a carter who had it from Walter Hale's own hand, and it named the factor rule plainly for what the Moot judged it to be: a state licence laid across a trade the north had carried on unaided since before the Severance, and a fifth part of every northern sack's worth handed, by that licence, to men who had done nothing to the wool but stand between the grower and the buyer with the council's own paper in their hand. It asked, as such letters generally asked, that the rule be looked at again. The council's answer, when it came, came slowly and said little: that the rule stood as licensed, that the fair's first year had shown it workable, and that the matter, having been considered, would not be reconsidered inside the year. The letter was filed at Cathair dhearg in the same box as the Moot's earlier letters, on the same shelf, in the same clerk's hand.

Oighrig herself never saw the Moot's letter, the council having no cause to send a toll-mistress a complaint written against a rule she had only been asked to word, and she learned of it, when she learned of it at all, from the same clerk who brought her the council's confirmation that spring, a young man not long in the office who mentioned it in passing, as one piece of the winter's business among several, and seemed faintly surprised that she troubled to ask him what the letter had said rather than merely that one had come. She asked him to read her the line about the fifth part twice over, and wrote it down afterward in her own book beside the rule itself, on a page she kept for nothing else, a habit her own clerks took, in the years that followed, for simple thoroughness and never once thought to ask her the reason for.

Oighrig heard of the council's answer at the fair's second opening, on the same field, by the ford, in an Dàmhair of SE 22, though her own chapter of the matter had already closed some months before that, in an Lùnastal, when the council's clerk who carried its confirmation to her read the whole of her own rule aloud before the assembled factors and the gathered maoir of the eastern shires, word for word as she had written it the autumn before by rush-light, stall-fee and court and the third clause together, and asked her, when he had done, whether the reading matched her own book. She told him it did, word for word, and watched the four factors nod at a rule they had had no hand in writing and every profit in keeping, and thought, though she did not say it aloud to the clerk or to anyone else that day, that a thing read aloud in the same words it was written in did not thereby become any less her own doing for the reading, whoever else's coin the reading was meant to serve.

# Chapter Twenty: Of the Way Niall Came

*SE 22 an Lùnastal – SE 23 an Lùnastal*

> *Mar a thàinig Niall.*
> The way Niall came.
>
> — entered once, and once only, in the hand of Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill, chronicler

## I. Of the Bells at Cathair dhearg

Word of it came out along the east road a day and a night after it happened, riding in the mouth of a maor's courier who had changed horses twice and slept once, on the floor of a tavern, in his boots. By the time it reached Muileann chaol the bells at Cathair dhearg had already been ringing since dawn, and would ring, in relays, until the following dusk.

That much the Library set down without difficulty: that Niall died and Brìghde was crowned on 31 an Lùnastal, SE 22; that the bells of Òrd Mhacha were rung a full day and a night for his death; that the streets about the old counting-house filled with a crowd larger than any the capital had seen since his own crowning; that the crowd was quiet, and stayed quiet, and went home before the second night; that within the week his daughter stood where he had stood, and the same rite that had made him king was said over her by the same order, and no voice in the crowd or the council was raised against it. Those were the facts, and the Library has never had more of them to give. What was said in the death-chamber, if anything was said, and by whom, went with the people who heard it, and none of them left an account that reached Muileann chaol. The chronicle does not guess at what it was never told.

For that first day the capital kept no market. No order shut the stalls round the old counting-house; nobody could be found willing to be the trader who cried his wares under a tolling bell, and by noon the empty stalls had become, without anyone declaring it, the custom of the day. Ships in the harbour struck their colours to half the mast, a habit some said the humans had left behind them and others said the island had always had, and the argument over which was true outlasted the mourning by a fair margin. Children were kept from the streets near the tower, since the noise of the bells at close range could be heard for days after in a small skull, and every mother in Cathair dhearg who had one seemed to know it.

The council of twelve sat within the week, as its minute-book shows it always sat, on its fixed day, and the first business entered that day is a dispute over a weir on the Abhainn ìseal that had run three sessions already and would run two more before it was settled. Between that entry and the one before it there is no blank page, no space left for the weight of what had happened, only the ordinary hand of the clerk who kept the book that year, going on to the next line as he had been taught to. A visitor turning the pages now might read past the crowning and never know a kingdom had changed hands in the gap, unless he thought to look for the single line, two entries down, noting that the council's oath of service had been sworn afresh before the new sovereign, in the same room, on the same afternoon as the weir.

The bells themselves were an old debt paid. They had hung in the tower of Òrd Mhacha since before the Severance, cast by hands nobody now living could name, and they had rung four times in seventy years: once for Niall's own crowning, twice for storms taken as omens that came to nothing, and now this. A boy set to work the smaller of the two, relieved every two hours by another boy, kept a tally chalked on the tower wall of how many times his arms had pulled the rope, and rubbed it out when his watch ended, so that no count of it survives, and the Library has none to give.

At Brìghde's crowning the market crosses of the south carried the proclamation within three days, in the same words that had carried Niall's twenty years before, with only the name changed and the year. A clerk at Ros dhomhain, copying it out for the harbour gate, wrote Niall's name by habit before he caught himself, scored it through with two strokes, and wrote Brìghde's above the line. The corrected copy hangs at Ros dhomhain yet, under glass, kept there mostly because nobody afterward could be troubled to have it taken down.

Of the new queen herself the record gives, for this year, only what any record gives of any crowning: the rite kept, the regalia carried out of Òrd Mhacha's keeping and back into it, the crowd that watched and dispersed. No word of hers survives from that week, and none was sought. The state she inherited went on being governed by the same twelve families and the same maoir the day after as the day before, gathering the same head-due by the same reckoning, and if anything in the machinery of the kingdom so much as paused to notice that the hand on the lever had changed, no minute of any council records it.

## II. Of the Word Gormshuil Let In

At Muileann chaol the chronicler kept a small room above the Library's reading-hall, with one window that looked down into the yard where the copyists sunned their vellum, and a table too narrow for the papers she put on it. She had held the office four years by then, and had written, in that time, several hundred entries in a hand her own clerks had learned to copy well enough that visitors could not always tell which lines were hers.

The office kept to a small routine that had grown up around her without much planning: two clerks besides Tormod, a copyist shared with the reading-hall below, and a courier's box nailed to the outer door for anything that came while she was at the Library proper, sorting the boxed rolls that still arrived, a decade on, from shires that had only just got round to clearing an old counting-house or a dead magistrate's chest. Most days the work was of that kind, patient and small: a grave-list from Doire shean copied fair, a parish register cross-checked against the humans' own numbering, a maor's return of the year's head-due entered against the last five years' and the difference noted without comment. The crowning, when word of it reached her desk between a grave-list and a return, looked like nothing larger than the rest of that morning's post, and she had learned, in four years of the office, to give it no more room on the page than its facts required and no less.

She wrote the crowning three times before she let any version of it stand.

The first draft said that the throne passed from father to daughter without incident, which was true and said nothing. The second said that no one contested the succession, though many in the country's temples counted years by lives that did not shorten as other lives did, and this she struck through before the ink had properly taken, because it was also true and said a good deal too much, and she was not the chronicler who would be the one to say it first. The third draft she left half a page long and unfinished, because in trying to explain why the thing seemed both ordinary and strange at once she had begun, without meaning to, to write an argument, and a chronicle is not an argument.

She sat with the three failed pages spread on the narrow table and the courier's letter weighted under an ink-stone, and thought, not for the first time, that words for what had happened came easily enough. What was hard was choosing, among the true things that could be said, which one the kingdom's grandchildren would be permitted to know had been thought at all.

It was her clerk, Tormod mac Sheumais, four years now at her side, who gave her the way out, without knowing he had done it. He came up with a fair copy of an unrelated entry for her to check, glanced at the crossed-out drafts on the table without meaning to read them, and said, by way of nothing, that the taverns of Cathair dhearg, where he had grown up, had a phrase for anything that went off without a quarrel: *the way Niall came.* He had heard it against a debt his father paid without an argument, and again against a marriage nobody in either family had opposed, and thought it a tavern saying, no more, the kind that gets into every account book in a town within a generation of one clean transaction and means nothing very much by the time it does.

Gormshuil sat with that a long moment.

It sat oddly with the chronicle's language, a line out of a debtor's ledger dressed as history. Turning it over, she saw it was also the only true thing in any of the four drafts on her table: a plain report of how smoothly the crowning had gone, in the very words the kingdom had already coined to say so. She had thought, for a long moment, that she would be inventing a judgment. She was, she decided, only recording one that had already been made, in taverns and market squares, by people with no office and no ink-stone, long before she sat down to write her own version of it.

She wrote it in, four words, and did not strike it out.

*The succession came mar a thàinig Niall*, she wrote, *and the record notes no voice against it.*

She looked at the sentence for some time afterward, the pen dry in her hand, weighing whether a phrase let in once could be kept from becoming a habit. Other offices had lost their plainness that way: an ornament allowed for one entry because it fit so well, then reached for again the next time something needed saying gently, until the whole record read like a poem trying to be a ledger. Sitting there, she resolved to let herself the one line and no other, for as long as the office was hers, and she kept that resolve to the end of her years at the desk, though nothing outside her own conscience would ever have held her to it. It is, in the whole span of her chronicle, the only idiom she ever entered.

Tormod himself never knew, until she told him years later over a different matter entirely, that the phrase he had offered in passing, meaning nothing by it, had gone into the kingdom's own record of its own history. When she did tell him he asked, reasonably, why she had not simply said so at the time, and she answered that a chronicler thanking her clerk for a turn of phrase in front of him was a chronicler inviting a second turn of phrase the following week, and a third after that, and she had seen offices ruined by less. He took the answer as the kind of thing she said, and went back to his copying, and the matter was not raised between them again.

Her mother, when she heard of it on a visit to her mother's village by Ceann àrsaidh that autumn, laughed longer than Gormshuil thought the thing deserved, and said that her daughter had spent four years learning to write like nobody in particular so that she could, in the end, write like everybody. Gormshuil said this was not quite fair, that she had chosen the one phrase precisely because it belonged to no one, having passed through every debtor's ledger and wedding contract in the south until nobody living could say who had coined it. Her mother said that was a fine distinction to draw over four words, and asked whether the same care went into every entry or only the ones that made a queen of somebody's daughter. Gormshuil said the care was the same throughout, and that this was rather the point of keeping a chronicle at all. Her mother said it was fair enough, and poured the tea, and the two of them sat some while in the kind of silence that did not need filling, of the sort that only happens between a mother and a daughter who have already said most of what needs saying, over many years, and found no cause to disagree twice about the same thing.

## III. Of the Hall at Seann Dunn

East along the coast, past the last of the shires the Crown troubled to garrison closely, the houses of the Seann Spioradan had never had a hall of their own, only the hearths of whichever family was keeping the year's rite, and a long custom of walking to a neighbour's fire when their own house had none living old enough to lead the naming. In the autumn after the crowning, forty households of that coast put up timber and stone at Seann Dunn for a hall that would hold all of them at once, and roofed it before the first frost, working by turns as a barn-raising is worked, with the women cooking for the builders and the builders arguing over the pitch of the roof.

The chronicle required nothing of her here; Gormshuil went to see it finished because word of an ancestors' hall reached a chronicler's desk the way any large gathering of the faithful did, and because her mother's own house, three valleys inland, kept the same rite at a hearth too small for half its dead. She went on a hired horse with one clerk, and arrived the evening before the hall's first naming, and slept badly in a fisherman's loft that smelled of nets.

The hall was plain enough to look at: four walls of undressed stone, a roof of new timber that still smelled of the axe, a hearth at either end so that no one house's fire should be taken for another's, and no image or carving anywhere in it, since the Seann Spioradan hold that a name spoken aloud is ornament enough and needs no likeness to stand beside it. Forty families had raised it in a season, working the stone by day and, Gormshuil was told, arguing by candlelight over whose hearth should stand nearer the door, an argument that had been settled, in the end, by the eldest woman of the coast simply sitting down at the hearth she preferred and daring anyone to move her.

The naming she watched from the door, where a chronicler belonged and no further. Forty heads of houses stood in turn and spoke the names of their dead, going back as far as memory or a grandmother's telling would carry them, some no more than three generations, one old woman of Seann Dunn reciting nine before her voice gave out and her son finished the tenth for her. A fisherman from the far end of the coast, a young man by his voice, named only his father and stood a long moment after saying it before sitting down again, and nobody in the hall thought this needed any comment, since not every house's dead came in long lists and a hall built to hold long lists had to hold the short ones too, or it was built for nothing. Nobody wrote any of it down that night. It was spoken, the way it had always been spoken, into a room full of people who already half knew it, and the only new thing in the room was the room.

Gormshuil, listening from the door with her clerk beside her, found herself counting, without quite meaning to, how many names her own mother's hearth could put up against the room's forty, and gave up the count somewhere past a dozen, less from any want of dead to name than because counting, standing where she stood, felt like exactly the kind of ledger-keeping she had come east to get away from for one evening.

An elder of the hall, a boat-builder called Fearchar Ruadh whose house Gormshuil did not know, found her afterward at the door and asked her plainly whether the Library kept such lists as his houses were now keeping. She told him, as plainly, that it did not, not yet, that the Library kept what came to it and asked for little else, and that if his hall chose to send a copy of its naming south each year, it would be received and kept as carefully as anything else that reached Muileann chaol.

"And if we do not send it," he said, "will the Library go looking for it?"

"No," she said. "It never has."

He seemed to find this the right answer, and said the hall would think on it over the winter. The following year, as it happened, they did send a copy, and the hall went on sending one every year after, each a little longer than the last, name by name. Gormshuil entered its arrival in her own hand, and noted, as she noted with every such gift, only the day it came and the number of names it carried, nothing of what she had seen at the door of the hall. That she kept, if she kept it at all, in the private book she had begun some years before and showed to no one.

## IV. Of the Light on the Mole

Far up the eastern coast, past even Seann Dunn, the town of Cuan ruadh had none of the five lighthouses the humans had left the kingdom to keep. It had a mole, built in the humans' time for a fishing fleet larger than the one that used it now, and at the end of the mole, that same autumn, the town council voted its own coal money to burn a light where no Board light had ever reached.

They built it plainly: an iron cage on a stone stand, a keeper's shed no bigger than a byre, and a boy paid a few coins a week to carry coal out along the mole in all weathers and keep the cage fed through the dark months, when the boats came home late and the rocks off the harbour mouth took a hull or two most winters that a light might have spared. The town called it nothing grander than the light, and burned it faithfully from the first frost.

The winter before the vote, a boat out of the town had come in through a fog so thick a man could not see the length of his own oar, and had found the harbour mouth only because her skipper had fished those rocks since he was a boy and could smell the change in the water before he could see the change in the light. Two boats that same winter had not been so fortunate, and lie yet, or lay then, broken on the same rocks the fog had hidden. It was that skipper, by the town's own telling, who stood up at the meeting that voted the coal money, and said that a harbour that could build a mole could build a light to stand on the end of it, and that the Crown's five lights had never once been built for a town too small to matter to anyone who did not live in it.

They wrote, too, in the same season, to Comhairle nan Taighean-solais at Cathair dhearg, asking that the light be taken onto the Board's roll and its coal paid from the Board's purse as the five older lights were paid. The letter that came back, some months later, on 25 an Gearran, SE 23, said that the Board's charter named five lights and no more, that a sixth had never been provided for, and that the town's own arrangement, being no charge upon the Crown, might continue exactly as it was.

It did continue exactly as it was, for the rest of the age. The boy who first carried the coal out along the mole grew old doing it, and trained his own boy to the work, and neither of them was ever paid by any hand but the town's own. Gormshuil, reading the Board's letter when a copy of it found its way south with the year's other papers, entered the refusal in four lines and no more, in much the manner Cathair dhearg's own council had once refused a wall it thought needless. She did not add that the fishermen of a town with no lighthouse of its own devising had, for as long as anyone there remembered, gone out and come home by no light but the moon and their own knowledge of the rocks.

## V. Of the Còmhrag

At Ceann leathan, two summers after the fair at Muileann òg had proved that the whole island would travel for a gathering if the gathering gave it reason, a smaller and rougher custom took its own first root. Men of the hewing towns had long settled disputes and simple boasts with their fists at the mine-head, on pay-days, under no rule but that a man who went down did not get up swinging; someone, nobody the Library can now name with certainty, thought to bring the custom to a field outside the town and dress it as a contest, with judges and a purse, so that the fighting that had always happened anyway might happen once a year, in daylight, where the fair-wardens could take a fee from every man who came to watch.

The first was fought on 4 am Màrt, SE 23, and they called it simply the Còmhrag, the melee; it drew men from every vein-town within two days' walk: Muileann dhearg sent the largest company, since its hewers had the most to prove and the least else to spend a wage on, and its lodging-houses emptied for the day into the crowd around the ropes. The rules, such as they were that first year, ran to little more than this: any man might enter who paid the fair-wardens' fee, no man might carry an edge, and the last man left inside the ropes took the purse. Nobody thought to write down more than that, because nobody expected the thing to need more than that, and for one summer they were right.

The field lay on rising ground outside the town where the fair-wardens had once grazed the fair's own horses, and by midday of the Còmhrag it held more people standing than Ceann leathan held in its beds. The ropes were strung in a rough square, four posts and a coil borrowed from the harbour store, and inside them the crowd that had paid its fee to fight stood together at one corner while the crowd that had paid its fee to watch pressed close on every other side, close enough that a man knocked hard against the rope felt the whole weight of the watchers lean into it with him. There was no bell to open the bout and no bell to close it; a fair-warden with a horn from a captain's old muster-call blew it once at noon, and the fighting did not properly stop again until the light was going and one man alone still stood inside the ropes.

Two men did not walk out of the ropes that first year. The Library's own words for it, entered by Gormshuil from the fair-wardens' own report and nothing more, run to a single sentence: the dead of the first Còmhrag were buried at Ceann leathan within the week, and the melee was fought again the following summer regardless. She was asked once, years afterward, by a visiting scholar, whether the chronicle ought not to have said more of who they were. She answered that the report she had been sent gave her nothing more to say, and that she had never yet found it her office to invent what a report withheld.

The man who won that first Còmhrag was a hewer out of Muileann chrom named Calum mac Aonghais, whom the crowd was already calling Calum Ruadh before the last bout was decided, for the colour of his hair and the state of his face by the end of it. He was young for the work he did underground, younger still for the crowd that carried him on its shoulders the length of the field when the judges called it, and he took the purse, a year's wages counted out on a trestle table by the fair-wardens' own clerk, and the second prize besides, which was the right, entered that same evening on the shire's roll at Ceann leathan, to bear arms in any shire of the kingdom for the rest of his life.

He had not looked, by the accounts that reached Muileann chaol afterward, like a man built for winning. A quarryman out of Baile thais, twice his age and half again his weight, had put him down twice in the first hour and stood over him laughing the second time, and it was said in the town afterward that Calum got up the second time only because the crowd nearest him had begun, without much kindness, to place their bets against him staying down, and a man will get up for less reason than that when there is a whole field watching. He did not win by any skill anybody could later describe in much detail; he won, the town agreed, by refusing for six hours to stay on the ground longer than it took him to breathe, until every man larger than him had either gone down himself or grown too tired to make use of being larger.

It was a strange gift to give a hewer, and everyone at the field that evening seemed to feel the strangeness of it a little, though nobody said so aloud. A man who spent his days with a pick and his nights in a lodging-house by the sidings had, by the ropes and the purse and a shire clerk's signature, become in the eyes of the law something his father had never been and his sons might never be again: a man the kingdom would let go armed. The inn-keepers of Ceann leathan, four of whom had built new houses that year purely to hold the crowd the Còmhrag brought, kept his table free of charge that night, and would go on doing so, by a custom nobody formally agreed to, for as long as he came back to fight.

He did not fight again that season. He walked out of the town before dawn the next morning, the purse in his coat and the shire clerk's paper folded inside it, and took the coal road north toward Muileann chrom on foot, alone, past the fair-wardens' new inns with their shutters still up and the field where the ropes had been taken down in the night, leaving nothing behind him but two flattened circles of grass and a debt the Còmhrag's keepers would spend the winter arguing over how best to collect from next year's crowd. Besides the purse he carried the right to go armed through any shire on the island, a right his own father, a hewer before him at the same face, had never held. For that one autumn it was simply his, earned with his own hands in a field outside a mining town, and he walked home with it the way a man walks home from work that has gone, on the whole, well: tired, a little proud, and not looking back.

# Chapter Twenty-one: Of the Sea-Feast Turned Away

*SE 24 am Màrt – SE 26 an Gearran*

> We ask that the widows of the Cuan bheag drowning be heard in this Moot on the same footing as any man who has paid his due, and heard first, since it is their dead we are speaking of and not our own.
>
> — a motion of the Moot at Caol mhòr, 10 am Màrt, SE 24, entire, as the Library renders it

## I. Of the Dock, the Twentieth, and the Names Given to Children

In these years the fair at Muileann òg was not the only place the shire's coin went to make stone stand up out of mud. At Ros gheal on the north-central coast the town gave over its whole spring to a dock built long enough to take three grain-ships lying abreast, for the Hawk country sent its barley and its oats down by cart no longer but by water, and the water paid better. The Hawk houses came down from Cnoc bheag to bless the stones before the first ship warped in, and asked, as the price of the blessing, a tithe of whatever the dock earned. The shire's factor haggled them down to a twentieth, and paid it, and has paid it every quarter since, so that to this day the clerks of Ros gheal call the due simply the Hawk's, and few of them could now say why a fishing town owes a grain due to a bird that flies inland.

It was a green early summer, that same year, when the shunting families of Muileann chrom, who lived apart in their rows beside the little engines and were counted apart in every roll the council kept, had a great crop of children born to them all at once, more than the row had cradles for. Two of that crowd were named Seachran and Brean, and of them, and of the rest born that season, this book says nothing more, for they had done nothing yet, and a chronicle that ran ahead of a child's life would not be a chronicle at all.

Further south that year, Seann Bhral on the southern coast, not the older Seann Bhral of the west, which is a different town and always has been, passed Ros dhomhain in the weight of fish landed, and its curing-sheds, which had been four, became eleven, and ran the whole length of the harbour so that a stranger walking it after dark could follow the smoke and not see the water at all. And near Seann Chwen, on the same coast, a travelling show pitched its poles for the first time, calling itself An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn, and the clerk who wrote its arrival into the local roll noted that he could not say what its acts were meant to show, nor, he added, could the crowd that filled the field to watch them, and came back the second night larger than the first.

These are the things the Library keeps of that year in the south: a dock, a due, a crowd of children too young to be named for anything but themselves, more fish than the year before, and a show nobody could explain and everybody paid to see twice. The clerk at Seann Chwen who could not say what the acts were meant to show tried, in his own defence, to set down what he had seen: a woman who walked a rope strung between two masts with her eyes bound in cloth; a man who ate fire from a spoon and spat smoke for a full minute after; a dog that counted to nine by barking and never, that the clerk could tell, miscounted. He gave it up as a bad job and wrote instead that the show had taken a good many pennies of the realm-coin from Seann Chwen in one night and would likely take as many more before it moved on, which was the kind of fact a roll could hold.

In the north the year is kept by a different kind of ledger. It begins with who stood up to speak.

## II. Of Mary Coyle Standing Up

The Moot's house at Caol mhòr had one door, low enough that a tall man ducked for it out of habit whether the lintel needed it or not, and inside, a table that had been a ship's hatch-cover before somebody planed it flat and gave it legs, the grain of it still showing the pattern of the rope that had once run over it in a coil. A stove at the far end took the worst of the chill off the room and none of the rest; men and women kept their coats on through every sitting from am Faoilleach to an Cèitean, and the breath of forty people in the small room fogged the one window until David Hale kept a rag on a string beside it, to wipe a clear patch for whatever daylight was left by the time the meeting rose.

Walter Hale sat at the head of the table still, an old man now, his hearing going, and he let the meeting run long past its hour because he had stopped trusting himself to know when an hour was up. He had chaired the Moot since before most of the room now sitting in it could walk, and the younger clerks had begun, that year, to write his rulings down twice, once as he gave them and once as David Hale judged he had meant them, in case the two should ever need reconciling.

Mary Coyle had come to every sitting of the Moot since the westerly took her husband and ten other men off Cuan bheag five years before, and for five years she had sat at the back near the door with the other widows. There were, that winter, eleven of them who came regular, in a pew of their own though nobody had built it as a pew, simply the bench nearest the door where a woman could slip out early if a child needed fetching. She had passed notes up when she had something to say, because that was how it was done, and nobody had told her different, and she had not thought to ask. Agnes Tulloch, who sat beside her most nights and had lost a brother on the same boat, used to fold the notes into the smallest square her fingers could manage before they went forward, as if a small enough fold might make the asking smaller too.

That night the matter before the Moot was the grain-ships. Ros gheal had agreed its twentieth with the Hawk houses, and the northern boats that had begun that year to land their fish at the new dock were to pay the same twentieth on what they landed, out of the Moot's common harbour purse; and that purse took its coin, in part, from a levy on every fishing family in the north, widows included, for the upkeep of the harbour lights. The widows of Cuan bheag had heard nothing of it until the coin was already gone. The man reading the account, a Moot clerk named for the evening only, ran through the figures in the flat unhurried voice of someone who did not expect to be stopped, and would not have thought to stop himself if he had known what was coming.

"We pay into that purse the same as any man," Mary Coyle said, standing, "and we have never once been asked what it should buy."

The room did not so much fall silent as forget, for a moment, what it had been doing. Nobody at the table had heard her speak before without a note going up first, folded small, for a man near the front to read out in her stead, in his own voice, so that the words arrived at the table already once removed from the mouth that made them.

Hale cupped a hand to his better ear. "Say that again, and stand where I can hear you."

She came round the table, past the stove, past the clerk with his flat voice stopped mid-figure, and said it again, louder, close enough now that Hale did not need the hand at his ear. "We pay into that purse the same as any man. Every quarter, out of what little the season leaves us. And no one has asked a widow of Cuan bheag what she would have that money spent on, though it is our dead the harbour lights are meant to warn other men's boats away from the rocks that took them."

"That is a fair question," Hale said, when he had turned it over, "and I do not know that anyone has ever put it to this table before."

"No one has," said Mary Coyle. "I have sat at the back of this room five years and watched other men's notes read out and voted on, and I thought, tonight, that I would rather be wrong to my own face than right in somebody else's mouth."

There was a laugh at that, not unkind, and one or two of the older men who had known Thomas Coyle rapped their knuckles on the table the way they would for a man's speech they approved.
