David Hale, the old man's son, kept the day-book at the Moot's elbow, and he wrote down what she said nearly word for word, because it was the first time in the minutes that any woman's speech was set down whole rather than summed in a line ("the widow Coyle spoke") as the clerks had always done before, when they troubled to note a woman's speaking at all.

It was resolved, before that sitting rose, that the widows of the drowned should be heard in the Moot on the same footing as any man who had paid his due, and heard first when the matter touched their own dead. Agnes Tulloch, from the bench by the door, was the one who moved that it be written down as a standing rule and not a courtesy for one night only, and old Hale, who had chaired the Moot longer than either woman had been widowed, said he could not see why it had taken the room so long to think of it, which was as near as he came, in front of the whole Moot, to admitting that it had not occurred to him either.

David Hale copied the motion twice, once into the day-book and once onto a loose sheet that Mary Coyle folded into her shawl and carried home, because she did not yet trust a book she could not open herself to keep a thing said.

She did not sit at the back again.

## III. Of the Muster for Seann Bhral

It was old Hale himself, turning the matter over by his fire that spring, who put the thought in her head, though he never claimed it after. "My grandfather," he said, "used to tell of a feast of the sea the western harbours kept at summer's end, for the safe return of the boats. He said our own folk learned it from the Dia-thìrich of those harbours in the first years after the Crossing, when the harbours still took in whoever came off a boat."

"Do we still keep it?"

"We keep the *shape* of it. A blessing at the boats, in an Gearran, before the season proper starts. But the old feast, the one it comes from, they keep still, he said, at a house on the west coast. Seann Bhral. Not this one." He tapped the table, meaning the near one, the fishing port to the south they had all heard of that year on account of its curing-sheds. "The other Seann Bhral. The first one."

Mary Coyle turned it over for the better part of a month, and what she found, asking among the older crews, bore Hale out: that the house of Manannan's order at Seann Bhral in the west was reckoned the oldest on that coast, and that some memory persisted, thin as a rope worn to its last strands, that the Tuathaich forebears had once been welcome at its feast of the sea, in the years just after the Crossing, before the island had settled into a kingdom with a north side and a south.

She put it to the Moot in an t-Iuchar: that a fleet of the northern boats should sail west-about, round the capes, to keep the feast where it had first been kept, as their own people's memory said they were owed the right to do. The Moot argued it two full sittings before it agreed. Nobody spoke against the sea-feast itself; half the room thought it a fool's errand all the same, to sail eleven boats round the worst capes on the island at the tail of the summer for a welcome that was not certain, and said so, plainly, and were not wrong to wonder it. Mary Coyle did not argue that they were wrong. She said only that a certainty was not what she was asking the Moot to send her after, and that she would go herself whatever the vote, with whoever chose to come, and the Moot, having heard that, voted to send its blessing after her rather than let her sail without it.

It was not a large fleet in the end. Eleven boats put out from Caol mhòr and Cuan bheag and Ros mhòr on a grey morning at the end of an Lùnastal, laden with little beyond themselves and the coin for the harbour dues at the far end, a keg of salt fish apiece to see them there and back, and, in the bottom of Mary Coyle's own boat, the folded sheet from the Moot's day-book that named her the one the north had sent. She sailed in the leading boat, not because she could handle a boat better than any man aboard (she could not, and said so plainly to the skipper who offered her the tiller out of courtesy the first morning, and he never offered it again) but because it had been her word that sent them, and she judged, rightly, that a thing said ought to be stood behind by the one who said it, in the bow if not at the helm.

The passage took the better part of four days, coasting inside the worst of the weather, putting in at night wherever a harbour would have them, which was not everywhere; the harbour-master at Ros bheag, on their second night's road, would not let them tie up at the quay proper and sent them instead to a mooring buoy off the point, with a lantern for courtesy and nothing warmer than that. Two nights they lay at anchor in open bays with the watch kept turn and turn about against the swell, wrapped in whatever oilskin and wool could be spared, and men who had fished together twenty years found out, in those two nights, things about each other's snoring and each other's praying that they had somehow never learned in twenty years of ordinary weather. On the third a squall out of the south-west put green water over the bow of the smallest boat and near enough finished it before the crew bailed her clear with anything that would hold water, boots included; Mary Coyle, in the boat behind, watched the smaller craft vanish twice into the trough of a wave and come up twice still afloat, and said afterward that she had made herself a promise in that quarter-hour that she kept the rest of her life and never once told anyone the wording of. Nobody was lost. It was, more than one of them said afterward, the hardest four days most of them had known, and they measured them, as the north measured every hardship, against the Crossing itself, which none of them remembered and all of them had heard told.

## IV. Of the House That Said the Sea Was the Same

They came into Seann Bhral on the eve of the feast, eleven boats riding low with salt on everything, and moored where the harbour-master's boy showed them, at the outer wall, away from the fishing fleet proper. The house of Manannan's order stood above the harbour on its own terrace, older than anything else in the town by the look of its stonework, its doorposts carved with a wave-pattern worn nearly smooth by long ages of hands touching it on the way in.

Word of eleven Tuathaich boats standing in had gone up to the house before the last of them was moored, carried by a harbour boy quicker with his feet than his manners, and by the time Mary Coyle and two of the older skippers climbed the terrace steps a small crowd of the town's own fisherfolk had gathered at the wall below to see what would come of it, some curious and some, by their faces, already certain.

The keeper who came out to them was a tall, spare man, not unkind in his manner, who heard Mary Coyle out to the end without once interrupting her, which she took, wrongly, for a good sign. She had rehearsed the asking the whole four days of the passage, turning the words over at the tiller and in the night watches until she judged she had them worn smooth, and she gave it to him now much as she had made it to herself: that the Tuathaich forebears had kept the feast of the sea at this house once, in the first years after the Crossing, before ever there was a kingdom with a north side to it; that the memory of it was thin in the north now but not gone; and that eleven boats had sailed a hard four days on the strength of that thin memory, asking nothing more than to stand at the harbour and see the rite done, and perhaps to say a word of their own over it, if the house would permit that much.

"You have the right of the history," he said, when she had finished. "It is true that in the first years the harbours took in whoever came off a boat, and asked no questions of blood before they let a man to the fire. I do not deny you that. But the order that keeps this house now keeps it for those who hold the rite of Manannan as it is held today, by right of blood and by the custodian's book, and that is not a thing four days' hard sailing can put right, however justly you sailed them."

"We are not asking for the rite," said Mary Coyle. "We are asking for the feast. Our own priests can say what needs saying over it."

"The feast is the rite," the keeper said, not unkindly, and that was the whole of his answer, said once and not repeated, though she asked it three further ways before she judged that a fourth would only make a hard thing harder to carry home. "The sea is the same sea it always was," he told her at the last, seeing her face, and meaning, she understood after, to soften it rather than close it further. "It is the house that is not the same house it was."

One of the skippers who had climbed the terrace with her, a hard, plain man named for nothing gentler than his trade, asked the keeper straight out whether it was blood he meant, or coin, since the house looked in no want of either. The keeper did not take offence at it. "Both, in their way," he said. "The order keeps this house on tithes from families who have held the rite for ages. If I let in every boat that could show a claim on the old welcome, I would have no house left to keep it in by the second winter, and no order behind me either. I do not say that gladly. I say it because it is true, and I would rather tell you a true hard thing than a soft one that costs me nothing."

She did not answer that, then. She has been reported, by more than one of the crews who stood behind her on the quay that evening, to have looked a long while at the carved doorposts before she turned back to the boats, the wave-pattern worn smooth by hands she would never be able to count and none of which were now hers to add to, and to have said nothing at all until she was aboard, at which point she said only that they would sail on the morning tide, and slept, or lay still enough to be thought asleep, through a night none of the rest of the eleven boats' crews slept much through at all. Below on the harbour wall a few of the town's own fisherfolk had stayed on past dark, and one woman among them, whose name the Library has not kept, came down to the boats with a jug of something hot before she went home, and said only that she was sorry for it, which was more than the house above had said, and which Mary Coyle remembered, she told people afterward, longer than she remembered the keeper's own words.

## V. Of the Feast They Made Their Own

The passage home took five days against a headwind that had not troubled them going out, and nobody aboard the eleven boats said much of anything about Seann Bhral for the length of it, beyond what was needed to work the sail and the helm. It was on the third day, off the northern capes, that one of the Ros mhòr men, an old hand who had said little the whole voyage, asked Mary Coyle plainly what she meant to do now, since the west would not have them.

"Keep it anyway," she said. "Not their feast. Ours."

She did not mean, and said she did not mean, to invent a rite out of nothing; she meant the blessing of the boats that the north already kept in a thin, half-remembered way each spring at the great church at Cnoc ghorm, and to make of it, deliberately and in full, the feast that Seann Bhral had refused them the whole of. It was decided among the crews before they raised Caol mhòr again, and the decision cost nothing but the saying of it, which by then Mary Coyle had some practice in.

Word of it went round the north coast faster than the eleven boats themselves had sailed, carried by every crew that had been on the passage and told, in every kitchen it reached, a little larger than it had left the last one; by the time an Gearran came round, boats were promising to come from as far as Inis mhin's country, a fair way further than any of the eleven had gone west. On the second Sunday of an Gearran, in SE 26, the boats of the north coast that could be got to Cnoc ghorm in a day's sail or a morning's cart were drawn up on carts and trestles in the field below the church, the hulls brought overland from the nearer harbours, more than fifty of them by the count David Hale kept for the day-book, far more than had ever gathered at Cnoc ghorm for the old thin blessing in any year before. The priest of An Eaglais who kept that parish, a young man new to the charge and glad of the crowd whatever brought it, said the old words over each hull in turn, dipping a bundle of dried heather in a bucket of harbour water and shaking it across bow and stern while the crews stood bareheaded in the cold, their breath going up white over the field in a line as long as the boats themselves. Mary Coyle's own boat, the one that had carried her both ways to the west, was blessed fourth in the row, and she stood at its bow through the whole of the rite with her hands folded and her shawl pulled close, and said nothing to anyone until it was done.

Afterward there was food on trestles set up in the churchyard, brought by whoever had a little to spare that week, and someone had got a fiddle working despite the cold, and the thing that had begun as eleven boats sailing west at the summer's end ended, that evening, as a crowd in a churchyard field that did not, by any account written down afterward, look like a people who had been turned away from anything at all.

The Library keeps this much of what followed: that the north kept its own Fleadh na Mara at Cnoc ghorm every year after, on the same Sunday, without asking leave of any house on the west coast again, and that within a generation more boats came to it than had ever, in the memory of anyone living, gone to the feast at Seann Bhral. Whether the house on the west coast ever heard how it had grown, the Library does not know, and has found no one who thought to write and tell it.

# Chapter Twenty-two: Of Iain Mapa's Survey

*SE 26 am Màrt – SE 27 an t-Iuchar*

> Received of Iain mac Ruairidh, called Iain Mapa, one survey of the faces of the Sloc Mòr, rolled and tied, this day. Filed.
>
> — the Mine Board's receipt, 9 an Cèitean, SE 26, entire, as the Library renders it

## I. Of the Faces of the Sloc Mòr

Iain mac Ruairidh was thirty-two years old and had spent the better part of a year on his knees, or bent double, or flat on his belly on stone that was always either wet or freezing, with a lamp on a string round his neck and a chain that two other men held taut while he called the figures back to them over his shoulder. He was a chainman by his first trade and a surveyor by the Board's later reckoning, and he had come up through the Sloc Mòr the slow way, gallery by gallery, learning the mountain's faces the way another man might learn a woman's, by long acquaintance and no great ceremony about it. He thought of himself as careful rather than clever, which the Board valued more, or said it did.

What he had found, over that year, he had not gone looking for. He had gone into the eastern galleries with the ordinary work of the season, to true up an old survey against the new digging and settle a dispute between two overseers about where one man's cutting ended and another's began, and he had come out of it with a set of figures that would not lie flat no matter which way he turned them. The vein was thinning, badly nowhere yet: to the east it ran narrower than the old maps showed, and to the south it pinched again in the same proportion, as if the mountain had made up its mind about something years before and only now got round to telling anyone.

He checked it twice before he let himself believe it, because a man who tells the Mine Board a thing it does not want to hear had better be right, and a third time because rightness alone, in his experience, was protection for no one. Working the eastern faces again at speed, chain out to its full length and back, in the wet cold of the spring with water finding its way down the back of his collar no matter how he stood, he got the same figures each time, to within an inch the chain itself could account for, and set them down in the plainest words he had: thinning to east and south, in a hand that did not shake, and did not argue.

The whole of it he drew fair on a single long sheet, rolled and tied with the plain string the Board's own store issued for the purpose, and carried himself the thirty-one miles from the Sloc Mòr to Cathair dhearg rather than send it by the carters, for a thing that mattered, in his experience, travelled better in a man's own hand than in anyone else's.

He had told no one at the Sloc Mòr what the figures showed, not the two men who had held his chain for him nor the overseer whose dispute had set him onto the eastern galleries in the first place, though both had asked, in the ordinary way men ask a surveyor coming up out of the dark what he has found down there. He had said only that the old maps wanted correcting, which was true as far as it went and told them nothing they could carry off and repeat, and he had told himself, walking the road south with the roll under his arm and the weather coming up cold off the hills, that this was caution and not cowardice, though he turned the distinction over more than once before he reached the capital and did not come to rest on it either way. The road ran two days by cart or a day and a half on foot at a hard pace, and he took the second, sleeping the one night at a carters' inn on the road where nobody asked his business and he offered none, and came into Cathair dhearg on the morning of the second day with the roll dry under his coat and his boots ruined by the last mile of it, which had run wet the whole way.

## II. Of the Receipt

The Board sat that season in three low rooms behind the old counting-house at Cathair dhearg, the same rooms it had sat in since the Sloc Mòr concession was first granted, with a single window between the three of them that let in less light than a man might have wished for reading survey work. Iain was shown in by a clerk who did not ask his business, because his business was written plainly enough on the roll under his arm, and he stood in front of a table at which three men sat, none of whom he had met before, though he knew all three by name the way a chainman knows the men who sign his wages.

He laid the roll on the table in front of them and untied the string himself, because it seemed to him the courteous thing, and waited for one of them to unroll it. None of them did. The man in the middle, who was older than the other two and dressed a shade better, put two fingers on the near edge of the sheet, as if to hold it down against a wind that was not blowing in that room, and left it at that.

"You've come far," he said, which was not a question and did not want an answer.

Iain gave him the short of it anyway, because he had walked thirty-one miles to say it and meant to say it whether it was asked for or not: the vein was thinning to east and south, the figures were on the sheet, the old maps wanted correcting, and a man ought to know it who was deciding where the next year's galleries went. He said it plainly, the way he had written it, without dressing it in anything worse or better than what the ground had told him.

The three men looked at the roll, and then at each other, and not very long at either.

"It will be considered," said the one in the middle.

Iain had walked thirty-one miles carrying a thing he believed, and he had thought, on the road, about a good many ways this hour might go, most of them worse than this one, some of them shouting. He had not thought about this one, a short sentence and a closed door behind it, and it took him a moment to find his own voice again, and when he did it was smaller than he had meant it to be, though it did not waver.

"I should like a receipt," he said.

The clerk at the side table looked at him as a man looks at another who has asked for something unaccountable in that room; no one told him no, and after a silence in which the three men at the table seemed to consult each other without a word passing between them, the youngest of the three nodded at the clerk, who took up a pen, wrote a few lines on a scrap no bigger than his own palm, and passed it across for the man in the middle to sign. He did not. He passed it on to the third man at the table, a broad, unhurried man named Ruairidh mac Ailein, who read what was written, found nothing in it he cared to argue with, and signed his own name under it without comment, in a hand a good deal quicker than the clerk's.

*Received of Iain mac Ruairidh, called Iain Mapa, one survey of the faces of the Sloc Mòr, rolled and tied, this day. Filed.* Nothing more. No word of what the survey said, no word of thinning or of east and south, nothing that a man reading it afterward, with no other knowledge, could have told from what it had cost to get.

Iain folded it once and put it in his pocket-book, where it lay against the ribs on the walk home closer than the coin he carried, and he thanked the room, which did not seem to expect thanks and did not offer any back, and went out past the clerk into the ordinary daylight of Cathair dhearg's street, which struck him, for a moment, as a strange place for nothing at all to have happened in.

The roll stayed on the table when he left it, and by the account the Library keeps of that room's business it was filed within the week, in a press with the two years' surveys before it, and shown to no one. Within the month Iain mac Ruairidh was told, without much explanation offered and none asked for, that he was wanted at the silver works at Muileann chiar, twenty-four miles east and a little south, where the Board had need of a man who could hold a chain straight and did not ask more questions than the work required.

He asked, once, of the clerk who brought him the posting, whether the move had anything to do with the survey he had carried in himself the month before, and the clerk, a younger man than the three at the table and not unkind, said only that he could not say, which Iain took to mean that the clerk could say and had chosen not to, and did not ask a second time. He asked nothing at all of Ruairidh mac Ailein, whom he passed in the corridor on his way out of the counting-house that same week and who nodded to him civilly enough, as one working man nods to another whose trade he has some respect for, and said nothing of the receipt he had signed, and Iain said nothing of it either, and the two of them went their ways down the same corridor without either mentioning the thing that stood between them, which was, Iain thought afterward, very much the manner of the Board in everything it did.

## III. Of the Rule Made at Cathair mhòr

The Library at Muileann chaol tells the rest of that year in fewer words than it gave to the receipt, and it is worth setting down what little it does say, because the Board's own account of itself, where the Board troubled to keep one, is thinner still.

The Mine Board had sat at Cathair dhearg since the Sloc Mòr concession was first cut, close by the counting-house whose rooms it borrowed and the mint that struck the coin its shafts paid for. In am Faoilleach of the following year it moved its clerks and its presses the sixteen miles to Cathair mhòr, into rooms taken on lease above the town's own wool market, on the stated ground that a board charged with the mountain's business ought to sit nearer the mountain than it had. No one who wrote of the move at the time troubled to explain why sixteen miles nearer counted for so much, when thirty-one had done well enough for the years before, and the Library, which asked the question of every clerk still living who might have answered it, records only that none of them thought the question worth much of a reply.

With the move the Board set down, in the plainest of its own minutes, a rule that had not existed in writing before that year, though men who had dealt with the Board a long while said afterward that it had always been the practice and only now got its own sentence: that the surveys of the Board's own men were to be kept at Cathair mhòr, in the Board's own presses, and were not to be sent on to the Library at Muileann chaol as the reports of other offices were sent, by the standing order that had governed the state's paper since Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill first asked every shire for its books. The rule gave no reason for itself beyond the Board's own convenience in having its working papers to hand, and it was written in four lines, and it was never once, in all the years it stood, brought before the council to be confirmed or struck down, because no one outside the Board's own rooms had reason to know it existed at all.

The Library, setting this down at the age's close with every paper the state ever sent it laid open on the table, notes only this: that from the year the rule was made until the year it was at last broken, the Board's surveys of the Sloc Mòr's faces went nowhere but into the Board's own presses, and that among them, filed and never circulated, lay the sheet Iain mac Ruairidh had carried thirty-one miles and a receipt had been the whole of his payment for.

No one on the council was asked to confirm the rule, and no one on the council thought to ask after it, for the Board's business had always been counted a small, dry corner of the state's affairs, more like a mill's own account book than a matter of law, and the men who sat on the council in those years had grain and roads and the fair at Muileann òg to occupy them, and little patience left over for a mountain that had, on the face of things, gone on giving as freely as it always had. The wool market's factor let the rooms to the Board gladly enough, for the rent was steady and the Board's clerks were quiet tenants who kept regular hours and troubled the market's own business not at all, and if he ever wondered what papers the Board kept upstairs that could not travel the sixteen miles on to Muileann chaol with every other office's, he left no word of the wondering behind him.

## IV. Of Small Trades and a Forbidden Night

Not every year's business was the mountain's. At Seann Vell on the capital shore, in those same seasons, the glass-houses that had lately begun blowing small flasks found a trade nobody had planned for them: the women of the town took to filling the flasks with waters they distilled themselves from bog-myrtle and meadowsweet and the honey pressed from heather, and selling them by the dozen to carters bound for the market towns of the western plain. Within a year or two the plain's own towns had taken the trade up on their own account, so that a woman travelling that country could buy the same scent from three different hands in three different towns and be told, by each, that it was made nowhere but where she stood. It was a small thing, and the Library sets it down chiefly because it happened in the same year as larger things that left less behind them: a magistrate's fine, a boat kept for a relic, a survey filed and forgotten. The glass-houses of Seann Vell are still standing, and the small trade in scent still runs from them, longer-lived by a good margin than the rule the Board made that same year and never told the council of.

Further north, at Baile chrom on the far cape where the lighthouse stood, the vigil-keeper Hannah Crane had for some years kept the vigil of the Grey Night in the open, on the headland below the light, as no keeper before her had kept it. In the summer of that same year a Dia-thìreach magistrate new to the district, who had heard the vigil described to him as an unruly gathering by men who had never troubled to watch one, forbade it as disorderly and had Hannah Crane brought before him and fined. She paid what she could of it herself and could not pay the rest, and word of the fine went south with the wool carts and reached the Moot at Caol mhòr before the summer was out. The Moot, which had by then grown used to paying for things the north's own purses could not quite stretch to, voted the balance of her fine out of its own small chest without much debate, on the motion of a councillor who said only that a woman fined for sitting on a headland in the cold and saying nothing to anyone was not, in his judgement, a threat the Moot need trouble itself to agree with.

The vigil did not stop. It went indoors, into a byre lent for the purpose by a family who kept the old rite themselves and asked no questions of those who came to it, and it was kept there, one night a year, in a silence the magistrate's order could not reach any better than it had reached the shingle, because a rule made against a sound cannot be made against its absence. Outsiders were still not told which night it was. The Library, which has asked, is not told either.

## V. Of the Boat Kept for a Relic

Far to the south, on the coast the Great Wave had scoured clean a generation before, the harbour at Cuan dhearg was opened again that same season, with a new mole of dressed stone laid where the old one had gone under the water in a single night. The masons who built it were largely the sons of the men who had lost the first harbour, and more than one of them said, working the stone, that they were laying it heavier than their fathers had, against a wave that had not troubled the coast again in all the years between, and that nobody in Cuan dhearg had stopped thinking about all the same.

The first boat warped into the new harbour was not a new boat at all. Among the hulls that the wave had cast up into the fields behind the old town, and that had lain there through more than twenty years of grass growing up around their ribs, one had been found sound enough, when the harbour-master's men went out to look at what the fields still held, to be dragged back down to the water and caulked and floated. It went in first, ahead of every boat built new for the rebuilt harbour, and the harbour-master, a woman named for her own grandmother who had drowned in the wave without ever seeing a harbour again, kept it afterward as a relic rather than putting it back to work, mooring it at the head of the quay where every boat coming in or going out passed close by it. The fishermen of Cuan dhearg came to call it simply the boat of the field, and told strangers, if they asked, that it had come home the long way round, by way of the barley, and taken its time about it.

## VI. Of Muileann chiar

Iain mac Ruairidh had come to Muileann chiar at the start of the summer the receipt was given, with his chain and his lamp and the pocket-book that held, among its other pages, the receipt the Board had given him, and he found the silver works a smaller business than the Sloc Mòr and a stranger one, the veins running in thin bright seams through rock that gave up its secrets more readily than coal ever had, if a man knew how to read the seams at all. He was set to measuring the eastern faces against the old plans, much as he had been set to the same work at the Sloc Mòr, and the overseer who took him on said only that the Board had sent word he was careful, which was, the overseer added, more than the Board generally troubled to say of anyone.

The town itself he found smaller too, and quieter, built along a single burn that the silver-washers used and that ran, by the season, either a clean brown or a faint grey depending on how the works upstream were going, and the guild that held the silver had kept its charter through the humans' time and into the restored kingdom without much interruption to its own ways, so that the men he worked beside spoke of the vein as a thing with moods of its own, to be coaxed rather than merely measured, in a manner the coal men at the Sloc Mòr would have thought soft. He did not think it soft, once he had spent a season at it. The silver ran truer to the old plans than the coal had, faces holding where the maps said they would hold, and there were weeks that spring and into the summer when he went a full day without once thinking of the sheet he had carried to Cathair dhearg, which he counted, when he noticed it, a kind of rest.

It did not last the whole season. A letter came to him the following summer, forwarded on from the Sloc Mòr by a clerk who thought he might want to see it, from one of the two men who had held his chain for him the year before, asking, in a rough hand and rougher spelling, whether the eastern galleries had been given up yet, since the overseer at the Sloc Mòr had begun talking of opening new ground to the west instead, where the going was harder but the yield, by the overseer's own reckoning, steadier. Iain read it twice and wrote back a short answer that said he had no way of knowing what the Board meant to do with the ground he had surveyed, which was true, and did not say what he privately believed, which was that the Board meant to do nothing with it at all beyond keeping it filed, because a mountain that has been told, in writing, that it is running out does not stop giving simply because the men who own it have chosen not to read the letter.

He did not speak of the survey he had left behind him, not to the overseer and not to the men who worked the faces alongside him, and if any of them wondered why a chainman with a name for care had been moved on so quickly from a working as large as the Sloc Mòr to one so much smaller, none of them asked him to his face, and he offered nothing. What he did, on his first free evening at Muileann chiar, in the room he had taken above a cooper's yard, was to take the pocket-book out and lay the receipt flat on the table under the lamp, and read it through once more, though he had it near enough by heart already, and then he took a pin from the small tin he kept for mending his own coat and pinned the scrap of paper into the back leaves of the book he kept his working figures in, where it would not fall out and could not easily be lost, and where, he thought, it would still be found by whoever came after him, whether that was the Board or no one at all.

He did not write beside it what it meant to him, because he was not a man who wrote such things down even when he thought them, and the figures on the sheet he had carried to Cathair dhearg said, as far as he was concerned, everything that needed saying about the vein and about the mountain and about what the Board had chosen to do with the knowing of it. But he kept the receipt pinned in his book from that evening on, through every posting the Board sent him to afterward, a small square of paper that said only that a thing had been received and filed, and nothing at all of what the thing had been, and he carried it, in the years that followed, the way another man might carry a debt he meant, sooner or later, to see paid.

# Chapter Twenty-three: Of the Bare Entry

*SE 28 am Faoilleach – SE 29 an t-Ògmhios*

## I. Of Achadh mhin's Fields

The clerk who carried the shire's return up from the south-west that winter was young enough to think the news in it worth a second horse, and rode the last stage in the dark to save the half-day it would have cost him to wait for light. Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill read it at her own table at Muileann chaol by a single lamp, the household long abed, and found nothing in it that a fresh horse had been worth, which was not the same as finding nothing in it at all.

Achadh mhin's fields bore again. It was the plainest sentence the shire clerk had ever sent her: the barley had come up along the old strips, the salt long since rained out of ground that had lain under the Great Wave's tide-mark for a generation, and three of the households that the council had moved off it in the year of the wave, or their children in their place, had asked and been granted their old ground back, measured out to the same lines the humans' surveyors had cut before any Dia-thìreach clerk had thought to draw a shire on top of them. The shire had gone to the trouble of the old humans' plat rather than draw new bounds of its own, since the old lines were the ones the families still walked by memory, their grandparents having farmed inside them, and a boundary a family can find in the dark by the line of a hedge is worth more than one a surveyor can find at noon with a chain.

She wrote the entry in four lines, gave it the category the record gave such things, and noted, because she always noted it when she could, the day the return had reached her and not only the day the fields were sown. It went into the chronicle between a drought at Baile chiar and a wedding at Doire shean, one line among the ordinary traffic of a kingdom's year, and she thought no more of it that night than she thought of any entry once it was written and the ink dry.

One of the three households was named in the return, since the shire clerk had thought it worth the ink: a family that had farmed the northernmost of the drowned strips before the wave, moved inland to a cousin's holding for a generation, and come back that spring to find the old boundary stone still standing where the tide had left it, tilted but not thrown down, and had righted it themselves before troubling the shire for a measurer at all. Gormshuil kept that detail out of the chronicle's own entry, which had no room for a family's name among a shire's ordinary returns, but she copied it into the private book she had kept these several years and showed to no one, on the ground that a record built only of what the office required would in the end tell a reader less about the kingdom's year than the office already knew, and that somebody, someday, might have use of the difference.

She thought more of it three weeks later, when the second courier came, this one no less young but riding no faster than the roads allowed, since nothing in his bag would be helped by haste and everything in it would be hurt by a torn seal. Gormshuil had kept the chronicle ten years by then and knew the weight of a packet by its wrapping before she broke it: a shire's ordinary return came loose in a merchant's satchel; a council packet came sealed twice, once by the clerk who wrote it and once by whoever above him had read it and agreed it should go. This one was sealed twice.

She broke it standing, which she did not usually do, and read it standing too, which she did even less, and when she had read it through she sat down at the same table where she had entered Achadh mhin's barley and found that her hand, reaching for a fresh sheet, was steadier than she had any right to expect, and steadier, she thought afterward, than the news deserved.

## II. Of the Bare Entry

Brìghde was dead, and the packet gave no more of the matter than that. It gave the day. No cause was made known, in words that made plain the office writing them expected the phrase to be believed and did not much mind whether it was. Eòghan, Brìghde's cousin, had been crowned within the week by Macha's rite, as the rite required when a throne could not sit empty past a certain number of days, and a line added at the foot, in a different, hastier hand, said that the council's own sitting on the matter had not passed as quietly as the crowning that followed it.

Gormshuil sat a long while with the sheet in front of her and wrote nothing. She had, in ten years, buried one king and crowned another, and had let one phrase into the record for it, weighed for a night and kept for good; she had told herself then that a chronicler who let herself one ornament, chosen with care, was safer than a chronicler who let herself none and then, some later year, gave way all at once to a worse one under worse pressure. She believed that still. It was not, she found, sitting with the lamp burning down and the packet's two seals broken on the table in front of her, an answer to the question the second death put to her, because the second death was not the same question as the first.

*Mar a thàinig Niall* had cost her nothing to write because it had cost the kingdom nothing to hear. A king had died in his middle years, and had been followed by a daughter nobody contested; the sentence she had borrowed had been light because the year it described had been light. This year was not light. A queen had died young, of a cause the office that wrote to her did not name and, by the turn of the sentence, did not intend ever to name, and the crowning that followed her had gone through a council sitting hard enough that someone thought the fact of its hardness worth adding in a different hand, though not worth explaining. A chronicler who reached for a soft phrase now, having reached for one once before, would not be choosing an ornament. She would be choosing a habit, and a habit chosen at the one moment the record most wanted to speak plainly was a habit chosen exactly wrong.

She wrote three drafts before she wrote the one that stood. The first ran to six lines and said, without quite saying it, that a young death was a hard death for a chronicler to leave unremarked, which she struck through before the ink was dry, on the ground that a reader wants to know what happened and has no use for what the chronicler found hard. The second ran to two lines and said only the day and the fact, and she looked at it a long time before striking it too, because a chronicle that gave a queen's death two bare lines when it had given the last one a name for what came after read, to her own eye, less like restraint and more like a door pulled shut on purpose, and a shut door draws the eye of anyone who later comes looking for what was behind it, which was exactly the attention she did not want to invite and could not, in honesty, say her entry was free of inviting regardless of how she wrote it. The third she began and left unfinished on the table past midnight, because it had begun arguing with its own middle before it reached its fact, laying out the case for saying more before it had said the thing plainly. An entry that argues before it states is no record at all, only a brief for one side of a question nobody had asked her to judge.

What she wrote in the end, on the fourth attempt, past the second hour of the morning, gave the day of Brìghde's death, the fact that no cause was made known, the day of Eòghan's crowning by the rite, and nothing else. Nothing was said of the council's hard sitting on the succession. Nothing was said of what the harder hand in the packet's second seal had wanted her to know without quite writing it down. Four bare lines carried a queen's death and a king's crowning together, the same length the chronicle would have given a lesser succession in a lighter year, and she signed the page, and did not strike it, and sat with it in front of her until the lamp guttered rather than trim it and give herself more light to doubt it by.

She knew, setting it into the chronicle the next morning in her own clean hand rather than trusting the copy to a clerk, exactly what the bareness would do. A reader coming to that page a hundred years on, or ten, would read four short lines after a long entry for the coming of Niall's own reign, would notice the shortness before noticing anything the lines actually said, and would ask, as she herself had asked of shorter entries in older books, what the silence was standing in for. She could not stop that asking. She had decided, over the third draft struck through on the table, that she did not want to. An entry padded to look full said, to anyone who read enough of them, precisely as much as an entry left honestly bare, and said it more dishonestly, since it dressed a silence as a fullness and hoped the reader would not weigh the two the same. She would rather the silence stood for what it was and let the reader do their own weighing than build a small deception into the kingdom's own record to spare a future reader the discomfort of wondering.

"You wrote nothing of the hard sitting," said Tormod, the following week, laying a fair copy beside her for checking, having read the packet himself as her clerks always did before she did, since a clerk who did not read what he copied was of no use copying it.

"I wrote what the office sent me and what I could stand behind," she said. "The hard sitting is the council's to enter in its own minutes if it chooses to. It is not the chronicle's business to tell a reader what to make of a silence it did not create."

He asked her, not for the first time in ten years, whether she thought a chronicler owed the truth or the record, as though the two were ever different questions, and she told him what she had told him before, that the two were the same question asked twice, and that the day she found them pulling apart from one another was the day she would know it was time to lay the office down, whatever the council thought of the timing.

## III. Of the Votes Recorded

The council's own minute of the sitting reached her some weeks after, forwarded by the same office that had sent the first packet, on no request of hers; she took this to mean that somebody above the clerk who copied it wanted the fact of it in the kingdom's permanent keeping even if nobody wanted it dwelt on, which suited her well enough, since dwelling on it was not the chronicle's office to begin with.

It was the first minute of its kind the council had ever kept, in the restored kingdom's whole span since the twelve first sat at Cathair dhearg. Every crowning before it, Niall's own included, had gone through the council's sitting as a formality entered without a division, the twelve rising as one body to swear the fresh oath the rite required of them and the clerk noting only that the oath was sworn. This time the clerk noted a division. He named the two who had stood against seating Eòghan, Tormod mac Iain Òig and Sìleas nic Artair, and he named nothing else: not the ground either had stood on, not the word either had used to explain a vote that no councillor within living memory had ever needed to explain before, not whether the two had spoken together or apart, not whether the nine who carried the sitting had answered them in the room or only outvoted them and moved on to the day's next business. Four lines, the same length she had given the queen's death and the king's crowning together, and the fourth line was the plainest of the four: *the two did not sit again.*

She entered it as it had come to her, changing nothing, since a council's own minute was not hers to soften or to sharpen, only to keep; and she found, doing so, that the four bare lines of the council's record sat oddly well beside her own four bare lines for the crowning, as though the two offices had reached, from opposite ends of the same season and without a word passing between them, the same conclusion about how much a hard year could safely be let say of its own hardness in the kingdom's own hand.

A later return told her of the two seats, and she entered it separately, since the record kept things in the order they reached her and not the order a reader might wish for a tidy story: before the year turned, the council filled both places, a landed man's son from the western shires taking the one and a widow of a coastal house the other, and neither newcomer, so far as any packet reaching Muileann chaol ever said, was asked in council to account for the vote that had opened the seat they now held. Tormod mac Iain Òig went home to his own lands, and his name does not appear in the chronicle again for some years. A separate note on Sìleas nic Artair, which Gormshuil entered without comment because it was not hers to comment on, told that she kept a house of her own kin's Old Spirits faith with more attention than the council's business had ever left her time for.

"Two names and no reasons," Tormod said, copying the fair page, "is a strange thing for a first of anything."

"It is the shape the council chose to give it," Gormshuil said. "I did not choose it for them. I only kept it."

She thought, though she did not say it to him, that the council's silence and her own were not quite the same silence, however alike the two entries read on the page. Hers was chosen with a night's argument behind it, three drafts struck through before a fourth stood, and she could have told anyone who asked exactly why she had chosen it. The council's, she suspected, watching the fair copy dry, had not been chosen at all, only arrived at, the way a room full of people who would rather not explain a hard vote will find, without deciding to, that four lines are as much as anyone in the room is willing to put their name to. A chosen silence and a fallen-into one looked the same on a page a hundred years on. She did not think they ought to, and knew of no way, within the office the chronicle gave her, to mark the difference for a reader who had not sat, as she had, with the packet's two seals broken open under a guttering lamp.

## IV. Of the Fire at Inis bhàn and the Letter of the Schools

The spring brought her a return of a plainer kind, one that asked nothing of her but the keeping. Fire had taken the warehouse quarter of Inis bhàn on the Abhainn ìseal, in the north-central country, and burned two days before the town beat it back street by street with buckets and wet sacking and whatever water the river would give up to a chain of hands; the loss was heavy, three storehouses and a dozen dwellings above them, but the dead were none, every soul in the burning quarter having got clear ahead of the flame or been carried clear by neighbours who did not wait to be asked. The town's Hawk house, which had never before opened its doors past the households sworn to it, took in every family the fire had put out of a roof, sworn or not, and kept them through the worst of the spring cold until new roofs could be raised; the return noted this without comment, as the town seemed to have taken it without much comment, a Hawk house doing in a hard week what a Hawk house existed to do and nobody troubling to call it remarkable.

What the town did trouble to call remarkable, and what its return spent three lines on where the fire had had one, was the bell the town bought that summer to stand where the old warehouse bell had burned with its tower under it: cast at the founders' yard at Cathair dhearg to the town's own order and no other's, and rung once on the quay before it was ever hung, so that half the town could say afterward they had heard it new before anyone else on the river did. It carried, by every account that reached the Library after, further up and down the Abhainn ìseal than any bell in the kingdom, farmers three miles off swearing they set their day by it whether they meant to or not, and Gormshuil, entering the fire and the bell in the same short passage, found herself giving the loud bell nearly as many words as the two days' burning, and let the imbalance stand once she had looked at it, on the ground that a town chooses what it wants remembered of its own hard year as much as any office in Cathair dhearg does, and a chronicle that overruled a town's own choice of what to dwell on was claiming for itself a kind of authority the office had never in fact been given.

In the north that same spring a child was born whom the chronicle of that year does not mention, and could not have: Dubhan, born mortal into the confinement the Severance had made, decades after the war that had shut the island against those from whom his line descended. No return carried his name south, and no packet brought it to Gormshuil's table.

The letter that closed her year, and that she entered last of the season's business though it had reached her some weeks before the summer's warmest days, came from the Moot at Caol mhòr, over Walter Hale's own hand, and it was neither bare nor argued with itself in the writing, which she noticed and was glad of, having spent the better part of the winter learning again how much could ride on four plain lines. It gave, in Hale's own flat count, the number of schools the north now kept for its own children, eleven in all, from Agnes Pike's byre at Doire ghlas to a room over a chandler's shop at Ceann mhòr that had opened only that autumn, and it gave, after the eleven, a second number that the letter itself called worth the Moot's separate notice: three of the eleven, Agnes Pike's among them, had begun that year to teach some measure of Dia-thìris alongside the humans' letters and the Moot's own minutes. No order from the council asked for it, and no maor gave leave for it; parents at all three schools had simply come to the teacher and asked, wanting their children able to read a proclamation, a ledger, a shire's boundary-line, in the tongue the kingdom wrote its business in, whatever tongue the household spoke at its own hearth.

Gormshuil read the letter twice, the second time more slowly than the first, and entered it whole rather than in the short hand she gave most returns, letting the eleven schools and the three among them stand in the chronicle in something near Hale's own words, since a fact this plain needed no chronicler's shortening and would have lost by it. She thought, setting the pen down on that entry longer and more fully than she had let herself set it down on the year's harder ones, that a record could be trusted to keep a great silence honestly only if it could also be trusted to keep a small fullness honestly, the one discipline standing or falling with the other; and that whatever a reader made, a hundred years on, of the four bare lines she had given a queen's death, they would at least find, not far past them in the same book, an entry that gave a plain northern letter every word it had asked for, and could judge for themselves which kind of year the chronicler had thought she was keeping.

She copied the letter's last line into her own hand before she filed the whole of it away: *eleven, and three of the eleven now teach both.* It went into the chronicle exactly as Hale had written it, and she let it close the year's entries, the bare and the full both behind her now.

Before she put out the lamp she opened the private book again, the one no clerk copied and no council packet ever asked to see, and set beside the year's two hardest entries a line of her own that would never go south to Cathair dhearg or stand in any fair copy: that a kingdom which could give a school's letter every word it asked for, and a queen's death four lines and no more, kept two records under one hand and one table, and that she had not yet decided, in ten years of keeping both, whether the difference was a fault in her or a fault in the year. She closed the book on the question unanswered, as she had closed it before, and set the next return, still unread, on the corner of the table for the morning.

# Chapter Twenty-four: Of Walls under the Ground

*SE 30 an Giblean – SE 32 an Cèitean*

> Found this season at Làrach an Dùin: walls of dressed stone, older than any building known to us, and no writing on them anywhere. Entered as of the Old Ones, purpose unknown.
>
> — the Library's register of finds, 3 an Giblean, SE 31, entire, as it stands at Muileann chaol

## I. Of the New Hall at Cathair mhòr

The house of Mac Ùisdein had been building in stone the better part of two years before it was finished, and when it was finished the town said there was no house like it between Cathair dhearg and the sea, which was very likely true, since no one else in the kingdom had a mountain of spoil sitting idle at the mouth of his own working to quarry it from for nothing. Uisdean mac Ùisdein had taken the stone that came up broken and unsellable from the Sloc Mòr's own galleries, cart-load on cart-load of it over two winters, and set masons to dressing it into a hall with a roof of slate and a stair of the same grey stone climbing to a gallery that ran the width of the house. The Guild of Hewers held its feast there the week it was finished, tables the length of the hall and torches in iron brackets the smith had made to match no pattern but his own fancy, and men who had gone down the Sloc Mòr's shafts for twenty years sat under a roof built, as more than one of them said that night with a dry look at the man beside him, out of the very rock they had spent those twenty years bringing up.

Ailean Leabhar was not at the feast. He heard of it after, from Mòrag nic Coinnich, who had gone as the Library's own witness because somebody from Muileann chaol always went to a thing of that size, whether the Library thought it worth the going or not, on the ground that a house built to outlast its builder was exactly the kind of thing a chronicle regretted not having a clerk present for once the builder and the house were both fifty years gone. She told him the hall smelt of new mortar and old smoke in about equal measure, and that Uisdean had stood at the head of the highest table and said almost nothing, letting the guild's own master speak for the evening, which she thought, knowing the man a little, was either modesty or the surest kind of confidence there was, and that she had not been able to decide which in one evening and did not expect a second evening to settle it for her.

The licences went out that same season, and drew less notice at the time than the house did, though they would draw more before the year was out. The southern fishing grounds off Caol mhòr had been open water to whoever put a boat on them since the shires were first drawn, Dia-thìreach and Tuathaich boats working the same banks without much comment from either side, since fish did not trouble to sort themselves by the terms of a truce their forebears had made a generation before either fleet was born. That spring the maor's office at Caol mhòr began issuing licences for the grounds, in writing, and kept them for Dia-thìreach boats. The Tuathaich fleet was left the northern grounds instead, where the fishing ran thinner and where, as every man on the quay at Caol mhòr already knew without the office troubling to say it, the raiders' own boats worked too, since a coast with no licence on it was a coast with no one to complain of who fished it.

The first boat turned away under the new rule was a Tuathaich craft out of Caol mhòr itself, her master a man named Sam Ridley who had fished the southern banks since before the licences were dreamed of and who brought his catch in to the maor's own quay the day the rule took force, as he had every fair-weather day for eleven years, and was told at the scales that the catch could be weighed but the boat that had taken it had no paper for the grounds it came from and would need one before it went out again, and that papers for those grounds were not, at present, being written for boats of his fleet. Sam Ridley said little at the scales and less on the walk home, by every account that reached the Moot's own minutes at Caol mhòr that summer, but the Moot entered the day and the name all the same, since a first of anything was worth the ink even when the man it happened to had nothing further to say about it.

Doire shean, in the south-west, built its own harbour that same season, the first new harbour raised anywhere in the kingdom since the Severance without a coin of the Crown's in it. The house of the Stone at Doire shean lent the money against the town's own dues, as the order's houses had taken to doing where a town's need outran a maor's patience for petitioning Cathair dhearg, and the masons who built the mole worked to the Stone's own measure rather than the Crown's, a fact the harbour-master noted with some satisfaction in his first return and the council, so far as any packet reaching Muileann chaol ever said, noted not at all. The house took its first quarter's dues off the new quay before the mole's last course was even dry, a plain figure entered in the town's own book beside the sum it had lent, and the return that reached Muileann chaol set the two figures side by side without comment, leaving a reader to work out for himself, as Ailean did when the return crossed his own table, how many years of quarter-dues it would take the town to owe the house of the Stone rather less than it had first borrowed from it.

Of the feast in the new hall he had one further account, sent him some weeks after Mòrag's own telling by a mason who had worked the dressing of the stone and had not been asked to the tables he had spent two winters cutting, a plain enough matter and no fault, by the mason's own words, of Uisdean mac Ùisdein's, since the feast had been called for the guild and the guild held no cutter of stone among its own sworn members, whatever the man's hand had done for the walls that housed the supper. The mason wrote it to the Library without complaint, only as a thing he thought worth the record's keeping, that he had dressed the stone of a hall he was not asked to sit in, and Ailean entered the letter whole rather than in his own shorter hand, on the ground that a fact stated this plainly, and without complaint attached to it, needed no keeper's shortening, and would only have lost by it.

## II. Of the Trenches at Làrach an Dùin

Ailean Leabhar was five-and-fifty that spring, keeper of the Library fifteen years, and he had learned in most of those fifteen years that the finds which mattered least to the kingdom's own business were very often the ones that cost him the most sleep, a fact he had stopped finding strange some time before he had stopped finding it troublesome. He went down himself to Làrach an Dùin on the south-east coast that year, which was not his habit, since a keeper who left Muileann chaol every time a dig opened would have had no library left to keep by the end of a season; but the diggers' first letter had used a word he did not care to take on trust from a letter, and the word was *older*.

The camp sat above a low headland where the ground had been broken by trenching since the early spring, a scatter of canvas and turf-roofed huts and a cook-fire that never quite went out, and the diggers, four of them under a foreman named Cailean who had cut trenches for the Library at three sites before this one and thought he had seen most of what the ground on Dia-thìr had to show him, met Ailean at the head of the longest trench with the particular quiet of men who wanted to be asked rather than to volunteer.

"Show me," Ailean said, and Cailean showed him.

The wall ran the length of the trench and further, a coursed stone founded so deep that the diggers had given up trying to find its footing and had cut sideways instead to follow the line of it, dressed on its face in a manner Ailean had not seen in any ruin the Library held a record of, the stone fitted so close along its joints that a knife blade would not have found the gap between one block and the next. There was no mortar in it anywhere they had cut. There was no carving on it anywhere they had cut, no sign scratched or cut or painted, nothing that a scholar could call a letter or a mark meant to be read by anyone who came after, only the wall itself, running on under the turf in a line the trenches had not yet found the end of.

"How old," Ailean said, not quite a question, since he already knew no answer he was given would satisfy him.

"Older than anything I've cut into," Cailean said, "and I've cut into the watch-fort ruins and thought those old. Whatever built this built long before any of them, and built better."

Ailean spent four days at the camp before he went home, most of them on his knees at the trench's edge with a lamp and a notebook, and what he found in those four days was less than what he did not find, which was the harder thing by far to carry back to Muileann chaol and set down in the Library's own hand. No writing. No image of a god or a beast or a man. Not a hearth-ash, not a broken pot, not a bone the diggers could say for certain was worked by a hand rather than gnawed by a fox, nothing that a scholar of any faith on the island could point to and say *this tells us who they were, or what they wanted, or what they called the stream at the foot of their own wall*. Only stone, laid with a patience and a skill that put every mason Ailean had ever watched at work to shame, and then, at some point no trench had yet reached far enough to find, left.

He wrote the entry himself rather than leave it to a clerk, sitting at the foreman's own trestle by lamplight on his last night at the camp, and he wrote it short, because the alternative to short was to write a page arguing with his own ignorance, and an entry that argued with itself before it stated its fact was no entry at all, only a chronicler's private trouble dressed up as a finding. *Walls of dressed stone, older than any building known to us, and no writing on them anywhere. Of the Old Ones, purpose unknown.* He read it back twice, struck nothing, and let it stand.

## III. Of Làrach an Teampaill

He rode east from Làrach an Dùin rather than straight home, since the season's letters had brought him word of a second matter that could not, in honesty, wait for a second journey, and reached Làrach an Teampaill in the district's own damp evening light with the ruin already half in shadow, a low mound of fallen stone that the local telling called a temple though nobody living, Dia-thìrich or Tuathaich, could have said whose.

He was met, before he had so much as dismounted, by three elders of the Seann Spioradan houses of the district, who had heard by the same letters that had reached him that the Library meant to open the ground, and who had come to the ruin themselves to be there when he arrived rather than trust the matter to a written petition that a keeper at Muileann chaol might set aside unread. The eldest of the three, a woman named Beathag who kept the district's own hearth-book and had walked, by her own account, to Làrach an Teampaill on every quarter-day of her life since she was old enough to be trusted with the road alone, spoke first and spoke plainly.

"We are not asking you to leave it standing," she said. "It will stand or fall as the ground under it chooses, and we have never asked the Library to prop up a wall it has no business propping. We are asking you not to open it. Whatever is under that stone, it is not ours to say what it is, and it is not yours either, and a hand that goes into the ground to find out makes a claim on the finding that neither of us has the right to make."

Ailean stood at the edge of the mound a long while before he answered, the light going out of the sky behind Beathag's shoulder and the ruin's own shadow lengthening across the ground between them, and he thought, standing there, of the wall at Làrach an Dùin four days behind him, laid by hands that had left no word anywhere for anyone who came after, and of the entry he had written by lamplight, *purpose unknown*, and of how little that entry had actually told a reader once the words were counted, and how much labour the not-knowing had cost him to set down honestly rather than paper over with a guess dressed as a finding.

"I can measure it without opening it," he said at last. "The shape of the ground, the fall of the stone, what stands and what has come down, none of that needs a spade. If that answers what you're asking, I'll take the measure and leave the ground as I find it."

Beathag looked at him a moment before she answered, the way a person looks at an answer they had expected to have to argue harder for. "It answers it," she said. "We had not thought to hear it offered before we asked twice."

"I've dug one wall this week that had nothing to tell me but its own patience," Ailean said. "I don't think this one owes me more than that either, and I'd rather leave it its patience than spend a season proving I was right to want an answer it never meant to give me."

He spent two days at Làrach an Teampaill with a chain and a level rather than a spade, walking the mound's own outline and setting down, in a hand as careful as any he gave the Library's own registers, the line of the fallen wall, the height of what still stood, the lie of the ground where a doorway might once have opened toward the morning sun or might, for all his measure could tell him, have opened toward nothing a living scholar would recognise as a reason. He entered it, back at Muileann chaol a fortnight later, in four words that cost him nearly as much thought as the four he had given the wall at Làrach an Dùin: *measured, and let be.*

## IV. Of the Obelisk at Cnoc bheag

The third of the season's ruins asked less of him and gave, in its own way, nearly as little back. A standing stone north of Cnoc bheag, cut with lines of a script no scholar at Muileann chaol or anywhere else on the island had ever been able to read, had stood in open pasture since before any record the Library held began, cattle rubbing their flanks against it and children chalking their own marks beside the old ones until a passing shepherd or a stricter mother scrubbed the chalk away again.

Ailean sent a scribe rather than going himself, a careful young woman named Ùna who had trained under him at copying the Library's oldest and most damaged leaves and who took to the obelisk's lines with the same patient hand she gave a torn page, kneeling at the stone's foot with a board and a soft pencil and a square of oiled cloth against the weather, and copying every stroke exactly as it stood, gap for gap where the stone had worn smooth and weathered edge for weathered edge, rather than smoothing a guessed line into a broken one the way a less careful hand might have been tempted to.

It took her the better part of three weeks, working only in fair weather, and when the copy came back to Muileann chaol Ailean set it against every script the Library's own shelves held a record of and found nothing that matched it closer than a chance resemblance any two alphabets might share by accident. He filed the copy as he had filed the walls and the temple's own measure, under the same plain heading, and sent word to the council, through the maor of Cnoc bheag, that the stone was worth a fence against the cattle if nothing else, since a thing that had stood unread for longer than the kingdom's whole span deserved at least that much keeping, whatever it turned out, in the end, to have been trying to say. The council found the money for the fence before the summer was out, four posts and a rail set well back from the stone's own foot, and the shepherds of the district, who had rubbed their cattle against it without much ceremony for as long as any of them could remember, grumbled for a season about the lost scratching-post and then, by the following spring, had mostly stopped grumbling.

## V. Of the Lighthouse's Shadow

He had one other matter that season that was not his own finding, brought to him only because the Library kept the copies of everything a shire's return chose to enter, and it came from the far north-west, from the keeper of the lighthouse at Baile chrom, a Dia-thìreach man fifteen years at the post and still reporting, as his warrant bade him, what he saw by land as well as by sea.

He reported, in a hand Ailean thought more careful than most such reports troubled to be, that the Grey Night sect kept its yearly vigil that spring in the lighthouse's own shadow, a knot of shapes standing silent in the dark at the foot of the tower through the small hours, gone before the light came up enough to put names to any of them, and that he had made no move against them, having no order that told him a silent vigil on open ground was any business of a keeper's whose charge was the light and not the shore beneath it.

The report went south to Cathair dhearg with the season's other returns, and Ailean, copying it into the Library's own register as he copied every such return that reached him, noted what came back from the council in answer, which was nothing at all. No order to the keeper, no word to the magistrate at Baile chrom who had fined the sect's own vigil-keeper once already for holding the same watch in the open, no instruction of any kind that a clerk at Cathair dhearg troubled to set down where a copy of it might reach Muileann chaol. He entered the silence as plainly as he had entered the walls and the temple, since a council's not answering was, in its own way, as much a fact of the kingdom's year as anything it had chosen to say, and a Library that kept only the answers and not the silences would, in the end, be keeping the smaller half of the record.

## VI. Of the Salt-Pans and the New Deputy

The last of the season's business reached him from the east coast rather than the west, a plainer matter than any of the others and, for that reason, one he was glad to set down last. The flats below Àth bheag had been dug for salt-pans that spring, shallow beds cut into the tidal ground and left to the sun and the slow work of the sea, and by the time the first return reached Muileann chaol the town was already supplying salt up the coast as far as the eye of the return's own writer cared to follow it, a trade that had begun, so far as anyone at Àth bheag troubled to say, from nothing more than a man noticing that the flats held the tide long enough after each ebb to leave a white crust worth the gathering, and a second man asking why nobody had thought to help the flats do more of it on purpose.

It was on the road home from that last errand, in the early days of the summer, that Ailean told Mòrag nic Coinnich what he had been turning over since the trench at Làrach an Dùin, which was that fifteen years of keeping the Library alone, riding out to every dig and every dispute and every return that seemed to want a keeper's own eye on it rather than a clerk's, had begun to cost him more than the walking, and that a Library with only one person who could speak for it was a Library one bad season from having nobody who could. Mòrag had come to Muileann chaol as a girl of the district and had worked under him the better part of a decade, careful with the older leaves in a way few of the younger clerks troubled to be and quicker than any of them at telling, from a shire's ordinary return, which lines wanted a keeper's own attention and which could wait for the season's slower copying.

"You want a deputy," she said, not quite a question, when he had finished saying rather less than that directly.

"I want someone the Library can trust to speak for it when I can't be in two places at once," he said, "which this season proved I very often can't. I'd want it to be you, if you'll take it."

She said she would think on it, which he had expected, and came to him three days later with her answer, which he had also expected, though not quite so soon: that she would take it, on the condition that the Library's own register note plainly, from the first day she signed anything in its name, that she signed as deputy and not as keeper, since a record that let the two blur together, even out of kindness to a woman doing the work well, would in the end tell a later reader less truth than a record that kept the two apart. He agreed to it before she had finished the sentence, thinking, as he agreed, that she had learned the office's own discipline rather better in ten years than some keepers managed to learn it in a lifetime, and that a Library with a deputy who thought that way about her own title was a Library considerably less likely to need worrying over the next time a keeper rode east and did not come home for a fortnight.

He set Ùna's copy of the obelisk into the Library's own presses himself that same week, alongside the measure of Làrach an Teampaill and the short entry on the wall at Làrach an Dùin, three findings that told, between them, almost nothing of who had raised the stone or built the wall or asked that the temple's ground be left to its own patience, and a great deal, if a later reader troubled to notice it, of what a keeper of the Library had judged worth doing with a question he could not answer. He had measured what could be measured, copied what could be copied, and filed the not-knowing as carefully as he would have filed a certainty, so that whoever came after him, with better tools or a longer patience or simply more time than a single season allowed, would find the ground exactly as he had left it, and the question exactly as open.

# Chapter Twenty-five: Of Walter Hale's Last Winter

*SE 33 am Faoilleach – SE 34 am Màrt*

## I. Of the Grain-Store at Cathair fhada

The Crown's grain-store at Cathair fhada was two winters building and one summer roofing, a hall of dressed stone on the southern plain long enough that a loaded cart could turn inside it without backing into the door, and when the last course went on in the dry season the masons signed their names in the mortar under the sill, in the way of a house that expects to stand. It was filled from the south's own harvest, sack on sack carried up from threshing floors within a day's cart of the town, and the keeper set to it, a quiet man named for no one in the record, walked the rows each morning counting the sacks against a tally he kept in his coat and telling no one the sum.

The store stood full and shut through the good years that followed it. The keeper walked his rows, turned the sacks against the damp, sold off the oldest grain each autumn to make room for the new, and let the south forget the store was there, which it very soon did.

In the same season, though the two had nothing to do with one another beyond the year they shared, the second count of the island's people since the Severance went out from Cathair dhearg: clerks with their books riding the shire roads a second time, tallying hearth by hearth as the first count had. This time a second column stood beside the first, one figure for what a household held and one for what its neighbour held, Dia-thìreach against Tuathach, town against country. The first count had only looked; it had set down numbers and let them lie side by side on the page for anyone with eyes to read the gap between them. The second count was built to measure the gap itself, a column of difference drawn out and summed at the foot of every shire's page and then summed again for the whole island at the bottom of the last one.

The clerks who carried the sums back to Cathair dhearg were young, most of them, riding roads they had never seen before that autumn, and not one of them was ever told the fate of the figures once they were handed over. They were bid write their own shire's page fair, seal it, and hand it across a table to a councillor's clerk who took it without a word of thanks and set it on a stack with the others, and every one of the riders who carried a page that autumn came away with the same plain sense, never spoken aloud between them on the road home, that they had been asked to measure a thing they would not themselves be shown the measure of.

The report went into the council's own keeping and stayed there. No proclamation followed it, no minute of the council's reading it was copied south to the Library, no word of its sum reached any shire clerk who might have carried it further, and the councillors who had called for the count in the first place gave out, when any of the twelve was asked directly, only that the figures wanted study before they wanted airing, a form of words that satisfied the asking without answering it. A report that measures a thing and is then locked away measures it no less truly for the locking, but it does not, for as long as the lock holds, change anything at all, and the council, whatever its reasons, chose that year to hold the lock rather than the change.

## II. Of Walter Hale's Last Sittings
