At Caol mhòr, that same dry season, Walter Hale sat the Moot's chair for what none of the men and women around the table yet knew to call his last winter of sitting it, though most of them, looking at him, suspected it without saying so. He was old by any account the north kept of its own, the first speaker the Moot had ever chosen, thirty-one years in the chair since a room of angry fishermen and shepherds had put him there because he could read a factor's ledger as fast as the factor himself and would not be talked past. His hands had begun to shake on a cold morning in a way they had not shaken the year before, a small tremor the room would have needed to be watching for to catch, and he had taken, without saying why, to letting David set the seal to a letter rather than doing it himself.

David Hale had kept his father's minute-books at his elbow since the year of the first fair, when the fair's toll-mistress had turned his wool from the gate to a factor's stall under a rule he had not known was written, and the lesson of that turning had stayed with him longer than the wool's loss ever had. He wrote a fair hand, faster than his father's now, and had taken, these last two winters, to writing the day's business twice, once in the rough book on the table and once again that same night at his own hearth in a second hand steadier than the first, telling himself it was only practice and knowing, without quite admitting it to himself, that he was keeping a second copy against a day he did not want to name.

"You needn't do it twice," Hale told him once, catching him at the second copy by lamplight, his voice thinner that winter than the room was used to hearing it.

"It keeps my hand in," David said, which was true as far as it went and no further, and his father, who had kept a Moot's minutes long enough to know a half-answer when he heard one, let it stand without pressing it, which was its own kind of answer back.

The business that winter was ordinary enough to look at from outside: a dispute over a weir on the Abhainn ìseal that two villages had fought over for longer than either could say why, a petition from Doire ghlas for a second well, the yearly reckoning of the head-due against what the shires had actually paid rather than what they owed. Hale sat through all of it steady enough, his voice carrying the length of the room as it always had even when his hands would not hold a pen without a slight travelling shake in the line, and only those who sat closest to him, David among them, marked how much longer the sittings left him afterward, sunk in his chair with his eyes shut while the room emptied around him, before he would rise and let himself be walked home.

He kept, that whole winter, a habit he had kept for thirty years without once breaking it: the first hour of any sitting given over to whoever had walked furthest to be heard, before the day's set business was opened, on the ground he had given the room the year he first took the chair and never troubled to give again, that a room which heard its own business before its furthest petitioner had already told that petitioner what it thought of the walk. A carter from beyond Àth fhada stood that hour one grey morning with a grievance over a toll he thought wrongly charged him, and stood a long while, the room patient around him while Hale let him finish without once hurrying the telling, and when the carter had done Hale answered him himself rather than passing the matter to a clerk, in a voice that had gone thin that winter but had not gone impatient, and settled the toll in the carter's favour before the day's proper business was called. David, watching, thought his father looked more tired setting down that one small matter than he had looked settling weightier things the winter before, and said nothing of the thought to anyone.

## III. Of the Twenty-Eighth of an Gearran

He died on the twenty-eighth of an Gearran, in his own bed at Caol mhòr with David beside him and Alice sent for from the school though she did not reach the house before the end, seventy-six years old by the count his own house kept, which was neither a young death nor a cruelly long-delayed one, only the ordinary close of an ordinary span, the kind the north had learned by then to expect of its own and no longer thought worth remarking on for its length alone. He had sat the Moot's chair four days before, the weir dispute settled at last in the villages' own favour rather than either party's, and had told David walking home that evening, in the flat way he said most things he meant seriously, that he thought he would let the next weir dispute be somebody else's to settle. David had taken it, at the time, for the kind of thing a tired man says after a long sitting and thought no more of it until the twenty-eighth came.

The Moot's business stopped for three days without a vote taken to stop it; nobody moved to open the room, and nobody needed to be told why not.

The whole north walked to his burial, or near enough to the whole north that the roads into Caol mhòr that week carried more feet than the fair itself had carried the autumn before, fishermen up from Cuan bheag and Ros mhòr, carters off every road into the town, shepherds off the hill country who had never once sat in the Moot's room but had heard his name read out at a dozen musters and knew it as the name a factor's letter answered to when a northern flock was turned away at a gate. They buried him at Caol mhòr within sight of the Moot's own house, the ground he had sat closest to for thirty-one years, and the Church's own rite was said over him by a priest who had not been born when Hale first sat the chair.

The chair itself did not sit empty past the week's mourning. The Moot met on the fourth day, the room fuller than any ordinary sitting, and put the choosing to a vote before the dust of the burial mound had properly settled. Two other names were spoken before hers, a factor's son from the fair road who had money enough to be heard and a shire clerk from Doire ghlas whom half the room knew only by his letters, and both names were set aside within the same hour without much debate, the room's own sense running, though nobody troubled to say it outright, that the chair Hale had built wanted filling by someone the widows and the fishing families would call their own before they would call it a factor's or a clerk's. Mary Coyle, a fisherman's widow of Caol mhòr who had first stood to speak in that same room some nine years before and had gone on standing to speak in it since, was named speaker at the last by a count that nobody in the room troubled to call close.

She had buried a husband to the sea before she ever spoke a word in the Moot's chair, and she took Hale's chair now with the same flat quiet she had used the first time she rose to speak for the widows of Cuan bheag, no speech beyond the plain words the office required of her, no promise offered beyond what the room could see for itself in the way she sat down once the vote was read: as a woman meaning to stay in the chair for exactly as long as the room wanted her in it and not a day longer than that. Fifty-two years old that winter, she took the seal David held out to her and turned it once in her hand before she set it down at her own place, the same seal Hale's own hand had set to thirty-one years of letters, and said only, to the room rather than to David in particular, that she supposed the books had better go on being kept the way they had always been kept, which the room took, rightly, for an asking that David stay on rather than an order that he must.

David kept the books under her as he had kept them under his father, the rough copy on the table and, that first night, though he told himself afterward there was no longer any reason to keep it up, the second copy again at his own hearth, in a hand that shook rather more than his father's ever had, on a night when the keeping of it seemed to want doing whether or not it served any purpose he could have named to another soul in the room.

## IV. Of the Report Asked For and Refused

Seonag nic Ille-Mhoire had ridden the shire roads with the second census the autumn before, one clerk among a dozen sent out from Cathair dhearg, and had carried her own shire's tally back to the council's clerks with her own hand on the sum at the foot of the page. Young for the work, no more than thirty, she had thought, riding home with the figures still fresh in her saddlebag, that a count taken with such care, hearth against hearth, column against column, would be read by somebody who meant to do something with what it showed. Some months on she asked whether she might see the whole of it, the island's sum rather than her own shire's part of it, telling the clerk at the door of the council's keeping-room that she had carried the figures herself and had a right, she thought, to know what they had come to add up to.

The clerk refused her, giving no reason beyond the plain fact of it, that the report was the council's own and shown to no hand that had merely helped gather it, and she did not press him further, having carried enough council business in her time to know a closed door when a clerk's flat face showed her one. That evening she wrote the asking and the refusal down in her own hand, in a private book she kept for herself and showed to no one. She could have pointed to no purpose the keeping served; she wrote it down because a thing asked and refused seemed to her worth a record all the same, in much the way a chronicler at Muileann chaol was that same winter keeping a second private book of her own for reasons she could not have named any more plainly.

## V. Of the Doctors of Àth àrsaidh

At Àth àrsaidh, an easy day's ride from Caol mhòr, Eachann mac Rath had practised physic under his guild's own charter for twenty years, a careful man who set a break as well as any hand on the island and had buried, in his own accounting kept privately and never shown to the guild that licensed him, rather fewer of his patients than the guild's own average allowed for a man of his years in practice. When the Moot wrote to him that winter offering to pay his fee for the teaching of it, two Tuathaich women in his own surgery, learning what he knew by watching him set a bone and mixing a poultice at his elbow rather than by any book, he took the offer without asking the guild's leave, on the plain ground, he told the two women when they first came to him, that a broken arm mended the same whichever hand mended it and he saw no reason a guild seal should decide who was taught to do the mending.

Ruth Ashby and Clara Tulloch came to him that am Faoilleach, two women of the fishing country about Caol mhòr who had nursed their own families and their neighbours' through fevers and birthings for years without any name for the knowledge beyond what their mothers had shown them, and Eachann set them, the first week, to nothing grander than rolling bandages and watching him work, telling them plainly that a physician's hand was built on watching before it was built on doing. They watched through the whole of that dry, hard season, the fevers that came with short water and poor grain filling his surgery faster than any two hands, his or theirs, could easily empty it, and by the spring thaw both women could set a simple break unwatched and had begun, under his eye still, to mix the plainer poultices themselves.

The guild found him out before the summer was old, a factor's wife of Àth àrsaidh mentioning at a fair stall, without malice or particular thought, that Eachann's new girls handled a lancet as steady as he did, and the word reached the guild's own hall inside the month. Two of the guild's own men rode out to see the surgery for themselves before the letter was written, and stood in the doorway watching Ruth Ashby set a child's wrist while Eachann talked her through it without once touching the arm himself, and left again without a word to either woman, which Eachann told them afterward was answer enough of what the letter would say when it came.

The guild struck him from its rolls before an Cèitean was out, the letter naming no fault in his physic, only the plain fact that he had taught outside the guild's own leave and to hands the guild's charter did not recognise as fit to be taught. He read it once at his own table, with Ruth Ashby and Clara Tulloch both there for the evening's lesson, and set it aside rather than answering it, telling the two women, when Clara asked whether the striking changed what he meant to teach them, that a guild seal had never yet set a bone and he saw no reason to let the loss of one stop him doing the one thing the seal had never actually done for him. His patients were no fewer for the guild's letter than they had been before it, and Ruth Ashby and Clara Tulloch kept coming to his surgery through that summer and the next, learning what he had left to teach them before any guild seal stood between the teaching and the two women who wanted it.

## VI. Of the Flood on the Abhainn ìseal

The Abhainn ìseal broke its banks along its lower reach in am Màrt, the longest river of the island carrying, in three days of rain harder than anyone had thought to plan against, three bridges clean away and a long stretch of the coal line's embankment with them, the rails left hanging over open water where the ground beneath them had simply gone. A carter caught on the middle bridge when the third day's rain brought the water up fastest got his horse free and lost the cart, and stood on the bank afterward watching the whole span go under inside the space of a single held breath, the timbers turning once in the current before the flood took them out of sight round the bend below the mill. No one drowned on that stretch of river that week, though two of the villages downstream lost more of their low ground than any flood in the shire's own memory had taken before, and the line's engineers, walking the embankment once the water dropped enough to let them, found nothing left to walk on for the better part of a mile.

The line shut for want of ground to run on, and the ports that had lived on the coal it carried, Ros dhomhain and the western harbours among them, turned to whatever they had laid by in their own stores against a leaner week, none of them having laid by against a season. Word of the shutting reached the yards before it reached any office that might have planned for it, and for two days the ordinary traffic of coal carts simply stopped at the washed ground and turned back the way they had come, their drivers no wiser than the townsfolk waiting at the far end for a delivery that was not coming.

Mary Coyle had sat the Moot's chair not yet a month when the first rider reached Caol mhòr with word of the washed embankment, and she called the room together the same evening rather than waiting on the week's ordinary sitting, on the plain ground, she told David as he opened the rough book to a fresh page, that a bridge does not wait on a schedule and neither, while she held the chair, would the room that had to answer for one. She gave her first order from that chair before the ink of the vote choosing her was properly dry on the older page behind it: every northern harbour that answered to the Moot to open its own coal store and share it out by the count of hearths rather than by whoever reached the yard first, since the north's coal came down that same line and would not come again until the line itself could be walked and mended.

David wrote it into the rough book in his own hand, the first order the book carried under her name rather than his father's, and did not, that night, trouble to copy it again by his own hearth, finding, when he sat down to his lamp as he had sat down most nights of the two years before, that he no longer felt the want of the second copy he had kept so long against a day whose need for it, he saw now, had already come and gone.

Mary sat on in the room after the vote was carried and the riders sent, David gathering the loose pages of the night's business into the rough book while she waited for the last of the council to file out. She had not, she told him once the room had emptied, expected to give her first order over a broken bridge rather than over any of the ordinary business she had sat through for nine years watching another hand settle; she had thought, if she had let herself think about the chair at all before the room put her in it, that her first order would be some small thing, a licence signed or a petition answered, not a whole coast's coal rationed out on the strength of one rider's word before the damage had even been properly walked. "It is what came first," David said, closing the book, "and a chair answers what comes first or it answers nothing." She thought about that longer than the plainness of it seemed to warrant, and said, rising at last to let him bank the fire and lock the room behind them both, that she supposed a chair had never once in Hale's thirty-one years been given the luxury of choosing which order came first, and she saw no reason her own first winter in it should be the one to break that rule.

# Part Five: Of the Fall and the Search

# Chapter Twenty-six: Of the Hawk's Own Custodian


*SE 35 an Cèitean – SE 36 an Dùbhlachd*

## I. Of the Naming at Inis ìseal

The Hawk houses of Siorrachd Cnoc bheag had kept their own hearths and their own altars for ages without asking leave of anyone south of them, and when the houses met at Inis ìseal in an Cèitean to name a custodian of their own, the asking was not for leave either. Every house sent a witness, and most sent two, so that the low stone hall by the water stood fuller than it had stood since the roof was last mended, benches carried in from three farms and set along the walls, and the smell of wet wool and peat-smoke thick enough that the door was propped from first light to last.

They named Raonaid nic Iain, whose mother's mother had kept the altar at Inis ìseal before her and whose own hands had kept it these nine years since, and they named her without a vote taken, only a standing up house by house until the hall stood, and a shout that the youngest present, a boy sent to watch the door, carried out to the road to tell whoever passed that the Hawk had its own custodian now, as the houses to the south had had theirs these thirty years.

She was not a young woman by then, past the years when a house sends its unmarried daughters to keep an altar and long past the years when anyone in the hall would have thought to ask whether she was fit for the office; she had buried a husband and raised two sons on the altar's own upkeep, gull-eggs and a widow's share of the fishing, and had sat the long vigils of the Hawk's own nights, the ones the southern Rite kept only at its greatest feasts, every year of the nine without missing one. When the shout went up she did not answer it at once, standing at the front of the hall with her hands folded into her shawl, and it was Murchadh Ruadh of Baile fhionn, the oldest man in the room, who crossed to her and set a strip of white feather into her hand, plucked, he said, from no living bird but kept in his own house three generations against a day the Hawk houses might want a custodian to give it to.

"You'll wear it or you won't," he told her, "but it's yours now either way."

She wore it, pinned at her collar, for the rest of that day and every day after that anyone in the north ever saw her.

The white billet on the shire's own arms, a plain bar the roll had given Siorrachd Cnoc bheag thirty years back for no reason any living clerk could give, hung on a board at the back of the hall that same afternoon, and more than one witness, filing out into the wet evening, looked at it and said to whoever walked beside them that a shire whose hills held the oldest hawk-altars on the island ought by rights to carry a hawk on its own seal and not a bar that meant nothing to anybody. Nobody thought, that evening, that the saying was more than an evening's grumble. The houses had said as much before, at other namings, and the roll had never once answered them.

Each house that had sent a witness sent also, as the custom of a naming asked, something of its own hearth to be set on the altar's own step before the hall broke, a handful of meal, a coil of new-spun wool, a jar of the honey the moor bees made in Cnoc bheag's own heather, so that by the time the last house had come forward the step held more than the altar would use in a season and the overflow was carried out afterward to whichever door in the town had the least behind it that winter. It was a small thing, the giving, and none of the five witnesses who later carried word of the naming south to Cathair dhearg thought it worth putting in their telling, but Raonaid, standing at the step through the whole slow giving of it, would say afterward that the shout had told her the hall's mind, but the step filling, house by house, with more than any one house could easily spare, had told her the houses' hearts, and it was the second telling she carried longer.

The rain that had held off through the naming came on hard as the last witnesses left, and those with the furthest roads home, the farms above Baile fhionn and the two lone houses out past the moor's edge, stayed the night in the hall rather than ride it, sleeping on the benches they had carried in that morning, so that Raonaid's first night as custodian was spent, whether she had planned it or not, with a full house of the Hawk asleep around her altar and the rain loud on a roof three farms had lately mended between them.

## II. Of the Letter from Seann Skell in the South

Word of the naming reached Seann Skell on the southern coast inside the month, carried, as such word always was, by a fish-buyer's factor who thought no more of the telling than he thought of the weather he reported in the same breath. The house of the Rite's high custodian sat above the harbour there, built to the design of the man who had first held the office, Dòmhnall mac Thormoid, eleven years dead by then and long since answered for by a successor the north knew only by his letters, a careful hand that gave away nothing of the man who held it.

The letter that came back to Inis ìseal that autumn was three lines long and cost, the houses reckoned afterward, more in the riding of it than the paper it was written on was worth. It named no fault in Raonaid nic Iain, gave no reason a house could argue with, and said only that the high custodian's own order of worship, written and read at every seating south of Cnoc bheag these thirty years, knew of no office called the custodian of the Hawk houses and could not, for want of knowing it, own one. It was signed with the seal the letter's own writer never troubled to explain, a seal the north had never seen before and never troubled to ask after, and it was read aloud once in the hall at Inis ìseal and then folded and put away, not burned, not answered, only kept, in the way a house keeps a thing it means to look at again.

"He doesn't own her," Murchadh Ruadh said, when the reading was done and the hall sat quiet with it, "so we'll carry on as though he had."

Nobody in the hall thought that a strange thing to say, and nobody troubled, that autumn or after, to write south again asking the high custodian to change his mind. The houses kept their own vigils as they had kept them before the letter came, brought their own disputes to Raonaid as a custodian's disputes had always been brought to whoever the altar answered to, and let the three lines from Seann Skell sit in their folded state at the back of the hall as a fact about the south rather than a judgment on the north, which was, in its own quiet way, the only answer the letter ever got.

Raonaid herself read the letter over twice more before it went into its keeping-place, once aloud to Murchadh Ruadh alone and once again silently, by herself, at the altar the night after. She was neither young enough to be stung by the refusal nor old enough, she told Murchadh, to have stopped caring what a house in the south thought of a house in the north, and she said, folding the letter the second time, that a woman could hold both those things at once without either one winning out over the other. The fish-buyer's factor who had first carried the word north was asked, the next time his cart came through Inis ìseal, whether the house at Seann Skell had said anything more of the matter to anyone in the port below it, and he answered, with the flat honesty of a man who had carried a great many messages he understood not at all, that nobody south of the harbour had spoken of the Hawk houses since the letter went, one way or the other, as though the asking and the answering of it had already used up whatever the south meant to say on the matter for a good while yet.

It was noticed, that winter and the winters after, that no house of the Hawk sent its dead south to be buried by any rite but its own, and that no house of the Hawk sent a son or daughter south to be married under any custodian's blessing but Raonaid's, a practice none of the elder witnesses could say had ever been written down as a rule and none of the younger ones thought to question, the north simply going on keeping its own as it had always kept its own, letter or no letter.

## III. Of the Order Set Down

The Hawk's own worship had never once been written in all the ages the houses had kept it, passed altar to altar by a custodian's own mouth to the ears of whoever stood the vigil beside her, each custodian carrying the whole of it in memory and handing it on the same way, a line here worn smooth by a hundred years of telling and a line there added by some long-dead keeper whose name the order no longer carried. Raonaid had it from her mother's mother the same way, sitting the long vigils as a girl and saying the words back until her tongue held them without her mind troubling over them, and she had never once, in nine years keeping the altar on her own account, thought to set any of it down.

It was a question from one of her own sons, home from the fair road that summer and asking her plainly who would carry the order whole if she died before she had passed it to whoever came after her, that turned her to the thinking of it. She had no daughter of the altar's own line grown yet to the age of learning it, only two sons neither called to the office, and she sat with the question longer than she sat with most things that were put to her, through the long evenings of an t-Sultain when the hall's business was thin and the nights long enough for a great deal of sitting.

Her son had meant the question idly, the kind of thing a man asks his mother across a hearth without expecting an answer that troubles him, and he was startled, telling it afterward to his own wife, at how long she had sat with her hands still in her lap before she answered him at all. "It would go the way the humans' own tongue went out of Ros bheag," she told him at last, "a little forgotten every year until nobody left could say what had been lost, only that something had." He had not known what to say to that, and she had not pressed him to say anything, only risen after a while and gone out to the altar alone, and it was that same night, by her own account given years later, that she first thought of the account-book with its blank pages standing unused on a shelf where her sons kept the farm's own tallies.

She began the writing in an Dàmhair of that same year, a stub of pencil and a farmer's account-book with more blank pages in it than any account had ever needed, and she wrote slowly, sounding each line to herself before she set it down to be sure the words on the page matched the words her own mother's mother had given her rather than some smoother version her own tongue might have worn them into over nine years of saying. More than once she found a line would not come to her whole until she had gone out and stood at the altar in the cold to say it, the words sitting easier in her mouth with the stone under her hand than they ever sat at a hearth with a pencil waiting, and twice that winter she woke in the dark certain she had set a word down wrong the evening before and lit a lamp to check it against the sound of her own memory rather than trust the page until morning.

It took her the better part of a season, the book filling a page at a time between the altar's ordinary business, weddings and buryings and the small disputes over grazing that a custodian was asked to settle as often as any greater matter, and there were weeks that autumn when the book saw no new line at all, set aside on its shelf while a dying man in Baile fhionn wanted sitting with or a boundary quarrel between two farms wanted a custodian's own eye on the ground. When it was done at last, in the thin light of an t-Samhain, she read it through once from the first line to the last, aloud, alone in the hall with the door shut against the wind, to hear whether it still sounded as the order had always sounded spoken rather than written, and found, she told no one but herself that morning, that it did, near enough, and that the near enough would have to serve, because a thing spoken and a thing written were never going to be the same thing entire, however careful the hand that wrote it.

She did not show the finished book to the houses, and she did not send word south of it either. She read it aloud once, on the night of an t-Samhain's full moon, to the full gathering of the Hawk houses in the hall at Inis ìseal, the only reading any of them would hear that year or any year after, and when the reading was done she closed the book, tied it with a strip of the same white feather Murchadh Ruadh had given her at her own naming, and set it into the iron box the altar had kept its lamp-oil in since before her mother's mother's time, and turned the key.

"It's heard once a year," she told the hall, when one of the younger witnesses asked why the book was not left out for any house to read at its leisure, "the way it was always heard. Writing it down was only so the hearing wouldn't die with me. It was never meant to be read the way a factor reads a ledger."

The box went back onto its shelf behind the altar, and the key went onto a cord Raonaid wore under her shawl from that night forward, alongside the white feather at her collar, and no house that came to Inis ìseal after that ever saw the book, only heard it, once a year, in Raonaid's own voice, exactly as the houses had always heard the Hawk's order before a single word of it had ever touched a page.

## IV. Of the Hawk on the Seal

The houses' own asking, the one Murchadh Ruadh had spoken at Raonaid's naming without much thought of its ever coming to anything, was carried to Cathair dhearg that same an t-Samhain by a delegation of five, Raonaid among them though she had never once before ridden further south than the fair at Muileann òg. She rode the two days south with the white feather still pinned at her collar and the iron box's key still on its cord, and found the capital, when the delegation reached it, louder and larger than any telling of it had prepared her for, the streets about the council's own hall crowded with clerks and petitioners from every shire on the roll, so that Murchadh Ruadh, riding at her side, remarked that a woman could stand a year's vigil at Inis ìseal and hear less noise in the whole of it than Cathair dhearg made in a single morning. They asked the council for what the houses of Siorrachd Cnoc bheag had asked at other namings and never been given: that the white billet the roll had carried on the shire's arms for thirty years be struck, and a hawk set in its place.

The council heard them in the same chamber where every other shire's petition was heard that season, a councillor reading the asking off the delegation's own written page in a voice that gave away no more of his own mind than the letter from Seann Skell had given of its writer's, while Raonaid stood at the front of the five with her hands folded into her shawl exactly as she had stood at her own naming, and answered, when a second councillor asked her plainly why a shire wanted a hawk rather than the bar it had always carried, only that the hills round Cnoc bheag had kept hawk-altars longer than the roll had kept its billets, and that a shire's arms ought by rights to say something true about the shire rather than nothing at all. The council gave them, against every expectation the delegation had ridden south carrying, exactly what they asked. No clerk on the council's own rolls could say what the billet had ever stood for, and a shire's arms that carried nothing anyone could read was, the council's own reasoning held, worth less to the roll than one that carried a mark the shire's own people would know at a glance for their own. The grant was written and sealed before the delegation had been a full week in the capital, the quickest business, Raonaid said afterward to the hall at Inis ìseal, that she had ever seen any council do, quicker by far than the letter from Seann Skell had taken to cross half the distance for half the news.

The maor of Siorrachd Cnoc bheag sent his own seal south with the grant to be recut, and it came back before the year was out, the plain billet gone from it and a white hawk set among the twelve crescents the shire's arms had always carried round its border, wings a little spread, the die-cutter's own touch rather than any pattern the houses had sent him. The maor himself broke the old seal's die on the flags of his own hall before the shire's assembled clerks, a small ceremony he had thought up himself and never afterward repeated for any other grant, and pressed the new one for the first time into a stick of wax held up so that every clerk in the room could see the hawk stand clear of it before the wax had properly cooled. It was the first change made to the roll at the asking of an order rather than a crown or a council's own reckoning, and the shire's clerks, entering the new seal into the rolls that autumn, wrote the fact of it plainly beside the old blazon they struck through, in the flat hand clerks kept for such things and nothing more.

Raonaid held the new seal in her own two hands the day it reached Inis ìseal, turning it once to catch the light off the wing the cutter had set spread rather than folded, and said nothing for a while that any of the witnesses standing round her troubled to write down. The book in the iron box behind the altar stayed locked as it had been locked the night of the reading, its key on its cord under her shawl, unread by any hand but her own and unheard by any ear but the houses' once a year; the seal, when it was pressed to the shire's next grant, showed a hawk to anyone who cared to look, north or south of Cnoc bheag, whether the high custodian at Seann Skell chose to own the house that had asked for it or not.

## V. Of What the North Carried That Year Besides

The order at Inis ìseal was not the only thing the north set down or gave up or fought over in those two years, and the Library's own later hand, gathering what Siorrachd Cnoc bheag had carried through them, set the rest beside it as its due.

At Ceann leathan in an Giblean of the following year the Còmhrag was fought as it was fought every year since the fair-wardens had first called it an old custom of arms, blades kept from the ring by a rule as old as the melee, bare hands and staves and the fighters' own weight against each other on ground already churned to mud by the crowd's own feet before the first pair was called. Six men died on the trampled ground before that year's melee was called at last, more than had ever died there in one year before, one of them a boy of Baile ghlas not yet twenty whose own mother had walked two days to stand at the ring's edge and see him fight, and stood there still when they carried him off it. The custodians of the southern Rite, who had never loved the Còmhrag and had said so quietly at every seating since it began, petitioned the fair-wardens that year to end it outright, sending a clerk with the petition written fair and sealed rather than trusting the asking to a rider's memory. The wardens read the petition in their own counting-room, above the very quays the melee's crowds filled every spring, and refused it inside the hour, on the plain ground, their answer said, that Ceann leathan lived off those crowds as much as it lived off anything the sea or the coal line brought it, and a town does not vote itself poor to please a custodian who does not keep its books.

The circus came to Ceann leathan that same autumn, An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn pitching its tents on the trampled ground within a week of the six burials, its wagons painted in colours the mud had not yet had time to dull and its callers crying a show of tumblers and a caged wolf from the eastern hills to crowds that the fair-wardens had counted rightly would stay on after the melee rather than scatter home early with their pockets still part full. It was said afterward, though no one who said it could point to the hand that had written the letter, that the wardens themselves had paid the circus to come that particular year, the timing too neat for anyone who had watched a Còmhrag before to call it chance, and the boy of Baile ghlas's own mother, so the telling went, walked past the tents on her way home without once turning her head toward them.

The railway reached Ceann leathan the same season, the last miles of embankment laid through ground the coal line's engineers had put off for two summers running for the softness of it, driven pile by pile until it would bear the weight, so that coal might be carried down to a second harbour and shipped from quays that had known nothing heavier than a fishing boat's catch before that year. The first coal-ship out of the new quays loaded by lamplight the following an Dùbhlachd, her master reckoning the tide would not wait on daylight and the shore gang working the chutes through a night colder than any of them had dressed for, so that the record of it, kept by the harbour clerk more from habit than from any sense that the night wanted remembering, noted only the hour and the tonnage and the men's own complaint of the cold, nothing more. The town's own walls, built to hold the Ceann leathan the fair had made of it, held nothing of the Ceann leathan the coal line made of it after, and by the second winter the quays had spread a good half-mile beyond the old gate with no wall following them, so that a stranger riding in from the coast road could no longer say with any certainty where the old town ended and the new one began.

On the west coast that same year Ros bheag opened its own yard for the building of coal-ships, the first yard the western ports had kept for themselves rather than sending south to Ros dhomhain for every hull they needed built or mended, its first keel laid on ground that had been a drying-green for nets the summer before. The shipwrights of Ros dhomhain, whose guild had held the whole coast's building trade to itself since before any of them now living could remember a rival yard, carried their protest to the guild court at Cathair dhearg and lost it there in a single sitting, the court's own ruling holding that a guild's charter bound its members to the guild's own standard of work and not to any single yard's monopoly of the coast. The eldest of the Ros dhomhain masters, who had ridden south himself to speak the protest, was heard to say on the road home that he had lost more trade to a single morning's ruling than his own father had lost in forty years of storms, and no one who heard him say it troubled to tell him he was wrong. Ros dhomhain's shipwrights went on building what work still came to them, and Ros bheag's new yard took the rest, and within the year the western ports no longer sent so much as a rowing-boat south for mending.

# Chapter Twenty-seven: Of the Silver at Depth

*SE 37 am Faoilleach – SE 39 an t-Ògmhios*

> Received of the silver guild of Muileann chiar, its charter renewed under the restored custom, seal and signatures entire, this day. Filed.
>
> — the council's receipt, 1 am Faoilleach, SE 37, as the Library renders it

## I. Of the Faces below the Old Working

Iain mac Ruairidh was past forty, and eleven years at the silver works at Muileann chiar, where the Mine Board had sent him the summer it gave him his receipt. He had stayed on long enough that the townsfolk no longer called him the Board's man from the west but simply Iain, the surveyor, as if the works had grown him themselves out of their own rock, and the old workings he had been sent to measure ran shallow, and the new ones, the ones he measured now, did not.

The silver at Muileann chiar had always been worked from the surface down, the old shafts no deeper than a tall house is high, sunk by hands that had learned the seam close to daylight and never troubled to ask what lay beneath it, since a seam that gave silver at arm's length gave a man no reason to dig further for it. It was Iain's own chain, run down a new shaft cut on the strength of nothing more than a hunch one of the guild's own captains had carried for thirty years and never had the coin to test, that first proved the seam ran richer the deeper it was followed. Every worked vein Iain had ever measured before had thinned with depth; this one thickened, the ore darker and heavier in the hand the further down the new gallery went. He checked the figures three times before he wrote them fair, the same habit that had served him at the Sloc Mòr, and found them holding each time, to within the chain's own inch.

He carried the new figures to the guild hall himself rather than send them by a boy, walking the short distance from the shaft's mouth to the hall's door with the roll under his coat against the rain, and found the guild's own masters gathered already, word of the deep gallery's yield having outrun his own walking by the better part of a morning. The old silver guild of Muileann chiar had kept its charter since before the Severance, a charter the humans' own Administration had let stand unaltered through the whole of their years on the island, on the plain ground, it was said, that silver troubled nobody's coal and a guild that troubled nobody was a guild worth leaving be. The charter had lapsed with the Administration's own going, along with every other paper the humans' hand had signed, and the guild had gone on working the shallow seam these thirty-odd years on custom alone, its captains meeting and its journeymen bound by no writing any court south of Muileann chiar would trouble to uphold if a dispute ever came to one.

He stood in the guild hall's doorway that morning longer than the walk from the shaft had left him breath for, the masters' own talk running ahead of him faster than he could get a word into it, one captain already reckoning aloud what a deeper gallery might be worth to the guild's own share and another asking, more soberly, whether the timbering that held for a shallow working would hold for a deep one, a question Iain thought worth asking and had not yet an answer for. He set the roll down on the hall's long table and let them argue over it a while before he spoke, on the plain habit, learned at the Sloc Mòr, that a room arguing over a survey it has not yet properly read will argue better once it has read it, and unrolled the sheet himself when the noise had thinned enough to let him.

"It will hold," he told the captain who had asked about the timbering, "if it is timbered the way I have drawn it and not the way custom drew the shallow shafts, and not an inch cheaper," and the captain, who had expected a surveyor's usual hedging, looked at him a moment before answering that he supposed a man who had walked the figures three times over had earned the right to say so plainly. A guild working a seam that ran to nothing was a guild the council could safely leave uncharted; a guild sitting on ore that ran the other way, richer with every fathom, was a different matter, and the charter that came back from Cathair dhearg that spring, under the restored custom the council had by then given a dozen older trades, bound the guild's captains to the Crown's own tithe on every bar struck and gave the guild, in return, the courts' own force behind its bindings. Iain's figures went south with the petition that asked for it, unrolled this time and read entire by three men who had not troubled to unroll his first survey eleven years before, a fact he noted to himself without saying it aloud to anyone at the guild hall, and pinned the noting, in his own private book, beside the older entry it answered.

## II. Of the Blanks and the Gold below Baile dhìreach

The deep gallery's silver came up faster, once the new shaft was properly timbered, than the mint at Cathair dhearg could refine it, more ore reaching the capital in a single season than the mint's own furnaces had ever been built to answer, and the council, rather than build the mint larger at the Crown's own cost, gave the refining out to the villages of the eastern hills, whose smiths had worked what little silver came their way for generations on nothing grander than a hearth-forge and a patient hand. The villages took the guild's rough bar and worked it down to the mint's own fineness and measure, paid by the pound of finished metal rather than by the day, a bargain the council's clerks reckoned cheap and the villages, who had never before been paid for anything by the Crown's own hand, reckoned otherwise.

It was at Baile dhìreach, lowest of the eastern villages and nearest the stream that ran off the hills above it, that a smith named for no particular skill beyond his father's trade before him found that the same stream which turned his forge's own wheel carried gold in its gravel, fine grains of it caught in the same pan a boy might use to wash grit from a well. He said nothing of it for a season, working the guild's silver bar as he had been bid and washing his own pan only of an evening when the forge was banked, until the gold he had put by, a modest handful, was worth more than he could easily account for to a maor's clerk who came asking why a village smith kept coin he had no wages to show for. He told the clerk the plain truth rather than invent a lie he would have to keep, and the clerk, to the smith's own surprise, thanked him for the telling and carried the matter south rather than fining him for the withholding.

The council added the stream's gold to the villages' own charge that same year, washed and weighed alongside the silver bar and struck into the same blanks the mint's own dies pressed for the realm-coin, so that a coin drawn at random from any shire's till that year might carry, unmarked and unremarked, a grain of Baile dhìreach's own stream in its weight. The first blanks struck under the new arrangement went west from the eastern hills in am Faoilleach, carried by the same clerk who had first asked the smith his question, riding a road he had ridden a hundred times before on the guild's ordinary business and reckoning, this once, that he carried something worth minding on the way. He handed the blanks to the mint's own master at Cathair dhearg with no more ceremony than a carter handing over a load of grain, and the master weighed them, found the sum true to the fraction the villages' own reckoning had promised, and signed for them without comment, which the clerk took, riding home, for the highest praise the mint's own hand was ever likely to give anybody.

The villages were paid by weight that spring and every spring after, the payment carried up from Cathair dhearg in a locked box a maor's rider brought once the quarter's blanks were counted, and the smith who had found the gold in his own pan, whose name the villages kept among themselves though no royal book troubled to record it, was said by his neighbours to have washed that same stream every evening of his life after, long past the years his own forge still needed the wage, on the plain habit, he told anyone who asked him why, of a man who has once found a thing worth finding and sees no reason to stop looking for it again.

## III. Of Mòr nic Dhòmhnaill

Domhnall the elder, Mòr's own father, had refined silver for the old guild longer than any other hand at Muileann chiar, a careful worker who could tell the fineness of a bar by its ring on the anvil before the assayer's own scale confirmed it, and his daughter had grown up at his elbow the way a smith's own daughter grows up at a forge, learning the work by watching it long before anyone thought to teach it to her outright. She was past thirty herself the year Iain's survey proved the deep gallery, unmarried by then longer than the town thought usual for a refiner's own daughter, having kept her father's books and weighed his bar since her mother's death without much time left over, she told anyone who asked her plainly why, for the kind of courting a town like Muileann chiar expected of its women.

Iain had known her some years before the guild's charter was renewed, the two of them meeting first over a dispute about the true weight of a bar the guild's own scale and the Board's own scale had returned two different figures for, a dispute Iain was sent to settle and Mòr was sent, by her father who trusted her hand more than his own that week, to argue her family's side of. She proved him wrong in front of three of the guild's own captains, walking him through the weighing twice to show him where his own scale's beam sat a hair's breadth off true, and he thanked her for it rather than taking offence, a response she found rarer in a Board man than she had been led to expect and said so to her father that same evening.

They were married in am Faoilleach of the year the deep gallery's charter was signed, a plain ceremony at the guild hall rather than any grander house, the same long table that had held Iain's survey the season before cleared and scrubbed and laid with what the guild's own wives could put together on short notice, bread and the guild's own store of dried fish and a cask a departing wool-factor had left against a debt nobody now troubled to collect. Mòr's father gave her hand himself, his own voice steadier at the giving of it than Iain had ever heard it over a disputed bar, and the guild's captains stood witness in place of any kin Iain had thought to bring from the west, since his own people were a hard two days' distance and a Board man's postings did not run to much visiting. One of the captains, the same who had doubted the timbering, stood and said, when the guild's own custom called for a witness to speak, that he had watched a great many surveys come through that hall and never one that had married into it before, which the room took for the nearest thing to a blessing the man was ever likely to give anybody, and Mòr laughed longer at it than the joke quite earned, which Iain took for the truer blessing of the two.

Mòr kept her own name at the guild's books after the marriage, as a refiner's daughter's name was worth more on a ledger than a surveyor's, and the two of them kept, that first year, two households' worth of habits under the one roof, Mòr rising before first light to weigh the night's cooling bar while it was easiest read and Iain gone before she had finished to whatever gallery the week's work called him to, so that David the guild's own boy, who carried messages between the forge and the shaft-head, joked that he served two masters under one roof and never caught them at the same meal twice running. Iain told her on their first evening as man and wife that he had reckoned, walking east from the Sloc Mòr those eleven years before, that he was walking toward a posting and had not once reckoned he was walking toward a wife, a confession she took, she told him, as the nearest thing to a compliment a surveyor's tongue was ever likely to manage, and answered that she had reckoned, watching him lose an argument over a scale's true beam in front of three of her father's own captains, that she was watching a man honest enough to be worth the losing of an argument to, which she meant, she told him, as the higher compliment of the two.

## IV. Of the Two Towns Called Dùn thais

There were two towns on the island that answered to the one name, Dùn thais, one on the west coast within a morning's ride of Ros bheag and the other far to the east, seat of its own shire and its own dues, and the confusion the two had caused the royal record since the drawing of the shires had never yet troubled anyone enough to be untangled, since neither town's business had often crossed the other's on any page a clerk at Cathair dhearg was likely to read in the same sitting. That changed, in its small way, the same year the eastern hills' first blanks went to the mint, when both towns' names reached the capital in the same season's post.

The western Dùn thais asked, that spring, for a court of the sea to be set over its own harbour, to judge salvage and wreck along a stretch of coast that had gone without any such ruling since the Severance, its fishermen having settled such disputes among themselves by custom until a wrecked hulk driven ashore the autumn before proved too rich a prize for custom alone to divide without hard words on both sides of it. The council granted the court within the season, and its first sitting, held on the strand with the hulk still canted where the tide had left it, awarded the wreck whole to the crews who had driven it aground rather than let it lie for whoever claimed it first, a ruling the fishermen carried home more pleased with the court's plain justice than with the timber it won them.

The eastern Dùn thais, in the same season, opened a covered market for the hill farms that had traded in its square uncovered since the town was first walled, a long timbered hall raised at the shire's own charge to keep the autumn's grain dry through a market day, its first trading held under a roof that smelled, the farmers said, more of new-cut wood than of the produce it sheltered. The clerk at Cathair dhearg who filed the eastern town's petition for its market alongside the western town's petition for its court, both arriving within the same week and both signed only "Dùn thais" without further marking, entered the two matters against the one town's name in the royal record before a second clerk, reading the file a fortnight later, caught that a market and a sea-court could hardly belong to a single harbourless hill town in the same season and set the error right by hand, a correction that held for exactly as long as it took the next season's post to bring the next confusion.

Neither town troubled itself over the mistake once it reached their own ears, each reckoning, in the way of a town used to being the only Dùn thais its own shire had ever needed to distinguish, that the fault lay in the capital's own carelessness and not in any likeness between the two of them, and the royal record went on confusing the pair a while longer yet, court and market alike filed sometimes rightly and sometimes not. A factor from the western town, riding south that same year on business of his own, was twice asked by clerks at Cathair dhearg after the covered market's own takings, a question he could not answer and thought, at first, a poor joke at his expense, until he understood that the clerk before him held no joke at all, only a file that had never once been told there were two towns to keep apart. He carried the tale home to the western harbour more amused by it than aggrieved, and it was told at that town's own hearths for years after, growing a little in the telling each time, that the capital itself could not tell a sea-court from a market roof so long as both bore the one name.

## V. Of the Petition from Baile chiar

Doire chaol, the village laid out south of the capital in the first years after the Severance for the families that served the royal household, had grown in the years since from a scattering of houses built for clerks and stewards into a town proper, its own market crowded of a market day and its own disputes running thicker than the maor of Baile chiar, whose shire the village sat within, had ever troubled to answer for when it was smaller. The maor wrote to the council that same year, plainly and without much ornament, that Doire chaol's business had outgrown a seat five miles distant and asked that the village be given a maor of its own rather than go on being governed, badly and at second hand, from a hall it took the better part of a morning to reach on the village's own worst roads.

The council read the petition alongside a dozen others that season and granted it before the summer was old, the only shire cut new from an older one since the original drawing had first set the island's bounds, Siorrachd Doire chaol entered onto the roll with its own arms, its own dues, and a maor of its own choosing rather than the Baile chiar man's deputy who had kept its peace, badly, these many years. The Baile chiar maor himself, reading the grant, was heard by his own clerk to say only that he was glad of the lightening, having governed a village he could not properly see to for longer than he cared to own, and sent the new shire's first dues south the same season with a note wishing its new maor better luck of it than he had had.

## VI. Of the Shepherd above Doire uaine

The hills above Doire uaine had been grazed thin by shepherds for as long as any flock had run there, save one stretch of high ground the shepherds themselves would not put a beast to, a shoulder of hill where the old writings the town's own keeper still had by heart told of a thing that was dead and did not rest, the Marbh-bheò the writings named it and no shepherd living had ever seen with his own eyes, though every one of them could point to the ground it was said to keep. It was custom rather than any written rule that kept the flocks off that shoulder, the kind of custom a hill country keeps without troubling to ask itself why, and it had held, the keeper reckoned, since before her own grandmother's telling of it.

A shepherd new to that country, a young man down from the north hired that season for want of local hands enough to cover the lambing, put his own flock to the shoulder's grass one evening rather than walk them the longer way round it, the grass there thicker than anywhere else on the hill and the light already going, and did not come down again. His dog came down alone the next morning, and the flock scattered wide over ground it had never before been let to graze, and the town searched the shoulder three days running without finding more of him than a crook left standing where the ground pitched steep, driven into the turf as a man might drive it who meant to climb rather than fall.

The magistrate who wrote the matter into the shire's own book, a careful man who had no more taste than his own clerks for setting an old story down as a court's own finding, entered wolves as the cause, a beast or beasts unaccounted for having come down off the higher ground that season, a finding the town's own shepherds neither argued nor believed, since no wolf had been seen on that hill in living memory and none was seen after, but a finding that let the book close on the matter without asking the court to rule on a thing older than any court the island kept. The keeper who held the old writings by heart said nothing against the magistrate's entry when it was read to her, only that the shoulder would go on being grazed thin and empty whatever the book called the cause of it, and the shepherds, who had never needed the book's word to keep off that ground before the finding and needed it no more after, went on keeping off it exactly as they always had.

The young shepherd's crook was brought down off the hill and given to his own family, who had walked three days from the north to claim what little of him the shoulder had left to claim, and the mother, standing at the magistrate's own door with the crook in her two hands, asked him plainly whether he believed his own entry, wolves being a thing she had shepherded thirty years herself without once losing a beast to. The magistrate, who had asked himself the same question more than once in the writing of it, told her only that the book wanted a cause it could hold, and that a mother burying a son deserved a finding she could carry home and set before a shire court if ever she wanted to, which a hillside's old writing, however faithfully kept, was never going to give her. She took the crook and the finding both, and thanked him for neither more nor less than the truth he had given her, and walked the three days back north with her son's own crook wrapped in her shawl the whole way.

## VII. Of the Copy Iain Kept

Iain wrote the guild's new charter into his own private book the same evening it was signed, in the plain hand he kept for entries he meant to be able to find again without searching, beside the receipt the Board had given him eleven years before and the deep gallery's own figures, set down fair the week he first proved them. He had kept the habit since his first survey, a second record held against the day the Board's own copy might be lost, mislaid, or simply not shown to the hand that had earned the showing of it, and he had never yet had cause to open the book for any purpose grander than his own satisfaction that the figures, wherever the Board's own copies went, still existed somewhere a man could put his hand to them.

Mòr found him at it one evening that autumn, the book open on the table between them while she totted the guild's own weekly weighing at his elbow, and asked him, not for the first time, why a Board man troubled to keep a second copy of business the Board itself was paid to keep straight. He told her what he had told nobody else in eleven years of the keeping, that the vein at the Sloc Mòr had thinned exactly as his first survey said it would and no living soul at Cathair mhòr had ever once told him so, the figures simply vanishing into the Board's own files the day he handed them over and never once being spoken of to him again, so that a man might work eleven years for a Board that had proved him right and never learn it from any mouth but his own reckoning. The silver at Muileann chiar ran the other way, richer with every fathom where the coal at the Sloc Mòr had run thinner with every one, and Iain told her, closing the book, that he meant to go on keeping his own copy of both truths for as long as the Board went on keeping its own counsel about either of them, a thing that seemed to him, though he did not put it in those words to her, less like caution now than like the plainest kind of accounting a man could keep against a kingdom that told him only what it chose to.

He put the book away on its shelf, silver charter and coal survey held the same distance from his own reaching hand, and walked out with Mòr to the stream below the town, where the light was going the way it went in that country at that season, thin and long over the hills, and said nothing more of the Board that evening, the two of them standing a while at the water's edge before the cold turned them back toward the forge's own banked warmth and the guild's ledgers waiting, unfinished, on the table they had left.

# Chapter Twenty-eight: Of the Fall at Muileann dhearg

*SE 39 an t-Iuchar – SE 40 an t-Samhain*

> *Cha d' fhuair a' bheinn fois a-riamh, is cha d' fhuair sinne.*
> The mountain never got its rest, and neither did we.

## I. Of the First Day of an t-Iuchar

Muileann dhearg had grown fat on the Sloc Mòr's overflow for thirty years, a town of narrow streets and spoil-stone chapels five miles from the great shaft, its own pits worked to keep the Sloc Mòr's yield steady in the seasons when the greater mine's own galleries wanted rest the Crown would not grant them. The Cill ghlas district under Muileann dhearg had stood shut from the humans' time until the Board reopened it, and the men who went down into it that first morning of an t-Iuchar knew its name the way every hewer on the mountain knew it, the way a house knows a grave it does not visit. Scàineadh Cill ghlas, the Rending, had taken the old workings in the Age of Strangers, and the timbers that came up afterward, what little of them came up whole, were kept for a season in the guild hall at Achadh dhomhain before anyone could bear to burn them. The new gallery ran a hundred fathoms east of where the old one had run, along a line the Board's own surveyors had walked twice and marked sound on the map both times. It had been working four months.

It gave at the fourth hour past midnight shift-change, when the day gang was down and the night gang not yet up, so that for one turn of the clock the gallery held more men than it would hold at any other hour of the twenty-four. Nobody afterward could say what brought it down, only that the roof let go along its whole length at once rather than falling face by face the way a bad roof usually gives a man time to run from, and that the noise of it was heard on the surface as a single long note, like a bell struck once and left to die away underground instead of in the air. Thirty-one men were in the gallery. None of them came up alive.

Word reached Muileann chiar the following evening, carried by a rider the Board sent without much urgency, since it was a mine matter and Iain mac Ruairidh was thirteen years at the silver works and no longer, by the Board's own reckoning, a mine matter himself. The rider found him at his own door with Mòr beside him, the two of them newly enough married that neighbours still called across the yard to wish them well of an evening, and he read the message once standing in the doorway and once again sitting down, and said nothing to his wife beyond that he would be a week gone, perhaps more.

He was chainman first at the Sloc Mòr before he was Board surveyor anywhere else, and Cill ghlas was ground he had walked as a boy learning the chain from Lachlann mac Iain Bhàin, who had walked it as a boy under the man before him. He rode through the night rather than wait for morning, the twenty miles by the coal road and then the cart track up from Achadh dhomhain, and came into Muileann dhearg with the horse blown and his own legs near as unsteady under him, to find the town already at its digging, torches ringing the pit mouth and women carrying water up from the wash-house in relays that had not stopped since the fall.

They let him down on the second rope, the first having been given to the guild's own overman, and he went the whole hundred fathoms with a lamp in one hand and the guild's rope in the other, over rubble that shifted under his boots in ways rubble should not shift, until the beam of his lamp found the roof-line where it had let go and he stood a long while looking at it before he spoke to the man behind him.

"Bring me a level," he said. "And send to Muileann chiar for the old sheets I keep there. Not the Board's. Mine."

They brought him the level before the old maps came, since the maps had to be sent for from Muileann chiar and would not reach him before the second day. He spent the dark hours of that first night on his knees along the fallen roof-line, the level laid flat and a boy holding the lamp steady over his shoulder, and marked chalk figures on a slate the rubble dust settled over as fast as he could write them. The overman, a broad man named for no reason this book keeps to it, crouched beside him a while and asked, once, whether the fault ran under the working faces still open to the north.

"It runs under half the district," Iain Mapa said. "I don't yet know which half is the safer half."

"Then we bring up what we can and shut the rest."

"That's my own thought, aye. I'll want it in writing that it was my thought and not the Board's, before I put my name to closing a working that four months of Board surveys called sound."

The overman said nothing to that beyond a short breath that was not quite a laugh, and went back to the rope.

## II. Of the Rules Made for the Dia-thìrich

It took four days to bring up the thirty-one, working by relays through galleries that groaned at every stroke of the pick, and on the fifth day the whole district was closed on Iain Mapa's own word before the Board at Cathair mhòr had so much as read his report. He had found the fault by the second day: a line of broken ground running north-east under the new gallery exactly where the Rending's own line had run under the old one in the humans' time, so close to the surface survey's marked boundary that a man drawing the map by lamplight, in a hurry, might have set his pencil a hair's width wrong and never known it. A Board that surveyed a district once and called the survey finished had made an ordinary error, the kind any board might make. The mountain itself had not finished moving simply because a map said it had stopped.

The old maps reached him on the third day, brought up from Muileann chiar by a rider who had ridden as hard coming as Iain Mapa himself had ridden going, three rolled sheets Iain had copied years before from the custodians' old rolls, older in their first drawing than any paper the Board kept at Cathair mhòr, drawn by hands long dead in a script the Board's own clerks could no longer easily read. He unrolled them on a trestle set up in the open air beside the pit mouth, weighting the corners with stones against a wind that wanted to carry them off toward the burying-ground, and laid his own new chalk figures over the old ink line by line until the two agreed to within a fathom along the whole length of the fault. The old surveyors, whoever they had been, had known exactly where the ground was broken. They had marked it, in a hand gone brown with age, with a single word he had to hold the lamp close to read: *fàgte*. Left. Let be.

The dead were buried at Muileann dhearg in a single ground broken for them at the edge of the town's own burying-yard, thirty-one graves dug in two days by every man in the town not needed underground, the custodian of the district reading over each in turn rather than once over all, since the families asked it that way and the custodian did not argue. Iain Mapa stood at the ground's edge through the whole of it, hat in hand, and was asked by more than one widow, in the flat voice grief leaves people with, whether the ground had been marked sound. He answered every one of them the same way. It had.

He did not tell the widows what the level had told him in the dark of the first night, that the ground had been marked sound by men who had walked it with a chain and a lamp and had not walked it far enough, or often enough, or with the old lists of the Rending laid open beside their own paper while they walked. It would have told the widows nothing they could use, and he had learned enough of the Board by then to know that a truth spoken over a grave and a truth written into a report the Board would read did not need to be spoken in the same words, or even, always, by the same man. The level's figures he kept on his slate until he could copy them fair, washing the chalk dust off with his own hand rather than a boy's, the way a man washes a thing he means to use again.

The Board's rules followed within the month, new orders for the digging of any gallery within a mile of ground the old lists named as struck by a calamity, timber doubled, a second survey required before any face was opened, a bell-line run the whole length of a new working so that a fall anywhere along it could be heard at both ends at once. They were good rules, and Iain Mapa, reading them at Muileann dhearg where the Board sent them to him first as the man who had closed the district, found nothing in them he would have changed. They were written for the Sloc Mòr and its daughter workings, where Dia-thìreach hewers held the guild's own oath and the guild's own voice to ask for them. At the western pits, where Tuathaich hands worked under Dia-thìreach overseers on ground the guild had never chartered, the same order went out on the same day's post and was kept the way an order is kept by men who know no one south of them will come to check.

It is told of Àth leathan, where the overseer's own name is not given in any record the Library holds, that the new rule for timbering was posted on the pit-head door within the week, in the Board's own hand, and that the timber the rule called for was ordered from the yard at Ceann mhòr the same week, and paid for out of the pit's own accounts, and never came. The overseer's books, kept in the flat hand overseers kept for such things, show the order and the payment both, entered on facing pages, with no third entry anywhere to say why the carts never left the yard. The hewers at Àth leathan went on working the old way, under the old timber, because a man with a family to feed does not stop hewing coal to ask a question the pit-head door has already answered him with a posted order he cannot read.

Iain Mapa did not go to Àth leathan that autumn. He heard of it the way the Board heard of most things from the western pits, sideways, in a clerk's letter meant for another matter that mentioned the timber order in passing, as a thing settled, and he kept the letter. Thirteen years before, at Cathair dhearg, he had learned what a receipt was worth against a Board that did not read what it filed, and he had begun, without quite deciding to, the habit of keeping every paper that crossed his own hand a second time before he let it go.

He wrote his own letter that same week, at the table Mòr kept for him by the window, naming the fault at Cill ghlas by its true line, citing the survey he had made thirteen years before of the faces of the Sloc Mòr, and setting the two beside each other on the page: a mountain that did not rest, and a Board that surveyed it once and called the matter closed. He wrote until past midnight, by his own lamp, and read it through twice, and folded it, and did not seal it.

"You'll send that," Mòr said, from the door, in a voice that was not quite a question.

"I sent one before," he said. "They gave me a receipt for it and moved me to the silver."

"This one names thirty-one dead, not a thinning seam."

"It names the same Board." He turned the letter over once on the table, as though weighing it in his hand might tell him something the words on it could not. "A receipt is a fine thing to have kept, thirteen years on. I've never once had cause to use it."

Mòr said nothing further that night. She had married a surveyor and not a clerk of the Moot, and she had learned in a year of marriage that there were silences of his best left alone, and this, she judged, was one of them. He put the letter in the drawer where he kept the receipt, unsealed, and left it there, and if he took it out again in the weeks that followed, to read over or to add a line to, no one at Muileann chiar ever saw him do it.

## III. Of the Sixty and the Forty

Muileann dhearg did not fill again the way it had filled in the first years of the concession, on wages and the promise of work. Forty families left Achadh dhomhain before the autumn was out, walking south to the fishing ports with what a cart would carry, and the town's own tally-clerk, entering their names off the roll, wrote against each one only *gone south*, since the roll kept no other word for it. Some had lost no one in the fall and went anyway, saying to whoever asked that a town could grieve thirty-one men once and go on living beside their graves, but a family did not choose to raise its own sons under a mountain that had shown, once, what it thought of a survey.

The Guild of Hewers, whose rolls the fall had thinned by thirty-one at a stroke, bound sixty apprentices that same season to fill them, boys sworn in at Achadh dhomhain with a hand laid on a lump of coal in the guild's own hall, the oath read out by the guild's eldest master in the same words it had been read in since the charter, each boy's father standing behind him in a line that ran the length of the hall and out its door into the yard. Not one of the sixty was Tuathaich. The guild's charter had said, since the Holy Age custom was taken up again, that it was for Dia-thìreach applicants, and the charter was kept, so that the pits that had just buried thirty-one Dia-thìreach hewers filled their rolls again with Dia-thìreach boys, and the western pits, where the dying was no less real for going uncounted, filled theirs with whatever hands the overseers could hire by the day and let go by the day when the work was thin.

At Caol mhòr, where the north's own minute-book had carried the fall as four lines the week it happened and nothing since, Mary Coyle read the Board's new rules when a copy reached the Moot by way of a carter who had seen them posted at Ceann mhòr, and sat with them a long while before she called for the book. She wrote to the Board that autumn, in her own hand, asking that the same rules be kept in fact as well as in the posting at the western pits, and named Àth leathan by name, and the timber that had not come. She sent it by the same carter's road the goods went south by, since the Moot had no faster road to send anything by.

The letter reached Cathair mhòr within the fortnight and was answered within the month, in three lines, thanking the Moot for its concern and stating that the matter had been referred to the district overseer for his report. No report was ever filed. The letter was kept, in the press where the Board kept what it had no further use for, and a clerk's hand noted its arrival on the cover in the same flat script that had noted the timber order at Àth leathan on facing pages a season before. Mary Coyle asked the carter, the next time he came north, whether he had heard anything more of it. He had not. She wrote nothing further that year. The book at Caol mhòr held her one letter and the Board's three lines, and nothing between them, and that was the whole of what the kingdom's own record held of Àth leathan's timber.

## IV. Of the Third Day of an t-Sultain

The Library at Muileann chaol kept its own account of that autumn apart from anything Iain Mapa saw or heard, and it is from the Library's own record, and not from any word that reached him at Muileann dhearg, that this book takes what follows.

Ailean Leabhar had kept the Library four-and-twenty years, first among the wet rolls in the cellar and then among the chests the shires sent up one by one, and he had grown old in the keeping the way the rolls themselves grew old, a little more brittle each year, the hand that had once carried a torch down a stair now needing a boy to carry the lamp for him. He was four-and-sixty that autumn, though he had stopped, some years before, letting anyone at Muileann chaol mark his birthday, saying that a keeper's business was other men's years and not his own.
