He kept to his desk through most of an Lùnastal and into an t-Sultain, reading, as he had read every autumn for a decade, the harvest returns the shires sent up, and he was found there on the morning of the third day of the month, at his own desk, with the returns for Siorrachd Doire chaol open under his hand and his pen laid down beside them rather than dropped, so that Mòrag nic Coinnich, who found him, said afterward that he looked to have finished the line he was writing before he stopped.

They buried him two days after, in the small ground behind the Library, where no keeper had been buried before him because no keeper before him had held the office long enough to be thought of as belonging to the place rather than merely working in it. The town of Muileann chaol turned out for it near to the last household, since there was scarcely a family in the shire the Library's own chests had not, in four-and-twenty years, asked something of, a grave-list copied or a boundary confirmed or a name set right against a parish book gone soft with damp. Mòrag nic Coinnich read nothing over him beyond his own words, the ones a clerk had once used in his hearing and that he had answered without meaning the answer to outlast him.

"The Library settles nothing," she said, at the grave's edge, in a voice that carried no further than the nearest rows of mourners. "It only keeps."

She was named keeper before the month was out, the council at Cathair dhearg confirming what Muileann chaol had already taken for settled the day Ailean Leabhar was found at his desk, and she began, within her first week in the office, a practice no keeper before her had kept: writing beside each item that came into the chests, in a small hand at the foot of its own entry, where it had come from and who had sent it and on what day. She gave no reason for the practice when she was asked, beyond that a thing a Library could not trace back to its own hand was a thing the Library could be told anything about, and she had watched, in all her years at Ailean Leabhar's own elbow, how often the Board's word and the shire's word and the north's word, laid side by side, did not agree.

Eight years his deputy by then, she knew which chests he had never finished sorting and which he had gone back to twice and still called unfinished, and she spent her first month as keeper doing what she told no one at the time she was doing: going through his own desk, drawer by drawer, in case some paper he had meant to file lay there still, undone. She found nothing from Muileann dhearg, and nothing from Àth leathan, since neither the Board's silence on the one nor its three lines on the other had ever been sent to the Library at all. What she found, at the back of the lowest drawer, was a single sheet in his own hand, headed only with a date some years old, that read, in its whole: *what we are not sent, we cannot keep. Ask the shires again.* She could not say, reading it, whether it was a note to himself or the first line of a letter he had never finished, and she kept it, unfiled, in the drawer of her own desk, where it stayed the whole of her time as keeper.

## V. Of the Fire at the Fair

The fair at Muileann òg had stood nineteen years by that Samhain, the greatest gathering the island kept, its stalls running three full days along the river meadow below the toll-house where Oighrig nic Mhathain had kept the rules since the first year, a woman of fifty now, grey at the temple, still walking the whole length of the ground herself each morning before the gates opened, the way she had walked it the first year with the rules not yet a season old.

The fire ran on the eve of the feast, after the gates were shut and most of the stall-holders gone to their lodgings, starting, so far as anyone could afterward say, in the timber stacked behind the weavers' row for the mending of trestles, and running before the wind caught it properly along a row of canvas and dry wood that had stood in the same ground, packed close, for three days running. It went from stall to stall faster than any man on the ground that night could outrun it on foot, the canvas roofs catching each in turn with a sound one witness likened to a sail taken aback in a hard squall, and by the time the bucket-chain from the river was properly formed the weavers' row and half the chandlers' beyond it stood already past saving.

Oighrig was in the ground herself when it started, having gone back for a ledger left in the toll-house, and she was seen by more than one witness beating at the canvas with her own cloak before the men who came running got the worst of it turned aside from the stalls that held the season's whole trade for a dozen towns. She did not leave the ground until the last of the flame along the weavers' row had been beaten down or burned out on its own, and it was only then, in the grey light before dawn, that anyone thought to look closely at her hands.

The court sat the next morning in the trampled field, since the toll-house had burned with the rest, Oighrig presiding from a chair a stall-holder carried out for her, her hands and one side of her face bound in linen already gone brown at the edges, and the fair went on that day and the next as the rules said it must, since a fair once opened could not, by the rules she herself had written nineteen years before, be closed before its third day without the toll-mistress's own word, and she gave no such word. She died of the burns before the month was out, at her own house at Muileann òg, the toll-mistress's chair going, for the first time since the fair began, to a woman who had not held it from the first year.

That same winter the Rail Board, asked by the Moot to carry the north's wool south to the fair as it had carried southern goods for twenty years, refused the carriage, citing the fair's own rule that Tuathaich goods be sold only through Dia-thìreach factors and holding that a rule written for the selling of goods bound the carrying of them as well, a reading no clerk at the Board had troubled to make in any of the twenty years before. Mary Coyle wrote a second letter that winter, shorter than the first, asking only whether the Board's reading of the rule was new or had always stood and simply never before been used against the north's own goods. The Board did not answer it. A clerk's hand noted its arrival on the cover, in the same flat script, and filed it beside the first.

The wool went south the old way that year, loaded onto carts at Caol mhòr in the first cold week of an Dùbhlachd, five days on the road by Cnoc ghorm and Àth fhada to the fair at Muileann òg, the carters wrapped against a wind that had not yet learned to be as hard as it would be by the time they reached the coast, the last of the north's trade for that year going south the way it had gone before there was ever a railway to refuse it. The new toll-mistress at Muileann òg, keeping the fair's rules as Oighrig had left them, sold the wool through its factors when it came, as the rule said she must, and entered the sale in the fair's own book under the makers' shire and not their names, as the book had always kept it.

Iain Mapa, at Muileann dhearg that same week, closing out the district's books before the district itself was let stand idle through the winter, wrote nothing new to the letter in his drawer, and sent nothing south beyond the district's own accounts, which the Board read.

# Chapter Twenty-nine: Of the Carters' Road

*SE 41 am Faoilleach – SE 42 an t-Iuchar*

> Entered this day, on the word of the widow at Àth fhada, one name: her husband, lost under the western pits in the spring gone by. No other book will hold it. This one will.
>
> — the first entry of Clàr nan Leòn, 28 an Dùbhlachd, SE 41, as the Moot's clerks kept it

## I. Of the Road the North Named

The Rail Board's refusal stood through the whole of that winter, and the wool of the north went south the only way left to it, by cart, five days on the road from Muileann leathan to the fair at Muileann òg, and Daniel Frayne rode with the second train of carts that left in am Faoilleach, having asked leave to go himself, the Moot having sent no one before him and nobody troubling that winter to say him no. He was thirty-six that winter, a clerk of the Moot since before he could properly be called a man, and he had spent most of those years at a table at Caol mhòr with other men's words in front of him and had not, until that winter, ridden further from the northern shires than a day's walking would carry him.

The road the carts took was no road the Board's own maps troubled to draw, being nothing more than the old way the Tuathaich had always known between one northern town and the next, worn by feet and cart-wheels rather than laid by any surveyor's chain: out from Muileann leathan by Cnoc ghorm, where the church built for the Ros bheag bell stood with its door open to the carters of a market morning, and on by Àth fhada, where the ford that gave the town its name ran shallow enough in that season for the carts to cross without unloading, and down at last by the old way to Inis àrsaidh, where the road proper began and the wool went on by a track the fair's own toll-keepers knew and taxed. Frayne rode the whole of it on a borrowed horse he handled worse than he handled a pen, and said as much to the carter beside him on the second day, who laughed and told him a Moot clerk's hands were worth more to the north whole than broken on a green horse's account, and to hold the rein looser.

It was at Àth fhada that the first house opened its door to the carters as an inn proper rather than as a household doing a neighbour's kindness, the family that kept it having fed carters at their own table for two winters running before one of them, a woman near sixty who had buried a husband under the western pits and raised four children on what the mine paid a widow, reckoned that a house that fed twenty men a night on its own charity might as well be paid for the feeding. She hung no sign, having none to hang and no coin to cut one, but she kept a lamp lit in her window past the hour any other house in the town kept one lit, and the carters came to know the lamp before they knew her name, and called the house by it. Within the season two more households on the road had done the same, at Cnoc ghorm and at a crossing short of Inis àrsaidh, each lit lamp answering the one before it, so that a carter riding that road by night in the second winter of the wool's going by cart could find his bed by the lights alone, without once asking a stranger the way.

Frayne asked the widow at Àth fhada, on the second night he lodged under her lamp, what the carters called the road they rode, having heard no one name it before that journey and having wondered, riding it, whether a way so plainly worn by use had ever been given a name at all. She told him plainly that the north had always called it the Carters' Road, and had called it so since before the wool went by cart at all, back to the years when the same track carried salt and grain between the northern towns before any fair at Muileann òg had reason to want either, and that the name had simply grown to fit the newer use as a coat is let out to fit a growing child, without anyone troubling to cut a new one. He asked her, being a clerk and unable to leave a fact alone once he had it, what the south called the same road, and she told him, without much interest in the answer, that she did not know the south troubled to call it anything, the road not existing on any map south of Cnoc ghorm that she had ever heard of a southern man consulting. Frayne wrote the two facts down in the small book he carried for the Moot's business, the north's name and the south's silence side by side, and thought, riding on the third morning with the carts strung out ahead of him on a road no southern chart would own, that a thing could be entirely real to one half of an island and entirely absent from the other half's account of the same island, and that this seemed to him, turning the thought over as the horse found its own footing better than his hands found the rein, the truest thing the journey had shown him.

The weather held fair the first three days and broke on the fourth, a cold rain out of the west that found every gap in a carter's coat and turned the road's worn ruts to standing water by the time the train came down off the higher ground short of Inis àrsaidh, and Frayne, who had never in his years at a Moot table learned what it was to sit a horse in rain that did not let up, understood before the day was out why the carters rode in wide-brimmed hats no Caol mhòr clerk troubled to own. The lead carter, an old man who had driven the same road for the wool before Frayne was born and for salt and grain before that, told him, when Frayne asked how the carts would cross the low ground with the water standing as it was, that a road worn as long as this one had been worn found its own way round a flood the way a stream finds its own way round a stone, and that the carts would sit a night at the crossing short of Inis àrsaidh and go on when the water dropped, which they did, losing half a day to the weather and none of the wool to it.

It was at that same crossing, waiting out the rain under the third of the road's new lamps, that Frayne fell into talk with a Tuathaich family of the western pits travelling the other way, north from the fair with a season's wages and a cart of goods a southern factor had let them buy against the wool not yet sold, and heard from them, for the first time in his own hearing rather than at second hand in a Moot report, how a family that had never owned land of its own reckoned the road's five days against a season's whole earning. The husband told him plainly that the road cost the north more than the south ever troubled to count, a cart and a team and five days of a man's labour spent getting wool to a fair that would have carried it in a single day by rail had the Board's own rule allowed it, and that the toll the carters paid in time was a toll no ledger at Cathair dhearg would ever be asked to enter against the fair's own profit. Frayne wrote the figure down as the man gave it to him, a season's wages set against five days twice over for every cart the north sent south, and thought, riding on once the water had dropped enough to let the carts through, that a fact set down in a clerk's small book travelled no further than that book's own covers unless someone with the standing to be heard troubled to carry it further.

The carts reached Muileann òg on the fifth day, as they always did, and the wool was sold by the factors the fair's own rule required, at a price the carters reckoned fair enough for the road behind them and mean enough for the road they knew the profit was truly measured against, and Frayne stood at the fair's own edge a while watching the factors' clerks weigh and mark the bales before he turned to find the inn the carts' own drivers used, a house that took Tuathaich custom without comment because its owner had learned, over enough seasons, that a carter's coin spent as well as any other man's. He rode home the same road he had ridden out, five days back by the same lamps, the water dropped now and the going easier, carrying nothing the Moot could point to as the fruit of the journey save the two facts in his small book, the north's name for the road and the south's silence about it, a season's wages weighed against five days twice told, and a callus on his right hand he had not had going out.

## II. Of the Boy Who Watched

In the north in those years Dubhan was a boy of twelve. He grew up watching a caste that did not age hold every true advantage on an island to whose edge his own forebears had been pushed, and the coal was never his to inherit. Of him the chronicle of those years says nothing more, and the Library has nothing more to give.

## III. Of the Register Begun

Mary Coyle called the Moot's clerks to the room at Caol mhòr in an Dùbhlachd of that same year, Frayne among them, home from the carters' road some months and back at his usual table, and told them plainly what she had told no one outside the room before that morning: that the Board kept no count of the Tuathaich dead and maimed in the western pits beyond what the census swept up in its own careless net, a number without a name attached to it anywhere a hewer's own family could ever put a finger to, and that the Moot, having no Board of its own to answer to and no council above it to forbid the keeping, would begin a book that named them one by one, on the families' own word since no other word was going to be offered.

"We have no rolls to draw the names from," Frayne said, the first objection any clerk in the room troubled to raise aloud, "and a name taken on a widow's word alone, with nothing to check it against, is a name a southern court would throw out before it read the second line." Mary Coyle answered him that she had not asked the room to keep a book a southern court would honour, only a book that would be true, and that a widow's own word, given in a room with her neighbours to hear it, was truth enough for any book the Moot troubled to keep, whatever a court south of Caol mhòr chose to call it.

The book was opened that same week, a plain ledger bound at Muileann leathan and carried north still smelling of the binder's glue, and the first name entered in it was the husband of the widow at Àth fhada whose lamp Frayne had lodged under not a year before, brought to the room by a neighbour of hers who had walked the road south on other business and thought, hearing the Moot's new business spoken of, to carry the widow's name along with him rather than let it wait for a season she might not trouble to make the journey herself. Frayne wrote the entry in his own hand, the widow's husband's name and the pit he had died under and the season it had happened in, and set the pen down a moment before the ink was dry, having understood, in the writing of that single line, that he had just done the one thing his years at a Moot table had never yet let him do, which was to put a Tuathaich name into a book that meant to keep it rather than to file it and forget it. He told Mary Coyle, handing her the ledger to read over, that he did not know how many names the book would want before it was done, and she told him that neither did she, and that not knowing was the whole of the reason for keeping it.

The register grew through that winter and the spring after, a name and a place and a season at a time, entered on no evidence stronger than a family's own remembering and checked against nothing but the room's own trust in the family that gave it. Frayne kept the second book himself, a working ledger where a name was first set down rough before it was copied fair into Clàr nan Leòn proper, and he found, within the first month of the keeping, that the work asked more of a clerk than the careful hand he had brought to it out of habit. A name given at second hand by a neighbour wanted checking, where checking could be had, against whatever other neighbour or kinsman might confirm the season and the pit, the Moot trusting the neighbour's word well enough and asking only that a register meant to outlast the men who kept it be made as right as a clerk's own care could make it; and more than one entry that winter was set down first as one thing and corrected within the season to another, a season misremembered, a pit's own name given wrong by a family that had moved twice since the death and forgotten which working had taken the man.

Mary Coyle read every entry before it went into the fair copy, a habit she kept up through that whole first year though the room's other business left her little enough time for it, and told Frayne, the evening he brought her the twentieth name, that she meant to go on reading each one herself for as long as her eyes held out, since a book kept for the dead deserved at least one pair of eyes that troubled to read it whole rather than trusting the work entire to a clerk's own hand, however careful that hand had proved itself. She asked him, that same evening, whether the work weighed on him more than the Moot's ordinary business had, and he told her, after a silence longer than the question seemed to want, that it did, and that he had not expected it to, having spent enough years copying grimmer reports than most clerks ever saw without the copying troubling his sleep before. What troubled him now, he said, was not the dying, which the north had always known and grieved in its own way, but the knowing that a name written nowhere else might, if his own hand slipped or his own memory failed some winter years off, be lost a second time, this once for good; and Mary Coyle told him that this was exactly why the book was bound in leather rather than stitched in paper, and kept in the Moot's own strongbox rather than on any clerk's open shelf, so that no single hand's slipping would be given the chance to lose it.

By the year's end the register held above thirty names, carried to every western pit's own captain that the Moot's clerks could reach and copied out a second time, against fire or flood, into a spare book kept apart from the first at a house in Muileann leathan that had never once been troubled by a southern search, so that a name lost to the Board's own count might yet be found in Clàr nan Leòn, the register of the hurt, kept at Caol mhòr and sent south to no court, no Board, and no council that had never once asked to see it.

## IV. Of the Chronicle Laid Down

Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill had kept the royal chronicle at Muileann chaol for four and twenty years by that summer, the first to hold the office, and she told the Library's own keeper, Mòrag nic Coinnich, in an t-Iuchar of SE 42, that her hand had begun to shake on a long day's writing in a way it had not shaken when she was young at the work, and that a chronicle written in a shaking hand was a poorer gift to the years after her than a chronicle handed, in good time, to a younger one. She wrote her last entry that same week, a plain list, kept in the same hand she had kept every list before it, of what the chronicle under her care had gone four and twenty years without setting down: the northern towns' own accounts of themselves, the humans' old treaties in their own tongue, and the Board's surveys, which the Board kept at Cathair mhòr. She struck nothing from the list once it was written, and asked no one's leave to write it, and set the pen down for the last time as chronicler on a page that named, more honestly than any page she had written before it, the shape of everything she had not been able to write.

Tormod mac Sheumais came after her, the clerk who had ridden the first chronicle circuit and had sat at her elbow at Muileann chaol ever since, and who wrote, once he sat at the desk Gormshuil had kept, in the hand so quick that it had long since won him the name Tormod Pinn. He copied Gormshuil's last list into the front of his own first book, word for word, and struck nothing out of it either, telling Mòrag, who asked him why a new chronicler would open his own book with an old one's account of what was missing rather than with a fresh page of his own, that a list of gaps was worth more copied whole than left behind to be found and re-written by whoever came after him with less patience for the finding.

## V. Of the Keel at Ros mhòr

The shipwrights turned out of the southern guild yards in the years the guilds first closed their doors to Tuathaich hands had scattered along the northern coast in ones and twos since, mending what boats the north already owned and building nothing new, the timber and the coin for a proper yard being beyond what any one of them could raise alone. It was at Ros mhòr, in am Faoilleach of SE 41, that enough of them came together at last to lay a keel of their own on the open strand, the harbour there deep enough for a hull of any size the north was likely to want and far enough from the southern yards that no guild master troubled to ride up and ask under what charter they worked.

Harry Marlow stood at the head of them, grey now and further from the boy who had first been bound apprentice at a southern yard than he had ever expected to find himself, and it was his own hand that laid the yard's first keel, cut and set to the lines he had taken, rib by rib, off the old wreck on the Cuan shean hard, the humans' own lines, low and full in the bow, that had gone out of southern fashion the year the guilds decided a Tuathaich hand had no business building anything a Dia-thìreach captain might one day sail. He told the men working beside him, the first morning the keel was laid true and pinned, that he had spent thirty years building other men's boats to other men's rules, and that he meant to spend whatever years were left him building his own boats to a rule he could stand behind, whatever a southern guild chose to call the result.

The hull went up through that year and the next on evenings and Sabbaths, and by an Cèitean of SE 42 the men had a shed over the slip and called the place a yard, the yard's men keeping their day's wage at whatever work would still have a Tuathaich hand and giving the boatyard what hours were left over, timber bought a plank at a time from whatever coin the yard's own men could spare and coin from Ros mhòr households who wanted no share in the finished boat beyond the knowing that it had been built. A southern factor riding through that spring, on business that had nothing to do with boats, stopped long enough at the harbour to look the frame over and told Harry Marlow, not unkindly, that a hull built on Sabbaths and evenings by men paid nothing for the building of it would want two years where a guild yard wanted one, and Marlow told him that two years of a man's own boat was worth more to the man than one year of another man's, an answer the factor turned over a while before riding on without troubling to argue it further.

It stood ready for the water in an t-Iuchar of SE 42, swifter in the eye of anyone who had built a boat before than anything the southern yards had launched in a long season, low in the bow and quick to answer, the humans' old lines proved again on northern water by hands the south had told, not many years before, that such lines were no longer theirs to build. Harry Marlow put his own shoulder to the launching with the rest of the yard's men, the rollers greased and the tide judged to the hour by a man who had judged tides at a southern yard before any of the younger hands beside him had been born, and the hull took the water clean, riding upright and true from its very first wave without the roll a badly trimmed hull will sometimes show a crowd on its first meeting with the sea. The men who had cut its timber and pinned its keel stood on the strand at Ros mhòr and watched it ride, the first boat the north had built entire to its own name since the yards first turned them away, and said little, having spent thirty years among them learning that a boat that answers true says more for itself than any man standing on the strand beside it ever could; and Harry Marlow, wading out to lay his own hand once more on the hull's cold planking before the crew took her out past the harbour mouth, told no one in particular, though more than one man on the strand heard him say it, that his father had cast dead coin into ploughshares in a smithy at Doire mhin and lived to see the north plough its own furrows with them, and that he meant, himself, to live long enough to see the north sail its own waters in hulls it had built with no southern guild's leave asked for and none given.

# Chapter Thirty: Of the Unlit Ships

*SE 43 an Giblean – SE 45 an Dùbhlachd*

> An Dùbhlachd, night the ninth. No moon. A sail crossed under the light going north, showing no lamp fore or aft. I could not read her build. Marked her heading and the hour and nothing else, having nothing else to mark.
>
> — the log kept at Taigh-solais Baile ìseal, its first year

## I. Of the List Copied and the Grain That Came North

Tormod Pinn kept, in the front of the first book he wrote as royal chronicler, the list his predecessor had left him of what no chronicle yet held, 25 an Giblean, SE 43, the northern towns' own accounts of themselves, the humans' old treaties in their own tongue, the Board's surveys; and it is told of him that in the second year of his keeping, riding the southern circuit Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill had ridden before him, he wrote on a leaf of its own, and not beneath her list, which he would not add to, a line of his own: that a gap named was worth more than a gap forgotten.

That same spring the dry years came again to the country about Achadh shean, 3 an Cèitean, SE 43, where the ground had failed once before in the humans' own time and been given a name for it that the shire's own people had never troubled to forget, Tiormachd Achadh shean, the drought of the old field. The rains that should have come with am Màrt held off through an Giblean and into an Cèitean, and the wells the households of the drove road had drawn from since before any living farmer's grandfather went first brackish and then, in three of them, dry to the stone, so that the maor of Siorrachd Achadh shean, a careful man who kept his own tally of every well's yield the way a miser keeps a coin-count, sent word south before the second month of the dry was out rather than wait, as an older maor might have waited, for the harvest itself to fail and prove the need past arguing. He wrote in his own petition, copied afterward into the shire's own chest, that a man could argue with a poor harvest for a season and still bring in enough at the edges to call it a harvest; a well gone to the stone argued with no one, and gave nothing back to be argued over.

The council answered faster than the north had ever known it to answer anything, and it is set down in the royal chronicle, in Tormod's own quick hand, why: the grain that went to Achadh shean that year came from a store built ten years before at Cathair fhada, on the southern plain, a Crown store raised great enough to feed the whole south a season and filled twice over from the south's own harvests before ever a dry year gave it reason to open its doors, and it was opened now for the first time since the masons had raised it, 9 am Faoilleach, SE 44, its grain carried north not by road, which would have taken a fortnight and lost a tenth of the load to spoilage on the way, but by the coal line, the same rails that carried the Sloc Mòr's coal south carrying grain north instead for the length of one season, the Rail Board charging the council in full for the carriage and the council paying it without the argument a poorer year might have forced. The first wagons of it reached the sidings at Achadh shean on a morning wet enough at last with the season's first proper rain that the maor stood in the yard to watch them unloaded with his own boots sunk an inch in mud he had prayed six weeks for, and told the carters, half in earnest and half as a joke against himself, that the grain had plainly waited on the roof to prove it was not wanted before it troubled to come.

No one in the shire died of the drought that year, a fact the chronicle set down in four words and no more, and the maor had twelve wells dug to the rock along the whole length of the drove road before the following winter, 6 an t-Samhain, SE 43, each one cut deep enough to answer a dry year worse than this one and each marked, at his own order, with the name of the shire and the name of the council that had paid for the digging, so that no household drawing water from them in a harder year to come would forget whose grain had answered the last one. Four of the twelve held water still, by the Library's later reckoning, long after the rest of that dry spring was a line in a chronicle and nothing more, and a fifth stood dry from the day it was dug, cut, as the well-diggers themselves owned afterward without much shame in the owning, on the word of a dowser's hazel rather than on any survey a Board man would have troubled to make first.

It is the way of a record kept at one desk to see a season's want answered and set the answering down as though the answering were the whole of the matter, and Tormod Pinn's own hand, careful as it was, did not trouble that spring to ask what a store built ten years before a want, and opened the very first time a want arose, might mean for a shire whose want came slower and less kindly than a single dry spring on the coal road. That question belonged, that year, to a different coast, and a different kind of keeper.

## II. Of the Keeper at the Point

The light at Baile ìseal stood on a low point of rock at the eastern edge of the island, south of the ford-town for whose salt-pans the coast was known, where the land ran out flat and treeless into a grey sea that showed nothing on a clear day but its own horizon and, on the worst nights of an Dùbhlachd, nothing at all beyond the reach of the lamp's own light. Murchadh mac Coinnich had kept it four years by the spring the dry years came to Achadh shean, a Dia-thìreach of one-and-thirty that spring, given the post by the Lighthouse Board on the recommendation of an uncle who had kept a smaller light on the western coast and judged the boy steady enough for a post where steadiness, more than any other virtue a keeper might be asked for, was the whole of the office.

He had a wife, and a daughter not yet three, and a house of two rooms built onto the lighthouse's own base so that the stair to the lamp-room rose straight out of the kitchen, an arrangement his wife complained of on a smoky evening and was glad of on a night the wind came hard enough off the sea to make the walk from any separate dwelling a misery. The work of the post was simple to describe and endless to perform: the lamp trimmed and lit an hour before the light itself was needed and kept burning through whatever hours the season demanded, the oil accounted for to the half-pint in a book the Board's own inspector checked twice a year, the glass kept clean of salt against a wind that fouled it within a week of any cleaning, and a log kept, as every light on the coast kept one, of the weather and the hour the lamp was lit and doused and nothing more than that, a book that in Murchadh's first four years at the post held nothing a stranger reading it after him would have called worth the keeping.

The inspector who rode out from the Lighthouse Board's own office twice a year to check the oil against the book was a dry, exact man who had kept a light himself in his own youth and judged every keeper he inspected against the standard of his own remembered diligence, and he told Murchadh, on the visit before the dry year at Achadh shean was three months old, that the log of Baile ìseal was the tidiest he read on the whole eastern round and the emptiest, both facts said in the same even voice and neither meant, so far as Murchadh could tell, as either praise or complaint. Murchadh took the remark for a compliment at the time, having nothing yet to set against an empty book but the honest fact that the coast had given him nothing to fill it with, and it was some months before he came to hear the same remark differently, as a question asked without the asking of it, whether a book kept tidy because nothing troubled it was the same thing as a book that answered for a coast truly at peace.

The coast below the light was a Dia-thìreach coast in name and a mixed one in fact, the salt-pans of Àth bheag worked by Dia-thìreach ford-keepers and the boats that ran the coast between Àth bheag and the towns north of it crewed as often by Tuathaich hands as not, since the fishing grounds off that shore paid no closer attention to a man's people than the fish themselves did. Murchadh knew most of the boats by sight before he knew half their owners by name, the way a keeper comes to know a coast, by the shape a hull makes crossing under his own light at an hour he has learned to expect it and by the absence of a shape at an hour he has learned to expect that too. He had watched, in his first four years, the ordinary traffic of an ordinary coast, herring boats out before first light and salt-barges working the tide up to Àth bheag's own quay, and had set none of it down beyond the bare fact the Board required of him, weather fair, lamp lit at the customary hour, nothing to report.

## III. Of the Burning of the Salt-Sheds

It was in an Gearran of the next year, the dry spring at Achadh shean not yet forgotten in the chronicle that had just finished setting it down, that ships flying no flag of any house or kingdom stood in toward the coast below Baile ìseal in the small hours of a night with cloud enough to hide a good part of the moon, 7 an Gearran, SE 44, and put men ashore who fired the salt-sheds at Àth bheag before the shore watchers on the dunes, doubled since the raiding off Cathair gheal some years before but still no more than two men and a lantern, had done more than raise the alarm. Murchadh saw the glow from his own lamp-room before he understood what it was, a low red smear along the coast to the south where no fire had any business standing at that hour, and he woke his wife and sent her for the nearest household with a horse while he kept the light burning as the Board required of him whatever else was burning along the same coast that night, since a keeper who let his own lamp gutter to run toward another man's fire left every ship still at sea to find the rocks by guesswork.

The sheds burned through what remained of the night and into the first grey of morning, three long low buildings where the salt was dried and stored against the winter trade, and by the time the alarm had carried far enough to bring men from Àth bheag with buckets and what the tide could spare them, there was little left to save beyond the stone footings and a stack of barrels too far from the fire's own heart to catch. The ships were gone before any boat could be crewed to follow them, standing off again into the same dark they had come out of, and it was two full days before the kingdom's own patrol boats, summoned from the harbour that kept them and rowed by men who had heard of the burning only when a rider reached them, came down the coast to look the ruin over and find, as the chronicle set it down afterward in a line that carried more in its plainness than any longer telling would have, the sheds cold.

Murchadh rode down to Àth bheag himself the second morning, once relief had come for the light and he could leave it in another man's hands for half a day, and stood with the ford-keepers among the wet ash and the barrel-hoops the fire had left standing when the staves inside them burned away, and heard from a woman whose own family's trade the sheds had held a season's whole salt for what she thought of a coast the kingdom's own patrol thought worth two days' notice to reach. "They will build it again," she told him, a plain fact she had settled with herself before he ever rode down rather than any comfort offered him, "and it will burn again, and the boats will come the third day next time as they came the second this time, being no faster for having been asked before." Murchadh had no answer for her that satisfied him at the giving of it, and rode home along the coast road turning the plainness of her fact over in a way the ordinary business of a lighthouse had never before given him reason to.

He asked her, before he left, how she had known to look for the ships coming rather than simply to grieve the sheds once they were gone, and she told him that her own father had kept the same trade before her and had taught her, as a girl too young to carry a full basket of the dried salt, to watch the horizon at an hour no honest boat troubled to be abroad, since a coast that made its living from the sea learned the sea's dishonest hours the way a farmer learns a bad neighbour's habits, by long unhappy practice and no help from any book. It struck him, riding home, that the woman's own father had kept a kind of watch for years that no Board had ever asked of him and no chronicle had ever thought to record, and that the watch had done the shed no good at all the one night it mattered, for want of anywhere further than her own two eyes to carry what she saw.

The sheds were raised again within the year, the Crown paying a third of the cost as it had paid a third of Cuan dhearg's relief a generation before and the shire's own households the rest, timber and stone going up through the autumn while the salt trade limped along on what the barrels spared from the fire could carry; and the patrol's own captain, called to answer for the two days before the shire's own maor, wrote a report that named the distance, the wind, and the hour the alarm had first reached his own harbour, a report the Board judged honest and the households of Àth bheag judged, when a copy of it was read to them at the market cross, an accounting that answered every question but the one that mattered, which was what a shore two days from help was worth calling a shore the kingdom kept at all.

## IV. Of the Log Begun

Murchadh went back to his light that same week no wiser than the woman among the ash had left him, but changed in a way that took him some months to put a name to, watching now, on every ordinary night the coast gave him, for a sail that carried no light where an honest boat would carry one, 12 an t-Samhain, SE 44. He said nothing of it to the Board, whose own instructions asked no more of him than the weather and the hour, and he set down nothing of it in the book the Board's own inspector checked, but he kept, from the first night after the burning that the sea gave him anything at all to watch, a second book of his own, bought with his own coin from a Muileann leathan binder a carter brought up the coast that autumn, in which he wrote what the Board's book had no line for: every ship that crossed under his light showing no lamp, her heading so far as the dark let him judge it, and the hour to the nearest half of the glass.

The first entry, made on a clouded night in an t-Samhain, nine months after the burning, ran to no more than the line the epigraph of this telling carries whole, a sail crossing north under no lamp of her own and a keeper with nothing to mark of her beyond the fact of her passing; and Murchadh, closing the book that first night, judged the entry worth less than the ink it had cost him, having named nothing a stranger reading it after him could use to know one dark sail from another. It was the fishermen of Àth bheag, more than any instruction the Board had ever sent him, who taught him within the season what a keeper's own eye alone would not have found, that a coast worked as long as this one had been worked came, in time, to know its unwelcome visitors nearly as well as it knew its own boats, by the cut of a sail against a grey sky or the particular black of a hull no honest builder on the island trimmed that colour, and had names for what it knew whether any book of the Crown's troubled to record them or not.

He heard the first of the names from an old salt-carrier at Àth bheag's own quay, a man who had watched the coast from a boat's deck longer than Murchadh had watched it from a tower, who told him, of a low black hull that had crossed twice under the light that autumn showing no lamp either time, that the coast called her An Ròn Dubh, the black seal, for the way she rode low and dark and vanished under a wave's own shadow before a watcher's eye had properly found her; and of a second, swifter and paler in her lines, that the coast called An Fhaoileag, the gull, for a habit of standing well out by day and closing only with the dark, the way a gull stands off a boat's wake until the catch is hauled and the guts go over the side. Murchadh set both names into his own book that same evening, against the two crossings he had already logged without a name to give them, and found, doing it, that a name changed what a bare heading and an hour had been until then; a sail without a name was one more unlit shape among however many the sea sent him, and a sail with one was a thing a keeper could watch for, expect, and, in time, begin to know the habits of, as surely as he knew the habits of the herring boats that crossed under his light by day with every lamp they owned burning honestly against the coming dark.

He kept the book from that season on with a care he had never given the Board's own log, ruling each page himself with a straight-edge before he ever wrote in it and setting a second lamp by the table where he wrote so that no error of a tired hand at a late hour might blur a heading he could no longer check by morning. His wife asked him once, watching him rule a fresh page by a lamp he could ill afford to burn twice in one night, why a book no one had asked him to keep should want a straighter margin than the Board's own book got, and he told her, turning the question over longer than a simple answer seemed to want, that a book nobody had asked for was the one book a keeper could be sure no one else would trouble to keep straight in his place, and that this alone made it worth more care rather than less.

By the following an Dùbhlachd, a full year into the keeping of his own book, Murchadh had entered above thirty crossings, most of them nameless still and a dozen given one or other of the two names the coast had furnished him, along with the weather of each night and, where the light let him judge it, the number of men he could make out at a hull's rail; and it was from that year's book, carried south by a Library clerk that winter, that the royal chronicle first drew the two names, An Ròn Dubh and An Fhaoileag, 9 am Faoilleach, SE 45, setting them into the realm's own record for the first time with no better source to credit them to than a lighthouse keeper's private ledger and the salt-carriers of a coast the kingdom's patrol had answered, once, two days too late. Tormod Pinn, reading the book a Library clerk had carried south for his own chronicle's sake, wrote beneath the copied names that a coast kept its own record whether the Crown troubled to ask for one or not, and that this book, more than the patrol's report or the shire's own petition, was the truest account the kingdom yet held of what sailed its eastern water unlit.

## V. Of the Champion of Àth ghlas

In that same winter, a good way south and west of the light Murchadh kept, the Còmhrag at Ceann leathan drew the largest crowd the fair-wardens of that town had yet built stands to hold, three sides of the field now timbered where two had answered before, the melee's own fame having grown, in the years since its first blood was shed, into the kind of gathering a man travelled a week to see rather than a day, 11 an Dùbhlachd, SE 45. The fighter who took the field's own honour that year, and the crowd's, was no man at all but Ealasaid nic Coinnich, of Àth ghlas in the west, a ford-market's daughter who had learned the staff and the fist from a father who kept no sons to teach it to and saw no reason a daughter should go untaught for the lack, and who stood, at the day's ending, the last fighter left the field, to a silence the fair-wardens' own chronicler afterward called longer than any cheer the ground had heard before it.

She was given the year's wages the Còmhrag paid its champion and the right to bear arms the custom granted along with them, and she took both without a speech, the crowd's own telling of it afterward making more of her silence than she had ever troubled to make of it herself; and she did not fight again, in that field or any other the Còmhrag's own custom kept, a fact the royal chronicle set down as plainly as it had set down the dry year at Achadh shean and the cold sheds at Àth bheag, without asking, in the setting down, whether she had gone once to prove a thing needed proving only the once or had simply found, having proved it, no further reason to return to a field that asked a fighter to prove it again each year for a crowd that came, more often than not, for the blood alone.

The fair-wardens asked her, the following spring, whether she meant to defend the year's own honour when the Còmhrag came round again, having never before had to put the question to a champion who might answer it either way, and she told them, by the account her own kin at Àth ghlas kept afterward, that a thing won once stayed won whether or not she troubled to stand on the same field a second year to keep it, and that she had a ford-market's own trade to see to that the field had never once paid her for keeping from. The wardens made what they could of the answer, which was little, and gave the year's honour after that to whoever the field itself decided, the way it had always decided such things before her single year among them.

The two accounts reached the Library within the same season, Ealasaid's silence and Murchadh's second book, carried south by different hands and read by the same chronicler's eye, and Tormod Pinn, closing that year's chest, found himself setting one beside the other without quite meaning to, a woman who had answered a question once and would not answer it again, and a keeper who had begun answering a question every night the sea gave him leave to and meant, so far as any book of his said otherwise, to go on answering it for as long as the light stood and the coast kept sending him ships that carried no lamp. Murchadh's own book, that Dùbhlachd, stood a full year deep, its first clouded entry no longer the poorest thing in it, and he set it on the shelf above his own bed each night beside the Board's own log, the one book asking nothing of him but the hour a lamp was lit and doused, the other asking, and answering as best a keeper's single eye could answer, what manner of coast the kingdom kept and how far its own keeping truly reached along it.

# Chapter Thirty-one: Of the Sacred Wood

*SE 46 an Dàmhair – SE 49 an Gearran*

> *Carson an làmh seo?*
> Why this hand?

## I. Of Cnoc bheag and the Waking Schools

By an Dàmhair of SE 46 the river quays of Cnoc bheag took in more grain in a season than the granaries of Cathair mhòr could show for a year, and the shire's own tale-keepers, who had watched the town's numbers year on year the way a farmer watches a field he does not own, wrote that Cnoc bheag had passed Cathair mhòr at last and would not be caught again. Its Hawk house, richer now than any order's house outside the capital, kept its own accounts apart from the Rite's and let no custodian south of the water see them; the grain barges tied three deep at the stone stair below the house on a market morning, sacks going up on men's backs from first light until the tide turned and took the empty boats back down river for another load, and a man could walk the length of the quay without once hearing the tongue of the south spoken, though he heard the Rite's bell and the Hawk's bell both, from towers a bowshot apart, telling two different hours to two congregations that did not otherwise speak. A factor of the Rite, come up from Cathair mhòr that autumn to see for himself whether the town's numbers were truly what the returns claimed, stood on the quay a whole market morning counting sacks with his own hand and gave it up before noon, telling the clerk who had come with him that a town could not be doubted that would not stop moving grain long enough to be counted.

The Library at Muileann chaol, keeping the years as they came in under Mòrag nic Coinnich's hand, set this beside a harder thing that same season, though no Board survey told it, the Board sending none: the hewers who came down to the fair said the coal came up thinner from the eastern galleries every year, and thinnest where it ran darkest, the shade the Rite called holiest. A vein that answered fewer hands than it once had was a mine matter to the Board and a coal matter to the Rite, and neither would own it as anything more, but it was the oldest question the island had, older than either of them, and that autumn it woke where it had slept.

The druid schools of Flidais, silent under the humans' rule and silent still for years beyond it, opened their doors again within the month, first at the old house near Muileann chiar in the east where the question had first been asked in the Holy Age, then within the year at two more houses that had stood empty so long that the roof-trees wanted new thatch before a lecture could be given under them without the rain coming through. Men who remembered the old houses only as places sheep were folded in a hard winter came with hammers and green timber before ever a lecture was given, mending a door here and a sill there for no wage but the promise of a bench kept for them when the teaching began. The Rite's own clerks, setting down what they knew of it for the high custodian's file, called it a nuisance of the vein's failing and nothing more, a habit of idle men asking why when they should be asking how much; the schools themselves called it, in the one word their own writings kept from before the humans came, the waking. Neither name mattered much to the students who walked to the old houses that winter with a slate and a knife to cut their own stylus, only that the houses were open and the question, the same one the vein-masters of the Holy Age had first put and never answered, could be asked aloud again without a hall shutting its gallery to the asker.

## II. Of the Lecture in Flidais's Wood

Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain came to the stag's grove near Muileann chiar on a morning in an Dùbhlachd with the frost still on the bracken and her own breath standing white in front of her, and found forty people waiting under the bare oaks where she had thought to find a dozen. She had taught the question in a small way for eleven years, to whoever of the old families would still send a son or a daughter to hear her, in a barn lent for the winter and in the corner of a market hall when the barn's owner wanted it back for lambing; she had never before stood in the holy wood to teach it, the wood the schools had kept since long before the humans came and had gone on quietly keeping even while the schools that owned it slept, a grove of old oaks and one white-barked stag's-tree at its centre that no axe had touched in living memory and none living now could say how long before that. Past fifty that winter, grey at the temple and stiff in one knee from a fall on wet stone some years before, she walked the last mile to the grove leaning on a hazel stick cut for her by a student, arriving with mud to the shin and no more ceremony about her than any farmer's wife come in from a field.

She had written the lecture out three times over and burned two of the drafts, standing that morning with neither paper before her, because the question did not want dressing. "Why does the vein answer this hand," she said, laying her own bare palm flat on the stag's-tree's white bark for the crowd to see, "and not that one." She let it stand a moment before she went on. The Holy Age had asked it of birth and of practice both and settled neither; the humans, who dug the vein deeper than any age before them and answered to it not at all, had asked instead why it should matter, and been told by their own masters that the question was not theirs to ask; and now, with the vein running thinner in the eastern galleries, the island's own people were asking it again, this time of a matter the census had begun to write down and neither the Rite nor the Crown would say aloud. She did not name the coal-touched that morning, not once, though every soul under the bare oaks knew well enough what hand she meant, and she let the silence that followed do what a plainer word would only have blunted. An old man near the back, whose own father had kept the strike-books in the last years before the schools shut, asked her when the silence had passed whether she meant to answer the question herself before she was done teaching it, and she told him plainly that she did not, that she had come to the grove to ask it in the open where it could be heard, not to settle in an afternoon what the island had failed to settle in all its ages, and the old man nodded at that as at an answer he had half expected and was not sorry to be given.

Word of that morning's lecture went out from Muileann chiar faster than any rider could have carried it, north and east through the shires where the old druid houses still stood roofless and waiting, and within the half-year the houses of Siorrachd Baile gharbh in the north-east, silent since the humans first ruled there, opened their doors on the same question and sent their own teachers walking the long road south to hear Seonaid herself before they dared teach it in their own halls. It was a walk of two days each way, by the accounts the schools themselves kept, over roads that saw little enough traffic beyond a carter's cart and a drover's flock, and the teachers who made it came in most years with their boots worn through and stayed only three nights before turning back, having judged the season too short and the sowing too near to spare a longer visit. The Library's own clerks noted, with the dry wonder of men who had watched fewer and fewer make such journeys for anything but a fair or a funeral, that no house among them missed a single winter's walk once it had begun, and that the youngest of the Baile gharbh teachers, a woman not yet twenty on her first journey south, wrote in the school's own minute-book on her return that she had walked two days to hear one question asked and not answered, and would walk it again gladly the next winter for the same.

## III. Of the Wet House at Caol shean

The stag's grove near Muileann chiar could not be taught in through the worst of the wet months, when the ground under the bare oaks stood ankle-deep and no fire could be kept lit long enough to warm a lecture, and by an Dùbhlachd after her first winter's teaching Seonaid had taken a house at Caol shean, one of the old druid towns of the east, to carry the school through until the ground dried. It was there, in a low room with a single smoking hearth and benches enough for thirty crowded to hold near fifty, the window shutters lashed against a wind that came off the coast with rain in it more days than not, that the school's students first laid the kingdom's own census beside the schools' oldest question and found the two would not sit apart.

The realm's returns carried a line for the coal-touched that gave a number and nothing else, the same bare figure the Rite's own doctrine called a settled matter and the Board's own clerks copied without comment year on year; the students at Caol shean, who had come to the school precisely because the settled matter did not sit easily with them, copied the same line into their own exercise-books and argued over it by the hearth in a way the Rite's own halls did not permit and had never permitted, not in the Holy Age and not now. A student new to the school that first wet winter, a miller's son from a village two days' walk south, asked aloud one evening why a line the Board would print and a custodian would bless should be a matter no one might question, when the vein, holier by far in the Rite's own reckoning, was questioned daily by every teacher under Seonaid's roof; no one in the room answered him outright, but no one told him to be silent either, and the talk ran on past the hour the hearth was banked, three students still arguing it by the last of the peat's own glow once the rest had gone to their beds. The Library's clerks, hearing of the evening from a student who kept the school's own minute-book, judged it worth the setting down, the first time on the record that the census line and the schools' old question had been spoken of in the same breath by anyone the Rite could not simply have shut a door on.

That same winter the hall at Muileann dhearg, the old druid hall that had served the hewers for a lodging and stood empty since the fall had closed the Cill ghlas district, was given back to the school by the Guild's own captains, more for want of any better use for a hall no miner would work under than for any love of the question taught in it, and the school took it gladly, glad above all of a roof that did not smoke and a floor that stayed dry through am Faoilleach. The captain who signed the grant over, an old man himself near the end of his own working years, told the schoolmaster who came to thank him that he wanted no thanks, only that the school keep the hall's roof sound, "since a roof kept is a roof kept, whoever prays under it." The Guild's grant carried one condition only, that the school teach nothing there that named a living captain or a living gallery, and the school kept to it without argument, having larger matters to ask than any one captain's name.

In the same season, at a council of the Rite called at Seann Skell on the southern coast, the high custodian's own clerks drew up a settlement long asked for and long refused: the Hawk houses of Cnoc bheag, grown too rich and too old a custom for the Rite to go on pretending had no place under it, were offered a place of their own within the order, answering to the high custodian in name and keeping their own bell and their own order of worship in fact. The terms ran to four pages, and the clerk who read them out to the assembled council read them slowly, watching the Hawk's own witnesses for the objection that had killed the same offer six times before; none came. The Hawk houses took the place, as the Library's own note of it says, "on the seventh reading of the terms and the first without an argument," and the quarrel between the two bells at Cnoc bheag, the Rite's and the Hawk's, was quieter after that, though it did not end; the two bells went on telling two hours to two congregations, only now under one roof of law that neither had troubled to ask for before.

## IV. Of the Bindery, the Breakwater and the Two Dùn thais

Daniel Frayne, who had walked to Agnes Pike's byre as a boy with nothing of his own but a slate, kept by SE 48 a small bindery at Muileann leathan where he taught young Tuathaich hands to sew a book's spine and cut its boards true, a craft the southern guilds had never yet let a Tuathaich apprentice learn under their own mark. The bindery was one low room behind his own house, a press he had built himself from a cider-press bought broken and mended, and three boards worn smooth with handling where his pupils learned first to fold a signature true before ever they were let near a needle or a knife. He had no guild's leave to teach it and asked none, having learned long since that the leave he wanted would not be granted him for the asking; he taught instead from what an old binder at Caol mhòr had let him watch as a boy and from what his own hands had worked out through failure since, ruined calf and split boards enough, by his own telling, to have clothed a smaller man's whole flock.

By an Giblean his first bindings, plain calf over boards with no maker's name pressed into the spine, were carried south with the wool carts and sold in three towns his own pupils had never seen, bought by Dia-thìreach households who praised the binding's neatness to Frayne's own face without knowing whose hands had made it. A carter who had sold three of the volumes at the fair told Frayne on his return that a Cathair mhòr merchant had asked twice over who bound them so true, and had been told only that they came from a northern house that kept its own methods close; Frayne laughed at that, the carter said, longer than the joke alone seemed to want, and then grew quiet and said that a closed mouth had sold more of his pupils' work than an open one ever would have. He kept every letter of praise that reached him by that roundabout road, unsigned as his own work was, in a box he showed to no one but the pupil whose hands had actually sewn the spine praised in it, and told the boy who asked him why he kept unsigned praise at all that a thing well made did not need his name on it to be true, only that he himself, and the hand that had made it, should know it.

That same spring the shires of the north-east coast, Caol chrom and its neighbour across the strait, laid the first stone of a breakwater the two had agreed between them to share the cost of, the longest the island had yet built, meant to close a strait that had drowned more boats in a hard winter than either shire's own harbour dues could easily bear alone; the work would want the better part of eight years to finish, by the masons' own reckoning, and the first stone went down to no ceremony beyond a blessing asked of whichever faith a man's own house kept, Rite or Hawk or the older reverence both together, the masons themselves caring more that the stone sat true than whose blessing had been said over it, and the two shires' own maoir standing together on the strand to watch the first block swung out on ropes and set, without either troubling to make a speech of it. In an Cèitean of the same year the old boatman at Cidhe Beag, who had carried passengers and small freight across the Abhainn uaine at his own landing for the better part of forty years without a licence asked or given, was granted one at last by the shire's own maor, more for the sake of the shire's records than for any change the boatman himself troubled to make in how he rowed his boat or reckoned his fare; he hung the licence's paper, framed behind a scrap of glass, in the one dry corner of his boat-shed, and told anyone who asked that he had rowed the crossing forty years without it and would row it forty more the same whether the paper hung there or not.

It was in these same years, the schools' clerks and the royal chronicler's both agreeing on it after their own fashion, that Tormod Pinn, keeping the royal record at his desk at Muileann chaol, first set down in plain ink what the map had begun to blur without anyone's intending it: that the realm held two towns of one name, Dùn thais in the west and Dùn thais in the east, and that the Crown's own returns had begun, in the press of a busy season, to run the two together as though they were one place answering for both a sea-court's ruling and a market's charter in the same twelvemonth. Tormod marked the confusion in his own hand, west against east, ruling a fresh line across the page where the two entries had begun to run together, and sent word to both shires that the Crown's clerks should take more care hereafter; it was a small matter beside a breakwater or a bindery, and Tormod himself thought it worth no more than the half-page he gave it, but the Library kept his half-page all the same, judging, as it judged most things, that a confusion caught early cost less to unpick than one left to grow into a dispute neither shire could afterward be talked out of.

Further north that same winter the fishermen of Loch chrom, the only great lake the island held, were licensed at last to net its trout for their own tables and their own markets, a right the Crown's own table had kept first call on since before any living fisherman's grandfather was born; the licence changed little in the practice of it, since the Crown's table was still served first as it had always been, the best of each week's catch set aside before ever a net was drawn to shore for the fishermen's own market, but it was written down now where before it had only been understood, and the fishermen of the loch, who set less store by writing than by the fish itself, thought the writing worth having all the same, against a day some Crown's steward less easy than the last might try to claim the whole catch instead of the first cut of it.

## V. Of the Pillar Set Beside the Obelisk

In an Gearran of SE 49, with the wet ground at Muileann chiar dried enough at last for the school to teach under the bare oaks again, three of Seonaid's own students rode out from the stag's grove to the standing pillar near Cnoc chiar and copied its marks onto three separate slates, chalk rubbed into the cut lines to bring them up under a low winter sun, before they rode on: one to the fenced obelisk in the pasture north of Cnoc bheag, and one to the column at Cnoc ghorm, standing alone in a field a farmer ploughed carefully round every spring without once being told to; they meant to lay the three copies side by side and see what any one of the three might tell that the others could not.

They rode back to Caol shean with slates wrapped in oiled cloth against the rain, and it took three wet evenings by the schoolhouse's single lamp before the students judged the copying careful enough to trust. They found signs in common between all three, cut, so far as anyone could judge, by no later hand than the oldest the island's own memory kept, a mark like a bent reed repeated at Cnoc chiar and at Cnoc ghorm both, and a straight double stroke that appeared on all three stones though nowhere else that any student present had seen it; and they found no meaning in the signs that any student of the school could bring out of them beyond the plain fact of their having been cut at all, by hands that had wanted, whatever else they wanted, to be remembered. One student, younger than the rest and less patient with a question that would not yield, asked why the school troubled to copy marks that told nothing; an older student, who had walked from Baile gharbh two winters running for less certain teaching than this, told him that a mark that told nothing was itself a kind of telling, if enough care was taken to notice that it had been left at all.

Seonaid herself, reading the three copies laid together on the long table at Caol shean by the last light of an afternoon in an Gearran, the shutters still lashed against a wind that had not yet let up since am Faoilleach, said nothing for a long while, turning each slate to the lamp in its turn and setting it down again. Then she took up her own pen and wrote, in the hand her own students copied afterward into every school's minute-book from Muileann chiar to Baile gharbh, the sentence the Library itself chose to close its own telling of that winter: that the Old Ones had been here, and had said so, in whatever tongue and by whatever hand had cut the stones, and that none living now could hear what they had said.

She did not write it as a discovery, having found nothing that a hundred generations before her students had not already half known and let lie; she wrote it, her own students said afterward, as a plain fact set down at last where it could not be unset, the way the census wrote its bare line for the coal-touched and the Board wrote its bare figure for the vein's own narrowing, a thing known and now written and no longer merely known. The question the schools had first asked at Muileann chiar in the Holy Age, why the vein answered some hands and not others, stood no nearer an answer for the winter's riding and copying than it had stood before it; but it stood now in the open, argued by lamplight at Caol shean and taught under bare oaks at Muileann chiar, where for the better part of the humans' whole rule it had been asked, if it was asked at all, only in a room with the door shut and no one outside to hear it.

# Part Six: Of the One Sheet and the Empty Floor

# Chapter Thirty-two: Of the Forty-One Shafts


*SE 50 am Màrt – SE 52 an Lùnastal*

> Forty-one shafts sunk between Dùn dhearg and Baile ruadh, and not one struck the vein. It had been tried before, long ages since, on the same ground, and the Library alone remembered.
>
> — the Library's own reckoning of the search, entered at Muileann chaol

## I. Of the Piles and the Six Schools

It is told at Muileann chaol, of the fiftieth year of the Severance Era, that the sea came into Inis chrom on the twenty-third day of am Màrt and did not trouble to knock. A storm tide out of the south-west rode the mouth of the river higher than any tide the town's own sailors could put a season to, and it went through the net-lofts and the rope-walk of the lower town the way a hand goes through a spider's web, leaving the timber standing in places and lying flat in others, and no reason a man could point to for the difference. Above ten families lost the whole of what they kept below the high-water mark, salt fish and cordage and a season's mending all gone together, and the harbour silted so that the deeper boats could not come in for the better part of a month, riding instead at anchor beyond the bar while their crews rowed the catch ashore in whatever smaller boat the flood had left them.

The town did not ask the Crown for its rebuilding. It asked its own carpenters, who had watched other towns on other coasts set their stores on piles against exactly such a tide and had always reckoned the cost of doing likewise not worth the bother of a flood that had never yet come. It came now, and the lofts and the rope-walk went up a second time on driven piles a fathom above the old floor, the timber cut from the woods inland and floated down the river on the spring flood, raft after raft of it, and the work was finished before the autumn herring, so that the only loss the second season carried was the labour. A sailor of the Stone's own order blessed the first pile driven and the last, and said, between the two blessings, that a town built twice on the same ground within one lifetime was a town that had learned what the sea meant to teach it only the once. The lofts stand so now, and the town's own telling of it, kept short and without much wonder in the keeping, is that the sea taught Inis chrom once what it would not trouble to teach twice.

In the east that same year Cnoc leathan opened a school in every one of its six parishes, on the twenty-first day of an Giblean, the first shire on the island to do so entire and out of its own dues rather than the Moot's purse or a chartered guild's charity. The sixth and last of the six, at a parish so small it had never before had cause to keep a room set apart for anything but a market day, opened with eleven children on its benches and a teacher hired from Baile chiar who had never taught so few in one room in her life, and said so to the parish's own maor, who told her that eleven taught well was worth more to the shire than sixty taught badly, and that the shire's own dues would stretch to the teacher's wage whatever the room held. The council at Cathair dhearg, hearing of the six schools together, sent a clerk to ask how a shire so far from the capital's own notice had found the coin, and was shown the accounts, plain columns in a plain hand, the dues that would otherwise have gone toward a road never built or a bridge never wanted, turned instead toward six rooms and six teachers and six sets of slates bought at Baile chiar. The clerk copied the accounts and carried them south, and nothing more was asked of Cnoc leathan, which went on keeping its six schools without further notice from the capital in either direction, the parish's eleven benches filling to twenty within two years and the teacher from Baile chiar staying on past the term she had first been hired for.

These are told first because they belong to the same year and to no great matter of state, and because the Library holds that a year should be known by what stood at its edges as well as by what stood at its centre. The centre of that year, for the mountain country and for the house whose name the mountain's yield had made, was a debt taken out against a hope, and it began in the month after Cnoc leathan opened its sixth school, when a grandson of the first holder of the Sloc Mòr rode to Cathair mhòr to ask the Mine Board for surveyors.

## II. Of the Borrowing

Alasdair mac Ùisdein was thirty-four that spring and had held his house's share in the Sloc Mòr for eleven years, since his father's death, without once having to ask the Board for anything beyond the ordinary courtesies a concession-holder was owed: a seat kept at the Board's own table, a first look at the yield figures before they went to the fair, a nod from whichever clerk was on duty when his own name was read from the roll. He came into the Board's chambers on the twentieth of an Cèitean with a paper already drawn, and laid it on the clerk's table before he had properly sat, which the clerk who received him thought, afterward, told him more about the man's temper that morning than anything Alasdair said aloud.

"My house holds the richest working the island has," he said, "and my house's own surveys, going back three generations, say plainly that the working thins to the east and to the south both. I am not the first Mac Ùisdein to read those figures. My grandfather read them and said nothing. My father read them and said nothing. I mean to be the first to act on them beyond reading them again."

The clerk asked him, since it was the clerk's own place to ask it, what he proposed the Board do that three generations of his own house had not already tried, and Alasdair told him that no Mac Ùisdein had ever gone looking for a second vein, having always had coal enough from the one they held not to trouble themselves over whether the island kept another, and that a house rich enough to ignore the question for three generations was, in his own reckoning, precisely the house that ought now to be asking it, before the first vein ran too thin to pay for the asking.

The act he meant was a search for a second vein, and the paper he laid on the table was a note of hand against his house's own share, coin enough to keep six surveying parties in the field a full season, more if the season wanted it. The Board did not need to be asked twice to lend its own surveyors alongside the hired ones, the search being, as the Board's own minute of that week put it without much modesty, "a matter touching the whole kingdom's coal and not the house of Mac Ùisdein's alone," and the Crown lent its name to the asking, which cost it nothing and bound it to nothing either, a fact the Board's clerks understood without needing it written down. A search that found a second vein would be the kingdom's triumph before it was Alasdair's; a search that found nothing would be a debt on one house's own books and no other's.

Catrìona nic Neacail was thirty-two that year, a surveyor of eight years' standing who had come up, as most of the Board's surveyors came up, through the vein-towns rather than through any school that troubled to teach the trade from a desk, chain-hand first at Muileann chiar and then at the Sloc Mòr itself before the Board took her on its own roll, and she was named to the search in the same week the note of hand was signed, one of eleven the Board sent east with their chains and their levels and their own field-books already half filled with other men's work on other ground. She had not asked to be sent. She had, she told the surveyor riding beside her on the road out of Cathair mhòr, a man twenty years her senior who had surveyed half the roads the Board now kept its own maps by, no particular hope of the search finding anything the house's own three generations of figures had not already told them, and she said this plainly, the kind of fact a careful woman kept in front of her so as not to be surprised by it later.
