"Then why go?" the man asked her, not unkindly, the two of them riding the east road past the last of the coal country's own smoke before the ground opened out into hill and moor neither had surveyed before.

"Because the Board pays me to go where it sends me," she said, "and because a search that finds nothing is still a search that someone has to walk the ground for, chain in hand, before the kingdom can be told plainly that nothing is there. I would rather be the one who walks it than the one who is told, years on, that nobody ever properly looked."

He said nothing further to that for the better part of a mile, and then told her, as the hills above Dùn dhearg came into sight for the first time, that he had surveyed for the Board twenty years and had learned in that time to tell, within a week of any new ground, whether it would answer or not, and that this ground, by every sign a man's eye could put to it before a chain was ever laid across it, gave him no particular feeling either way, which was, he said, the worst kind of ground a surveyor could be sent to, since hope at least gave a man a thing to be disappointed by.

## III. Of the Forty-One

The ground the search was set to was a stretch of hill and moor running from the rise above Dùn dhearg north-east to the red-earth fields about Baile ruadh, some thirty miles by the road and rather less as a bird would fly it, ground that had never held a working shaft in living memory and that the house's old surveys marked only with the word *unproved*, which in a surveyor's hand meant no more and no less than that nobody before had troubled to find out. The first shaft went down above Dùn dhearg in the early summer, cut through stone that gave every sign a hopeful man could ask of it, layered and dark and not unlike the stone that ringed the Sloc Mòr's own outer galleries, and for the better part of a fortnight the diggers worked it with the particular good humour of men who believe the next stroke of the pick may be the one that changes everything, singing at the windlass in the evenings and wagering small coin among themselves on the very day the vein would show.

It was not. Nor was the second, sunk three miles north-east of the first on a rise Catrìona herself had chosen for the lie of its strata, walking the ground twice with a level before she would mark it, nor the third, nor any of the eleven that went down that first season between the hill above Dùn dhearg and the moor's edge north of Baile ruadh. Each shaft was logged in the field-books the Board's clerks kept, depth and stone and water and the day it was judged dry, and each log ended the same way, in Catrìona's own hand more often than any other surveyor's on the search, with the single word the Board's own form asked for and no surveyor on the ground had yet found a kinder way to write: *barren*.

The camp the search kept that first summer, a scatter of tents and one timber hut on the moor's own edge, held eleven surveyors and near sixty diggers hired from the vein-towns and the shires round about, men glad enough of the season's wage whatever the ground gave up, and a cook who fed the whole of it from two great pots and a fire kept burning from first light past dark. Catrìona took her own meals with the diggers oftener than with the other surveyors, having learned young that a chainman's grumbling told a surveyor more about the ground than another surveyor's own reckoning ever did, and it was from a digger of Dùn dhearg, an old man who had cut peat on those same hills as a boy, that she first heard the moor's own name for the ground they were searching, *am Fearann Falamh*, the empty ground, a name the moor's own shepherds had used long before any Board surveyor came near it and had meant, the old man told her, nothing more mysterious than that no shepherd had ever found a spring on it worth the digging.

The second season brought thirty more shafts, spread wider now across the same stretch of country as the house's coin and the diggers' patience allowed, some sunk within sight of the first season's covered mouths and others carried further out onto ground the first year's surveyors had judged too poor to trouble with, and Catrìona kept, apart from the Board's own field-books, a private tally in the back pages of her own, a line for each shaft with its number and its depth and the date it was abandoned, so that by the close of that second summer she could tell a man asking, without troubling to add the column, that the search stood at thirty-eight shafts sunk and thirty-eight shafts dry. The diggers' songs had thinned by then to nothing much, and the wagers had stopped after the twentieth shaft or thereabouts, no man on the ground caring any longer to put coin against a stone that had shown them, thirty times running, exactly what it meant to show.

The thirty-ninth found nothing. The fortieth, sunk on ground so unpromising that even the diggers who cut it said afterward they had expected no better, found nothing either, the water coming in at a depth that told Catrìona, reading the borings by lamplight in the timber hut that evening, that the ground below it held no more promise than the ground above, and by the time the forty-first was marked out on the moor south of Baile ruadh, in the last days of the second summer, there was a temper on the ground that Catrìona had not felt on the earlier shafts, the particular tiredness of men who have done careful work for two years running and have nothing to show a passing stranger for it but a row of covered holes and a moor's own name proving truer with every one of them.

The forty-first shaft went down through an t-Sultain and into an Dàmhair, the diggers working it in weather no earlier shaft had asked them to work through, the first frosts in the ground by morning and the windlass rope stiff with them, and it was Catrìona who stood at its head on the morning the chief digger came up to tell her, not with any particular ceremony, his hands still black to the wrist from the last boring, that the water table had been struck at a depth where no vein had ever been found on the whole island and that the ground below it, so far as the borings could tell, held nothing but the same barren rock the other forty had held. She wrote the word in her own field-book, *barren*, in the same hand she had written it forty times before, and then sat a while on the shaft's own spoil-heap in the cold before she rode back to report it, a thing she judged, that particular morning, the ground had earned of her before she left it for good, whatever the Board's own form asked.

## IV. Of the Same Week

It happened, as such things happen more often than either chroniclers or surveyors care to admit, that the very week Catrìona rode into Cathair mhòr with the word of the forty-first shaft, Mòrag nic Coinnich at Muileann chaol was working her way through a press of Holy Age rolls that had lain unread in the Library's lower room since before her own keepership began, part of the long cataloguing she had set herself the year she took the keepership, tallying each roll against a list that had never once been made and setting aside, as she went, whatever the list did not already answer for. She came upon, near the bottom of a press she had nearly finished with that week, a list from the Holy Age, the ink browned and the vellum stiffened with age, that named, in terms she had to read twice by the light of her own lamp before she trusted them, the same hills above Dùn dhearg and the same moors south of Baile ruadh, searched once already, and found barren once already, by surveyors whose own names the roll no longer troubled to keep, the last line of it worn to little more than a shape where a hand had once written a plain word she could still, holding the vellum close, make out as the same word Catrìona had been writing all that season: barren.

She sent word south the day she found it, not to the Board directly, which was not the Library's habit, the Library keeping no correspondence with the Board as a body and preferring, where a fact touched one person's own work, to send it to that person plainly, but to Catrìona herself, whom she had never met but whose name stood at the head of more of the search's own logs than any other surveyor's, a short letter that said only what the roll said and asked nothing beyond that it be read. Catrìona received it the same week she filed her own report of the forty-first shaft, the two papers arriving on her table at Cathair mhòr within two days of each other, one saying that the ground before her had just failed to yield what two years and forty-one shafts had asked of it, the other saying that the same ground had failed the same way once already, ages before either of them, and that somewhere in the Library's own keeping the failure had been sitting the whole time, waiting for someone to think to ask.

She read Mòrag's letter twice before she set it beside her own field-book, and told the clerk who had brought it in that she did not know, that morning, whether the Library's find made the two years' digging easier to bear or harder, and the clerk, who had carried enough of the Board's own bad news in his time to have an opinion on the matter, said that a thing known twice over and forgotten once already was, in his own reckoning, harder to bear than a thing simply not known, since the not-knowing at least left a man free to hope the next shaft might be the one. Catrìona did not answer him directly. She copied Mòrag's letter into her own field-book, word for word, beside the entry for the forty-first shaft, and let the two stand together on the page, which was, she told the clerk afterward, the nearest thing to an answer she had, and wrote beneath the two a line of her own, that she meant, before the Board's own record of the search was closed and filed past reading, to see the Holy Age roll sent a copy south so that the next surveyor sent to that ground, if any Board ever sent one again, would not have to wait on a keeper's own private cataloguing to learn what the last search had already cost.

It was in that same season, before the search's papers were fully closed, that Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain's letter to the Board, written before the digging had properly begun and filed unread at the time in the ordinary way of letters the Board judged it had no immediate use for, was found again by a clerk sorting the Board's own correspondence for the year, and read this time with more attention than it had been given the first. She had written, when the search was still no more than Alasdair's note of hand and the Board's own minute, that the search asked the wrong question, that her school had always asked why the vein answered some hands and not others, and that in all the kingdom's asking about the mountain, in all the ages of digging it and forty years of the Board's own surveys, nobody had thought to ask why there was only the one vein at all, on the whole of an island otherwise so rich in stone and metal both. The clerk who found the letter a second time carried it to Catrìona along with Mòrag's, and Catrìona read it standing at the same table, and said to the clerk, when he asked her whether it changed anything, that it changed nothing the search could act on, a school's question and a surveyor's chain answering to different masters, but that she meant, all the same, to keep a copy of it beside the other two, so that whoever next read her field-book entire would have all three papers together and could judge for themselves what the season had actually found, and what it had failed, three separate ways, to ask.

## V. Of the Fence

The reckoning that followed the search fell to others than Catrìona, who had done the digging and left the accounting to the Board's own clerks, though it touched the ground she had walked all the same. The town of Dùn dhearg, whose hills had held a dozen of the dry shafts among the forty-one, brought its claim to the circuit court that summer, the shire's own advocate walking the shafts himself with two shepherds who swore, plainly and without much heat, that grazing spoiled by a digger's spoil-heap was grazing lost for longer than any digger troubled to reckon, one of them telling the court that a ewe would not graze within a stone's throw of a fresh spoil-heap for two full seasons after the diggers moved on, whatever grass grew there, and the other adding only that he had lost more lambs to the search's own open ground in two years than to wolves in the ten years before it. The court found for the town, and the house of Mac Ùisdein paid a third of the damages that same season and, its coin by then thinner than its note of hand two years before had allowed for, sold half its own share in the Sloc Mòr back to the Crown to meet what remained, on the fifth day of an t-Iuchar in the fifty-second year, a clerk of the Board carrying the deed south to Cathair dhearg the same week it was signed. Its stone house at Cathair mhòr, kept in the family since the first holder's own day, its hall still hung with the same crest the first Mac Ùisdein had cut for it, was let to the Board that same season, which moved its offices into it the following spring, so that a house built to hold one family's wealth came to hold, instead, the ledgers of a search that family's own coin had paid for and not answered, and a Board clerk was heard to remark, carrying the first press of files up the house's own stair, that the family had at least left the fires drawing well.

The shafts themselves, forty-one dry mouths in the ground between two towns that had asked for none of them, were left as the diggers had left them when each was judged barren in turn, covered loosely where the diggers troubled to cover them and not at all where the season's weather or the Board's own thinning purse left the work half done. On the moor south of Baile ruadh, where the ground was softest and the covering poorest, sheep began falling into the old shaft-mouths before the first winter after the search was out, three that the shire's own reckoning could put a number to and likely more that no reckoning troubled to count, and before that summer was out a child of the town, out after a stray lamb on ground she had walked a hundred times without harm, went down one of the same shafts and was not found again until the following day, past any help the finding could give her. The parish's own book at Baile ruadh holds her name and the day, and nothing more than that; her mother, it is told locally and nowhere written, would not walk that road again for the whole of the year that followed, and took the longer way round by the mill instead, whatever the weather asked of her for it.

The shire of Baile ruadh met the week after, in the same low room where its own dues had once been argued over school-money the shire had never had cause to spend, and voted, without much debate that the record troubled to keep, to fence every one of the shafts on its own ground at the shire's own cost rather than wait on a Crown that had shown, in the matter of Dùn dhearg's grazing, no great haste to pay for what its own search had spoiled. The shire's claim against the house of Mac Ùisdein for the fencing's own cost was entered the same week, and has never yet been paid. The fencing went up through that same summer, plain posts and wire strung by the town's own hands round each covered mouth, one shaft a day where the ground allowed it and two where a family gave its own labour free for a shaft that had taken a measure of their own, a fence for every hole on the moor, holes that had cost two years, a house's half-share, and one child, and had found, at the end of it, nothing but the stone the Holy Age's own forgotten surveyors could have told them, had anyone thought, before the digging began, to ask the Library what it already knew.

Catrìona nic Neacail rode past the last of the fences on her way south that autumn, on Board business that had nothing further to do with the search, and stopped a while at the rail nearest the road, where a boy of the town, too young to remember the digging, was mending a gap the last winter's frost had opened in the wire. She did not tell him what the shaft behind him had cost, in coin or in the other coin, and he did not ask her, taking her, from her dress and her horse, for no more than a Board rider passing through on ordinary business, which by then, in every particular the boy could see, she was. She rode on before the light went, the fences falling behind her one by one in the grey of the evening, each one holding nothing but the dark the search had proved, and thought, coming down at last onto the coal road with Cathair mhòr's own smoke ahead of her, that a kingdom which kept a Library at all and still had to be told twice, by its own ground, what that Library already held, was a kingdom that had not yet learned to ask its questions of the right book first.

# Chapter Thirty-three: Of the Reef Bell

*SE 53 an Giblean – SE 55 an t-Ògmhios*

> Cha do dh'fhàillig an solas ach aon turas; cha do dh'fhàillig an nighean idir.
> The light failed once; the daughter did not fail at all.
>
> — said of the keepers of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg, entered at Muileann chaol

## I. Of Bark and Rope and a List Alone

It is told at Muileann chaol that in the fifty-third year of the Severance Era the mills of Muileann dhomhain, in the ground south-east of the capital where the grain of three shires had gone to be ground since before the humans came, began for the first time in any keeper's memory to grind bark instead of grain. The orders from the vein-towns had thinned with the vein, coin scarcer at Cathair dhearg and Muileann chiar than it had been in Iain mac Ruairidh's own young years, and a miller who wants his wheel turning will turn it on whatever is brought to him. The tanners of the coast paid in silver for ground bark where the vein-towns had once paid in silver for ground grain, and the miller-families of Muileann dhomhain, who had cut their mark into a millstone before any shire kept a chest to hold the charter that let them, kept the mark and changed the trade under it without troubling the Board for leave. The Library set down the change in one line and asked the millers nothing further, there being, as the keeper who entered it wrote, no law yet made against a mill that ground what came to it.

The eldest of the Muileann dhomhain millers, a woman near seventy who had ground grain at the same wheel her mother had ground it at, was asked once by a passing clerk whether it troubled her that the wheel her family's mark had stood over for four generations now turned bark for a tanner's vat instead of flour for a baker's trough. She answered, the clerk's own note says, that a wheel does not know what is under it, and a family that has kept its mark through worse than a change of grist has no cause to start weeping over this one; the grain would come back when the vein-towns had coin again to buy it with, and until then the tanners' silver spent the same in the shire's own market as any other silver ever had. The clerk carried the answer back to Cathair dhearg unglossed, there being nothing in it, by his own account, that wanted a gloss.

Further north, on the coast where the coal line did not run, the rope-walks of Seann Tarr were that same year chartered as a guild by the restored custom, the last trade the humans had never touched to be given a charter of its own, its hemp brought down from the fields about Doire uaine and Achadh naomh by cart roads older than the survey lines that had tried, more than once, to straighten them. The shire keeper of Seann Tarr, being asked by a rider from Cathair dhearg to send the new charter south to be filed among the council's own papers, answered that the charter would stay in the shire's own chest at Seann Tarr, as every paper of the shire had stayed since the chest was first locked, and that the rider might carry south, if the Board required a paper at all, a list of what the chest held and no more. The rider carried the list south. The chest stayed where it was, and has stayed there since, and no clerk at Cathair dhearg has yet sent a second rider to ask again. It was said afterward at Seann Tarr, not without some pride taken in the saying of it, that a shire which will not send its papers south need never trouble over what is done with them once they arrive, and that a list is a cheaper thing to lose than a charter.

That same season An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn, which no chronicler now living can say for certain when it was first pitched or by whom, came again to the common near Inis àrsaidh in the west, and the magistrate who licensed its acts, being unable or unwilling to put a name to half of what he had watched from the front row with his own two daughters on his knee, entered the whole of it in his book as various, and the fee as paid, which was, of every entry a magistrate of that shire made that year, the one that gave the Library's own copyists the most trouble to gloss. His own note, appended some years after by a hand not his, says only that a man who has seen a thing done with fire, three knives and a length of rope, and cannot afterward say to his own satisfaction whether it was a trick or a wonder, does his shire no disservice by writing various and letting a wiser age decide the matter, if any age ever troubles to.

Ceann mhin, the great port south-east of the capital, opened in the same year a covered market over its old strand for the fish that came up from Seann Bhral and the grounds to the east, so that for the first time the buyers of the capital could stand dry-shod under a roof of the port's own raising while they haggled over a catch that had been wet from the sea an hour before. The old strand traders, who had cried their fish in the open for as long as any of them could remember and their fathers before them, grumbled at first that a roof over a fish stall was a roof over nothing a fish had ever asked for, and grumbled rather less once the first wet winter under the new roof let them keep a fire going by the scales that no open strand had ever let them keep, and their catch drier and better priced for it besides.

And at Ceann leathan, where the Còmhrag was fought every summer for a purse and a year's wages and the right to bear arms after, a fighter was killed that season with a hewer's pick brought in under a borrowed coat, and the fair-wardens, who had buried enough young men already without a tool from the vein finishing what a fist or a stave would have left standing, banned edged iron from the ring from that day forward. Staves and fists were still allowed, and the dying went on, only slower, which was as much as the wardens, by their own account, had ever promised to make of it; a warden of long standing, asked by a Board rider whether the ban would hold, said only that it would hold as long as a man could be searched at the ring's own gate for what he carried, and no longer than that, which the rider set down and carried away without further question, there being, in that answer, nothing a further question could have improved.

## II. Of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg

Of Ciorstaidh nic Artair, who kept after that year the light at Tobar dhearg on the south coast, it is told first what was done to her father, for the one cannot be told without the other.

Artair mac Mhurchaidh had kept the light at Tobar dhearg for above thirty years, since before his daughter could walk the gallery round the lamp-room without a hand on the rail, and in all that time the reef below the light had taken, by his own count kept in the log he left behind him, eleven boats and no lives, the light and his own watching having been, until that year, enough to answer for the second half of the reckoning. He had trained his daughter to the lamp from the age of nine, the wick and the oil and the turning of the great glass, and to the watch-book beside it, and had said to her often enough that a light which stands and a keeper who watches are two different things kept in one tower, and that the tower could be trusted to do the first of these many years after any keeper set to do the second was dead and gone, which she had taken, at nine and at nineteen both, for the kind of thing an old man says to fill a night watch and not for anything she would be asked to prove.

On a night in an t-Ògmhios when the wind stood hard out of the south-west and the light could do no more than show a hull where the light already knew a hull to be, a fishing boat out of Doire shean struck the reef in the black water below the beacon and hung there, taking the sea over her low side with every swell, her crew of four lashed where they could lash themselves and crying out in a wind that carried the sound away from the shore as fast as it was made. Artair heard them from the gallery before he saw them, the cry coming and going with the gusts the way a gull's cry comes and goes, and knew the sound for what it was before the next flash of his own lamp showed him the hull lying over on the reef's own teeth. He woke no one in the house below; the log he kept, found afterward open on the table with the ink still wet where he had broken off writing it, records the hour and the bearing and nothing of what he meant to do about either, as though the doing of it were too plain a thing to trouble a log with.

Artair, fifty-three that spring, went down from the light alone in the small hours with a coil of rope and the shore-boat that the lighthouse kept for no purpose but this one, and got the rope to the wreck, and got two of the four crew into the shore-boat, and put them ashore himself on the strand below the tower with no more than a word to make fast and wait, and went back a second time for the other two, and did not come back a third time himself. The two men he had put ashore said afterward, when the shire's own clerk came to take their account, that he had said nothing to them of the sea he was going back into, and had looked, in the one lamp's-worth of light they had of his face before he pushed off the second time, no more troubled by it than a man setting out to check a fence line he had checked a hundred times before.

Ciorstaidh, three-and-twenty and asleep in the keeper's house below the tower when her father went down, woke to the empty rail and the boat gone and understood, before anyone told her anything, what an empty rail and a gone boat meant at that hour in that wind. Leaving the two men her father had put ashore where they lay, past use to her or to themselves, she took the second boat, the one her father had not thought to take because two boats cannot do together what an old man's arms could no longer do alone in one, and went out after him along the line his own rope still marked in the water, the wind taking the oars out of true with every third stroke and the tower's own lamp swinging its light past her and away again with a regularity that told her nothing of where the wreck lay and everything of how little time the telling would take if she did not find it soon. The wreck she found at last by the sound of it before the sight, the timbers grinding on the rock under the wind the way a door grinds on a hinge too long unoiled, her father's rope still fast to it and the last two of the crew still lashed to what remained of the mast, past speech but not past living, the one holding to the other by a grip that had stopped being a choice some while before she reached them.

Rowing a boat built for a lighter woman than she then knew herself to be against a sea that had already taken the one keeper the reef had never before been able to take, with the two rescued men lying in the bilge doing nothing to help her and everything, by their dead weight alone, to make the pulling harder, she brought them in, and did not once, by her own account given years afterward to a niece who asked her, let herself think past the next stroke of the oar to what waited for her back at the tower once the pulling was done. Her father's own body came ashore three days after, a mile down the coast at a place the tide favours for such things, and was carried back to Tobar dhearg and buried in the ground above the light where every keeper of that beacon before him had been buried, the parish clerk entering against his name in the register no more than the day, the manner, and the word drowned, the same word the register had entered against every other name it had ever taken from that water. The night before the burial she stood the watch herself, the lamp trimmed and turning as her father had trimmed and turned it, there being, as she told the clerk who came to note the death, no law of the sea or of the Board either that excused a light from burning because its keeper was being buried in the morning.

The keeper's warrant does not pass by any law the council ever troubled to write down; it passes, where it passes at all, by the plain fact of who is left standing at the light when the last keeper is not, and by whether the Board at Cathair dhearg, being asked, can find any reason worth the ink to refuse what has already, in every particular but the paper, been decided by the sea. Ciorstaidh nic Artair asked for nothing beyond what the plain fact already gave her; the Board, being asked by the shire's own maor whether the daughter of a keeper who had died bringing in four lives with two boats and one rope might keep the light her father had kept, wrote back inside the month that she might, and the warrant that had been her father's was entered in her own name at Cathair dhearg without a word of debate that any clerk troubled to set down.

## III. Of the Bell in Fog

She did not let the matter rest at the warrant. Through that same summer she had an iron post sunk into the reef at low water, at the place her father's rope had marked and her own boat had found by it, driven and cemented by two masons brought up from Seann Vell who worked the tides for the better part of a month to get it standing, working only in the hour either side of the ebb when the reef stood clear enough of the water to be worked at all, and cursing, by their own later account, every tide that came in on them before the last bolt was set. She had the post painted the red that every chart from Cathair mhòr to Seann Skell now uses for a danger marked and known, and hung from an arm at its head a bell cast at Muileann chiar and paid for, the Board's own ledger shows, half from the Board's purse and half from a purse the fishing families of Doire shean and Tobar dhearg between them made up themselves, not being minded to wait on the Board's own half arriving before the bell was hung, a factor at Doire shean having gone door to door with a slate and a stub of chalk until the sum stood full.

The bell was rung by no hand and no clock; it hung loose enough on its arm that any sea with weight enough to be dangerous set it swinging and sounding of its own accord, and a sea too slight to trouble a boat left it silent, so that the bell told a master exactly what the master needed told and nothing more. When the Board's own engineer came down from Cathair dhearg, some months after the post was set, to inspect what the Board's half of its own money had bought, he walked the whole length of the reef at low water with his own instruments and pronounced the post sound and the casting good, and asked Ciorstaidh, more out of an engineer's habit of admiring his own trade than out of any doubt of hers, whether she meant in time to have the bell struck by some clockwork, on the pattern the Board had lately fitted to the light at Baile ìseal, so that a master out on the water might know the hour as well as the danger. She answered that a clock could tell a man the hour whether or not the sea agreed with it, and that she had built the bell to tell him only the one thing a clock could never tell him, which was whether the sea that hour meant him harm; if he wanted the hour as well, she said, he had a tide table and two eyes, and needed neither her bell nor the Board's clockwork to supply what his own almanac already owed him. The engineer, by his own report to the Board, wrote down that the keeper's design was sound and her reasoning sounder, and that he had no improvement to suggest that the keeper had not already considered and set aside for good cause.

The bell was heard first, by any account the Library troubled to gather, on a night in an t-Ògmhios of the fifty-fifth year, when a fog came down off the water thick enough that the light, for all its lamp and its glass and its keeper's own long practice at trimming it, could not be seen from a boat's length beyond where the reef began, and every boat working that stretch of coast that night steered by the bell alone, which the fog could not silence as it silenced the light, and came home. No boat went aground on the reef below Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg that year, nor in any year after that Ciorstaidh nic Artair kept the light, and the fishermen of that coast, who name most things for what they are and few things for what they hope, began that same year to call the reef, which had held no name before beyond a plain warning to keep clear of it, an Sceir Aithnichte, the known reef, there being, as one of them told a Board rider who asked him why, no longer anything about it that a man working that water by night needed to be told twice.

## IV. Of the Chair Laid Down

That same year, in Caol mhòr, Mary Coyle laid down the chair of the Moot she had held two-and-twenty years, since the winter Hale died and the widows of the northern crews had first put her name forward over her own protest that a fisherman's widow had no business speaking for clerks and hewers both. She had kept the chair through the beginning of the register of the dead and maimed that bore her own name in the north long after it bore any other, through the Rail Board's refusals and the Moot's own lean years when the chair was little more than a bench in a room the south did not trouble to send anyone to argue in, and had said of the work often enough, to the few who asked her why she kept at it, that a chair nobody wants to sit in is the one chair a body dare not leave empty, there being no one else who will trouble to fill it if she does not.

The laying-down came, the Moot's own minute records, on a morning in an t-Ògmhios with no more ceremony than the minute required, and she said what she had to say of the register her own hand had begun and the Rail Board her own petitions had never once moved, a plainer accounting, those who were in the room said afterward, than the years it summed had any right to fit into so few words. Of the widows who had first put her name forward, most of them dead now themselves, and of the register of the western pits' dead and maimed that she had begun and Daniel Frayne had kept in his own hand, the minute records her speaking at some length: a book, she said, that had grown by a name a season for fourteen years and would go on growing by a name a season for as many years again as the vein lasted, whoever sat in the chair to keep it. For herself she asked the Moot nothing, having asked it nothing on her own account in two-and-twenty years of asking it for everything else, and named, before the Moot rose that morning, the man she asked it to choose after her.

Daniel Frayne of Muileann leathan, who had bound books for the north's own schools when the southern guilds would not have a Tuathaich name on their rolls, and who had sat at Mary Coyle's own right hand in the Moot's chair for above ten years before that morning, keeping her own accounts steadier, by more than one account, than she had ever troubled to keep them herself, was chosen that same day without a voice raised against him, the first speaker of the Moot to have been born, as the minute troubled to note, after the Severance had already closed and not before it, a fact that meant little to the Moot's own business that morning. He had been a pupil of Agnes Pike's school before the guilds of the south would take a Tuathaich boy to bind their books, and had learned the trade in the end from his own reading and an old bookbinder of Caol mhòr who asked no questions of a boy's birth so long as his stitching held straight, and had come to the Moot's own clerking, in the years since, by much the same road: asked no leave, and given the work once it was plain he could do it better than the man before him.

He took the chair from a woman who had held it since before he could write his own name, in a room where the Moot's own chest held the north's tallies for every census the kingdom had taken and not published, a chest that Mary Coyle, in the last minute she gave as speaker, pointed to once and said nothing further of, there being nothing further, by her own account, that the pointing did not already say. Frayne said, by the Moot's own record, no more than that he would keep what she had begun and add to it only what the Moot itself asked him to add, which the clerk who wrote the minute set down exactly as he said it and no more warmly than that; and when an older man at the back of the room asked him, half in jest and half not, whether a speaker born after the Severance meant to speak any differently for it than a speaker born before, Frayne answered that he could not say, having no other speaker's whole life to set against his own, and that the Moot would find out, as it found out everything else that mattered to it, by watching what he did and not by asking him first what he meant to do, an answer the minute records without troubling to say whether the room took it for wit or for plain caution, it being, in Frayne's own mouth, not always easy to tell the one from the other.

It was told afterward, at Muileann chaol and at Tobar dhearg both, though never in the same telling, that the bell on the reef and the chair in Caol mhòr were rung and taken in the same season for the plainest of reasons, that a coast which cannot always keep its light burning against the weather it is given had learned, in the end, to hang a bell that needed no one's hand to sound it truly; and that a Moot which could not yet move a line of rail or unlock a chest of figures had learned, in its own time and by its own slower road, to choose a chair that needed no one born before the Severance to sit in it rightly. Neither telling troubled to say which lesson had come first, or whether either had come from the other at all; the Library, asked once by a student at Caol shean which of the two had taught the other, entered only that both were true and both were entered the same year, and left the rest of the reckoning to whoever wanted it badly enough to work it out alone.

# Chapter Thirty-four: Of the One Sheet

*SE 55 an Dùbhlachd – SE 57 an t-Iuchar*

> Duilleag na Fèithe, the sheet of the vein, held on one leaf what forty years of the Board's own files had kept apart across two towns and four presses: that the mountain had little left in it, and that the mountain had known this a long while before the kingdom troubled to ask.
>
> — the Library's own note on the map, entered at Muileann chaol

## I. Of the Fair's Northern Day

It is told at Muileann chaol that the court of the fair at Muileann òg, in the cold week before the turn of the fifty-fifth year of the Severance, gave over one whole day of its ten to goods carried down out of the northern shires, the first day in all the fair's history set aside so, and that the wardens who cried it from the fair's own steps did so in the flat voice men use for a thing they have not yet decided whether to be proud of. The goods still went to Dia-thìreach factors, as the court of the fair had ruled thirty years before and had never troubled to unrule; a northern weaver's cloth was still weighed, priced and sold by a southern hand at a southern table. But the day was named, and the stalls it filled stood in a row of their own along the fair's eastern wall, and over each stall, for the first time in the fair's keeping, hung a maker's own mark and not only the factor's.

Daniel Frayne of Muileann leathan stood that morning at the head of the row, the Moot's chair six months old on him and sitting no more easily than a coat bought for a taller man, and watched the first cloth of the day go up on its pole: a grey twill of Doire ghlas, plain wool dyed with the shire's own bark, and along its selvedge a single thread of undyed white running the length of the bolt, so fine a stranger might have taken it for a flaw in the weave before he took it for a mark. The weavers of Doire ghlas called it An Snàthainn Geal, the white thread, and had woven it into their own cloth for three years without asking the fair's leave, selling it under a factor's stamp as they sold everything else, until the court's new rule let them sell it, for the first time, under their own. The factor who had carried Doire ghlas cloth to that fair for eleven years stood by the pole with his ledger open and his face giving away nothing either way, and when a buyer from Cathair mhòr asked him what the thread meant, he said only that it was the shire's own habit and had never lowered the price of a bolt, which was, in its way, the truest thing said at the fair that day about what the day was worth.

Frayne walked the row twice before the light went, the factors' bell being rung early against the short afternoon, and stopped longest at the Baile chiar stall, where the southern weavers, who had sold cloth at that fair since before the row existed, had begun that same season to weave a thread of their own into the selvedge of their finer bolts, a pale grey scarcely darker than the wool, the mark being spoken for already at Doire ghlas, so that a buyer who did not know to look for it would carry the cloth home none the wiser. He asked the Baile chiar weaver, an old woman who had been at the loom since before the first Còmhrag, why her house troubled to copy a northern habit it need not have noticed at all, and she told him that a mark worth having was a mark worth taking, wherever it began, and that she had woven for forty years without her own name on a bolt and did not propose to die without it. Frayne wrote nothing of the exchange in the Moot's own book that night, there being no column in it for a compliment paid sideways by a stranger's loom, but he told Mary Coyle of it the next time he rode to Caol mhòr, and she said only that a thread the south troubled to steal was worth more, in the end, than a thread the south only bought.

The frost came down hard that afternoon, as it does most years at Muileann òg once the light begins to fail, and the wardens who had cried the northern day from the steps that morning were the same men who walked the row at dusk telling stallholders to bank their braziers and mind the canvas, the ceremony of the morning having given way, as every fair's ceremony does by nightfall, to the ordinary business of getting a hundred stalls safely through a cold night. Frayne stayed later than most, walking the row a third time with a lantern of his own after the buyers had gone, and found the Doire ghlas weaver's daughter, a girl of perhaps fifteen sent to mind the stall while her mother slept in the cart, sewing by the lantern's own light a second length of the white thread into a bolt not yet sold, working it in slow and even though nobody stood by to buy it that night or to see it done. He asked her why she troubled with it in the dark and the cold when the day's trade was over, and she told him, not looking up from the needle, that her mother had taught her the thread went in whether a buyer was watching or not, since a mark sewn only for show was no mark at all, only a better sort of lie. He carried that answer home with him too, and told it to no one, judging it a thing better kept than spent.

The court's minute of that day, four lines in a clerk's small hand, records the northern day kept, the goods sold, and the dues taken, and nothing of the thread at all. It is the Library's own habit, and not the court's, to keep such things; the sheet the fair's clerk filed that winter and the roll the Library keeps of it agree in every figure and disagree, entirely, in what either thought worth the keeping.

## II. Of the One Sheet

Catrìona nic Neacail was seven-and-thirty in the year the fair kept its first northern day, a surveyor of the Board thirteen years standing, chain-hand no longer but not yet the thing the Board would shortly make her, and she spent that whole winter and the better part of the following spring doing a piece of work nobody at Cathair mhòr had asked her for in so many words, though every surveyor on the Board's roll had known for years it wanted doing and none had troubled to do it entire. She meant to draw, on one leaf if the leaf would hold it, every stretch of the vein the Board's surveys called unworked: not the search's forty-one dry holes between Dùn dhearg and Baile ruadh, which were another matter and a closed one, but the true seam that the Sloc Mòr and its daughter workings had followed for ages, wherever any surveyor's chain had ever laid a line across ground still unopened.

She began with her own field-books, which by then ran to eleven, and worked outward through the Board's own rolls a shire at a time, riding where the rolls disagreed with each other or with the ground beneath them, which happened oftener than the Board's own clerks liked to be told. The riding took her that winter into weather no surveyor chose for the work if the choosing were left to him, frost in the saddle-leather most mornings and the short daylight gone before a chain could be properly laid twice over the same ground, and more than once she and whichever surveyor rode with her that week were glad of a shepherd's bothy or a maor's own kitchen fire to see out a night the road would not have forgiven them.

A surveyor named Griogair mac Aonghais, junior to her by six years and lent her for the season's riding, asked her once, the two of them sat by a fire on the moor above Muileann dhearg with the day's chain-work done and the light going, what she expected the finished sheet to show that every surveyor on the roll did not already know in his own gut, and she told him that a thing known in the gut and a thing drawn on a sheet were not the same fact, whatever a tired man on a cold hill might wish to believe of them, and that she meant the Board to have the second kind whether it wanted it or not. Griogair said, not unkindly, that a sheet was still only ink, and ink had never yet mined a pound of coal nor left a pound more in the ground than was there to begin with; she agreed with him, and told him that she had not undertaken the drawing to change what was in the ground, only to change how long the Board could go on not knowing it, which she judged, whatever ink's other failings, a thing ink was entirely equal to.

The drawing, when it was finished in the early summer, fitted on one sheet the size of a door, every stretch of the true vein still unopened marked in a red the ink-maker had mixed for her specially, since no ink already on the Board's shelves would hold its colour against handling. It was smaller than she had let herself believe it would be while she was still drawing it a shire at a time, small enough that a man could stand at the Board's own long table and take in the whole of what remained with one turn of his head, where the same fact spread across forty separate rolls in forty separate hands had never once been taken in whole by anyone, herself included, until the ink was dry. She called it, in her own record and then in the Board's, Duilleag na Fèithe, the sheet of the vein, and she published it before the year was out, in an Dùbhlachd, in the plainest way the Board knew how to publish anything, which was to hang it on the wall of its own chamber at Cathair mhòr where every surveyor, clerk and concession-holder who came through the door could read it for himself.

Within the month of its hanging, the sheet had done more to the Board's own chamber than any minute the Board had passed in years. Concession-holders who had come in on ordinary business, a licence to renew or a boundary to dispute, took to stopping before it on their way to the clerk's own table, some counting the red stretches with a finger held an inch from the paper as though the counting might yet change the sum, others asking whichever clerk was nearest what the sheet meant and receiving, more often than not, an answer no clearer than the question. A concession-holder of the western galleries, whose family had worked the same three shafts for four generations, stood before it the better part of an hour one wet forenoon and then asked to see the surveyor who had drawn it, and when Catrìona was fetched down from the upper room where she kept her own field-books, he asked her plainly whether the red she had used for his own family's ground meant ten years or thirty, since he had daughters to settle and would rather know now than be told later that the Board had known all along and had simply never troubled to colour it in. She told him she could not put a year to it without walking his own ground again herself, which she offered to do within the season, and he thanked her for an answer that gave him nothing certain but was, he said, the first honest nothing the Board had ever offered him.

The Board had named her surveyor-general that spring, when word of the drawing first went round its chamber, the office having stood empty three years since the last man who held it retired to his daughter's farm and not troubled to be filled again until the drawing on her table made plain that somebody ought to be answerable for the whole of what it would show. She was eight-and-thirty that year, and the clerk who read her the Board's own minute of the appointment, a young man new enough to his desk to still find such things worth remarking on, told her it was the youngest the office had been filled in living memory. She said only that the office had waited three years for want of anyone troubling to ask what it was for, and that she did not propose, now she held it, to let it wait so idle again.

## III. Of the Press at Cathair mhòr

A sheet the size of a door, once it is hung on a wall, wants explaining in a way a shire's own separate rolls, scattered across forty presses, never troubled anybody to explain; a fact spread thin is a fact nobody has to answer for, and a fact drawn whole is a fact somebody will shortly be asked how long it has been true. Catrìona knew this before the first concession-holder asked her the question outright, standing before the sheet with his own family's share of the vein marked in red not four miles from where his grandfather had first opened it, and asking her, in a voice that wanted an answer and not a courtesy, how long the Board had known the ground he stood on would not last his own grandson's lifetime.

She did not have the answer, and told him so plainly, which he did not thank her for; and she went down, that winter, into the Board's own files at Cathair mhòr to find it, a room in the cellar of the house the Board had taken from the house of Mac Ùisdein some years before, where every survey the Board had received since the rule that kept them there and not at the Library was pressed flat in bundles by year and by district, none of it catalogued past the bundle's own outer label, and most of the labels themselves faded past reading by a lamp that gave, on its best evening, light enough to read one line in three.

It took her the better part of a week, by that same smoking lamp, working through bundle after bundle with a clerk's boy to fetch and carry, a lad of twelve named Ruairidh who had been sent down to the cellar so often on other men's errands that he knew the presses better than any surveyor on the Board's own roll, and who told her, the second evening, that she was the first person in his own three years of fetching who had ever asked him to read a label aloud rather than simply hand the bundle across. The cellar gave up its own kind of cold that no fire lit at the top of the stair ever quite reached, damp in the stone and a smell of old paper and mouse that neither of them remarked on past the first evening, and she kept, through all five days, a tally of her own in the back of her latest field-book, a line for every bundle opened and a word for what it held, much as she had once kept a tally of shafts sunk and shafts dry on a moor some thirty miles east of that same cellar.

She found what she had expected to find in the main, surveys thinning steadily in what they reported the further east and south she read, the language of each one's own year a little more careful than the last about saying outright what the figures already said plainly, a caution she recognised, by the third day, as the particular caution of a clerk who has learned that a plain word costs him more than a careful one and a plainer fact none of his own concern. Twice that week she thought she had found the roll her instinct told her must exist somewhere in that cellar, and twice the date proved wrong or the hand too recent, and she set each aside with a small, private disappointment she did not trouble to name to the boy, until, near the bottom of a press she had all but finished with that week, her hand closed on a roll bound with a cord gone stiff with age and a knot nobody had troubled to untie in longer than the cord's own stiffness argued.

She untied it at the table, by the lamp's worst light of the whole week, and unrolled a survey of the Sloc Mòr's own faces, drawn in a hand she did not know, the vellum stiffened and the ink browned to the same tea-dark colour age gives every ink in the end, her own red not four feet away on the wall above, however brightly it still held its colour that morning. It showed the vein thinning to the east and to the south in terms that matched her own sheet stroke for stroke, in ground she herself had walked and marked red not eighteen months before, and it was dated, in the same unknown hand, thirty years before the year she sat reading it.

She read it through twice before she let herself do the arithmetic the date asked of her, and then a third time, more slowly, for the note pinned to its corner in a second hand, a Board clerk's, dry and brief: *received, filed*. Nothing more. No minute of a decision taken or a decision deferred, no record of who had read it, or whether anyone had, before it went into the press to wait thirty years for a lamp bright enough and a hand patient enough to find it again.

Ruairidh, watching her sit motionless over the roll longer than she had sat over any of the week's other finds, asked her at last what it was, and she told him only that it was proof somebody had already asked the question she had spent a year asking again, and that he need not trouble to fetch her anything further that evening, since whatever the rest of the cellar held, it would not now hold anything to match what her own two hands already did. Rather than leave the roll to be sent up with the rest, she carried it up the stair herself, and sat a long while that night at the Board's own long table, beneath her own sheet on the wall, reading the two surveys side by side by a better lamp than the cellar had given her, hers in red and the stranger's in ink gone the colour of tea, the same ground marked out in the same failing terms thirty years apart, and found, when she had finished the comparing, that she could not have said which of the two surveys troubled her more: the one that had found the truth, or the one that had been believed too late to matter.

## IV. Of Muileann chiar

She sent the Library a copy of the survey that same week, with a note of her own giving the day the Board's own bundle showed it had first been received, and then, rather than wait on the Library's answer, rode east herself, the road she had ridden a hundred times on the Board's ordinary business now carrying a different weight than any of those hundred rides had, toward Muileann chiar, where the Board's own oldest rolls still gave the surveyor of record for the district thirty years back as one Iain mac Ruairidh, called, in every roll that troubled to give him a second name at all, Iain Mapa.

She had never met him, though the name was known to her the way a chain-hand knows a predecessor's marks left on old survey pegs. He had left the Sloc Mòr's own surveying for the silver works at Muileann chiar before she came up through the vein-towns herself, and the Board's roll listed him now only as retired, on a small pension the silver guild paid out of its own funds rather than trouble the Crown for it, a fact she had not thought worth remarking on until she stood at his own door in the last week of an Giblean and saw, through the window, an old man bent over a workbench doing nothing she could name from the glass, moving small objects from one side of the bench to the other with a slowness that had nothing hurried in it and nothing idle either.

Mòr, his wife, a refiner's daughter of the same town who had kept his house near twenty years, let her in and told her plainly, before Catrìona had said above three sentences of who she was, that her husband had been failing since the turn of the year and tired easily, and that whatever business had brought a Board rider so far east had best be short. The house was small and warm and smelled of the silver-work he had long since given up doing himself but had never given up keeping the tools for, fine files and a scale under glass and a tray of ore samples gone dull with handling, each one, Mòr told her while the kettle came to the boil, labelled in his own hand with the gallery it had come from and the year, a habit she said he had never once broken in twenty years of marriage, whatever else about him the years had worn away.

Iain mac Ruairidh, three-and-sixty that spring, did not look, to Catrìona, like a man failing; he looked like a man who had set down, some years before, whatever weight a younger man carries without knowing he carries it, and had not troubled to pick it up again since. His hands, when he took hers in greeting, were steadier than she had expected of a man his wife called failing, though slow, and his eyes went first, before her face, to the mud still on her boots from the ride, a surveyor's own habit of reading a stranger by the ground she had lately walked. He asked her, before she had properly sat, whether the roll he had filed thirty years back still had his name on it, and when she told him it did, in another man's hand pinned to the corner, he smiled in a way she did not at first know how to read, and told her to fetch, from the second drawer of the same workbench she had watched him through the window, a folded paper he had kept there longer than his own children had been alive.

It was his own copy of the survey, the twin of the one she had found in the Board's own press, folded small and soft at the creases from thirty years of handling, and pinned to it, in ink gone no less brown than the Board's own copy, a receipt: *Received of Iain mac Ruairidh, called Iain Mapa, one survey of the faces of the Sloc Mòr, rolled and tied, this day. Filed.* It was signed by a Board man, Ruairidh mac Ailein, whose name meant nothing to her and would have meant nothing to anyone who had not, as she had that same week, read it once already at the foot of a Board minute thirty years old.

"I asked for it," he told her, "because a man who hands a fact to three other men in a room and walks out again with nothing to show for it has, by the next morning, no way of proving he ever handed it to them at all. It did not occur to me, asking for it, that I should still be showing it to anyone thirty years on. If I thought anything at all that day, it was that someone would read the survey long before the receipt for it ever wanted reading."

She told him what her own sheet showed, the red ink and the door-sized leaf and the shire's own concession-holder asking her, before the whole Board's chamber, how long the ground had been known to be failing, and he listened to the whole of it without once interrupting her, which she came to understand, before she had finished, was not patience so much as a want of surprise; he had known, in his own gut, exactly what her sheet would show, long before she had ever begun drawing it. Mòr, standing at the door with the kettle still in her hand, asked once whether he wanted to rest before hearing more, and he told her, gently enough that Catrìona judged it an old exchange between them and not a new one, that a man did not tire of hearing, after thirty years, that he had been right.

He asked her, when she had done, a little about the search for a second vein, which he had followed at a distance from Muileann chiar and judged, at the time, a search worth making even knowing it would fail, since a kingdom that has never troubled to look cannot afterward claim the looking would have made no difference; and he asked her, too, whether the school at Caol shean still kept its old question about why the vein answered some hands and none others, a thing he said he had wondered himself more than once in thirty years of watching men dig ground that answered nobody at all. When she had done he said only that it was a strange thing, to be believed at last by a woman not born when he had first gone unbelieved, and that he did not know whether the strangeness of it was better or worse than the thirty years that had come before it. He did not answer his own question, and she did not ask him to. Before she left, he walked her as far as the gate, slower than the distance asked for, and told her there, at the gatepost, that he did not propose to make old friends of thirty years' silence now that one woman had troubled to break it, and that she was to ride safe and mind the ford below Muileann chiar, which flooded most springs and had taken a surveyor's horse from under him once, years before, though not, he added, his own.

## V. Of the Bell at Caol shean

He died not a fortnight after her riding home, in the first days of an Cèitean, at his own workbench, and Mòr found him there in the evening in much the position Catrìona had first seen him through the window, small objects still laid out before him in an order only he had ever understood. The silver guild that had paid his small pension for the ten years since his retirement sent, as its own custom asked, a single ounce of refined silver to be laid in the ground with him, a mark of a working life spent honestly among its faces, and the guild's own master said over him, at a burial the whole street of retired surveyors and refiners turned out for, that Iain mac Ruairidh had gone down into more of the mountain's own dark than any three men living and had never once come up lying about what he found there, which the master judged, of a surveyor, the only epitaph worth the cutting.

Among his papers, going through them in the weeks that followed with a patience her own grief did not much help her to, Mòr found the folded survey where he had always kept it, the receipt still pinned to its corner exactly as Catrìona had seen it, and sent the whole of it south to the Library at Muileann chaol, with a note in her own hand saying only that her husband had asked, more than once in his last years, that it not be lost a second time, and that she did not know a safer place to send it than the one place in the kingdom that had never once told him his work was filed and nothing more. The keeper who received it, Mòrag nic Coinnich, entered it in the Library's own hand, as her practice was, with a note of where it had come from and who had sent it, so that a roll thirty years lost and a widow's own letter came, in the end, to be kept side by side on the same shelf, each answering for the other.

Catrìona resigned the office of surveyor-general before that same year was out, the Board's own minute recording it in four lines as flat as any minute the Board had ever kept, and went, within the season, to teach at the druid school at Caol shean, where the old question the schools had never stopped asking, why the vein answered some hands and not others, had begun, in the years since the search's own failure, to sound less like a riddle and more like the only honest question left to ask of a mountain that had, by every sheet the Board could now draw, very little answering left in it. She told the school's own teachers, in the letter that secured her the place, that she had spent all her working years learning to read what the ground would give and meant now to spend what years remained her learning to teach others to read it sooner than she had, which she judged, on the evidence of one thirty-year-old roll and one dry receipt, the only lesson in her own trade worth the passing on.

Muileann dhearg, in the few years that followed, lost near a third of its households to the ports and the southern yards, its people going where work still answered a chain and a lamp, families that had cut coal at Muileann dhearg for three and four generations loading a cart with what it would hold and leaving the rest, and the maor's own count of empty houses, kept at first out of ordinary habit and then out of something closer to alarm, ran by the third year to above sixty within the shire's own walls alone. Its Fèidh hall, given back to the druid school not ten years before, was shut for want of a congregation left to keep it, the last teacher there locking its door herself and carrying the key to the maor's own house rather than leave it with no one, and its bell taken down and sold, on the shire's own vote, to the same school at Caol shean that had lately gained a surveyor for a teacher, the sale bringing the shire less coin than the bell's own casting had cost a hundred years before, which nobody at the vote troubled to remark on aloud.

At Ceann leathan the coal-ships waited at the quay for cargoes that came in half loaded where they had once come in full, their masters pacing the harbour wall through whole afternoons waiting on a hold that filled slower every season, and the harbour dues falling by half within two seasons, and the fair-wardens, whose town lived as much off the coal trade as off the Còmhrag's own purse, raised the gate-price of the melee that autumn to make up what the quay no longer earned them, a rise the fair's own crowds paid without much complaint, there being few among them, by then, who had not already heard what a door-sized sheet at Cathair mhòr was said to show.

Of the sheet the Board's own minute has nothing further to say; it hangs still, so far as the Library's last word of it goes, on the wall of the chamber at Cathair mhòr where Catrìona nic Neacail first put it up, the red ink holding its colour better than the ink-maker had dared promise her. Any concession-holder who cares to stand before it and count can read, in that one leaf, exactly how much of the mountain's one true vein remains to be worked before the counting is done.

Catrìona gave her first lecture at Caol shean on a bright morning in an t-Iuchar, the students of the school gathered in the house at Caol shean where Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain had carried the old question through the wet months, and as she began to speak the bell that had rung out the last vigil at Muileann dhearg's own shut hall, hung now in the school's own modest tower, was rung for the first time to call the school in, its note carrying clear and a little strange across ground that had never before heard it, an old sound finding, at Caol shean, a use its makers at Muileann dhearg had never once intended for it.

# Chapter Thirty-five: Of the Crown Alone

*SE 58 an t-Sultain – SE 60 an Lùnastal*

> The charter names the Board a carrier of the Crown's people and their goods. A carrier that will take one man's coin and refuse another's answers to no charter at all.
>
> — Ruairidh mac Phàdraig, ruling given at Seann Bhral in the west, 31 an Dàmhair, SE 59

## I. Of the Market that Passed the Fair

The news came north the way most news came to Caol mhòr that decade, a season behind the fact and by way of a carter who had heard it from a factor who had heard it from someone nearer the matter: that the market day at Baile Mòr dhomhain, on the deep river in the hill country, had for two years running drawn more carts than the fair at Muileann òg, the old fair the whole island had measured its trade by since before the restored kingdom had a name of its own. Daniel Frayne heard it from a wool-buyer at the Moot's own table, a man come down from the hills to sell what Baile Mòr dhomhain's own market no longer had room to take, and turned it over a while before he wrote it into the room's ledger of the year's business, under no heading that fit it well, since it was not a Moot matter and yet seemed to him, turning three-and-fifty that autumn, a thing the room ought to have set down somewhere.

"The vein feeds fewer hands each year," he said to Mary Coyle's old clerk, who still kept the room's figures though the chair was Frayne's own now, "and the hill country feeds more of them than it did. A market goes where the coin already is, and stops waiting on a fair that has had the same coin coming to it every year since anyone living can remember." The clerk said this was truer than the room had leisure to argue with that morning, there being three causes waiting and a letter from Muileann shean not yet opened, and Frayne let the matter go for the day, though he kept the wool-buyer's fact in his own private book beside the register of the hurt, a habit he had never broken since the winter he first began it.

The crown changed hands that same season, and of it the room at Caol mhòr knew only what any household on the island knew: that Eòghan's reign had ended, at two-and-sixty, the notice giving no word of how, and that Mairead, eight-and-thirty, had been crowned at Cathair dhearg by Macha's rite, as every ruler of the restored line had been crowned before her. The room's clerks noted the day and the name and went back to their own ledgers, the Moot having no place in a rite it was never asked to, nor coin to spare for a journey south to watch it, and Frayne, reading the notice a second time before he filed it, found in it nothing to say beyond what the notice already said, a fact and no more, the kind he had learned young to set down plainly and leave alone. He noted only, in his own book and nowhere else, that Eòghan had held the throne since Frayne was a young man at Agnes Pike's benches, and that the coin that winter would be minted new with another name on it.

The mint's own notice reached Caol mhòr some weeks after the crowning, later than the news of it had come by mouth, and told the room only what such notices ever told it, that the die was changed and the old coin still good until the new one was struck in sufficient number, a fact of no more moment to a clerk's ledger than the changing of a season, save that Frayne, weighing one of the last old coins in his own hand before he passed it across the table for a debt owed the Moot, thought it a strange thing that a face stamped on metal should outlast, in most households' own reckoning, the man who had worn it, no household at Caol mhòr troubling any longer to name Eòghan at its own table where once his name had been the one every household knew.

He had seen the fair at Muileann òg only a few times in his own life, the first with the wool carts down the Carters' Road, and he remembered it as a crowd too large for any one man to take the measure of, the factors' own tents strung the length of a field that seemed, to a boy from the north, to have no far edge at all. He asked the wool-buyer, before the man rode on, whether the fair still looked so to a stranger's eye, and the man told him that it did, near enough, to a stranger who had never seen it in its better years, but that a man who had stood in that field every autumn for thirty years running, as the wool-buyer had, could see the gaps now where the tents had once stood three deep, gaps the fair's own wardens filled each year with a wider aisle and called it room for the crowd to move, though the crowd had not grown to want the room.

The letter from Muileann shean, when he opened it, asked a different question of him entire, and one he had some part in answering. The mill-town in the north had that spring opened a school of its own for the sons and daughters of hewers the Guild would not bind, the Guild having voted, for the first time since its charter, to bind no new apprentices at all beyond the sons and daughters of its own masters, the vein by then thinning under enough of the old galleries that a guild grown used to feeding every willing pair of hands had, that year, more hands than it any longer had work to give them. Muileann shean's school meant to teach those turned away to read, to reckon, and to survey, on the reasoning of the shire's own maor, who had written the letter himself, that a hewer's child shut out of the pit might still find his father's own trade from the surface rather than the gallery, chain in hand instead of pick, if someone thought to teach him the chain. He asked the Moot for primers, there being none in the north fit for the purpose and no coin in the shire's own dues to have new ones bound.

Frayne read the letter twice and then a third time, standing at the window of the room he had sat in as a clerk for more years than he had sat in it as speaker, and thought of Agnes Pike, dead that same year, who had taught him his letters in a byre at Doire ghlas on slates the school could not always find chalk for, and of the room she had kept, and of what she had once told him, a boy of ten with more questions than sense, that a trade a man could carry in his own head weighed nothing on the road and could not be taken from him by any Board that ever sat. He wrote back to Muileann shean that he would bind the primers himself, at his own bench, and send them north with the first cart that had room, and did so within the month, forty copies of a reading-book he had set the type for himself twenty years before and kept the forms for since, the ink still smelling of the press when the bundle went out on the cart. The shire's maor wrote back in the spring to say that the eleven children the school had opened with had grown, within the year, past thirty, and that three of the first eleven had already gone south to the ports to hire themselves out as chain-hands, the surveying trade being one, as it turned out, the ports had more use for than the Board's own vein-towns did just then.

## II. Of the Doire ghlas Bolt and the Suit

The mills at Doire ghlas were three years building by the time they turned their first cloth, raised with the Moot's own money on ground the Church had let stand idle since the Severance, the first works the north had ever owned that owed nothing to the vein and nothing to any southern charter either. Frayne had sat on the room's own committee that voted the money out of the Moot's slender chest, a vote he had argued for on grounds he set down plainly in the room's minute, that a people who wove their own cloth need not buy the south's, and that a mill built with the north's own coin answered to the north's own reckoning and to no factor's. The first bolt came off the looms in the last week of an t-Iuchar, a grey twill with a white thread run through the selvedge, the same mark the weavers of Doire ghlas had first been let sell under their own name at the fair some years before, and the mill's own overseer sent word to Caol mhòr the same week, a short letter that said only that the cloth was good, better than the south's own factors had reckoned a northern loom could turn out, and that the mill stood ready to sell it wherever a buyer's coin was willing.

The buyer's coin, when it came, found no way to travel. The Rail Board's own factors at Àth leathan, the railhead nearest the north, asked to carry the first wagon-load down the coal line to the fair at Muileann òg, where the southern trade was and where the cloth would fetch a price the north's own markets could not match, refused the load without troubling to give a reason beyond the one the Board had given every Tuathaich cargo since the line was laid, that the line carried what the Board judged fit to carry and answered to no one for the judging. The mill's overseer wrote to Caol mhòr a second time, angrier than the first, and Frayne read the letter to the room himself, standing at the same table Mary Coyle had once stood at to open the register of the hurt.

"We have asked the Board before to carry what we make," he told the room, "and been told before that the asking was not the Board's to answer. I mean, this time, to ask a court instead, since a Board that will not answer a letter may yet answer a summons." The room's older clerks, who remembered every earlier asking and every earlier refusal, doubted a Dia-thìreach court would hear a Tuathaich complaint any more kindly than the Board had, and said so plainly, but the room voted the coin for the journey all the same, there being, as one of them put it, little enough left to lose in the asking that the mill had not already lost in the refusing.

Frayne rode west that autumn to Seann Bhral, the circuit's own western seat on the coast, three days' road from Caol mhòr and one he had never ridden before, carrying the mill's own ledgers and the Board's own letter of refusal, kept whole rather than answered, in the same satchel he carried his private book in. He was four-and-fifty that year, and told the clerk who took his papers at the courthouse door, a young man who had plainly never before entered a Tuathaich name on the circuit's own roll, that he had come to bring a cause and not a petition, the distinction, he said, mattering rather more to him than the clerk seemed at first to grasp it did.

The justice who heard it was Ruairidh mac Phàdraig, four-and-forty that year, a man who had sat the western circuit for a dozen years and had, by his own account given later to a clerk who asked him, never before had a Tuathaich cause brought properly before his own bench rather than settled or dropped before it reached him. He heard the Board's own factor first, a well-dressed man from Ceann leathan who argued that the line was the Board's own property, raised with the Board's own coin and the Crown's own charter, and that a carrier might choose its own cargo as freely as a merchant chose his own stock. Ruairidh mac Phàdraig asked him, when he had finished, whether the charter that raised the line had named the Board a merchant or a carrier, and the factor, after a silence the court's own clerk noted in his record without comment, allowed that the charter's own words called it a carrier, there being no way to answer otherwise with the charter lying open on the bench between them.

Frayne spoke for the mill himself, having no advocate the Moot's own coin could stretch to and no wish, he told the court, to hire one, since the facts of the matter were plain enough that a plain man could lay them out without a trained tongue to dress them.
