He read the Board's letter of refusal aloud, word for word, and set beside it the mill's own account of the coin it had offered to pay for the carriage, a rate no lower than any southern mill paid for the same road, and asked the court only the one question the room at Caol mhòr had sent him west to ask, whether a carrier chartered by the Crown to carry for the Crown's own people might refuse one people among them and take another's coin freely.

The factor pressed his own point a second way before the court rose that first day, saying that the Board had carried Tuathaich cargo before, wool by the cartload in years the road had allowed it, and that the refusal touched only the line, the Board's own rails being a different property from the Board's own carts and answerable, in the factor's own reading of the charter, to a different clause entire. Ruairidh mac Phàdraig had the charter read aloud a second time at that, the whole of it, clause by clause, by the court's own clerk, a reading that took the better part of an hour and left the factor, by its end, with no clause left to point to that named the rails apart from the carts, the charter's own drafters having written, as the justice observed when the reading was done, of "the carriage of the Crown's people and their goods" without once troubling to say by what wheel or what rail the carriage was to be made. Frayne, listening from the bench set aside for him, wrote the justice's own words into his private book that same evening, judging them, he told the room afterward, worth keeping whole rather than in his own paraphrase.

Ruairidh mac Phàdraig gave his ruling three days later, at the same bench, in words the court's clerk copied fair and Frayne carried home whole, that the Rail Board was a carrier of the Crown and bound, by the Crown's own charter, to carry for any who paid the rate it set, whatever the cargo's maker, and that it had no more right to refuse the Doire ghlas mill's cloth than it had to refuse a southern factor's grain. The Board appealed the ruling to the council at Cathair dhearg within the month, as Frayne had expected it would, and the appeal sat unanswered on the council's own table through that winter and the spring following, until it was let lapse in the summer without a word given either way, the council's own minute of the matter, when the room at Caol mhòr at last obtained a copy of it, noting only that the matter had not been reached in the session's business, a phrase Frayne read three times before he understood it meant the council did not mean to reach it at all.

"It is not a victory they have given us," he told the room, the letter open before him, "only a defeat they have declined to trouble themselves with undoing. I will take it. I have taken smaller things for larger names before now." The room's older clerks, who had doubted him at the start of the asking, said nothing against him that day, and one of them, the same who had first doubted a Dia-thìreach court would hear a Tuathaich cause kindly, wrote in the room's own minute, in a hand Frayne kept and read again more than once in the years after, that it was the first ruling of any Dia-thìreach court the Moot had ever won standing, and that a first was worth the keeping whatever came after it.

## III. Of the Copper and the Last Shafts

The same seasons that carried the Board's own refusal to Seann Bhral and back carried other news south of the north entirely, news Frayne read of rather than rode to. The house of Mac Ùisdein, which had sold half its own share in the Sloc Mòr some years before to answer a search that had found nothing, sold what remained of its working shafts to the Crown outright the next summer, keeping only its share in the spoil-heaps and the quarry-stone the mine's own waste still yielded, and the Board's own clerks, moving the last of the house's papers out of the stone house at Cathair mhòr, wrote in their minute that the vein was thenceforth worked in the Crown's name alone, no house's own charter standing beside the Crown's upon it any longer. Frayne, reading the notice at Caol mhòr, thought of Alasdair mac Ùisdein, whom he had never met, and of the note of hand that had begun the search, and set the thought down nowhere, there being no place in the room's own business for a southern house's own ruin, however plainly it answered a question the vein had been asking the whole kingdom for years. He thought too, reading it, of the Board's own surveyor who had drawn the search's last sheet and then resigned her post to teach at the druid school at Caol shean, a woman he had never met either and knew only by the name a Board clerk had once let fall to him in passing, and wondered, folding the notice away, whether a surveyor who had walked forty-one dry shafts for a house now selling what little the shafts had left it found any particular satisfaction in the selling, or only the same flat notice the rest of the kingdom was left to read.

Copper was found that same year in the hills behind Àth fhiadhaich, in the eastern country, and the Board opened a working there within the season, hiring men laid off from the Sloc Mòr's own thinning galleries at a wage the Board's own notice called fair and the men themselves, by what word of it reached Caol mhòr, called better than nothing, which in that season was the higher praise. It was not the vein, and no one at Àth fhiadhaich troubled to call it so; the town's own house of the Old Spirits, keeping the oldest folk rite on the island by the ford where its river fishers still blessed their nets, gave the new working no blessing when it was asked, the house's own keeper telling the Board's factor, by the account that reached the north secondhand and perhaps not word for word, that copper dug for a wage was copper dug like any other stone, and that a house which blessed the fishers' nets for their own sake, not the catch's, saw no cause to bless a working got up only to keep men fed who had lost a richer trade. The Board took the answer without argument and worked the copper regardless, blessed or not, the men themselves glad of the wage whatever the house at Àth fhiadhaich thought fit to say over it.

Frayne set both notices, the last shafts sold and the copper unblessed, into his own private book that autumn, beside the wool-buyer's fact about Baile Mòr dhomhain and the letter from Muileann shean, and read the four together one evening at his own table, the room at Caol mhòr empty around him and the lamp burned low. A kingdom whose founding wealth was failing, he wrote, might sell its last shafts to itself and dig for copper it could not bless and still call itself the same kingdom it had been the year before, since a crown changes nothing of what it stands over merely by changing the head it sits on; but a mill that had stood three years building and a court that had ruled for it once, however grudged the ruling, were the north's own doing entire, owing nothing to any southern coin or any southern charter's goodwill, and he judged, closing the book that night, that this was the larger fact of the two, whatever the council's own minutes chose to spend their ink on.

The first bale went out from Doire ghlas on the coal line in the last days of an Lùnastal the following summer, the ruling near a year settled and the Board's own factors at Àth leathan weighing it onto the wagon without comment, as they weighed any other cargo that paid the rate. Frayne rode down to see it loaded, having business in the west that week regardless and no wish to let the day pass unwitnessed, and stood at the wagon's side as the bale went up, the grey twill wrapped in sacking against the road's own dust, the white thread at its hidden selvedge the only mark that told a stranger's eye it had not come off a southern loom at all. Two of the mill's own weavers had ridden down from Doire ghlas to see the bale off, young women neither of whom had been born when Frayne first rode the Carters' Road with the wool carts, and one of them asked him, watching the sacking go up, whether the cloth would fetch a fair price at Muileann òg or a mean one, the same question the fair had answered every year of his own working life without ever quite answering it the same way twice. He told her he did not know, and that no clerk of the Moot's had ever known it in advance, only after, but that a bale which travelled at all, carried by right and not by grudging leave, was worth more to the room at Caol mhòr than any single season's price could be, whatever that price turned out to be. She said this sounded to her like a speaker's own answer, given to spare her a plainer one, and he allowed, laughing despite himself for the first time that week, that it was exactly that, and that a speaker who had spent thirty years in the trade owed her at least the honesty of saying so. The factor who signed the wagon's own manifest was the same man, by chance or by the Board's own thin bench of factors at that station, who had refused the first load the year before, and he gave the bale no more notice now than he gave the crates of nails beside it, which Frayne judged, watching the wagon pull away toward the south and the fair it would reach in two days' time, the truest measure the Board could have given of what the ruling had actually won them, the same plain weight any other cargo carried, asked for once and carried without a second asking.

# Chapter Thirty-six: Of the Pumps and the Panthers

*SE 61 an t-Ògmhios – SE 63 an Lùnastal*

> A crossing is a crossing, and a hungry year is a hungry year, and neither waits on the other so exactly that a man may set his harvest by it. I set mine down all the same, and struck it through when the wheat proved me wrong, since a chronicle that will not own its own bad guesses is worth less than the guessing.
>
> — Tormod Pinn, note appended to his entry on 11 an Lùnastal, SE 62

## I. Of the Street Named for the Pit

The copper at Àth fhiadhaich drew men the way any new working draws them in a kingdom whose old one is thinning, and by the second summer of the digging the town had built, on the slope above the ford, a street of new stone houses for the miners come down from the Sloc Mòr's own failing galleries, men who had learned their trade in one pit and carried it, wage and tools and all, to another. The town's own council named the street before the last house on it had a roof, in the way a council names a thing quickly so as not to leave the naming to whoever finishes building last, and the name it chose was for the pit the miners had come from rather than the one they had come to: Sràid an t-Sluic, the street of the pit, so that a man walking up from the ford at Àth fhiadhaich passed under a sign naming a mountain he could not see from any window on the street at all.

The house of the Old Spirits at Àth fhiadhaich, which had given the new copper working no blessing when it opened, gave the naming no blessing either, and its keeper, the same woman who had told the Board's factor two summers before that copper dug for a wage was copper dug like any other stone, told the council now, by the word that reached Tormod Pinn at Muileann chaol some months after and which he judged worth the keeping, that a street should be named for the ground it stood on and not for the ground its people had left, and that a town which named its own streets after another town's mountain risked forgetting which mountain it lived under. The council heard her out, as councils do, and kept the name, there being no other ready to hand and no time, with winter coming on and roofs still unfinished, to argue one out. Tormod set the exchange down in four lines, the keeper's words nearly whole and the council's answer reduced to the one fact that mattered, that the name stood; he had learned young, from the chronicler who had trained him, that a chronicle owed a speaker her own words and owed a council only its own decision, the two debts being of a different weight entire.

The miners themselves, by every account that reached the Library that year, troubled the name less than their own council or their own priesthood did, a man newly down from the Sloc Mòr's own thinning galleries having, as Tormod judged when he set the matter down, a keener interest in the roof over his family's own new-built house than in the word painted above its door; two of the households on the street had brought with them, folded in a chest with the rest of their goods, small lumps of coal from the Sloc Mòr's own upper galleries, kept less for any use than for the plain fact of having carried something out of a mountain that had otherwise given their households nothing back for the digging. He set down, in the same entry and in fewer words still, what little came to him that season out of the north: that a man there had begun trying to draw a fuel from the waste of the mines, to stand in the coal's place, and that the trying had come to nothing. Tormod wrote the sentence once and moved on to the next matter waiting on his desk, and it is very nearly the whole of what the record of those years troubles to say of it.

Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh, who had come to the Library three years before as a clerk of the second circuit and been kept on since at Tormod's own asking, copied both entries fair into the day-book that evening, a task she had done for him most evenings of those three years, and asked him, setting down her pen, whether a street's wrong name mattered enough to trouble a chronicle with four lines when the season had brought harder matters. Tormod told her that a chronicle worked as a net rather than a court, taking in what came its way rather than weighing each thing first against what mattered more, and that a net which let the small fish through on the grounds that they were small ended, after enough seasons, holding nothing at all worth the hauling. She said this sounded like a saying he had used on her before, and he allowed, not looking up from the letter he had begun on the desk's other corner, that a chronicler who found himself a new saying every year had probably stopped chronicling and started only talking, and that he hoped, at five-and-seventy, not yet to have crossed that particular line.

## II. Of the Galleries Let Go

The letter he had begun that evening was to the Board's own clerk at Cathair mhòr, asking, as he had asked twice before that year without an answer worth the copying, what truth lay behind the word that had reached Muileann chaol from three separate quarters that the Sloc Mòr's lowest galleries stood flooded and the Board's own pumps idle above them. The answer came at last in the new year, a single sheet signed by a clerk whose name Tormod did not know, saying that the lowest workings had been let stand under water since the turn of the season, the cost of running the pumps against so little coal as the lowest seams still gave having outrun, by the Board's own reckoning, whatever that coal was worth at the fair; the sheet called it a pause, in the Board's own hand, and gave no day by which the pause was expected to end.

Tormod rode south that spring to see the thing himself, a journey he made perhaps once in three years and only when a report troubled him past the patience of a second letter, and stood at the pit-head above Achadh dhomhain on a morning cold enough that the pump-house's own chimney, drawing no fire that day, showed no more smoke than the empty sheds beside it. The overseer who walked him down to the lip of the lowest shaft, a man Tormod had met twice before in twenty years of such visits and each time greyer, told him that the water had come up eleven fathoms in the flooded galleries and showed no sign yet of finding its own level, and that the pumps which might have held it down had stood cold since the turn of the season on the Board's own order, an order the overseer read to him from a slip of paper he kept folded in his coat as though he expected, someday, to need to prove he had not imagined it. Tormod asked him whether the Board meant the pause for a season or for good, and the overseer said that a pause a man's own coat had to carry proof of was a pause that had already outlasted whatever the word was meant to promise, and that he for his own part called it by its right name among the other overseers, though never where a Board clerk might hear him say it.

The pumps themselves, three great engines the Board's own founders had cast at Cathair mhòr thirty years before, when the lowest galleries had still paid for the coal to run them, stood drawn out of their housings and loaded onto flat wagons before the summer was old, sold, by the Board's own notice, to the harbour works at Seann Bhral in the south, where a new dry dock wanted draining faster than its own smaller engines could manage. Tormod watched the first of the three go down the coal line from a siding above Achadh dhomhain, the engine lashed under canvas against the road's own dust and rain, and thought, watching it, of the wool-buyer's fact that had reached Caol mhòr some years before, that a market goes where the coin already is; a pump, it seemed to him, went where the water was, and cared no more than any bolt of cloth for the ground it had been built to serve. He wrote in his own book that evening, in words he judged too plain for the day-book's own hand and kept instead for himself, that a kingdom which sold the engines that held its own mountain dry to drain another man's harbour had answered, without troubling to say so anywhere in its own minute, the question the search of ten years before had failed outright to answer, and had answered it the way such questions are answered oftenest, by a bill of sale and not by a chronicle's own reckoning.

The overseer at Achadh dhomhain wrote to him once more that autumn, a shorter letter than the first, to say that the second pump had followed the first to Seann Bhral and the third stood ready to go, and that the men who had tended the three of them between them, six in all, had been found work on the working galleries still above water, the Board's own notice calling it no loss to any household, which the overseer, signing his own name this time rather than none, judged worth passing on without comment of his own, there being comment enough, he wrote, in the plain fact for anyone troubling to read it.

## III. Of Imrich nam Pantar

The word that reached Muileann chaol from the south-west that same summer came by a rounder road, a shire's own maor writing first to the Board of a stock loss he judged too large for the ordinary account of wolves and weather, and the Board's clerk, having no ledger of his own fit to hold it, passing the letter on to the Library as a thing more fit for a chronicle than a rent-roll. The maor wrote that a great host of the great cats the south-west herders called panthers, tawny beasts the size of a two-year calf that came down out of the high passes by the same road every so many years and had not been seen, by any herder's own memory then living, in longer than any of them could put a number to, had crossed the hill country near Baile dhomhain that spring by the old road the maps still called Imrich nam Pantar, and that for the better part of a month the flocks pastured along that road had lost more stock to the crossing than the shire's own dues could easily bear the loss of.

Tormod set the letter beside an older paper the Library kept, a list drawn up in the days of An Aois Naomh naming the years such a crossing had come before, a list he had first found reason to open only twice in the whole of his own chronicling, and found the crossing named there under a year whose distance from his own he worked out with a care he gave few other sums, the interval between one crossing and the last being, by the old list's own reckoning, longer than any single herder's working life, so that no man now living at Baile dhomhain had seen it before and none now living there was like to see it again. He wrote the entry longer than any other that year, setting the maor's own count of the stock lost beside the old list's count from the crossing before it, the two figures agreeing near enough that he judged the coincidence worth remarking, and noted, at the entry's foot, that the old list named the year following such a crossing a hungry one, the cats' passing having been reckoned, by whatever reasoning the Holy Age's own tellers had kept, to trouble the land's own bearing for a season after as much as it troubled the flocks during.

The herders themselves, by the second half of the maor's letter, had done what the old road's own name promised they would, driving what stock they could off the path beforehand and keeping the crossing days as a season of watching rather than working, and had lost, in the end, fewer beasts than the first week's count had feared, though more than any recent year had cost them. The tanners of Baile ghorm on the coast below, hearing of the crossing before the herders had finished counting their own losses, sent buyers up into the hills within the fortnight to take the hides of whatever cats the herders' own dogs and spears had brought down defending the flocks, paying a price the herders judged fair for a skin they had no other use for and the tanners judged cheap for a hide unlike any that came to their vats in an ordinary year. Baile ghorm's own tanners cured the skins through that summer by a craft the maor's letter did not trouble to describe and Tormod did not think to ask after, and the fair at Muileann òg the following year saw, for the first time in any chronicler's own memory, saddles and belts of panther-hide sold under the Baile ghorm mark, a fashion that took the southern buyers by surprise enough that the mark's own price doubled twice before the fair's ten days were out.

Tormod wrote of the saddles too, the following spring, a shorter entry than the crossing's own, noting only that the trade in the hides had outlasted the crossing by longer than any single season and that Baile ghorm's tanners meant, by every word that reached him, to keep the mark going as long as a hide came to hand to sell under it. Beathag, copying the entry, asked him whether it was proper for the chronicle to note a trade that might, for all either of them could tell that year, come to nothing within a season or two, and Tormod told her that a chronicle's business was what a year had actually done and not what a later year might undo, and that a note honestly wrong in ten years' time cost the Library less than a note never set down at all for fear of being wrong.

## IV. Of the Lent Lamps and the Yard at Muileann chrom

The same summer that carried the panthers south brought a smaller trouble north, one that reached Tormod first through the coal-line's own carters, who complained of it at every siding between Muileann mhin and Muileann chaol long before any shire's maor troubled to write it down. The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin, whose forges turned out the greater part of every shaft-lamp the vein-towns burned, had halved their own making that year for want of coal enough to fire the forges properly, the coal that reached Muileann mhin coming thinner and dearer with every season the Sloc Mòr's own galleries gave less of it up, and a town that made lamps by burning coal to shape the iron those same lamps then burned more of had found, that year, the two ends of its own trade closing on each other like a door.

The pits themselves, left short of new lamps and unwilling to send men below without light enough to see the roof by, took to lending shaft-lamps from gallery to gallery and pit to pit as need moved, a habit no charter had ever set down rules for and the Guild of Hewers, finding itself with no clause to govern it either, met by keeping a minute-book at its own hall, a plain ledger in which any overseer borrowing a dozen lamps from a neighbouring pit entered the number, the day, and his own name against repayment. Tormod sent to the Guild's hall for a copy of the book's first year, judging it a thing the Library ought to hold against the day some later chronicler asked how the pits had managed a coal so scarce it could not always light its own diggers, and found in it, when the copy came, more names entered against debts than names entered against repayments, a ledger that told, in its own dry column of borrowings, a plainer account of the vein's own thinning than any letter the Board had troubled to write him that year.

The trouble at Muileann chrom, when it came that same summer, was of a different order, and reached him first as three lines in a Board notice and only later, and at greater length, in a letter from the custodian of the yard's own small house of the Rite, a man Tormod had corresponded with before on lesser matters and trusted more than he trusted the Board's own notices. The yard families who kept the coal trains running between the Sloc Mòr and the coast, seeing their own wages cut that spring by an order the Board judged no more than the coal's own falling price required, stopped the trains outright for three days running, the first stoppage of its kind the line had known since it was laid, and put forward as their spokesman a man of one-and-forty named Dòmhnall Ruadh mac Ailein, whose father had laid the first rail at Muileann chrom with his own hands and who had worked the yard himself since he was a boy of twelve.

Dòmhnall Ruadh, by the custodian's account, asked the Board's own factor for nothing more than the wage restored to what it had stood at the year before, and told him, in words the custodian judged worth the copying whole, that a family which had laid the rail, tended it, and kept it running through every season the line had known could not be paid less for the same work merely because the mountain the rail served had grown poorer, the mountain's own poverty being the Board's misfortune and not the yard's making. The Board's factor answered, on the third day, that the wage would stand as it had before the cut, the stoppage having cost the Board more in halted coal than the cut itself had saved it in a season, and the trains ran again on the fourth day at the old rate; on the fifth, the Board's own notice named eleven men dismissed from the yard for their part in the stopping, Dòmhnall Ruadh among them, the settlement of the wage and the dismissal of its askers arriving, by the custodian's own dry observation, in the same week and from the same hand.

The custodian who wrote to him of it kept, besides his house's own register, a small book of his own in which he set down the yard's grievances as its families brought them to him, a habit Tormod recognised at once as a chronicler's own habit worn by a man who had never called it that, and told him so in his answering letter, adding that a house which kept such a book against the day some larger matter needed it had done the Library's own work a season before the Library knew to ask for it.

Tormod set the whole of it down at greater length than the panthers had had, the wage restored and the eleven put out being, he judged, a thing later readers would want in full rather than in summary, and wrote at the entry's close, in the day-book's own plain hand and not merely his private one this time, that a Board which answered a stoppage by giving the families their wage and taking their spokesman's own place from him had settled nothing it meant to keep settled, and that a chronicle owed its readers the plain fact of both halves of such a bargain, not only the half that looked, on the Board's own notice, like a kindness.

## V. Of the Strike-Through

The harvest that autumn, across the whole of the south and west both, came in better than any the shires had reckoned on since before the search for a second vein had first been spoken of, the wheat standing thick enough at Cathair fhada that the maor there wrote to Muileann chaol of granaries built for a leaner year now wanting a second storey to hold what the first year's fields had actually given. Tormod read the maor's own letter at his desk in the last week of an Lùnastal, the panthers' crossing more than a year behind the kingdom by then and the old list's warning of a hungry year to follow it a full season overdue with no want anywhere the letters reached him to bear it out, and sat some while with his own book open at the entry he had written the spring before, the ink long dry and the words, read again in a good year's light, sounding to him now less like a chronicler's careful reckoning and more like an old man's fright dressed in an old list's borrowed authority.

He took up his pen, dipped it, and drew a single line through his own sentence, the one naming the year to come a hungry one by the Holy Age's own reckoning, leaving the words legible beneath the stroke as the Library's own practice required of every correction, a chronicle owing its readers its wrong guesses as plainly as its right ones, and wrote beneath it, in the same hand, that the harvest of the year following the crossing had proved thick rather than thin across the south and west, and that the old list, whatever true word it had kept of crossings a dozen lifetimes gone, had kept no word this time that the wheat troubled to answer to.

Beathag, coming in from the outer room with the day's letters, found him sitting with the book still open before him and the ink not yet blotted, and asked whether he meant the line to stand, a chronicler striking through his own words being a thing she had not seen him do in the three years she had kept his book. Tormod told her that he meant it to stand exactly as struck, the line and the words both, since a chronicle that quietly rewrote its own bad year earned, season on season, the trust of no one, and that he had rather be read, seven-and-seventy years old and wrong once in a season, than be believed infallible by readers who had never troubled to check him. She blotted the page for him without being asked, as she had learned to do that summer without spoiling the stroke beneath the blotting sand, and set the book back on its stand open at the struck line, where it stood, by Tormod's own wish, through the whole of that harvest month, so that any clerk who came to the desk on Library business might read, before he read anything else that year, a chronicler's own hand owning that he had once been afraid of a summer that came in kind.

# Chapter Thirty-seven: Of Now Written

*SE 64 an Dàmhair – SE 67 an Lùnastal*

> A column of figures is no argument, until it has been read aloud in a room that never wished to hear it read. After that it is a fact the room must carry, and carries as long as the room keeps its own minutes.
>
> — Daniel Frayne, private book kept at Muileann leathan, 6 an t-Samhain, SE 64

## I. Of the Clerks Who Came for the Figures

The census clerks who rode north to Caol mhòr that autumn were the first the Moot's room had ever seen come asking rather than come telling, and Daniel Frayne, nine-and-fifty that year and speaker long enough that he no longer troubled to count the seasons of it, found the change stranger than anything the clerks themselves said to him. Two men came, both Dia-thìreach, both younger than his own eldest clerk, riding a cart with a chest of blank forms lashed under a tarpaulin against the rain that had followed them the whole road from Cathair dhearg, and they asked at the door of the room, with a courtesy Frayne had not met from any southern office in thirty years of dealing with them, whether the Moot kept a count of its own people that the third census might use, the shire's own maor having told the council's census office that no southern clerk had yet set foot in the northern towns to take one and none was like to before the printing date the council itself had chosen.

Frayne sat with them the better part of a day, the room's ledgers open on the table between them, and gave them what the Moot had: the school registers Agnes Pike's and Alice Hale's houses had kept since before he could write his own name properly, what the vigil-keepers of Baile chrom would lend of their own books, the bindery's own tally of every family in Muileann leathan that had ever brought him a book to mend, and the Moot's own count of heads taken every third year since the room was first opened, a count no southern office had ever asked to see before that autumn. The younger of the two clerks copied the figures into his own book in a fair, careful hand, and asked, when he had done, whether the Moot would swear to them before a justice if the council required it, a question Frayne answered by telling him that the Moot had sworn to smaller things for larger names before that day and would swear to this one gladly, there being nothing in the figures the room had any cause to soften.

The rain that had followed the clerks up from Cathair dhearg did not let up while they sat at the room's table, and Frayne, watching it run down the small window behind the younger clerk's shoulder, thought it a fitting enough weather for the asking, the road north having never been an easy one for a southern office to trouble much with in any season, wet or dry. He offered the two men what the room's own chest could spare of Caol mhòr's own bread and its own beer, poor fare beside what a council office kept for its travelling clerks, and the elder of the two, a man near Frayne's own age who had ridden the circuit for the census twice before in the south and never once in the north, said over it that he had heard the road called worse than he found it, and that a man might have told him, before he set out, that the room at the end of it kept better order in its own ledgers than half the southern shire halls he had visited that same season. Frayne took the saying for the courtesy it plainly was and no more, having heard courtesies enough from southern mouths over thirty years to know the weight a wise man gave them, but he set it down in his own book that night beside the rest, judging that even a courtesy, once written, outlived the mouth that had spoken it.

"They will print what we give them," Frayne told the room's own clerks that evening, when the cart had gone south again with the chest of forms filled and the blank ones still lashed beneath the tarpaulin for want of use, "and I do not know yet whether that is a kindness or only a shorter road to the same silence we have always been given. But we have never before been asked, and a room that keeps a minute-book keeps this in it: that in the sixty-fourth year of the reckoning, we were asked." He wrote the day into his own private book that same night, the figures given and the manner of the giving both, a habit he had kept since the winter he first began it and had no thought of breaking now that the figures, for once, were wanted rather than merely tolerated.

The census was published that same autumn at Cathair dhearg, in the last week of an Dàmhair, and it was the first in the kingdom's history to be printed and sold openly at the fairs rather than filed unread in the council's own cellar, a small reform the notice that announced it called a token of the Crown's own confidence in its people, though the room at Caol mhòr, reading the notice a season later than the south had read it, found in the phrase nothing that the figures, once they arrived, did not answer more plainly than any notice could.

## II. Of the Reading and the Two Words

The figures reached Caol mhòr early in an t-Samhain, a bound sheaf of printed columns the council's own press had run off in numbers enough to sell at every market town on the roll, carried up the last stretch of road on a carter's own cart because the autumn's rain had closed the higher road to anything lighter, and the room that gathered to hear them read was fuller than it had been in years, benches carried in from the vestry next door and the fire built up past its usual evening measure against a cold that had kept the windows white with frost since the first hard nights. The Moot's clerk who read the columns aloud, a woman who had kept the room's own books since before Frayne himself had held the chair and had buried, by her own account, two speakers and meant to outlast a third at the same table, read them in the flat voice a clerk keeps for figures that trouble her more than she means to let the room see. Frayne sat in the chair Mary Coyle had once sat in, his hands laid flat on the table the way he sat when he meant to keep them still, and listened to every column the census had chosen to take, the counted heads, the counted hearths, the counted trades a family owned to, read out in turn for the northern towns and set beside the same columns for the south.

In every column the clerks at Cathair dhearg had troubled to take, the northern towns stood at about half the measure the southern shires showed for the same count, a fact the room had known in its own bones for two generations and had never once seen printed in the kingdom's own hand before that winter. Nobody in the room was surprised at the figures themselves; what silenced them, Frayne wrote afterward, was hearing figures they had always known made into a fact the council itself had signed its own press to. The clerk read the last column and set the sheaf down, and the room kept a quiet long enough that the fire's own settling in the grate was the loudest thing in it.

Frayne drew the minute-book toward him when the quiet had held as long as he judged it should, and wrote two words in it, and let the room see him write them before he spoke a word himself: *Now written.* He offered the room no gloss on the two words, then or after, though more than one clerk asked him in the years following what he had meant by them and got, from each asking, much the same answer, that a figure the Moot had always known and the kingdom had never printed was one kind of fact, and a figure both the Moot and the kingdom now held in the same paper was another kind entire, and that the difference between the two kinds was the whole of what he had meant to set down and no more than that.

One of the room's younger clerks, a man barely into his own second year at the table and too new to the work to keep the stillness the older hands kept by long habit, asked Frayne afterward, walking out with him into the frost, whether the two words meant the room ought now to expect the south to answer for what it had printed. Frayne told him no, that a fact set down was not a promise kept, and that a room hoping for the one from the other had not yet learned the difference the room's own long history ought to have taught it by then; but he told the young man, too, that a fact once printed could not be unprinted, whatever the council chose to do or not do about it, and that this was worth having even where a promise was not, a distinction the young clerk turned over some while in the cold before he owned that he took the sense of it, if not yet the comfort.

The census carried, as the first one had, a line for the coal-touched, a number given without gloss or comment, and Tormod Pinn, copying the published figures into the royal chronicle at Muileann chaol that same winter as he had copied every census before it, entered the line exactly as Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill had entered it a generation before him, without a word added either side of the number. He was eight-and-seventy that winter and had kept the chronicle three-and-twenty years, and the clerks who worked beside him at Muileann chaol said afterward that his hand had grown no less steady for the years, only slower, so that a page that had once taken him an evening now took the better part of two.

In the south-west that same season, the houses of the Stone published, for the first time in their own province's memory, a count of their own people to set beside the kingdom's, a reckoning kept by the province's own scribes rather than by any council clerk, and the two counts, when word of them reached Muileann chaol, agreed within a hundred souls of each other, a closeness the chronicle noted with the same flat hand it gave every other column that winter, though more than one clerk at the Library remarked, reading the entry, that a province which could check the kingdom's own figures against its own and find them true had been given a trust the north had never once been offered.

## III. Of Tormod Pinn's Last Winter

Tormod Pinn had come to the chronicler's desk at Muileann chaol in the forty-second year of the reckoning, called Pinn for the speed of his own hand rather than for any name his father had given him, and he had kept, since the day Gormshuil laid the pen down, the same habit she had left him: the list of what the record did not hold, copied into the front of every year's book and never once added to nor struck from in three-and-twenty years of keeping it. He had told the Library's younger clerks, more than once over those years, that a chronicler's business was to keep the list honest rather than to shorten it, and that a man who struck a line from another's list without first filling the gap it named had done nothing but tidy a shelf he had no right to tidy.

A junior clerk who copied returns beside him that last winter said afterward that Tormod Pinn had grown, in his last years, given to reading a page twice where once he had read it once, from a wish, the clerk judged, to be sure of a figure before he trusted his own hand to it, a carefulness the younger clerks about him took at first for slowness and only later, once his desk stood empty, understood for what it had been. Tormod kept to his own desk through most of that winter and into the spring following, reading, as he had read every season for twenty years, the returns the shires sent up and the figures the census had newly given him to set beside them, and the clerks who passed his door those months said he looked, by the spring, thinner in the face than the winter before, though none of them thought to trouble him with the saying, a chronicler's own health being, by the Library's long custom, a matter he was left to keep to himself unless he chose otherwise. They found him at his own desk on a morning in an t-Sultain, the returns for that year still open under his hand and his pen laid down beside them rather than dropped, in much the manner, an old clerk remarked who had served under Ailean Leabhar too, that a man of the Library seemed always to be found, as though the desk taught a certain way of leaving it.

He was buried at Muileann chaol within the week, in the small burying-ground behind the Library that held every keeper and chronicler the house had kept since Ailean Leabhar's own day, and Mòrag nic Coinnich, who had known him the whole of his three-and-twenty years at the desk, spoke over him only that he had kept the list honest and struck nothing from it that was not yet earned, words the Library's own younger clerks copied down and kept, by their own account, truer to the man than any longer eulogy could have been. He was nine-and-seventy at his death, by the Library's own reckoning of his years, an age no chronicler before him at Muileann chaol had reached at that desk, and the clerks noted the fact in the margin of his own last page, the only line in the whole of his tenure that he had not written himself.

Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh took the desk that same summer, three-and-fifty years old and the first woman to hold the chronicler's chair since Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill, chosen by Mòrag nic Coinnich from among the house's own senior clerks for a steadiness of hand the keeper judged the desk would want after Tormod's long, quiet tenure. She had kept the Library's own gazetteer returns seven years before that summer and told the clerks who worked under her, on her first morning at the chronicler's own desk, that she meant to change nothing of the desk's furniture nor its hours, only its habit of silence where the record had none to give, a saying the clerks who heard it did not at first take her full meaning of, until her first year's book was closed and its foot-note read. She kept his habit of the list at the front of the year's book, unchanged, and added to it a habit of her own that no chronicler before her had kept: a foot-note at the close of every year's entries, set apart from the chronicle proper, naming what the record could not learn that year and why, where the why could be told at all.

Her first such note, written at the foot of her first year at the desk, concerned the northern figures the census had printed. The clerks who had gone to take them, she wrote, had been told the figures at Caol mhòr and had not troubled to count them for themselves, and the figures they were told were the Moot's own, given freely by its speaker to two clerks who asked. So the kingdom's first honestly printed census was honest in the north, she set down, only because the north had done the counting the south's own clerks had been sent to do and had not done. Frayne read the note some months later, a copy of it sent north by a Library clerk who thought the room at Caol mhòr ought to see what its own giving had been made into, and kept the copy in his private book beside the day he had first given the figures, judging, he told the room, that a chronicler who would write such a thing plainly, of her own kingdom's own clerks, was a chronicler the north might yet have some use trusting.

## IV. Of the Chests Called In

Mòrag nic Coinnich, keeper of the Library these six-and-twenty years, had long held that a history kept in forty scattered shire-chests was no history at all but forty separate hopes that someone, someday, would trouble to read them together, and in the year after Tormod Pinn's death she sent her own clerks out along the roll to call every shire's record-chest in to Muileann chaol, the maors' own returns, the town chronicles where any town kept one, the vigil-books and rite-rolls the shires' own faiths had filed apart from the Crown's business, all of it, whatever a shire had troubled to keep, to be copied or kept whole as the Library judged fit.

Most shires sent what they held without complaint, some gladly and some only because a council notice had told them to, but at Seann Tarr the shire's own keeper, an old man who had held the chest's key since before Mòrag herself was born and had never in that whole tenure let a stranger's hand touch the chest without his own standing by it, burned the chest in his own yard the night before her clerks arrived rather than let it travel south. He met the clerks himself at the gate the next morning, the ash still warm behind him and his own coat smelling of the smoke he had not troubled to wash from it, and told them, when they found only ash where the chest had stood, that the shire's record belonged in the shire and would stay there in whatever form he judged fit to leave it, a plain answer given without heat and without apology, the clerks noted, as though the burning had been no more than the ordinary close of an ordinary evening's business. He was fined by the council for the burning, a fine the Library's own clerk noted he paid without argument and without apology either, and the chest, and whatever it had held of Seann Tarr's own two centuries, was lost entire, the only shire record of the whole calling-in that the Library never had the chance to read.

Cathair naomh, in the north, sent its own rolls in two carts that same season, together with the town's own chronicle, kept by a single family through four generations without a council's asking, the crates packed by the family's own eldest daughter, who rode the two carts south herself rather than trust them to a hired carter, and told Mòrag's clerks, unpacking the crates at her own hand once the road was done, that her grandmother's grandmother had begun the chronicle on the back of an unused rent-roll for want of paper better suited to it, and that every hand since had kept to the same plain page rather than buy finer stock the family judged an extravagance no plain chronicle wanted. Mòrag nic Coinnich, going through it at her own table with a clerk standing by to lift out whatever the crates held, entered it in the Library's own register as the best-kept shire record the calling-in had yet returned, a judgment she let stand even after every other shire's chest had reached Muileann chaol and been weighed against it. Seann Toll sent its own chest willingly and asked, when the clerks came for it, for a copy of everything the chest held to be returned to the shire once the Library had made its own, an asking no shire before it had thought to make, and Mòrag's clerks made the copy as asked, a full transcription bound in the same hand and set beside the original before either left the shire's own hall, and the copy they made for Seann Toll became, in the years after, the pattern every later shire's copy was cut to, the Library having found, in the asking, a better custom than the one it had begun with.

The Library's own holdings doubled that year with what the calling-in returned, and it took into one keeping, for the first time since its founding, the lesser archives several provinces had kept apart from the Crown's own rolls, so that from that season the history of Dia-thìr was written and held in one place at Muileann chaol and not scattered, as it had been since the Severance, across forty shire halls each keeping its own account of its own corner and no other's.

No Tuathaich record was called in that season, nor any season after it, the calling-in's own notice having named only the shires the council's roll accounted for, and the north's own record stayed where it had always stayed: the Moot's minute-books at Caol mhòr, the school registers Agnes Pike's and Alice Hale's houses had begun, the churches' own registers, the vigil-books of Baile chrom, all of it in private keeping and none of it asked for. Frayne, reading the calling-in's notice when word of it reached the room the following spring, called the room together and put the question to them plainly himself, whether the Moot ought to offer its own books south now that the council had shown, by the calling-in, a wish to gather every record the kingdom held: a question, he told them, the room had never once been asked by any southern office and had, this once, the choosing of for its own.

The room debated it the better part of an evening, the older clerks arguing that a book offered was a book the council might one day demand rather than merely receive, and the younger arguing that a history kept only in the north was a history the kingdom's own printed figures would go on outweighing however true the north's own count remained. "We gave them the figures once," the room's oldest clerk said, near the debate's close, "and they made of the giving a mark against us, however honestly it was meant. I will not vote to give them the books as well and trust the giving to fare better." Frayne, who had sat the whole evening without speaking his own mind either way, told the room only that he had not called them together to be told which way to vote, and that he would set down whatever the room decided and no more of his own judgment beside it, a promise the room's own minute of that night bears out.

The room's minute of that evening, in Frayne's own hand, records no vote taken by show or by count and no reason given beyond the two words its own clerk set down at the sitting's close, words that answered the calling-in more plainly than any longer argument the room could have offered instead: *kept north.* No cart went south from Caol mhòr that year or any year following, and the Moot's own books, whatever the kingdom's Library now held of every other shire's record, stayed where they had always been kept, in the room at Caol mhòr, in the hands that had written them.

# Chapter Thirty-eight: Of the Empty Floor and the Banked Fire

*SE 68 an t-Ògmhios – 18 an t-Ògmhios SE 71*

> A floor raised and left bare speaks only years afterward, once the ledgers show plainly what was left unsent.
>
> — Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh, foot-note to the chronicle, entered at Muileann chaol, 2 an t-Ògmhios, SE 68

## I. Of the Fourth Floor

The new wing at Muileann chaol was raised of the grey stone that came up out of the Sloc Mòr's own spoil, cut and dressed by masons who had learned the trade cutting galleries rather than walls and cut it, by old habit, in blocks the size a gallery's own timbering would have wanted. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh, three years into the chronicler's chair by the summer it was finished, walked its three built floors before a single chest had been carried up to them and thought that a library housed in a mountain's own leavings kept, in its stone if nowhere else, an honest account of where the kingdom's wealth had gone. The first floor took the provinces' returns, shire by shire, in presses built to the same measure so that no shire's chest stood taller or grander than its neighbour's. The second took the town chronicles, where any town had troubled to keep one, and the third the vigil-books and rite-rolls the shires' own faiths had filed apart from the Crown's business. The fourth floor, built to the same measure as the three beneath it, stood empty, its presses raised and its shelves cut and planed and never loaded, and Mòrag nic Coinnich, walking it with her that first morning, told Beathag only that a floor was easier built now than added later, and that the Library had learned, over its long keeping, to build for what it did not yet hold.

The clerks who carried the chests up from the carts that autumn worked the first three floors in the order the wing had been given them, a chain of hands up three flights of a new stair that still smelled of its own mortar, and more than one of them, setting a chest down at last in its press, remarked to the clerk behind him that the fourth flight climbed to nothing and asked, half in jest, whether they were to carry chairs up there instead of chests to save the stair the indignity of standing idle. Beathag heard the jest twice that autumn from two different mouths and wrote neither of them into the chronicle, judging a chronicle no place for a joke that would want explaining to a reader fifty years on, though she kept the sense of it, she owned in her own private book, longer than she kept most things said to her that season.

Beathag asked Mòrag plainly, since the keeper had not offered it, what the fourth floor was built to hold, and Mòrag answered that it was built for the north's own record, should the north ever choose to send it, and that she had asked the masons to raise it all the same, whatever the Moot's own answer proved to be. The two women stood some while at the head of the empty stair, the fourth floor's own door unlocked and its room bare of everything but light coming in low through windows cut the same size as the floors below, and Beathag wrote that evening, in the private note she had kept since her first year at the desk, that a room built and left empty said more of the kingdom's own habits than any room the kingdom had troubled to fill. She had kept, since Tormod Pinn's death, his own front-of-the-year list of what the Library had never been sent, unchanged; she added now, at the year's close, her own foot-note beneath it, a habit no chronicler before her had kept, and she wrote of the fourth floor only that it stood ready and that no cart had come, a sentence she judged plainer than any she could have set beside it.

The calling-in of the shires' chests that had filled the wing's first three floors was two years finished by the time the wing stood ready to take them, and Beathag, reading the whole tally that summer for the first time set out floor by floor, found in it a fact the calling-in's own notice had never troubled to state outright: every shire the council's own roll accounted for had sent something, willing or unwilling, whole or in part, and the one record asked for and not received was the one record never asked for at all. She set that down in the same plain hand, and kept the note in the book the Library's own younger clerks were beginning, by then, to read before they read the chronicle proper, a small book that had, by the wing's second year, outgrown the drawer she had first kept it in.

## II. Of the Arrears at Àth leathan

The Rail Board's own minute that summer gave one line to the branch line at Àth leathan, closed for the falling yield of the western pits, and Beathag, copying the minute into the chronicle as the Board had written it, found nothing in the line to trouble a reader who did not already know the western hills. The pits did not close with the branch. The Board's overseers were withdrawn, their wages costing more by then than the coal they oversaw was fairly worth to a house working the vein in the Crown's name alone, and the Tuathaich hewers who had worked those pits under the overseers' watch for two generations went on working them under pit captains of their own choosing, men chosen from among their own number for the trust of the rest, in a manner the Board's own charter had never troubled to forbid because it had never once thought a Tuathaich pit might be left to govern its own affairs.

The last overseer to leave Àth leathan, a man named in no book Beathag ever read but remembered at the pit-head for years after by the hewers he had watched, is said to have handed the pit-head scale's own key to the hewer standing nearest him without a word of ceremony either way, and to have ridden south the same afternoon without looking back at the headgear behind him. The captains the hewers chose kept the Crown's fifth by the Leòid ruling, as the ruling required of them, weighing every cart at the pit-head and setting the fifth part by before a cart went anywhere, and sent word south each season of what was owed, in a hand as careful as any overseer's had ever been. The Board took the payments when a carrier troubled to bring them and entered them in its own books as arrears, a word that named a debt owed rather than a due paid, though the hewers at Àth leathan had never once failed to send what the ruling asked of them. Beathag, reading the Board's own ledger a season later at a clerk's asking, wrote in her private note that a kingdom which could not tell the difference between a debt and a payment made in good faith had chosen, in the choosing of that one word, to keep a grievance where none was owed, and that she did not know whether the choosing had been made in malice or only in the ordinary carelessness of a Board that had stopped looking at what it did not have to look at.

In the second summer after the branch closed, the pit captains at Àth leathan sent the season's first coal south by cart rather than by rail, the road being longer and the going slower but the loading and the sending both theirs to order, down through the western hills to the yards at Seann Bhral, where the coal factors bought it at the pit-head price and asked no questions of the hand that had cut it. It was the first coal out of Àth leathan to travel a road the Board had not chosen for it, four carts and a spare axle carried against the road's own roughness, and the carters who drove it said afterward, at Cnoc thais and at the pits above it, that the going had cost them three days more than the rail would have and had cost the Board nothing at all, the Board having washed its hands of the branch and of everything the branch no longer carried. The factors at Seann Bhral, the carters said too, weighed the coal twice over before they paid for it, as though a cart come down from a pit with no overseer's mark on its papers were a cart to be doubted until the scale itself had spoken; but they paid, each time, the full pit-head price, and asked, in all the seasons of the carts coming, no question beyond the weight.

A younger clerk at the Library, reading the Board's own minute beside Beathag that same season, asked her whether the word ought to be struck from the ledger and a truer one put in its place, since the chronicle, of all the kingdom's books, might have the standing to ask for it. Beathag told him no, that a chronicle's business was to copy the word the Board had chosen and let the choosing stand against the Board's own name, not to soften it for a reader who ought to be trusted with the plain fact of it; she had learned the habit, she told him, from a chronicler who struck through his own bad guesses rather than hide them, and a chronicler who mended another office's bad words was practising a different trade entirely. The clerk did not raise the matter again, though he copied, that same week, the word arrears into three further ledgers of his own without once, by his own later account, writing it easily.

## III. Of the Register at Cnoc thais

At Cnoc thais, in the same western hills, the pits passed to their own hewers in the same season and by the same withdrawal, and the man chosen to keep the accounts was Sam Varley, four-and-fifty that year, who had worked the pit-head scales under the Board's own overseer for eleven years before the overseer left and had kept, in that time, a private tally of his own beside the Board's, out of a habit he could not afterward explain except to say that a scale watched by one pair of eyes alone was a scale worth checking against a second pair. He opened, that first season, a book of the pit's own accounts, the earliest page of it headed in his own plain hand with the day and the pit's own name and nothing else, a book the town's own register still keeps and still calls by no finer title than the day it was begun.

His small son Tom, not yet old enough for the pit, ran the errands the book wanted: a figure carried to a captain waiting at the pit-head, a weight called down from the scale-house to the table where his father sat with the ledger open, a message sent to the next valley when the carts were due and had not come. Sam kept him at it through that first summer and every summer after, and once, when the boy asked why the figures mattered so much to a book nobody south would read, told him plainly, without looking up from the page, that a book kept honest for nobody was worth more than a book kept honest for someone watching, since the one habit would hold when the other failed. Tom did not, by his own account, take the full sense of the saying that summer, standing in the scale-house door with the cold coming in behind him and his father's pen not once pausing over the page; but he carried the figures all the same, and carried them straight, and Sam never once had to send a second boy after the first.

That same season, on the southern road a country away, the far-off house that the carters called An Sligeanach Fad' às passed from the family that had kept it three generations to a family of drovers new to the trade. The old keepers left the way the tellers of that road say a house is properly left, the last of them sweeping the hearth clean before he handed the new family the key, and the drovers built a second hall beside the first for a trade the old house had never troubled to serve; a hall built, the carters who watched it rise said, faster and cruder than the first, of green timber that would want a year's settling before a door in it hung true. Within a few years the house that had once fed a carter dried deer and black water and asked no questions had become the largest house on the old mining roads, its yard crowded of an evening with beasts and men from every valley the roads still served, its new hall louder than the old one had ever been in three generations of quiet keeping. Beathag noted the sale in the chronicle in a single line, the house's changing hands being, by the Library's own measure, a small thing beside a branch line closed or a pit passed to its own hewers, though she wrote, in her private note that year, that a house grown fat on the drove trade while the coal roads emptied told its own kind of truth about which trade a failing kingdom still had use for.

The book's first year closed, as every year after it would close, on the last evening of an Dùbhlachd, when Sam sat up late by the scale-house lamp to draw the final line beneath the season's figures and set the total against what the captain's own count made of it, the two sums agreeing, that first year, to within a single basket-weight neither man troubled to chase down further. Tom, sent to bed an hour before, came down again in his nightshirt to see the line drawn, having asked, the week before, whether a book's first year ought not to be watched closed the way a house watches its own hearth banked for the night, and Sam let him stand by while the ink dried, saying nothing of the asking either way, though he did not send the boy up again until the page was blotted and shut.

## IV. Of the Failing Grounds

The herring did not come, that year or the year following, to the grounds off the mouth of the river below Seann Dunn, and the east-coast boats, finding their own waters empty a second season together, went north to fish the grounds off Caol mhòr instead, grounds the licence law had kept for Dia-thìreach boats since the licences were first written and that few east-coast boats had troubled to fish while their own waters answered. The law gave them the right, and they used it, in numbers the law had never anticipated, and the Tuathaich boats that worked the edges of those grounds were pushed farther out by hulls they did not know and could not, by any law written, turn away.

The boats of Inis mhin, pushed from the grounds nearest their own harbour by the crowding, took to the deep water beyond the northern isles, a water no boat of that coast had fished within living memory for the roughness of it and the distance a crew had to keep from land overnight, days on end with no headland in sight and the swell running longer than any inshore man cared to trust. Two boats were lost there in the first year, gone out and not come back, and the harbour kept, after that, a stricter watch on the weather than it had ever kept before, a horn sounded from the point whenever the glass fell fast; but none was lost in any year following, the crews having learned, in the losing of the two, what the deep water asked of a boat that meant to fish it and return. Before the second summer was out the catch that Inis mhin brought in from that water had passed what Caol mhòr brought in from all the grounds about it, a fact the chronicle sets down without comment, since a comment would only have said what the figures said more plainly: that a people pushed from what the law protected had found, in what the law did not trouble to reach, a living the law had never thought to grant them.

## V. Of the Keeper Laid Down

Mòrag nic Coinnich laid down the keepership of the Library in the autumn of the seventieth year, two-and-seventy that season and thirty years and more in the chair, the longest any keeper had yet held it, longer than Ailean Leabhar's own founding tenure, and she named, before the council that confirmed such things, her own deputy Raghnall mac Mhuirich to come after her, a man fifty that year who had kept the Library's own catalogue in order through every calling-in and every new wing raised over it without once, by Beathag's own account, losing a single shelf's place in the reckoning. Mòrag's own last act at the desk was to walk the fourth floor once more with Beathag beside her, the floor no less empty than it had stood the day the wing was finished, their two lamps the only light in a room built for four hundred chests that had never held one. "I built the room," she said, when Beathag asked her, at the head of the stair, whether the emptiness troubled her after thirty years of watching it. "The asking who fills it belongs to Raghnall now, or to nobody, and a room built stands built either way." She left the key to the fourth floor's own door with Raghnall the same week, unremarked among the other keys, a room being, in her own long judgment, worth more built and empty than never built at all.

Raghnall took the chair that same season and changed, in his first year, nothing of the Library's own hours nor its own custom, a steadiness the clerks under him took, at first, for a want of ambition and came later to value as the surest thing the house had left it, in a season when little else about the kingdom's own coal held steady. He asked Beathag, in that first year, whether her own foot-notes ought to be gathered separately from the chronicle proper, a question she answered by telling him that a note kept apart from what it corrected was a note easily lost, and that she meant to keep hers bound into the very pages a reader could not skip past. He did not ask her again, and the foot-notes stayed where she had put them.

That same autumn the price of coal-fuel at the fair of Muileann òg doubled over what it had stood the season before, the Board having cut its own sales to spare the lowest galleries the pumping its dwindling profit could no longer answer for, and the fair's own court, whose long custom it was to fix a ceiling on any good the crowd grew angry enough about, set a ceiling price on coal-fuel that same week, cried three times from the fair's own steps as the custom asked. It found, within a season, that no factor troubled to sell at the price named, the coal simply not reaching the fair's stalls at all rather than reaching them cheap, so that a buyer who came asking for coal-fuel at the court's own ceiling was told, at stall after stall, that none was to be had that day, a true answer and a hollow one both. The ceiling stood written in the court's own book and broken in every stall beneath it, and the wardens who had cried it from the steps did not trouble to cry its breaking, a silence Beathag noted in the chronicle as plainly as she had noted the ceiling.

## VI. Of the Watchmen and the Banked Fire

At Cnoc fhiadhaich, where the spoil-heaps of the old coal galleries still stood unlevelled above the town, the Board posted watchmen the following spring against the households that had taken, in the doubled price of the fair, to picking coal off the heaps to burn in their own grates rather than buy what they could no longer pay for. The watchmen the Board hired were men of the town, chosen for their knowledge of the ground and paid a penny a day above a labourer's wage for the watching, and set two to a shift, one at the north heap and one at the south, with a lantern between them against the winter dark. The chronicle records, in a line Beathag set down without any gloss beside it, that the watchmen saw nothing, every night the posting lasted, though the heaps grew visibly lower by the season and the town's poorer grates burned warmer than the price of the fair could otherwise have bought them. A clerk who rode out from Muileann chaol to note the posting for the Library's own record wrote home to Beathag that he had watched the north heap an hour himself one evening and had seen, in that hour, three separate baskets carried down from it by three separate doors, none of them the watchman's own; she kept his letter but did not print it, judging a clerk's single hour no fair measure of a whole season's watching, whatever it seemed to prove.

In the capital that same season, and worse as the summer came on, the streets of the poorer quarters burned their lamps shorter hours than the council's own lighting order required, the keepers of those streets having found, by the doubled price, that an order written for a coal that cost half what it now cost was an order the poorer wards could no longer afford to keep in full. A lamp lit at dusk and let go out before the middle watch left a street dark for the hours a labourer walked it home from a late shift, and more than one such labourer, Beathag's own clerks reported to her, had taken to carrying a rushlight of his own rather than trust the council's order to see him the whole way. The council's own notice on the matter, when one came at all, named the shortening a saving rather than a want, a word Beathag copied into the chronicle exactly as the notice gave it and set beside it, in her own private note that year, that a saving and a want looked much alike from a street too dark to tell the one from the other.

Her foot-note for that year, entered the following spring at the close of the chronicle's own account of it, named what the record could not learn: how many grates in the capital's poorer wards had gone unlit that winter for the price of what should have warmed them, a figure no census had troubled to ask for and no shire had troubled to keep, so that the Library, which now held in one place the fullest count the kingdom had ever kept of its own coal, its own dead, and its own dues, held no count at all of its own cold. She wrote the note in the same hand she had written every note before it, and changed, in the writing of it, nothing of the desk's own hours nor its own custom, as she had told Raghnall, on his first morning at the chair beside her, that she meant to do.

She climbed the fourth stair once more before she sealed the year's book, alone this time, Mòrag being by then a season retired from the desk, and stood again in the room the masons had built and the masons alone had ever filled, the light coming in as low and as even as it had the first morning she had seen it. A shire's chest could be called in by a letter and a cart, she wrote that evening, and a fair's own price could be set down in a court's own book whether the coal answered to it or not; but a floor built for a book that was never sent stayed exactly what it had been built as, a question asked once and left standing, and she judged, closing the year's account, that the Library had grown practised, in seventy years of the kingdom's keeping, at building rooms for what it did not yet have the courage to ask for outright.

In the north Dubhan was at his work still, as he had been for ten years, boiling and burning what the pits threw away. Nobody in the capital was watching him, and nobody in the Library knew his name. On a night near midsummer in the seventy-first year, the tellers of the north say, he banked his fire and slept beside it, as he had on a hundred nights before.

Here this book ends, the fire banked in the north and the kingdom asleep around it, the Library's fourth floor standing empty still, the ceiling broken in every stall that sold beneath it, and no word set down of what the morning brought.

# The Annals of the Age

## The Years SE 1 – 5

- <a id="ev-V-0001"></a>**22 am Màrt, SE 1** — *The Tuathaich homeland fixed*. The descendants of the humans stranded by the Severance are settled by law in the north of the island and held there. It is a confinement; yet their children's children call it home.
- <a id="ev-EVI-1000"></a>**26 an Giblean, SE 1** — *The Hale household lodged at Caol mhòr* (Caol mhòr). Walter Hale comes north with his wife Ellen and their children David and Alice among the households the guard walks into the homeland that summer, and is given a loft over a net-store on the harbour street at Caol mhòr, his for as long as nobody wants it back.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0001"><em>The Tuathaich homeland fixed</em>, 22 am Màrt, SE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-1001"></a>**28 an Giblean, SE 1** — *Hale takes to copying the Caol mhòr harbour slate* (Caol mhòr). With no office and no book of his own, Walter Hale begins copying the catch weighed at the Caol mhòr quay from the fishermen's slate before it is rubbed clean each evening, the first written record the harbour keeps of itself under the new homeland.
- <a id="ev-EVI-1002"></a>**31 an Cèitean, SE 1** — *The north's first harvest falls short* (Caol mhòr). Sown late on ground half the settled households have never worked, the Tuathaich shires' first harvest comes in thin, short in the straw and light in the ear, while the stores that once came over the water from an Tìr Thall do not come again.
- <a id="ev-EVI-1003"></a>**2 an t-Ògmhios, SE 1** — *The Caol mhòr catch shared by households* (Caol mhòr). As the herring run late and thin that autumn, the Caol mhòr boats stop selling their catch to whoever comes first to the quay and begin sharing it out by households instead, a change no minute records and every household in the town keeps to.
- <a id="ev-V-0002"></a>**3 an t-Ògmhios, SE 1** — *The Severance companies stood down* (Cathair dhearg). The war-companies of the last campaign against the human administration are disbanded at Cathair dhearg. Their rolls go to the council unburned, and the companies are never abolished; they live on as names on a list.
- <a id="ev-EVI-1004"></a>**26 an t-Ògmhios, SE 1** — *Fearchar mac Raghnaill's plea that his company's roll be kept* (Cathair dhearg). At the muster in Cathair dhearg's drill-yard, Captain Fearchar mac Raghnaill asks neither for pay nor for arms but that the roll of his company's names not be burned with the loose paper of the stand-down, since every name on it stood where the roll says he stood.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0002"><em>The Severance companies stood down</em>, 3 an t-Ògmhios, SE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-1005"></a>**7 an t-Iuchar, SE 1** — *The disbanded companies' rolls kept, not burned* (Cathair dhearg). On a clerk's asking, the master of the chests orders that the rolls of the stood-down war-companies be kept and boxed rather than burned with the rest of the muster's loose paper; Fearchar mac Raghnaill's roll is the first spared, though he never learns it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0002"><em>The Severance companies stood down</em>, 3 an t-Ògmhios, SE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-1006"></a>**18 an t-Iuchar, SE 1** — *Ailean's list of the chests begun* (Cathair dhearg). Carrying sixty-one companies' rolls down into the council's vault, Ailean mac Iain keeps, unasked, a written list of which roll went into which chest and in what order, the first record of its kind the council's vault has ever had.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0002"><em>The Severance companies stood down</em>, 3 an t-Ògmhios, SE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-1007"></a>**29 an t-Iuchar, SE 1** — *The war-vault sealed at Cathair dhearg* (Cathair dhearg). The council's vault of war papers is closed and bricked over at Cathair dhearg, the seal meant to stand until some later year gives cause to break it; the master of the chests signs Ailean mac Iain's list of the vault's contents before it is filed.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0002"><em>The Severance companies stood down</em>, 3 an t-Ògmhios, SE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0003"></a>**31 an t-Iuchar, SE 1** — *The boundary stones set* (Caol mhòr). Stones are set on the north roads where the Tuathaich country begins. No wall follows them. Many stand by the roadside yet, and no one has been paid to move them.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EVI-1001"><em>Hale takes to copying the Caol mhòr harbour slate</em>, 28 an Giblean, SE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-1008"></a>**2 an t-Samhain, SE 1** — *The boundary stone set on the Caol mhòr road* (Caol mhòr). The council's masons set a stone where the drove path crosses the road out of Caol mhòr, cut in Dia-thìris and left without a wall to follow it.
