The Cathair fhada store's grain reaches the sidings at Achadh shean by the coal line on the morning the season's first proper rain falls at last, and the maor, standing in the mud he had prayed six weeks for, tells the carters the grain waited on the roof to prove it was not wanted.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0156"><em>Grain by the coal line</em>, 9 am Faoilleach, SE 44</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0157"></a>**7 an Gearran, SE 44** — *Raiders at Baile ìseal* (Spùinneadairean-mara). Raiders land near Baile ìseal on the far east coast and burn the salt-sheds of Àth bheag. The kingdom's patrol boats come two days later and find the sheds cold.
- <a id="ev-EVI-5515"></a>**30 an Cèitean, SE 44** — *The salt-sheds of Àth bheag rebuilt* (Àth bheag). The burned salt-sheds of Àth bheag are raised again within the year, the Crown paying a third of the cost as it once paid a third of Cuan dhearg's relief, and the salt trade limps through the interval on what the barrels spared from the fire can carry.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0157"><em>Raiders at Baile ìseal</em>, 7 an Gearran, SE 44</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-5516"></a>**17 an t-Ògmhios, SE 44** — *The patrol captain's report on the two days* (Àth bheag). Called to answer before the shire's maor, the patrol's captain writes a report naming the distance, the wind and the hour the alarm reached his harbour; the Board judges it honest, and the households of Àth bheag, hearing it read at the market cross, judge it an accounting that answers every question but the one that matters.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0157"><em>Raiders at Baile ìseal</em>, 7 an Gearran, SE 44</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0158"></a>**12 an t-Samhain, SE 44** — *Murchadh mac Coinnich's log* (Taigh-solais Baile ìseal). Murchadh mac Coinnich, keeper of Taigh-solais Baile ìseal, begins to enter in the lighthouse log every unlit ship he sees, with her heading and the hour. His logs, kept most of his life, are the fullest record of the eastern raiders in the library.
- <a id="ev-EVI-5517"></a>**14 an t-Samhain, SE 44** — *The Board's inspector calls the Baile ìseal log the emptiest on the round* (Taigh-solais Baile ìseal). The Lighthouse Board's own inspector, checking oil against entries at Taigh-solais Baile ìseal, tells Murchadh mac Coinnich that his log is the tidiest on the eastern round and the emptiest, a remark Murchadh takes for a compliment until he comes, within the year, to hear it differently.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0158"><em>Murchadh mac Coinnich's log</em>, 12 an t-Samhain, SE 44</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-5518"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, SE 44** — *Murchadh buys a second book at his own coin* (Taigh-solais Baile ìseal). Murchadh mac Coinnich buys, from a Muileann leathan binder a carter brings up the coast, a book of his own beside the Board's, in which he means to set down what the Board's own log has no line for: every ship that crosses under his light showing no lamp.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0158"><em>Murchadh mac Coinnich's log</em>, 12 an t-Samhain, SE 44</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0159"></a>**9 am Faoilleach, SE 45** — *The pirates' names* (Àth bheag). The raiders fly no flag, and Murchadh mac Coinnich's log names their ships as the fishermen of Àth bheag name them. From his log the names pass into the royal record.
- <a id="ev-EVI-5519"></a>**24 an t-Ògmhios, SE 45** — *The salt-carrier names the raiders' hulls* (Àth bheag). An old salt-carrier at the Àth bheag quay gives Murchadh mac Coinnich the coast's own names for two dark hulls that have crossed under his light unlit, An Ròn Dubh for her low black run and An Fhaoileag for a habit of standing off by day and closing only with the dark.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0159"><em>The pirates' names</em>, 9 am Faoilleach, SE 45</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-5520"></a>**23 an t-Sultain, SE 45** — *Murchadh's book copied fair for the royal chronicle* (Muileann chaol). A Library clerk carries Murchadh mac Coinnich's private log south, and Tormod Pinn draws the names An Ròn Dubh and An Fhaoileag into the royal record from it, crediting no better source than a keeper's own ledger and the salt-carriers of a coast the patrol once answered two days late.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0159"><em>The pirates' names</em>, 9 am Faoilleach, SE 45</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0160"></a>**11 an Dùbhlachd, SE 45** — *The Còmhrag at its height* (Còmhrag Ceann leathan). The Còmhrag draws its greatest crowd yet to Ceann leathan, and the fair-wardens build timber stands along three sides of the field. The champion is Ealasaid nic Coinnich of Àth ghlas, the first woman to win it. She does not fight again.
- <a id="ev-EVI-5521"></a>**30 an Dùbhlachd, SE 45** — *Ealasaid nic Coinnich declines to defend the year's honour* (Àth ghlas). Asked by the fair-wardens whether she will defend the champion's honour the following year, Ealasaid nic Coinnich tells them a thing won once stays won whether or not she stands the field a second year, and returns to her family's trade at Àth ghlas.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0160"><em>The Còmhrag at its height</em>, 11 an Dùbhlachd, SE 45</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-5522"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, SE 45** — *Murchadh's first full year of the unlit ships* (Taigh-solais Baile ìseal). By the second an Dùbhlachd of his own keeping, Murchadh mac Coinnich's private book holds above thirty crossings, most nameless still, ruled by a straight-edge and set on the shelf beside the Board's own log as the truer account of what sails the eastern water dark.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0158"><em>Murchadh mac Coinnich's log</em>, 12 an t-Samhain, SE 44</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0159"><em>The pirates' names</em>, 9 am Faoilleach, SE 45</a>.</span>

## The Years SE 46 – 50

- <a id="ev-V-0161"></a>**14 an Dàmhair, SE 46** — *The Hawk river port of Cnoc bheag* (Cnoc bheag). Cnoc bheag, greatest town of the Hawk country, passes Cathair mhòr in its numbers. Its river quays take the grain of the north-central country, and its Hawk house is the richest of any order outside the capital.
- <a id="ev-V-0162"></a>**12 an t-Samhain, SE 46** — *Scoiltean nan Draoidhean revived*. The druid schools of Flidais, silent since the humans ruled, open again. Their first question, why the vein answers some and not others, presses hard once more, for the vein itself is failing.
- <a id="ev-V-0163"></a>**11 an Dùbhlachd, SE 46** — *Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain's lectures* (Coille Naomh Muileann chiar). The first teacher of the revived school is Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain. She lectures in the sacred wood of Flidais near Muileann chiar in the east, where the druids last met under the humans, and opens with the school's oldest question, plainly put: why the vein answers some hands and not others.
- <a id="ev-EVI-5523"></a>**28 an Dùbhlachd, SE 46** — *The old druid houses mended before the teaching* (Muileann chiar). Before a single lecture is given, villagers near Muileann chiar mend the doors and sills of the long-shut druid house with green timber and their own hands, asking no wage beyond a bench kept for them once the teaching begins.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0162"><em>Scoiltean nan Draoidhean revived</em>, 12 an t-Samhain, SE 46</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-5524"></a>**29 an Dùbhlachd, SE 46** — *An old cutter's son questions Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain* (Muileann chiar). After her first lecture in the sacred wood, an old man whose father kept the Holy Age strike-books asks Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain whether she means to answer her own question before she finishes teaching it. She tells him plainly that she does not.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0163"><em>Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain's lectures</em>, 11 an Dùbhlachd, SE 46</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0164"></a>**9 an t-Ògmhios, SE 47** — *The druid schools in Siorrachd Baile gharbh* (Baile gharbh). The houses of the druid schools in Siorrachd Baile gharbh in the north-east, silent since the humans' time, open again at Baile gharbh and Àth fhada. Their teachers walk to the sacred wood to hear Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain, and walk back.
- <a id="ev-V-0165"></a>**5 an Dùbhlachd, SE 47** — *The school at Caol shean* (Caol shean). The druid school takes a house at Caol shean, one of the great druid towns of the east, and teaches there in the wet months, when the wood is too sodden for lectures. Its students copy the census note on the coal-touched and dispute it openly.
- <a id="ev-V-0166"></a>**13 an Dùbhlachd, SE 47** — *The Hawk given a place* (Cnoc bheag). A council of the Rite at Seann Skell offers the Hawk houses of Cnoc bheag a place under the high custodian with their own order of worship. The Hawk houses take the place and keep their order. After this the quarrel is quieter. It does not end.
- <a id="ev-EVI-5525"></a>**20 an Dùbhlachd, SE 47** — *The Baile gharbh teachers' first walk south* (Baile gharbh). Teachers of the reopened druid houses in Siorrachd Baile gharbh walk the better part of a week to hear Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain teach in the sacred wood before daring to open the question in their own halls, and do not miss a winter's walk after.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0164"><em>The druid schools in Siorrachd Baile gharbh</em>, 9 an t-Ògmhios, SE 47</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-5526"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, SE 47** — *The census line argued by lamplight at Caol shean* (Caol shean). In the wet-house at Caol shean a miller's son newly come to the school asks why the census line for the coal-touched should be a matter no one may question, when the vein itself is questioned daily under the same roof; the argument runs past the hour the hearth is banked.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0165"><em>The school at Caol shean</em>, 5 an Dùbhlachd, SE 47</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-5527"></a>**22 an Dùbhlachd, SE 47** — *The Muileann dhearg hall given back to the school* (Muileann dhearg). The Guild of Hewers' captains give the school the hall at Muileann dhearg, shut since a gallery there closed three years before, on the one condition that nothing taught in it name a living captain or gallery; the school keeps to it gladly.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0165"><em>The school at Caol shean</em>, 5 an Dùbhlachd, SE 47</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-5528"></a>**23 an Dùbhlachd, SE 47** — *The Hawk's terms read a seventh time* (Seann Skell). At a council of the Rite at Seann Skell on the southern coast, the high custodian's clerks read the Hawk houses of Cnoc bheag the same settlement offered six times before; this time no witness raises the old objection, and the terms stand.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0166"><em>The Hawk given a place</em>, 13 an Dùbhlachd, SE 47</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0167"></a>**7 an Gearran, SE 48** — *The north-eastern harbours* (Caol chrom). Caol chrom and Caol gharbh on the north-east coast join their harbour dues to pay for a breakwater across the strait between them. It is eight years in the building and is the longest on the island yet.
- <a id="ev-V-0168"></a>**23 an Giblean, SE 48** — *Daniel Frayne's copying school* (Muileann leathan). At Muileann leathan in the north Daniel Frayne, a clerk of the Moot, teaches young Tuathaich to copy and bind books, since the guilds of that craft in the south will not take them. The bindings of Muileann leathan are found afterwards in Dia-thìrich libraries without their makers' names.
- <a id="ev-V-0169"></a>**22 an Cèitean, SE 48** — *The Abhainn uaine ferries* (Cidhe Beag). The boat-landing at Cidhe Beag on the Abhainn uaine is licensed as a ferry, to carry passengers and small freight down the river toward the coast. The first to hold the licence is an old boatman who had worked the landing without one for forty years.
- <a id="ev-EVI-5529"></a>**23 an Lùnastal, SE 48** — *Daniel Frayne opens his bindery at Muileann leathan* (Muileann leathan). Daniel Frayne builds a press from a mended cider-press and teaches young Tuathaich hands to fold, sew and board a book, a craft the southern guilds have never let a Tuathaich learn under their own mark; he asks no guild's leave to teach it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0168"><em>Daniel Frayne's copying school</em>, 23 an Giblean, SE 48</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-5530"></a>**1 an t-Sultain, SE 48** — *Frayne's first bindings sold south without his name* (Muileann leathan). The bindery's first plain-calf volumes, carrying no maker's name, are carried south with the wool carts and sold to Dia-thìreach households who praise the binding's neatness to Frayne's own face, none of them knowing whose pupils' hands had actually sewn the spine they hold.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0168"><em>Daniel Frayne's copying school</em>, 23 an Giblean, SE 48</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-5531"></a>**10 an t-Sultain, SE 48** — *The first stone of the Caol chrom breakwater* (Caol chrom). Caol chrom and its neighbour across the strait lay the first stone of a shared breakwater, the longest yet built on the island, meant to close a strait that has drowned more boats in a hard winter than either shire's harbour dues could bear alone.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0167"><em>The north-eastern harbours</em>, 7 an Gearran, SE 48</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-5532"></a>**19 an t-Sultain, SE 48** — *The old boatman's licence at Cidhe Beag* (Baile thais). The boatman who has rowed the crossing at Cidhe Beag on the Abhainn uaine for forty years without leave asked or given is granted a licence at last by the shire's maor, more for the shire's own records than for any change in how he rows or reckons his fare.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0169"><em>The Abhainn uaine ferries</em>, 22 an Cèitean, SE 48</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-5533"></a>**20 an Dàmhair, SE 48** — *Tormod Pinn marks the two Dùn thais west and east* (Dùn thais). Finding the Crown's returns beginning to run its two towns of one name together, Tormod Pinn rules a fresh line across the royal record marking Dùn thais in the west against Dùn thais in the east, and sends word to both shires' clerks to take more care.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0166"><em>The Hawk given a place</em>, 13 an Dùbhlachd, SE 47</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0170"></a>**24 am Faoilleach, SE 49** — *Loch chrom* (Loch chrom). The fishermen of Loch chrom, the only great lake of the island, are licensed to net its trout, which was kept for the Crown's table. Each year the Crown's table is served first.
- <a id="ev-V-0171"></a>**22 an Gearran, SE 49** — *The pillar at Cnoc chiar* (Colbh Cnoc chiar). Students of the druid schools try to read the pillar near Cnoc chiar by setting it beside the obelisk at Cnoc bheag and the column at Cnoc ghorm. They find signs in common and no meaning. Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain writes that the Old Ones were here and said so, and that none living can hear it.
- <a id="ev-EVI-5534"></a>**27 an Cèitean, SE 49** — *Three slates carried to Caol shean* (Cnoc chiar). Three of Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain's students ride from the sacred wood to copy the pillar near Cnoc chiar, the obelisk over Cnoc bheag's quays and the column at Cnoc ghorm onto separate slates, and carry them back through the rain to lay side by side.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0171"><em>The pillar at Cnoc chiar</em>, 22 an Gearran, SE 49</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-5535"></a>**16 an t-Iuchar, SE 49** — *A mark in common on three stones* (Caol shean). Comparing the three copied slates by lamplight, the students of Caol shean find a mark like a bent reed and a straight double stroke cut on all three stones and nowhere else known to them, and no meaning in either that any among them can bring out.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0171"><em>The pillar at Cnoc chiar</em>, 22 an Gearran, SE 49</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-5536"></a>**24 an t-Samhain, SE 49** — *Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain writes the Old Ones' sentence* (Caol shean). Reading the three slates laid together at Caol shean, Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain writes that the Old Ones were here and said so, and that none living can hear what they said; her students copy the sentence into every school's minute-book after her.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0171"><em>The pillar at Cnoc chiar</em>, 22 an Gearran, SE 49</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0172"></a>**23 am Màrt, SE 50** — *Flood at Inis chrom* (Inis chrom). A storm tide floods the lower town of Inis chrom on the south-west coast and drowns the net-lofts and the rope-walk. The town builds both again on piles, and so they stand now.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6000"></a>**26 am Màrt, SE 50** — *Inis chrom's lofts rebuilt on piles* (Inis chrom). After the storm tide drowns its net-lofts and rope-walk, Inis chrom does not ask the Crown for its rebuilding. Its own carpenters raise both a second time on driven piles a fathom above the old floor, timber floated down the Abhainn ghorm from the woods above Àth gharbh, the work finished before the autumn herring.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0172"><em>Flood at Inis chrom</em>, 23 am Màrt, SE 50</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0173"></a>**21 an Giblean, SE 50** — *Cnoc leathan's schools* (Cnoc leathan). Cnoc leathan in the east opens a school in every one of its six parishes, paid from the shire's dues, the first shire to do so. The council asks how it paid for them and is shown the accounts.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6001"></a>**13 an Cèitean, SE 50** — *Cnoc leathan's sixth parish school* (Cnoc leathan). The last and smallest of Cnoc leathan's six new parish schools opens with eleven children on its benches and a teacher hired from Baile chiar. The council's clerk, sent to ask how the shire paid for six schools at once, is shown plain accounts and asks nothing further.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0173"><em>Cnoc leathan's schools</em>, 21 an Giblean, SE 50</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0174"></a>**20 an Cèitean, SE 50** — *Alasdair mac Ùisdein's loan* (Cathair mhòr). Alasdair mac Ùisdein, grandson of the first holder of the Sloc Mòr concession, borrows against his house's share to pay for a search for a second vein. The Mine Board lends its surveyors. The Crown lends its name.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6002"></a>**27 an Lùnastal, SE 50** — *Catrìona nic Neacail lent to the search* (Cathair mhòr). The Mine Board names eleven surveyors to Alasdair mac Ùisdein's search for a second vein. Catrìona nic Neacail, thirty-two, a chain-hand risen through the vein-towns, is one of them, and tells a senior surveyor riding out with her that she would rather walk ground and find nothing than be told years on that nobody looked.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0174"><em>Alasdair mac Ùisdein's loan</em>, 20 an Cèitean, SE 50</a>.</span>

## The Years SE 51 – 55

- <a id="ev-V-0175"></a>**13 an Giblean, SE 51** — *The druid school on the search* (Coille Naomh Muileann chiar). Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain writes to the Mine Board that the search asks the wrong question. The school has always asked why the vein answers some hands, she says, and no one has asked why there is one vein. The Board files the letter.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6003"></a>**18 an Giblean, SE 51** — *Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain's letter read a second time* (Cathair mhòr). A Board clerk sorting the year's correspondence finds Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain's letter on the search, filed unread when it was first sent, and carries it to Catrìona nic Neacail along with Mòrag nic Coinnich's. Catrìona keeps a copy of both beside her own last entry, though she judges the school's question and the Board's chain answer to different masters.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0175"><em>The druid school on the search</em>, 13 an Giblean, SE 51</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0176"></a>**21 an Giblean, SE 51** — *The search for a second vein*. The search for a second seam of the coloured coal elsewhere on the island is costly, and finds nothing. The same search had been made in the Age of Ailean, thousands of years before, and had failed in the same way; it had been forgotten.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVI-6002"><em>Catrìona nic Neacail lent to the search</em>, 27 an Lùnastal, SE 50</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6004"></a>**18 an Cèitean, SE 51** — *The first shaft above Dùn dhearg* (Dùn dhearg). The search's first shaft goes down above Dùn dhearg in stone that gives every hopeful sign, the diggers wagering small coin among themselves on the day the vein will show. It is judged barren within the fortnight, the first entry in a tally that will run to forty-one.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0176"><em>The search for a second vein</em>, 21 an Giblean, SE 51</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0177"></a>**17 an Dàmhair, SE 51** — *Forty-one dry shafts* (Dùn dhearg). The borings of the search run from the hills above Dùn dhearg to the moors south of Baile ruadh. Forty-one shafts are sunk, and none strikes the vein. Afterwards Mòrag nic Coinnich finds in a list of the Holy Age at the library the same hills named as searched and barren.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVI-6004"><em>The first shaft above Dùn dhearg</em>, 18 an Cèitean, SE 51</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6005"></a>**31 an Dàmhair, SE 51** — *The moor's own name, am Fearann Falamh* (Dùn dhearg). An old digger of Dùn dhearg tells Catrìona nic Neacail the moor's shepherds have long called the search's ground am Fearann Falamh, the empty ground, meaning only that no shepherd ever found a spring there worth the digging. The name outlasts the search's own hope of it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0177"><em>Forty-one dry shafts</em>, 17 an Dàmhair, SE 51</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6006"></a>**28 an t-Samhain, SE 51** — *The forty-first shaft struck dry* (Baile ruadh). The last shaft of the search, sunk on the moor south of Baile ruadh through the hardest weather any of the forty had asked, strikes water at a depth no vein has ever answered. Catrìona nic Neacail writes the word barren in her own field-book a forty-first time and sits a while on the spoil-heap before riding to report it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0177"><em>Forty-one dry shafts</em>, 17 an Dàmhair, SE 51</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6007"></a>**11 an Dùbhlachd, SE 51** — *Mòrag nic Coinnich finds the Holy Age roll* (Muileann chaol). Cataloguing the Library's lower room, Mòrag nic Coinnich finds a Holy Age survey naming the same hills above Dùn dhearg and moors south of Baile ruadh, searched once and found barren ages before, the surveyors' own names worn from the roll. She sends Catrìona nic Neacail word the same week the forty-first shaft is closed.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0176"><em>The search for a second vein</em>, 21 an Giblean, SE 51</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0177"><em>Forty-one dry shafts</em>, 17 an Dàmhair, SE 51</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6008"></a>**29 an Dùbhlachd, SE 51** — *The Library's copy of the old survey promised south* (Cathair mhòr). Catrìona nic Neacail copies Mòrag nic Coinnich's letter into her own field-book beside her last entry and resolves to see the Holy Age roll sent south in copy, so that any surveyor sent to the same ground again will not have to wait on a keeper's own cataloguing to learn what the last search cost.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0177"><em>Forty-one dry shafts</em>, 17 an Dàmhair, SE 51</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0178"></a>**6 an t-Ògmhios, SE 52** — *Dùn dhearg's claim* (Dùn dhearg). The town of Dùn dhearg, whose hills held a dozen of the dry shafts, claims damages from the house of Mac Ùisdein for spoiled grazing. The circuit court awards them. The house pays a third before it sells.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6009"></a>**12 an t-Ògmhios, SE 52** — *Dùn dhearg's shepherds testify at the circuit court* (Dùn dhearg). At the circuit court's hearing of Dùn dhearg's claim, two shepherds swear that grazing spoiled by the search's spoil-heaps is lost longer than any digger reckoned, one saying he lost more lambs to the search's own open ground in two years than to wolves in ten. The court finds for the town.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0178"><em>Dùn dhearg's claim</em>, 6 an t-Ògmhios, SE 52</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0179"></a>**5 an t-Iuchar, SE 52** — *The house of Mac Ùisdein sells half* (Cathair mhòr). To meet its debts the house of Mac Ùisdein sells half its share in the Sloc Mòr back to the Crown. Its stone house at Cathair mhòr is let to the Mine Board, which moves its offices there.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6010"></a>**17 an t-Iuchar, SE 52** — *The Mac Ùisdein stone house let to the Board* (Cathair mhòr). Its coin thinned by the search and Dùn dhearg's damages, the house of Mac Ùisdein lets its stone house at Cathair mhòr, kept in the family since the first holder's day, to the Mine Board, which moves its offices into it the following spring.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0179"><em>The house of Mac Ùisdein sells half</em>, 5 an t-Iuchar, SE 52</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0180"></a>**3 an Lùnastal, SE 52** — *The shafts at Baile ruadh left open* (Baile ruadh). The dry shafts of the search are left open on the moors near Baile ruadh. Sheep fall into them, and one child, before the shire fences them at its own cost. The shire's claim on the house of Mac Ùisdein for the fencing is never paid.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6011"></a>**1 an Dàmhair, SE 52** — *The child of Baile ruadh lost to an open shaft* (Baile ruadh). A child of Baile ruadh, out after a stray lamb on ground she has walked without harm a hundred times, falls into one of the search's uncovered shafts and is not found until the day after. The parish's own book holds her name and the day, and nothing more.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0180"><em>The shafts at Baile ruadh left open</em>, 3 an Lùnastal, SE 52</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6012"></a>**27 an t-Samhain, SE 52** — *Baile ruadh votes to fence the forty-one shafts* (Baile ruadh). The shire of Baile ruadh votes to fence every one of the search's forty-one shafts at its own cost rather than wait on the Crown, and enters a claim against the house of Mac Ùisdein for the fencing's cost that is never paid. The fencing goes up through the summer, post and wire round every covered mouth.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0180"><em>The shafts at Baile ruadh left open</em>, 3 an Lùnastal, SE 52</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0181"></a>**9 an Giblean, SE 53** — *The Muileann dhomhain mills* (Muileann dhomhain). The mills of Muileann dhomhain in the south-east ground grain for the vein-towns. When the vein-towns' orders fall they turn to grinding bark for the tanners. The miller-families of the town keep their mark and change their trade.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6013"></a>**11 an Giblean, SE 53** — *Muileann dhomhain's mills turn to bark* (Muileann dhomhain). With the vein-towns' grain orders thinned by scarce coin, the mills of Muileann dhomhain begin grinding bark for the coast's tanners instead of grain. The miller-families keep the mark cut into their stone before any shire held a charter to license it, and change the trade under it without asking the Board's leave.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0181"><em>The Muileann dhomhain mills</em>, 9 an Giblean, SE 53</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6014"></a>**30 an Giblean, SE 53** — *A Muileann dhomhain miller answers a Board clerk* (Muileann dhomhain). Asked by a passing clerk whether it troubles her to grind bark at a wheel her family has ground grain at for four generations, the eldest of the Muileann dhomhain millers answers that a wheel does not know what is under it, and the grain will come back once the vein-towns have coin to buy it with again.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0181"><em>The Muileann dhomhain mills</em>, 9 an Giblean, SE 53</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0182"></a>**5 an t-Iuchar, SE 53** — *The rope-makers of Seann Tarr* (Seann Tarr). The rope-makers of Seann Tarr on the north-east coast are chartered as a guild, the last guild the restored custom makes for a trade the humans had not touched. Their hemp comes from the fields about Doire uaine and Achadh naomh.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6015"></a>**9 an t-Iuchar, SE 53** — *The rope-makers of Seann Tarr chartered* (Seann Tarr). The restored custom charters the rope-walks of Seann Tarr as a guild, the last trade the humans never touched to be given a charter of its own. Its hemp is carted down from the fields about Doire uaine and Achadh naomh by roads older than the survey lines that have tried more than once to straighten them.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0182"><em>The rope-makers of Seann Tarr</em>, 5 an t-Iuchar, SE 53</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0183"></a>**1 an t-Sultain, SE 53** — *Seann Tarr's chest remembered* (Seann Tarr). By the shire's own rule the rope-makers' charter at Seann Tarr is kept in the shire's chest and not sent to Cathair dhearg. The shire keeper of Seann Tarr keeps a list of what the chest holds and sends the list alone.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6016"></a>**15 an t-Sultain, SE 53** — *Seann Tarr's chest sends only its list* (Seann Tarr). Asked to send the new rope-makers' charter south to the Board's own files, the shire keeper of Seann Tarr answers that the charter will stay in the shire's own chest, and sends a rider south with a list of what the chest holds and no more. No second rider is sent to ask again.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0183"><em>Seann Tarr's chest remembered</em>, 1 an t-Sultain, SE 53</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0184"></a>**30 an t-Sultain, SE 53** — *The Circus at Inis àrsaidh* (An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn). An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn is recorded again, pitched this time on the common near Inis àrsaidh in the west. The magistrate who licenses it enters the acts as 'various' and the fee as paid.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6017"></a>**15 an Dàmhair, SE 53** — *The circus at Inis àrsaidh licensed as 'various'* (Inis àrsaidh). An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn pitches again on the common near Inis àrsaidh. The magistrate who licenses its acts, unable to put a name to half of what he has watched, enters the whole of it in his book as various and the fee as paid, an entry the Library's copyists find hardest of the year to gloss.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0184"><em>The Circus at Inis àrsaidh</em>, 30 an t-Sultain, SE 53</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0185"></a>**11 am Màrt, SE 54** — *Ceann mhin's fish-market* (Ceann mhin). Ceann mhin, the great port south-east of the capital, opens a covered fish-market over the old strand. Fish from Seann Bhral and the eastern grounds is sold there for the capital.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6018"></a>**4 an Cèitean, SE 54** — *Ceann mhin roofs its fish-market* (Ceann mhin). Ceann mhin opens a covered market over its old strand for fish carried up from Seann Bhral and the eastern grounds, the first roof the port has raised over the trade. The strand's old traders grumble at first, and grumble less once a wet winter lets them keep a fire by the scales.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0185"><em>Ceann mhin's fish-market</em>, 11 am Màrt, SE 54</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0186"></a>**8 an Cèitean, SE 54** — *Edged tools banned from the Còmhrag* (Còmhrag Ceann leathan). A fighter is killed with a hewer's pick, and the fair-wardens of Ceann leathan ban edged tools from the Còmhrag. Staves and fists are still allowed, and so the deaths go on, fewer.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6019"></a>**17 an Cèitean, SE 54** — *Edged iron banned from the Còmhrag* (Ceann leathan). After a fighter is killed at Ceann leathan with a hewer's pick carried in under a borrowed coat, the fair-wardens ban edged iron from the ring. Staves and fists are still allowed, and the dying goes on, slower, which a warden of long standing calls the whole of what the ban was ever meant to promise.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0186"><em>Edged tools banned from the Còmhrag</em>, 8 an Cèitean, SE 54</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0187"></a>**6 an t-Ògmhios, SE 54** — *The drowned lighthouse keeper* (Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg). The keeper of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg on the south coast drowns going out to a boat aground on the reef below the light. The boat's crew are saved by his daughter, Ciorstaidh nic Artair, and she is given the keeper's warrant in his place.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6020"></a>**29 an t-Ògmhios, SE 54** — *Artair mac Mhurchaidh drowns off Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg* (Tobar dhearg). When a Doire shean fishing boat strikes the reef below the light in a hard south-west wind, keeper Artair mac Mhurchaidh, fifty-three, goes out alone with a rope and brings two of the four crew ashore, then goes back for the other two and does not return the third time, after above thirty years keeping that light.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0187"><em>The drowned lighthouse keeper</em>, 6 an t-Ògmhios, SE 54</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6021"></a>**14 an t-Sultain, SE 54** — *Ciorstaidh nic Artair brings in the last of the crew* (Tobar dhearg). Waking to find her father's boat gone, Ciorstaidh nic Artair, three-and-twenty, takes the second boat out along his own rope's line and finds the wreck, her father's rope still fast to it. She rows the last two of the Doire shean crew ashore herself, a boat built for a lighter woman than she then is.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0187"><em>The drowned lighthouse keeper</em>, 6 an t-Ògmhios, SE 54</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6022"></a>**7 an t-Samhain, SE 54** — *Artair mac Mhurchaidh buried above the light* (Tobar dhearg). Artair mac Mhurchaidh's body comes ashore three days after the wreck and is carried back to Tobar dhearg, to the ground above the light where every keeper before him lies. The parish register enters against his name the day, the manner, and the single word every drowning of that water is given: drowned.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0187"><em>The drowned lighthouse keeper</em>, 6 an t-Ògmhios, SE 54</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6023"></a>**30 an t-Samhain, SE 54** — *The Board confirms Ciorstaidh nic Artair's warrant* (Cathair dhearg). Asked by the shire's own maor whether the daughter of a keeper who died bringing in four lives with two boats and one rope may keep the light he kept, the Board at Cathair dhearg writes back within the month that she may, and enters the warrant in her name without recorded debate.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0187"><em>The drowned lighthouse keeper</em>, 6 an t-Ògmhios, SE 54</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0188"></a>**11 am Màrt, SE 55** — *Ciorstaidh nic Artair's reef mark* (Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg). Ciorstaidh nic Artair has an iron post set on the reef below Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg, painted and hung with a bell. While she keeps the light no boat goes aground there.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6024"></a>**22 am Màrt, SE 55** — *The reef post raised by subscription* (Tobar dhearg). Ciorstaidh nic Artair has an iron post sunk into the reef at low water, painted the red of danger marked and known, and hung with a bell cast at Muileann chiar. Half the cost comes from the Board's purse and half from a purse the fishing families of Doire shean and Tobar dhearg make up between them.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0188"><em>Ciorstaidh nic Artair's reef mark</em>, 11 am Màrt, SE 55</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6025"></a>**8 an Cèitean, SE 55** — *The Board's engineer approves the reef bell* (Tobar dhearg). The Board's engineer walks the reef at low water and pronounces the post sound and the casting good. Asked whether she means to add clockwork to strike the hour as well as the danger, Ciorstaidh nic Artair answers that a man wanting the hour has a tide table and two eyes, and needs neither bell nor clockwork for that.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0188"><em>Ciorstaidh nic Artair's reef mark</em>, 11 am Màrt, SE 55</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0189"></a>**13 an t-Ògmhios, SE 55** — *Mary Coyle lays down the chair* (Caol mhòr). Mary Coyle lays down the chair of the Moot at Caol mhòr. Daniel Frayne of Muileann leathan follows her, the first speaker born after the Severance.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6026"></a>**3 an t-Iuchar, SE 55** — *The reef bell first rings in fog* (Tobar dhearg). In a fog thick enough to hide the light itself, the bell on its post rings of its own weight as the sea moves it, and every boat working that stretch of coast steers home by the sound alone. No boat goes aground on the reef below Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg that year, nor in any year Ciorstaidh nic Artair keeps the light after.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0189"><em>Mary Coyle lays down the chair</em>, 13 an t-Ògmhios, SE 55</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6027"></a>**23 an Lùnastal, SE 55** — *Mary Coyle lays down the chair of the Moot* (Caol mhòr). After two-and-twenty years in the chair, Mary Coyle lays it down at Caol mhòr, speaking of the register of the western pits' dead and maimed her hand began and the coal line her petitions never once moved south of Àth leathan, and names before the Moot rises the man she asks it to choose after her.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0189"><em>Mary Coyle lays down the chair</em>, 13 an t-Ògmhios, SE 55</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6028"></a>**7 an t-Samhain, SE 55** — *Daniel Frayne chosen speaker of the Moot* (Caol mhòr). Daniel Frayne of Muileann leathan, who bound books for the north's schools when the southern guilds would not take a Tuathaich name, is chosen speaker without a voice raised against him: the first to have been born after the Severance closed, and Mary Coyle's own right hand in the chair for above ten years before it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0189"><em>Mary Coyle lays down the chair</em>, 13 an t-Ògmhios, SE 55</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0190"></a>**9 an Dùbhlachd, SE 55** — *The Fèill's northern day* (Fèill Muileann òg). The court of the fair at Muileann òg sets aside one day of the fair for goods from the northern shires. They are still sold through Dia-thìrich factors, but under the northern makers' own marks. It is the first time a Tuathaich name is written on anything sold there.

## The Years SE 56 – 60

- <a id="ev-V-0191"></a>**12 am Faoilleach, SE 56** — *The Tuathaich marks at the fair* (Baile chiar). The first northern mark sold under its own name at the fair is the cloth of the weavers of Doire ghlas, a grey twill with a white thread at the selvedge. The southern weavers of Baile chiar begin to weave a white thread into their own.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6029"></a>**24 am Faoilleach, SE 56** — *The Doire ghlas weaver's daughter sews by lantern* (Achadh mhin). At the fair's close on its first northern day, a Doire ghlas weaver's daughter left minding her mother's stall sews a second white thread into an unsold bolt after the buyers have gone. Asked why she troubles with it unwatched, she says the mark goes in whether anyone buys it or not, since a thread sewn only for show is no mark at all.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0191"><em>The Tuathaich marks at the fair</em>, 12 am Faoilleach, SE 56</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6030"></a>**26 am Faoilleach, SE 56** — *Baile chiar's weavers name their own thread pale* (Baile chiar). Rather than claim the white thread already spoken for, the weavers of Baile chiar work a grey scarcely darker than the wool into the selvedge of their own finer bolts. An old weaver tells Daniel Frayne, who asks why the south troubles to copy a northern habit, that she has woven forty years without her name on a bolt and does not mean to die without it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0191"><em>The Tuathaich marks at the fair</em>, 12 am Faoilleach, SE 56</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0192"></a>**11 am Màrt, SE 56** — *The Depletion laid bare*. The quiet note of the survey in SE 26 is now an open trouble. The last unworked stretches of the vein are found, and they are smaller than any wish to own.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6031"></a>**4 an t-Iuchar, SE 56** — *Catrìona nic Neacail begins the one sheet* (Cathair mhòr). Catrìona nic Neacail, a Board surveyor sixteen years standing, begins drawing every stretch of the true vein still unopened onto a single leaf, working outward through the Board's own scattered rolls a shire at a time and riding to settle every ground the rolls disagree on.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0192"><em>The Depletion laid bare</em>, 11 am Màrt, SE 56</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0193"></a>**14 an Dùbhlachd, SE 56** — *Catrìona nic Neacail's map* (Achadh dhomhain). Catrìona nic Neacail, surveyor-general of the Mine Board, publishes the map of the vein's last unworked stretches. It fits on one sheet. Within the year she gives up her post and goes to teach at the druid school at Caol shean.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6032"></a>**15 an Dùbhlachd, SE 56** — *A concession-holder asks the sheet a plain question* (Cathair mhòr). A concession-holder of four generations' standing stands before the finished sheet the better part of an hour, then asks Catrìona nic Neacail plainly whether the red marked over his own family's ground means ten years or thirty, having daughters to settle and no wish to be told later that the Board had always known and never troubled to colour it in.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0192"><em>The Depletion laid bare</em>, 11 am Màrt, SE 56</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0193"><em>Catrìona nic Neacail's map</em>, 14 an Dùbhlachd, SE 56</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6033"></a>**28 an Dùbhlachd, SE 56** — *Catrìona nic Neacail named surveyor-general* (Cathair mhòr). The Board names Catrìona nic Neacail surveyor-general, an office left empty three years for want of anyone troubling to ask what it was for, until her one-sheet map of the vein's last unworked stretches made plain that somebody ought to answer for the whole of what it showed. She is the youngest to hold it in living memory.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0193"><em>Catrìona nic Neacail's map</em>, 14 an Dùbhlachd, SE 56</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0194"></a>**9 an Giblean, SE 57** — *Iain Mapa's survey found* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Among the Board's files Catrìona nic Neacail finds Iain Mapa's survey of thirty years before, which shows the same thinning she has just measured. She sends a copy to the library, with a note of when the Board received it.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6034"></a>**19 an Giblean, SE 57** — *Two surveys read side by side* (Cathair mhòr). Catrìona nic Neacail sits late at the Board's own table beneath her own sheet, reading her map and Iain Mapa's thirty-year-old survey side by side by lamplight, the same failing ground marked out in the same terms three decades apart, and cannot say which survey troubles her more, the one that found the truth or the one believed too late to matter.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0194"><em>Iain Mapa's survey found</em>, 9 an Giblean, SE 57</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6035"></a>**28 an Giblean, SE 57** — *Catrìona nic Neacail's visit to Muileann chiar* (Muileann chiar). Catrìona nic Neacail rides east to Muileann chiar and sits with Iain mac Ruairidh, three-and-sixty and failing, in what proves his last spring. He shows her his own copy of his old survey with the Board's receipt still pinned to it, and asks whether the school at Caol shean still keeps its old question about the vein.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0194"><em>Iain Mapa's survey found</em>, 9 an Giblean, SE 57</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0195"></a>**8 an Cèitean, SE 57** — *Iain Mapa dies* (Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid). Iain mac Ruairidh, called Iain Mapa, dies at Muileann chiar, where the Board sent him. His own copy of his survey is found among his papers with the Board's receipt pinned to it.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVI-6035"><em>Catrìona nic Neacail's visit to Muileann chiar</em>, 28 an Giblean, SE 57</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6036"></a>**17 an Cèitean, SE 57** — *Iain Mapa buried by the silver guild* (Muileann chiar). The silver guild of Muileann chiar, which had paid Iain mac Ruairidh's small pension ten years, buries him with an ounce of its own refined silver laid beside him, its master saying over him that he had gone into more of the mountain's dark than any three men living and had never once come up lying about what he found there.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0195"><em>Iain Mapa dies</em>, 8 an Cèitean, SE 57</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6037"></a>**5 an t-Ògmhios, SE 57** — *Mòr nic Dhòmhnaill sends her husband's papers south* (Muileann chiar). Going through her husband's papers, Mòr nic Dhòmhnaill finds the folded survey with the Board's old receipt still pinned to it and sends the whole of it to the Library at Muileann chaol, writing only that he had asked more than once it not be lost a second time, and that she knew no safer place to send it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0195"><em>Iain Mapa dies</em>, 8 an Cèitean, SE 57</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0196"></a>**6 an t-Ògmhios, SE 57** — *Muileann dhearg empties* (Muileann dhearg). In a few years Muileann dhearg loses a third of its households to the ports. Its druid hall is shut, and its bell sold to the school at Caol shean, where it rings for lectures still.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6038"></a>**8 an t-Ògmhios, SE 57** — *Muileann dhearg's maor counts the empty houses* (Muileann dhearg). Muileann dhearg's maor keeps a count of houses left empty as families leave for the ports and the southern yards, a tally kept at first from ordinary habit and then from something nearer alarm, running within three years to above sixty within the shire's own walls.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0196"><em>Muileann dhearg empties</em>, 6 an t-Ògmhios, SE 57</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6039"></a>**17 an t-Ògmhios, SE 57** — *The Fèidh hall's last teacher locks its door* (Muileann dhearg). The last teacher of Muileann dhearg's Fèidh hall, given back to the druid school not ten years before, locks its door herself for want of a congregation left to keep it and carries the key to the maor's own house rather than leave it with no one.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0196"><em>Muileann dhearg empties</em>, 6 an t-Ògmhios, SE 57</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0197"></a>**5 an t-Iuchar, SE 57** — *Ceann leathan's coal quays idle* (Ceann leathan). Coal-ships wait at Ceann leathan for cargoes that come in half-loads. The harbour dues fall by half, and the fair-wardens raise the gate-price of the Còmhrag to make it up.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6040"></a>**26 an t-Iuchar, SE 57** — *Ruairidh the cellar boy* (Cathair mhòr). A clerk's boy of twelve who has fetched bundles in the Board's own cellar at Cathair mhòr for three years tells Catrìona nic Neacail she is the first to ask him to read a label aloud rather than simply hand a bundle across. He helps her keep the tally of the week's search among the old presses.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0194"><em>Iain Mapa's survey found</em>, 9 an Giblean, SE 57</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6041"></a>**21 an Lùnastal, SE 57** — *Catrìona nic Neacail resigns the surveyor-general's office* (Cathair mhòr). Within the year of finding Iain Mapa's old survey, Catrìona nic Neacail resigns as surveyor-general, the Board's own minute recording it in four flat lines, and asks a place teaching at the druid school at Caol shean, judging the mountain's own answers now the only lesson in her trade worth the passing on.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0193"><em>Catrìona nic Neacail's map</em>, 14 an Dùbhlachd, SE 56</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6042"></a>**11 an Dàmhair, SE 57** — *Ceann leathan raises the Còmhrag's gate-price* (Ceann leathan). With the harbour dues at Ceann leathan fallen by half as coal-ships wait for cargoes that come in half loaded, the fair-wardens, whose town lives as much off the coal trade as off the yearly melee, raise the gate-price of the Còmhrag to make up what the quay no longer earns.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0197"><em>Ceann leathan's coal quays idle</em>, 5 an t-Iuchar, SE 57</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6043"></a>**1 an Dùbhlachd, SE 57** — *The Muileann dhearg bell rings Catrìona's first lecture* (Caol shean). Catrìona nic Neacail gives her first lecture at Caol shean in the same wood where Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain once first put the old question to her students, and the bell taken down from Muileann dhearg's shut hall, hung now in the school's own tower, is rung for the first time to call the school in.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0196"><em>Muileann dhearg empties</em>, 6 an t-Ògmhios, SE 57</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0198"></a>**30 an t-Sultain, SE 58** — *Baile Mòr dhomhain's market* (Baile Mòr dhomhain). As the trade of the coal-towns falls away, Baile Mòr dhomhain in the northern hills becomes the market for the wool and hides of the hill country. For two years together its market day draws more carts than the fair at Muileann òg.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6500"></a>**2 an Dàmhair, SE 58** — *Daniel Frayne notes the gaps at Muileann òg* (Fèill Muileann òg). A wool-buyer at the Moot's own table tells Daniel Frayne that the fair at Muileann òg now stands with gaps between its tents where none stood before, the fair's own wardens filling them each year with a wider aisle rather than own that the crowd has thinned.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0198"><em>Baile Mòr dhomhain's market</em>, 30 an t-Sultain, SE 58</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0199"></a>**29 an Dàmhair, SE 58** — *Mairead crowned* (Cathair dhearg). Eòghan's reign ends in the decade that the Depletion becomes known to all. Mairead inherits a kingdom whose founding wealth is plainly failing, for the first time since the restoration.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6501"></a>**13 an t-Samhain, SE 58** — *The old die broken at Cathair dhearg* (Cathair dhearg). With Mairead crowned, the die that struck Eòghan's own likeness on the realm-coin is broken at Cathair dhearg by the mint's custom, the old coin kept good until the new is struck in number enough to answer for it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0199"><em>Mairead crowned</em>, 29 an Dàmhair, SE 58</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0200"></a>**23 an t-Samhain, SE 58** — *The Hewers bind no apprentices* (Achadh dhomhain). For the first time since its charter the Guild of Hewers binds no new apprentices. Its masters vote to keep the rolls open to the sons and daughters of members only.
- <a id="ev-V-0201"></a>**19 an Giblean, SE 59** — *Muileann shean's school of hewers* (Muileann shean). Muileann shean in the north opens a school for the sons and daughters of hewers who will not be bound, and teaches them to read, reckon and survey. Most of its first pupils go to the ports.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6502"></a>**20 an Giblean, SE 59** — *Daniel Frayne binds primers for Muileann shean* (Muileann leathan). Asked for primers by Muileann shean's own maor, Daniel Frayne binds forty copies of a reading-book at his own bench at Muileann leathan and sends them north on the first cart with room, the forms unchanged since he first set the type twenty years before.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0201"><em>Muileann shean's school of hewers</em>, 19 an Giblean, SE 59</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6503"></a>**25 an Giblean, SE 59** — *Muileann shean's benches pass thirty* (Muileann shean). The school Muileann shean opened for hewers' children the Guild will not bind grows within the year from eleven pupils to above thirty, though three of the first eleven have already gone south to hire themselves out as chain-hands in the ports.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0201"><em>Muileann shean's school of hewers</em>, 19 an Giblean, SE 59</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0202"></a>**27 an Giblean, SE 59** — *The Doire ghlas mills* (Doire ghlas). Wool mills are built at Doire ghlas with the Moot's money, the first works in the north that owe nothing to the vein. The Rail Board refuses their cloth, until a ruling of the circuit court at Seann Bhral compels it to carry any goods that pay the rate.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6504"></a>**7 an Cèitean, SE 59** — *The first bolt off the Doire ghlas looms* (Doire ghlas). The wool mills raised at Doire ghlas with the Moot's own coin turn their first bolt, a grey twill with a white thread at the selvedge, and the overseer writes to Caol mhòr that it is better cloth than the south's own factors reckoned a northern loom could turn out.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0202"><em>The Doire ghlas mills</em>, 27 an Giblean, SE 59</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6505"></a>**7 an Lùnastal, SE 59** — *The Rail Board refuses the first wagon* (Muileann leathan). The Rail Board's factors at Muileann leathan refuse to carry the Doire ghlas mill's first wagon-load south to Muileann òg, giving no reason beyond the Board's own long custom of judging for itself what the line will carry.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0202"><em>The Doire ghlas mills</em>, 27 an Giblean, SE 59</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6506"></a>**23 an t-Sultain, SE 59** — *The Moot brings its suit to Seann Bhral* (Seann Bhral). Daniel Frayne rides west to the circuit court at Seann Bhral with the mill's ledgers and the Board's letter of refusal, asking Ruairidh mac Phàdraig to rule whether a carrier chartered by the Crown may refuse one people's cargo and take another's.
- <a id="ev-V-0203"></a>**31 an Dàmhair, SE 59** — *The Seann Bhral ruling* (Seann Bhral). Ruairidh mac Phàdraig, circuit justice at Seann Bhral, rules that the Rail Board is a carrier of the Crown and must carry for any who pay. It is the first ruling the Moot wins in a Dia-thìreach court. The Board appeals, and the council lets the appeal lapse.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVI-6506"><em>The Moot brings its suit to Seann Bhral</em>, 23 an t-Sultain, SE 59</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0204"></a>**30 an t-Iuchar, SE 60** — *The Crown's share of the Sloc Mòr* (Achadh dhomhain). The Crown buys the last working shafts of the house of Mac Ùisdein at the Sloc Mòr and leaves the house its share in the spoil and the quarry. Thenceforth the Board works the vein in the Crown's name alone.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6507"></a>**20 an Lùnastal, SE 60** — *Word of Catrìona nic Neacail's going* (Achadh dhomhain). A Board clerk's notice of the Mac Ùisdein sale reaches Caol mhòr with a passing word that the surveyor who drew the search's last sheet has resigned her post to teach at Caol shean, a name Daniel Frayne knows only at second hand.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0204"><em>The Crown's share of the Sloc Mòr</em>, 30 an t-Iuchar, SE 60</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0205"></a>**28 an Lùnastal, SE 60** — *The copper at Àth fhiadhaich* (Àth fhiadhaich). Copper is found in the hills behind Àth fhiadhaich in the eastern hills. The Board opens a working with men laid off from the Sloc Mòr. It pays wages. It is not the vein, and the town's Seann Spioradan house gives it no blessing.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6508"></a>**10 an Dàmhair, SE 60** — *The first Doire ghlas bale rides the coal line* (Muileann leathan). A year after the ruling, the Rail Board's own factor at Muileann leathan weighs the first Doire ghlas bale onto the wagon without comment, the same weight given any cargo that pays the rate, and Daniel Frayne rides down to see it loaded.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0203"><em>The Seann Bhral ruling</em>, 31 an Dàmhair, SE 59</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0202"><em>The Doire ghlas mills</em>, 27 an Giblean, SE 59</a>.</span>

## The Years SE 61 – 65

- <a id="ev-V-0206"></a>**2 an t-Ògmhios, SE 61** — *Àth fhiadhaich's copper-town* (Àth fhiadhaich). The copper workings at Àth fhiadhaich draw miners from the failing vein-towns. The town builds a new street for them and names it for the Sloc Mòr, and the Seann Spioradan house there speaks against the name.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6509"></a>**29 an t-Ògmhios, SE 61** — *The street named for the Sloc Mòr* (Àth fhiadhaich). Miners settled on Àth fhiadhaich's new street carry small lumps of coal from the Sloc Mòr's own upper galleries among their goods, keeping them for the plain fact of the carrying rather than for any use, while the Old Spirits' keeper tells the council a street named for another town's mountain risks forgetting the ground it stands on.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0206"><em>Àth fhiadhaich's copper-town</em>, 2 an t-Ògmhios, SE 61</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0207"></a>**1 an t-Iuchar, SE 61** — *Dubhan begins his experiments*. Dubhan makes his first attempts to draw a fuel to stand in the coal's place from the waste of the mines. They fail, and little is set down of them.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6510"></a>**9 an t-Iuchar, SE 61** — *Dubhan's first working set down*. Tormod Pinn enters a single sentence in the day-book on a report from the north, that a young man there has made trials at drawing a fuel from the waste of the mines and that they have come to nothing; he writes no more of it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0207"><em>Dubhan begins his experiments</em>, 1 an t-Iuchar, SE 61</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0208"></a>**13 an t-Iuchar, SE 61** — *The Sloc Mòr's pumps* (Achadh dhomhain). The lowest galleries of the Sloc Mòr are let flood, for the pumps cost more to run than the coal beneath is worth. The Board's minute calls it a pause.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6511"></a>**26 an Lùnastal, SE 61** — *The last pump drawn out* (Achadh dhomhain). Tormod Pinn rides to Achadh dhomhain and finds the Sloc Mòr's lowest galleries eleven fathoms under water, the pumps cold on the Board's own order; the overseer there has kept the order's own slip folded in his coat since the turn of the season, as though he expected someday to need to prove it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0208"><em>The Sloc Mòr's pumps</em>, 13 an t-Iuchar, SE 61</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6512"></a>**29 an Dùbhlachd, SE 61** — *The first pump goes down the coal line* (Achadh dhomhain). The first of the Sloc Mòr's three great pumps goes south under canvas on a flat wagon from a siding above Achadh dhomhain, bound for the new dry dock at Seann Bhral in the south; Tormod Pinn watches it pass and sets down that a pump goes where the water is and cares no more for the ground it served than a bolt of cloth.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0208"><em>The Sloc Mòr's pumps</em>, 13 an t-Iuchar, SE 61</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0209"></a>**17 an Giblean, SE 62** — *The pumps sold* (Seann Bhral). The Board sells the great pumps of the Sloc Mòr to the harbour at Seann Bhral in the south, where they drain the new dry dock. In the next generation they are the only engines of the vein still at work.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVI-6512"><em>The first pump goes down the coal line</em>, 29 an Dùbhlachd, SE 61</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6513"></a>**26 an Giblean, SE 62** — *The third pump follows and six men are found other work* (Achadh dhomhain). The overseer at Achadh dhomhain writes that the third and last pump has gone to Seann Bhral in the south after the second, and that the six men who tended the three between them have been found work on the galleries still above water, a thing the Board's own notice calls no loss to any household.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0209"><em>The pumps sold</em>, 17 an Giblean, SE 62</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6514"></a>**5 an Cèitean, SE 62** — *The maor of Baile dhomhain writes of the crossing* (Imrich nam Pantar). A shire's maor writes to the Board of stock lost along Imrich nam Pantar near Baile dhomhain, a loss too large for wolves and weather; the Board's clerk, having no ledger fit to hold it, sends the letter on to the Library.
- <a id="ev-V-0210"></a>**16 an Cèitean, SE 62** — *The panthers cross the south-west* (Imrich nam Pantar). A great host of panthers crosses the south-west near Baile dhomhain. For a month the herders lose stock. Tormod Pinn writes it down as a thing named in the lists of the Holy Age and not seen in living memory.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVI-6514"><em>The maor of Baile dhomhain writes of the crossing</em>, 5 an Cèitean, SE 62</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6515"></a>**16 an t-Ògmhios, SE 62** — *The old list of An Aois Naomh opened again* (Imrich nam Pantar). Tormod Pinn sets the maor's letter beside a Library list from the days of An Aois Naomh naming the years the panthers crossed before, an interval longer than any living herder's working life, and writes the crossing's entry longer than any other that year.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0210"><em>The panthers cross the south-west</em>, 16 an Cèitean, SE 62</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6516"></a>**27 an t-Ògmhios, SE 62** — *The herders keep the crossing days* (Imrich nam Pantar). The herders of the south-west drive their flocks off the old road beforehand and keep the crossing as a season of watching, losing fewer beasts in the end than the first week's count had feared, though more than an ordinary year costs them.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0210"><em>The panthers cross the south-west</em>, 16 an Cèitean, SE 62</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0211"></a>**13 an t-Iuchar, SE 62** — *The hides of Baile ghorm* (Baile ghorm). Tanners at Baile ghorm on the south-west coast buy the hides of the panthers the herders kill, and their trade outlasts the crossing by ten years. Saddles of panther-skin from Baile ghorm are sold at the fair at Muileann òg under the town's mark.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6517"></a>**18 an t-Iuchar, SE 62** — *Baile ghorm's tanners buy the hides* (Baile ghorm). Buyers from Baile ghorm ride up into the hills within the fortnight to take the hides of panthers the herders' dogs and spears have brought down, paying a price the herders judge fair for a skin they have no other use for.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0211"><em>The hides of Baile ghorm</em>, 13 an t-Iuchar, SE 62</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6518"></a>**23 an t-Iuchar, SE 62** — *Panther-skins first at the fair* (Baile ghorm). The fair at Muileann òg sees, for the first time in any chronicler's memory, saddles and belts of panther-hide sold under the Baile ghorm mark, the southern buyers taken by surprise enough that the mark's own price doubles twice before the fair's ten days are out.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0211"><em>The hides of Baile ghorm</em>, 13 an t-Iuchar, SE 62</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0212"></a>**11 an Lùnastal, SE 62** — *Imrich nam Pantar in the chronicle* (Imrich nam Pantar). Tormod Pinn's entry on the panthers is the longest in his book for that year. He sets it beside the list of the Holy Age, and notes that the old list names the year after the panthers as a hungry one.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVI-6515"><em>The old list of An Aois Naomh opened again</em>, 16 an t-Ògmhios, SE 62</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6519"></a>**25 an t-Samhain, SE 62** — *Muileann mhin halves its lamp-making* (Muileann mhin). The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin halve their making for want of coal to fire their forges properly, the coal reaching the town thinner and dearer each season the Sloc Mòr's galleries give less of it up.
- <a id="ev-V-0213"></a>**10 an Gearran, SE 63** — *The coal-lamp shortage* (Muileann mhin). The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin halve their making, for want of coal to burn in the lamps they make. Shaft-lamps are lent from pit to pit, and the guild's minute-book records who lent to whom.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVI-6519"><em>Muileann mhin halves its lamp-making</em>, 25 an t-Samhain, SE 62</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6520"></a>**14 an Gearran, SE 63** — *The Guild's lending-book*. The Guild of Hewers keeps a plain minute-book at its hall for shaft-lamps lent from pit to pit, and Tormod Pinn, sending for a copy of its first year, finds more names entered against debts than against repayments, a dry column that tells the vein's own thinning more plainly than any Board letter.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0213"><em>The coal-lamp shortage</em>, 10 an Gearran, SE 63</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6521"></a>**16 an Gearran, SE 63** — *The yard families stop the trains* (Muileann chrom). The yard families at Muileann chrom stop the coal trains for three days over a cut wage, putting forward as their spokesman Dòmhnall Ruadh mac Ailein, one-and-forty, whose father laid the yard's first rail; a Tuathaich minister there keeps his own book of the families' grievances.
- <a id="ev-V-0214"></a>**18 an Gearran, SE 63** — *Unrest at Muileann chrom* (Muileann chrom). The yard families at Muileann chrom stop the coal trains for three days over cut wages. On the fourth day the Rail Board settles; on the fifth it dismisses eleven men.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVI-6521"><em>The yard families stop the trains</em>, 16 an Gearran, SE 63</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6522"></a>**8 an Cèitean, SE 63** — *The Board settles and dismisses eleven* (Muileann chrom). The Board's factor restores the old wage on the third day and the trains run again on the fourth; on the fifth the Board's own notice names eleven men dismissed for their part in the stopping, Dòmhnall Ruadh mac Ailein among them, the settlement and the dismissal arriving from the same hand in the same week.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0214"><em>Unrest at Muileann chrom</em>, 18 an Gearran, SE 63</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6523"></a>**29 an Cèitean, SE 63** — *Cathair fhada's granaries want a second storey* (Cathair fhada). The maor of Cathair fhada writes to Muileann chaol that the year's harvest has proved thicker than any since before the search for a second vein was spoken of, granaries built for a lean year now wanting a second storey to hold it.
- <a id="ev-V-0215"></a>**7 an Lùnastal, SE 63** — *The hungry year that was not* (Cathair fhada). The harvest after the panthers' crossing is good across the south. Tormod Pinn records it and strikes through his own note of the year before.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVI-6523"><em>Cathair fhada's granaries want a second storey</em>, 29 an Cèitean, SE 63</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6524"></a>**14 an t-Sultain, SE 63** — *Tormod strikes through his own note*. Tormod Pinn draws a line through his own entry naming a hungry year to follow the panthers' crossing, leaving the words legible beneath it and writing that the harvest proved thick rather than thin, since a chronicle owes its readers its wrong guesses as plainly as its right ones.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0215"><em>The hungry year that was not</em>, 7 an Lùnastal, SE 63</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0212"><em>Imrich nam Pantar in the chronicle</em>, 11 an Lùnastal, SE 62</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0216"></a>**8 an Dàmhair, SE 64** — *The third census after the Severance*. For the first time in the Rìoghachd the numbers of the people are published openly. It is a small token of openness, and nothing else is changed.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6525"></a>**13 an Dàmhair, SE 64** — *Census clerks come north for a count* (Caol mhòr). Two census clerks ride to Caol mhòr, the first southern office to ask the Moot for its own count of its own people rather than take none, the shire's own maor having told the surveyor-general no clerk had yet gone north.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0216"><em>The third census after the Severance</em>, 8 an Dàmhair, SE 64</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6526"></a>**14 an Dàmhair, SE 64** — *The Moot's figures given to the census clerks* (Caol mhòr). Daniel Frayne gives the visiting clerks the Moot's own count, kept every third year since the room was opened, along with the school and vigil registers, and offers to swear to the figures before a justice if the council should ask it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0216"><em>The third census after the Severance</em>, 8 an Dàmhair, SE 64</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6527"></a>**23 an Dàmhair, SE 64** — *Frayne's private book notes the asking* (Caol mhòr). Daniel Frayne writes the day's giving into his own private book, judging it worth the keeping that the Moot had, for once, been asked for its figures rather than merely tolerated in the giving of them.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0216"><em>The third census after the Severance</em>, 8 an Dàmhair, SE 64</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0217"></a>**6 an t-Samhain, SE 64** — *The figures read at the Moot* (Caol mhòr). The published figures are read aloud at the Moot at Caol mhòr. They show the northern towns at about half the Dia-thìrich measure in every column the clerks chose to take. The Moot's minute says only: 'Now written.'
- <a id="ev-EVI-6528"></a>**2 am Faoilleach, SE 65** — *A young clerk asks what the two words mean* (Caol mhòr). Walking out of the room into the frost, a junior clerk asks Daniel Frayne whether the minute's two words oblige the south to answer for what it has printed; Frayne tells him a fact set down is not a promise kept, but cannot be unprinted either.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0217"><em>The figures read at the Moot</em>, 6 an t-Samhain, SE 64</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0218"></a>**8 am Faoilleach, SE 65** — *The count of the touched* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). The published census, like the first, has a line for the coal-touched. It gives a number and nothing more. Tormod Pinn copies it into the chronicle without comment, as Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill did for the first.
- <a id="ev-V-0219"></a>**28 an Lùnastal, SE 65** — *The census in the Stone's shires* (Doire shean). In the shires of Òrd na Cloiche in the south-west the houses of the Stone publish for the first time their own count of their people beside the kingdom's. The two agree within a hundred.
- <a id="ev-V-0220"></a>**26 an t-Sultain, SE 65** — *Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Tormod Pinn dies at his desk at Muileann chaol. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh becomes royal chronicler. She is the first to add at the foot of each year a note of what the record could not learn.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6529"></a>**31 an Dàmhair, SE 65** — *Tormod Pinn buried at Muileann chaol* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Tormod Pinn, chronicler nine-and-seventy years old, is buried in the small ground behind the Library among every keeper and chronicler the house has kept since Ailean Leabhar; Mòrag nic Coinnich speaks over him that he kept the list honest and struck nothing from it unearned.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0220"><em>Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh</em>, 26 an t-Sultain, SE 65</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6530"></a>**20 an t-Samhain, SE 65** — *Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's first morning at the desk* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh, chosen from the Library's own senior clerks, tells the house on her first morning as chronicler that she means to change nothing of the desk's hours, only its habit of silence where the record itself keeps none.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0220"><em>Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh</em>, 26 an t-Sultain, SE 65</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0221"></a>**10 an Dùbhlachd, SE 65** — *The Hawk houses' registers* (Ros gheal). The Hawk houses of Siorrachd Ros gheal send their birth-rolls to the library for the first time, on condition that they be filed under Òrd an t-Seabhaig and not under Òrd Bhrìde. Mòrag nic Coinnich agrees.

## The Years SE 66 – 70

- <a id="ev-V-0222"></a>**6 an Gearran, SE 66** — *Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's first foot-note* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's first note of what the record could not learn concerns the northern shires: the census clerks were told the figures and did not count them, and the figures they were told were the Moot's.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVI-6526"><em>The Moot's figures given to the census clerks</em>, 14 an Dàmhair, SE 64</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6531"></a>**8 an Gearran, SE 66** — *Beathag's note sent north to Frayne* (Caol mhòr). A Library clerk sends Daniel Frayne a copy of Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's first foot-note, naming the census clerks' reliance on the Moot's own figures; Frayne keeps it in his private book beside the day he gave them, judging her a chronicler the north may trust.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0222"><em>Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's first foot-note</em>, 6 an Gearran, SE 66</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0223"></a>**7 am Màrt, SE 66** — *The record-chests called in* (Seann Tarr). Mòrag nic Coinnich's clerks go to thirty shire towns to bring their record-chests to Muileann chaol. At Seann Tarr the shire's keeper burns the chest sooner than send it, saying that the shire's record belongs in the shire. He is fined; the chest is lost.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6532"></a>**8 am Màrt, SE 66** — *Mòrag nic Coinnich calls the shire chests in* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Mòrag nic Coinnich sends her own clerks along the roll to bring every shire's record-chest to Muileann chaol, judging a history kept in forty scattered chests no history at all but forty separate hopes of one day being read together.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0223"><em>The record-chests called in</em>, 7 am Màrt, SE 66</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6533"></a>**27 am Màrt, SE 66** — *The Seann Tarr keeper meets the clerks at the gate* (Seann Tarr). The shire keeper who burned his own chest at Seann Tarr meets Mòrag's clerks at the gate the next morning, his coat still smelling of the smoke, and repeats to them plainly that the shire's record belongs in the shire.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0223"><em>The record-chests called in</em>, 7 am Màrt, SE 66</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0224"></a>**5 an Giblean, SE 66** — *Cathair naomh sends its rolls* (Cathair naomh). The keeper of Cathair naomh in the north sends her shire's rolls to the library in two carts, with the town's own chronicle, kept by one family for four generations. Mòrag nic Coinnich enters it as the best-kept shire record received.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6534"></a>**19 an t-Iuchar, SE 66** — *Cathair naomh's chronicle carried south by its own keeper* (Cathair naomh). The eldest daughter of the family that has kept Cathair naomh's town chronicle four generations rides the two carts south herself and unpacks them at Mòrag nic Coinnich's own table, the chronicle begun by her great-grandmother on the back of an unused rent-roll.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0224"><em>Cathair naomh sends its rolls</em>, 5 an Giblean, SE 66</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0225"></a>**29 am Faoilleach, SE 67** — *The Seann Toll chest* (Seann Toll). Seann Toll in the north sends its chest willingly and asks for a copy of all that is in it. Mòrag nic Coinnich's clerks make the copy, and the shire's copy is the pattern for every copy the library has made since.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6535"></a>**26 an Gearran, SE 67** — *Seann Toll's copy becomes the pattern* (Seann Toll). The full transcription Mòrag's clerks make for Seann Toll, bound and set beside the original before either leaves the shire's hall, becomes the pattern every later shire's copy is cut to.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0225"><em>The Seann Toll chest</em>, 29 am Faoilleach, SE 67</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0226"></a>**26 an t-Iuchar, SE 67** — *The library enlarged* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Leabharlann Muileann chaol doubles its holdings and takes several lesser archives of the provinces into one record. From this time the history of Dia-thìr is kept in one place and not in many.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6536"></a>**28 an t-Iuchar, SE 67** — *Frayne puts the calling-in to the Moot's own room* (Caol mhòr). Reading the notice of the calling-in, Daniel Frayne calls the room at Caol mhòr together and asks it plainly whether the Moot should offer its own books south now that the council has shown a wish to gather every shire's record.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0226"><em>The library enlarged</em>, 26 an t-Iuchar, SE 67</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0227"></a>**3 an Lùnastal, SE 67** — *No northern chest* (Caol mhòr). No Tuathaich record is called in. The Moot's minute-books, the schools' registers, the churches' registers and the vigil-books of Baile chrom stay in the north, in private keeping, as they always have.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EVI-6536"><em>Frayne puts the calling-in to the Moot's own room</em>, 28 an t-Iuchar, SE 67</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6537"></a>**19 an Lùnastal, SE 67** — *The Moot's minute declining to send its books* (Caol mhòr). After an evening's debate, the room's minute at Caol mhòr records no vote by count and no reason beyond two words its clerk sets down at the close of the sitting: *kept north.* No cart of the Moot's own books goes south that year or after.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0227"><em>No northern chest</em>, 3 an Lùnastal, SE 67</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0228"></a>**2 an t-Ògmhios, SE 68** — *The library's new wing* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). The enlarged library is housed in a new wing at Muileann chaol, built of the grey stone of the Sloc Mòr's spoil. The chests of the provinces fill three floors. The fourth is left empty for what was not sent.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6538"></a>**15 an t-Ògmhios, SE 68** — *The new wing's three floors and the empty fourth* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh walks the new wing at Muileann chaol before its chests are carried up, and finds three floors built to hold the provinces' returns, town chronicles and vigil-books, and a fourth, raised to the same measure, left empty for a record that has not been sent.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0228"><em>The library's new wing</em>, 2 an t-Ògmhios, SE 68</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6539"></a>**18 an t-Ògmhios, SE 68** — *Beathag's first foot-note on the empty floor* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh keeps Tormod Pinn's list at the front of the year's book unchanged and adds, beneath it, her own foot-note that the fourth floor stands ready and that no cart has come, judging the sentence plainer than any she could set beside it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0228"><em>The library's new wing</em>, 2 an t-Ògmhios, SE 68</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6540"></a>**29 an t-Ògmhios, SE 68** — *The tally of the calling-in read floor by floor* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Reading the whole tally of the calling-in set out floor by floor for the first time, Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh finds that every shire the council's roll accounted for sent something, willing or not, and that the one record never asked for is the one never received.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0228"><em>The library's new wing</em>, 2 an t-Ògmhios, SE 68</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0229"></a>**30 an t-Iuchar, SE 68** — *The branch line to Àth leathan closed* (Àth leathan). The Rail Board shuts the branch line to Àth leathan, pleading the falling yield of the western pits. The Tuathaich pits go on working, and their coal goes by cart to the western ports and by boat from there.
