- <a id="ev-EVI-6541"></a>**2 an Lùnastal, SE 68** — *The Àth leathan branch shut for falling yield* (Àth leathan). The Mine Board withdraws its overseers from Àth leathan along with the branch line, its own wages no longer answering for the western pits' falling yield, and the pits pass, without any charter forbidding it, into the keeping of the hewers who work them.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0229"><em>The branch line to Àth leathan closed</em>, 30 an t-Iuchar, SE 68</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0230"></a>**28 an Lùnastal, SE 68** — *The Moot's hewers take the pits* (Àth leathan). The Board's overseers are withdrawn from Àth leathan, and the Tuathaich hewers there go on working the pits under their own pit captains, paying the Crown's fifth under the Leòid ruling. The Board takes the payments and enters them as arrears.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6542"></a>**9 an Dùbhlachd, SE 68** — *The Àth leathan hewers pay the fifth and are entered in arrears* (Àth leathan). The pit captains the Àth leathan hewers choose from their own number weigh every cart and set by the Crown's fifth under the Leòid ruling, sending word south each season; the Board takes the payments when a carrier brings them and enters them in its own books as arrears.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0230"><em>The Moot's hewers take the pits</em>, 28 an Lùnastal, SE 68</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6543"></a>**18 an Gearran, SE 69** — *The first Àth leathan coal carted to Seann Bhral* (Àth leathan). The pit captains at Àth leathan send the season's first coal south by cart rather than by rail, three days slower on the road but loaded and sent on the hewers' own choosing, down to the coal factors' yards at Seann Bhral in the west.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0230"><em>The Moot's hewers take the pits</em>, 28 an Lùnastal, SE 68</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0231"></a>**7 am Màrt, SE 69** — *Cnoc thais in the western hills* (Cnoc thais). At Cnoc thais in the western hills the Tuathaich pits pass to their hewers when the Board's overseers leave, and the father of the pit captain Tom Varley is chosen to keep the accounts. Here the town's own register of the pits begins.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6544"></a>**9 am Màrt, SE 69** — *Sam Varley opens the pit's own book at Cnoc thais* (Cnoc thais). When the Board's overseer leaves Cnoc thais, Sam Varley, who has kept a private tally beside the Board's own scale for eleven years, opens a book of the pit's own accounts headed only with the day and the pit's name, the earliest page the town's register still keeps.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0231"><em>Cnoc thais in the western hills</em>, 7 am Màrt, SE 69</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6545"></a>**18 am Màrt, SE 69** — *Tom Varley runs the book's errands* (Cnoc thais). Sam Varley's small son Tom, not yet old enough for the pit, carries the figures the book wants between the scale-house and his father's table; told that a book kept honest for nobody outlasts one kept honest only for someone watching, he carries them straight all the same.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0231"><em>Cnoc thais in the western hills</em>, 7 am Màrt, SE 69</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0232"></a>**5 an Giblean, SE 69** — *The Sligeanach's great year* (An Sligeanach Fad' às). An Sligeanach Fad' às, the roadside tavern by Ceann bhàn on the southern road, is sold to a family of drovers from Achadh mhòr, who build a second hall for the drove trade. It becomes the greatest house on the old mining roads.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6546"></a>**25 an Giblean, SE 69** — *An Sligeanach Fad' às sold to a family of drovers* (An Sligeanach Fad' às). The family that kept An Sligeanach Fad' às three generations sells it to drovers new to the trade, who raise a second hall beside the first; within a few years it is the largest house on the old mining roads, grown fat on the drove trade as the coal roads empty.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0232"><em>The Sligeanach's great year</em>, 5 an Giblean, SE 69</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0233"></a>**4 an Cèitean, SE 69** — *The eastern fishing grounds fail* (Seann Dunn). For the second year together the herring do not come to the grounds off the mouth of the Abhainn chaol below Seann Dunn. The east-coast boats go north to fish the grounds off Caol mhòr, which the licence law keeps for them, and the Tuathaich boats are pushed farther out.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6547"></a>**24 an t-Samhain, SE 69** — *The herring fail a second year off Seann Dunn* (Seann Dunn). The herring do not return, a second season together, to the grounds off Seann Dunn, and the east-coast boats, finding their own waters empty, take to fishing the grounds off Caol mhòr that the licence law has long kept for the northern boats.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0233"><em>The eastern fishing grounds fail</em>, 4 an Cèitean, SE 69</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0234"></a>**30 an t-Iuchar, SE 70** — *Inis mhin's boats* (Inis mhin). Pushed from their grounds by the eastern boats, the Tuathaich boats of Inis mhin fish the deep water beyond the northern isles. Two are lost in the first year and none after, and the catch of Inis mhin passes that of Caol mhòr.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6548"></a>**5 an Lùnastal, SE 70** — *Inis mhin's boats pass Caol mhòr's own catch* (Inis mhin). Pushed from their nearer grounds by the crowding of east-coast boats, the boats of Inis mhin take the deep water beyond the northern isles; two are lost the first year and none after, and within three years the catch they bring in passes what Caol mhòr itself takes from the grounds the law still calls its own.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0234"><em>Inis mhin's boats</em>, 30 an t-Iuchar, SE 70</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0235"></a>**28 an Lùnastal, SE 70** — *Raghnall mac Mhuirich, keeper* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Mòrag nic Coinnich lays down the keepership after some thirty years. Raghnall mac Mhuirich, her deputy, becomes keeper of Leabharlann Muileann chaol.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6549"></a>**12 an t-Sultain, SE 70** — *Mòrag nic Coinnich lays down the keepership* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Mòrag nic Coinnich, two-and-seventy and thirty years and more in the chair, lays down the keepership of the Library, walking the fourth floor once more with Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh and saying only that she built the room and leaves the asking to whoever holds the chair after her.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0235"><em>Raghnall mac Mhuirich, keeper</em>, 28 an Lùnastal, SE 70</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6550"></a>**14 an t-Sultain, SE 70** — *Raghnall mac Mhuirich made keeper* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Raghnall mac Mhuirich, fifty that year, takes the chair Mòrag nic Coinnich lays down and changes nothing of the Library's hours or custom in his first year, a steadiness the clerks under him come to value in a season when little else about the kingdom's coal holds steady.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0235"><em>Raghnall mac Mhuirich, keeper</em>, 28 an Lùnastal, SE 70</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0236"></a>**26 an t-Sultain, SE 70** — *The coal price at the fair* (Fèill Muileann òg). The Board cuts its sales, and the price of coal-fuel at the fair at Muileann òg doubles. The fair's court fixes a ceiling price and cannot hold it.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6551"></a>**29 an t-Samhain, SE 70** — *The fair's ceiling set on coal and broken in every stall* (Muileann òg). When the Board cuts its sales and the price of coal-fuel at Muileann òg doubles, the fair's court sets a ceiling price by its long custom; within a season no factor sells at it, the coal not reaching the stalls at the named price, and the wardens do not cry the ceiling's breaking.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0236"><em>The coal price at the fair</em>, 26 an t-Sultain, SE 70</a>.</span>

## The Years SE 71 – 71

- <a id="ev-EVI-6552"></a>**21 am Màrt, SE 71** — *Beathag's foot-note on the capital's cold* (Leabharlann Muileann chaol). Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's foot-note for the year names what the record cannot learn: how many grates in the capital's poorer wards went unlit for want of coal, a count no census asked for and no shire kept, so that the Library holds no reckoning of its own kingdom's cold.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0236"><em>The coal price at the fair</em>, 26 an t-Sultain, SE 70</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-V-0237"></a>**26 an Cèitean, SE 71** — *Coal thieves at Cnoc fhiadhaich* (Cnoc fhiadhaich). Households of Cnoc fhiadhaich are found picking coal from the spoil-heaps to burn, and the Board posts watchmen there. The watchmen are men of the town, and see nothing.
- <a id="ev-EVI-6553"></a>**10 an t-Ògmhios, SE 71** — *The watchmen at Cnoc fhiadhaich see nothing* (Cnoc fhiadhaich). The Board posts watchmen of the town itself over the spoil-heaps at Cnoc fhiadhaich against households picking coal to burn; every winter of the posting the watchmen see nothing, though the heaps grow lower and the poorer grates burn warmer than the fair's price could otherwise buy.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0237"><em>Coal thieves at Cnoc fhiadhaich</em>, 26 an Cèitean, SE 71</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EVI-6554"></a>**17 an t-Ògmhios, SE 71** — *The capital's poorer streets burn short hours* (Cathair dhearg). In the capital's poorer wards the street lamps burn shorter hours than the council's lighting order requires, the keepers no longer able to afford in full an order written for coal at half the price it now costs; the council's own notice calls the shortening a saving.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-V-0237"><em>Coal thieves at Cnoc fhiadhaich</em>, 26 an Cèitean, SE 71</a>.</span>

# A Gazetteer of the Age

#### A

**Achadh dhomhain** (Muileann chrom). Founded 10 an t-Ògmhios, FE 272. The pit town under the Sloc Mòr, at the head of the coal line. The line was mended through to its pithead in the twelfth year, and the first train out of it had its blessing said over the coal in the first wagon, the old custodian from Muileann dhearg being unwilling to walk the footplate. A quarry was cut above it in the thirteenth year and its dressed stone went south under the Mac Ùisdein wave-mark. The Guild of Hewers was chartered in the yard before its pithead on a cold day of an t-Samhain in the thirteenth year, each Dia-thìreach hewer swearing on a lump of coal, its Tuathaich families kept at their work. The guild bound sixty apprentices in its hall after the fall at Muileann dhearg, none of them Tuathaich, and forty households left for the ports that autumn. In the sixty-first year its lowest galleries lay eleven fathoms under water and its three great pumps went south by rail to Seann Bhral's new dry dock. Known for the Sloc Mòr's pithead, the hewers' oath, and the pumps.

**Achadh gharbh** (Caol shean). Founded 13 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,597. A village on the eastern road where the walkers to the holy well of Allt an Àigh lodge on their way. In the tenth year it was raising a long hall for them, and in the eleventh the hall stood; its keeper, an old woman, wrote each walker's name and shire in a cracked-spined ledger, which held travellers from better than twenty shires that first summer and from fifty by the end of the decade, north and south and east and west of the island together on the one road. The under-clerk Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill lodged here a night with her mother, of an Old Spirits house, on their walk to the well in the tenth year, and thought of the ledger growing a name longer every year while the wall the council had talked of went undrawn. The cairn at the well itself, the keeper told them, grows a little taller every year. Known for the walkers' hall and its ledger.

**Achadh mhin** (Cnoc naomh). Founded 1 an Lùnastal, FE 738. A township a little way inland on the south coast, on fields the sea had never in living memory reached, until the Great Wave of the fourth year ran over its low ground and salted in one night what three generations had ploughed. The council moved its survivors to higher ground a mile inland before the winter closed the roads and paid for their seed from the treasury without a due asked, the first relief the restored kingdom granted anyone. The fields lay under salt for a generation. In the twenty-eighth year they bore again, and three households moved away after the wave, or their children in their place, asked for their old ground and were given it; the shire measured them back onto the same strips the humans' surveyors had cut, since those were the bounds the families still walked by memory. The chronicler entered its barley the night before word came of Brìghde's death. Known for the first relief, and the fields that bore again.

**Achadh shean** (Achadh shean). Founded 21 an Giblean, GE 3,125. A shire of the drove road where the ground failed once before in the humans' time and was given a name for it that its people never forgot, Tiormachd Achadh shean, the drought of the old field. In the forty-third year the rains of am Màrt held off into an Cèitean and the wells of the drove road went brackish and then, three of them, dry to the stone. Its maor, a careful man who kept his own tally, wrote south before the second month of the dry was out, holding that a man argues with a poor harvest but a well gone to stone argues with no one, and cut twelve new wells along the road, one of them dry from the day it was dug on a dowser's word. The council answered faster than the north had ever known it to answer: grain from the Crown store at Cathair fhada reached the town's sidings by the coal line on the morning the first proper rain fell. Known for the dry years and the grain by rail.

**Àth àrsaidh** (Àth àrsaidh). Founded 12 an t-Samhain, GE 3,458. A town an easy day's ride from Caol mhòr, seat of a northern shire. Its maor's chest was the one the northern shires filled for the first chronicle circuit in the nineteenth year, and Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill found in it the maor's returns and nothing more, not a line in a Tuathaich hand, and wrote the fact down without a further word. Eachann mac Rath practised physic here twenty years under his guild's charter. In the thirty-fourth year he took Ruth Ashby and Clara Tulloch, two women of the fishing country, to learn by watching him set bones and mix poultices through a fever season; a factor's wife let slip at a fair stall that his new girls handled a lancet as steady as he did, and the guild struck him from its rolls. He kept his surgery open all the same. Known for the Tuathaich doctors.

**Àth bheag** (Àth bheag). Founded 26 an Cèitean, GE 4,347. A salt town on the tidal flats of the east coast below Taigh-solais Baile ìseal, worked by Dia-thìreach ford-keepers, its boats crewed as often by Tuathaich hands as not. Its flats were dug for salt-pans in the thirty-second year and it was soon supplying salt up the coast. In an Gearran of the forty-fourth year flagless ships came in under cloud and burned its three salt-sheds; the patrol came two days late, and the households judged the captain's honest report an accounting that answered every question but the one that mattered. The sheds were raised again within the year, the Crown paying a third. An old salt-carrier on its quay gave Murchadh mac Coinnich the coast's names for the raiders' hulls, An Ròn Dubh and An Fhaoileag, which the royal chronicle took from the keeper's own log. Mòrag nic Coinnich was made the Library's deputy on the road home from it. Known for the salt-sheds burned, and the raiders named.

**Àth fhada** (Cnoc ghorm). Founded 18 am Màrt, LE 908. A Tuathaich village on the old road the north calls the Carters' Road, between Cnoc ghorm and the low ground short of Inis àrsaidh. When the Rail Board would not carry the north's wool in the fortieth and forty-first years, the carts went south through it five days to the fair at Muileann òg, and a widow of the village who had fed carters at her own table for two winters, her husband lost under the western pits, began to take payment and keep a lamp lit past every other house's hour; it was the first inn on the road, and two more households lit lamps within the season. Daniel Frayne lodged under her lamp and learned from her the road's northern name, and her husband was the first name entered in Clàr nan Leòn. A carter from beyond it brought Walter Hale the last grievance he settled. Its druid house opened again in the forty-seventh year with Baile gharbh's. Known for the first lamp on the Carters' Road.

**Àth fhiadhaich** (Àth fhiadhaich). Founded 13 an Dùbhlachd, GE 4,325. A town of the eastern hills by a ford where its river fishers still bless their nets, whose Seann Spioradan house keeps the oldest folk rite on the island. Copper was found in the hills behind it in the sixtieth year, and the Board opened a working within the season with men laid off from the Sloc Mòr's thinning galleries. The house gave the copper no blessing, its keeper telling the Board's factor that copper dug for a wage was copper dug like any other stone. By the second summer the town had built a street of new stone houses for the miners on the slope above the ford and named it, before the last house had a roof, for the pit they had come from, Sràid an t-Sluic; the miners kept small lumps of the Sloc Mòr's coal among their goods, and the house's keeper told the council a street named for another town's mountain risked forgetting the ground it stood on. Known for the copper, and the street of the pit.

**Àth leathan** (Seann Skell). Founded 8 am Màrt, LE 1,303. A gathering of pits and shanties in the western hills where Tuathaich hewers had worked the coal since before the kingdom drew a road to them. In the thirteenth year the Rail Board built a spur of thirteen miles to it off the western branch, because the coal was cheap to lift and the carters' road worse each winter. After the fall at Muileann dhearg the Board's new timbering rule was posted on its pit-head door and the timber ordered from Ceann mhòr, and the timber never came; the hewers went on under the old props, and Mary Coyle named the town in her letter to the Board. In the sixty-eighth year the Board withdrew its overseers and the branch together, and the pits passed to the hewers, who chose captains, weighed every cart and set by the Crown's fifth under the Leòid ruling; the Board entered the payments as arrears. From the sixty-ninth year its coal went to Seann Bhral by cart. Known for the pits the hewers kept.

#### B

**Baile chiar** (Baile chiar). Founded 1 an Gearran, FE 869. A weaving town of the south whose weavers took a guild charter in the fifteenth year: the council's clerks cut them a seal of a shuttle over a fleece and entered the grant in a calf-bound book at Cathair dhearg after a fee and a feast, and the guild barred any weaver who had not served seven years under a master. Its pipers played for coin at the first fair at Muileann òg, and its cloth came to that fair from its looms. A drought at the town went into the royal chronicle in the twenty-eighth year beside Brìghde's death. Its maor petitioned in the thirty-eighth year that Doire chaol, five miles off, had outgrown being governed at second hand, and the new shire was cut from his, the only shire cut new since the drawing; he sent its first dues south with a note wishing its maor better luck. In the fifty-fifth year its weavers began a grey thread of their own in the selvedge of their finer bolts. A teacher from the town kept the smallest of Cnoc leathan's six schools. Known for the weavers' seal, and the cutting of Doire chaol.

**Baile chrom** (Baile chrom). Founded 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,464. A scatter of grey houses above a shingle beach where the coast turns, its nets strung to dry on frames mended every spring with the fathers' twine. It kept one of the five beacons on the capes, whose keeper wrote on the first morning of the age that no ship came. Its small church in a net-store answered to the same distant bishops as the great one at Cnoc ghorm. In the ninth year the vigil-keeper Hannah Crane kept the Mystery of the Grey Night in the open on the headland below the old light, as no keeper had kept it before; the bishops called it irregular in a letter that stayed folded behind the altar-cloth. The magistrate fined her for it in the twenty-seventh year, the Moot paid the fine, and the vigil went into a lent byre. In the seventeenth year the town's light was given a Dia-thìreach keeper under a warrant bidding him report what he saw by land as well as by sea, and in the thirty-second year he reported the vigil kept silent in the tower's shadow; the council answered nothing. Known for the Grey Night on the headland, and the fifth light.

**Baile gharbh** (Baile gharbh). Founded 15 an Lùnastal, GE 2,662. The seat of a north-eastern shire whose old druid houses had stood roofless and silent since the humans first ruled there. Within half a year of Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain's first lecture in the sacred wood, in the forty-seventh year, the houses of the shire at the town and at Àth fhada opened their doors on the old question again, and their teachers walked the better part of a week south to hear her before daring to teach it in their own halls, and did not miss a winter's walk after. The youngest of them, a woman not yet twenty on her first journey south, wrote of it in the school's own minute-book. Seonaid's sentence on the three stones was copied into every school's minute-book from Muileann chiar to this town. Known for the druid houses reopened.

**Baile ghorm** (Baile ghorm). Founded 7 an t-Ògmhios, GE 622. A tanning town of the south-west coast. When the panthers crossed the hill country near Baile dhomhain by Imrich nam Pantar in the sixty-second year, its tanners heard of it before the herders had finished counting their losses and sent buyers up into the hills within the fortnight for the hides of the cats the herders' dogs and spears brought down, at a price the herders judged fair. They cured the skins through the summer, and the next year's fair at Muileann òg saw saddles and belts of panther-hide sold under the town's mark for the first time in any chronicler's memory; the price of the mark doubled twice before the fair's ten days were out. Known for panther-hide under the town's mark.

**Baile Mòr dhomhain** (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Founded 24 an t-Samhain, FE 101. A market town on the deep river in the northern hill country. As the coal-towns' trade fell away its market became the market for the wool and hides of the hills, and in the fifty-seventh and fifty-eighth years its market day drew more carts than the fair at Muileann òg, a thing no one living could remember any market doing. A wool-buyer from its hills told Daniel Frayne of it at the Moot's table, and Frayne entered it in the room's ledger under no heading that fit, since it was not Moot business and yet seemed to him to be. Known for the market that passed the fair.

**Baile Mòr fhionn** (Caol leathan). Founded 6 an t-Samhain, FE 584. A town of the south-west, seat of houses of Òrd na Cloiche, the Stone, whose Clach is the Lia Fàil and not Crom's stone. In the seventh year its houses were bidden to send witnesses to the settling of the Rite at Seann Skell; they sent none, and a letter wishing the Rite well and promising nothing further, which Dòmhnall mac Thormoid copied onto the first page of his ledger of letters. The Stone kept its own houses, its own mark cut plain over its doors, and its own dealings through the age: it lent coin against a town's dues where a town's need outran a maor's patience, and its paper stood for coin at Inis thais until the coin came. Known for the Stone standing aside.

**Baile Mòr mhòr** (Baile Mòr mhòr). Founded 13 an t-Sultain, GE 2,616. The market town of the middle country, seat of its own shire. Its courthouse burned in the last summer of the war, and when Coinneach mac Ailein, a custodian's younger son, came as its first maor in the fourth year he held his court under the market roof among the fish-scales. When a new courthouse was raised two years on he sat in it for exactly one sitting and moved back to the market hall the week after, and the two maoir who followed him did the same, until holding court under the scales became simply how justice was done in the town and no one thought to write down why. Ailean mac Iain had ridden no further north than its market before the Severance, and he rode its letters to it again when the maoir were named. Its roll of arms and its dues were entered in the fourth year with the rest of the kingdom's. Known for the court held under the market roof.

**Baile ruadh** (Baile ruadh). Founded 3 an Dàmhair, FE 971. A town of red-earth fields in the east, where the barley fails on the thin soils every few years; in the hungry year of the twelfth, families walked from it to the pit towns for wages paid in coin. The search for a second vein ended on the moor south of it in the fifty-first year, the forty-first shaft striking water at a depth no vein had ever answered. The shafts were left uncovered; sheep fell into them the first winter, and before the next summer was out a child of the town fell into one and was not found until the day after. The parish book holds her name and the day. The shire met in the same low room where it had argued its dues and voted to fence every shaft on its ground at its own cost, post and wire round every mouth, and entered a claim against the house of Mac Ùisdein for the fencing that was never paid. Known for the fenced shafts.

**Baile thais** (Muileann dhearg). Founded 5 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,086. The town where the coal road from the central mountains comes down to the Abhainn uaine above the gulf. It grew a different way from the pit towns in the twelfth year, taking in carters, inns and a ropewalk, doubling its people within a decade and being given a shire court. Its carters carried the news of the coast south; it was from a carter of the town that Iain Mapa first heard of the raiders off Cathair gheal, third-hand and late. A quarryman of the town put Calum Ruadh down twice in the first hour of the first Còmhrag, and stood over him laughing the second time. Known for the coal road's river crossing.

#### C

**Caol chrom** (Caol gharbh). Founded 13 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,275. A harbour of the north-east coast, facing Caol gharbh across a strait that had drowned more boats in a hard winter than either town's harbour dues could bear. In the forty-eighth year the two shires joined their dues to pay for a breakwater across the strait between them, and laid its first stone that spring. It was eight years in the building and is the longest yet built on the island. Known for the shared breakwater.

**Caol leathan** (Caol leathan). Founded 12 am Faoilleach, GE 1,560. A small harbour town and the seat of the greatest house of Òrd na Cloiche, a low stone hall behind the harbour with the Stone's own mark cut plain over the door and nothing of the state's arms on it. In the twenty-first year the order rebuilt the house at its own cost and raised a low tower over its western gable, and hung in it a bell cast, the priests said, from coin given by every ship that had put in at the harbour and come home again. It is not a large bell, nor heard much past the town walls, but the town needed nothing heard past them: from that year the bell rang the hours, the market opened by it, and the harbour court and the fair court both sat by it, until within a year nobody in the town reckoned the time any other way. Known for the Stone's bell that rings the hours.

**Caol mhòr** (Caol mhòr). Founded 31 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,462. The harbour town where the council's word fixing the Tuathaich homeland was read aloud on the twenty-second of am Màrt in the first year, and where Walter Hale rendered it into the humans' tongue. In the second year the households met in the long room behind the harbour and opened the Moot's book, and the Moot sat here for the rest of the age: it voted grain against the winter, petitioned for the exchange of the cried-down coin, opened lifeboat and school purses, paid Cathair gheal's fine and Hannah Crane's, and kept its own minutes, counts and registers in the north. Walter Hale sat as its first speaker for thirty-one years and was buried in sight of its house in the thirty-third year; Mary Coyle followed him, the first woman in the chair, and Daniel Frayne after her. Its fishermen lost the southern grounds to the licence law of the thirtieth year. In the sixty-seventh year the room declined to send its books south to the Library, and the clerk entered two words, kept north. Known for the Moot, and the two words kept north.

**Caol shean** (Caol shean). Founded 21 an Lùnastal, GE 4,196. A town near the stag's grove of Muileann chiar, where the druid school kept a wet-house for the months when the grove stood ankle-deep and no fire would stay lit under the bare oaks. Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain took the house after her first winter's teaching, and in it her students argued the census line for the coal-touched by lamplight past the banking of the hearth. Three of them laid on its long table in the forty-ninth year slates copied from the pillar near Cnoc chiar, the obelisk at Cnoc bheag and the column at Cnoc ghorm, and found a mark like a bent reed and a straight double stroke on all three, which none could read. Catrìona nic Neacail came to teach here in the fifty-seventh year after resigning as surveyor-general, and the bell from Muileann dhearg's shut hall, bought on that shire's vote, rang in the school's tower to call her first lecture. Known for the druid school's wet-house, and the three slates.

**Cathair dhearg** (Cathair dhearg). Founded 6 an Dàmhair, GE 18. The capital held the council of twelve from the second year of the age, seated at a table too large for the room that held it, and every warrant, ruling and refusal of the kingdom went out from it. In the first summer the disbanded companies waited in its market square to be stood down, and sixty-one company rolls were carried into the vaults under the counting-house and bricked in. Niall was crowned here in the third year, Brìghde in the twenty-second and Eòghan in the twenty-eighth, and Mairead in the fifty-eighth; the bells of Òrd Mhacha rang a day and a night for Niall's death. The mint struck the realm-coin here from the fifth year, the Rail Board kept its low grey office here, and the Mine Board sat here until the twenty-seventh year, when it went to Cathair mhòr. The guild court heard the indentures and the yards' protests in its chambers. A second census was locked in the council's keeping-room in the thirty-third year and never aired. By the end of the age the lamps of its poorer wards burned shorter hours than the council's lighting order required, for want of coal at the price the order was written for. Known for the council's table, the mint, and the crownings.

**Cathair dhomhain** (Cathair dhomhain). Founded 25 an t-Iuchar, FE 634. A harbour town of the south-west, where the custody-book of the old vein-house on the hill above the harbour was kept until the house closed it. Eilidh nic Leòid was born here and spent her whole working life in its counting-house and harbour court, copyist, recorder and at last justice in all but name. In the eighth year she was made circuit justice of the south-west and held her first assize here before she had properly left the town, measuring an orchard boundary with knotted cord. She set out from it with Murchadh Clàrc and a satchel of blank record-books, and it was here, within sound of the harbour, that she died in the sixteenth year with the gathered book of her rulings finished on the table by her bed. The fishing villages that feed its market lie along the coast road south from Seann Bhral. Known for Eilidh nic Leòid's town.

**Cathair fhada** (Cathair fhada). Founded 13 an Cèitean, GE 2,523. A town of the southern plain. In the thirty-third year the Crown's grain-store here was finished, two winters building and one summer roofing, a hall of dressed stone long enough that a loaded cart could turn inside it, great enough to feed the south a season, filled from the south's own harvests. It opened its doors first in a poor season that same year, and in the forty-third it fed the dry country about Achadh shean, its grain reaching the sidings there by the coal line on the morning of the first rain. In the sixty-third year the harvest came in so thick that the maor wrote to Muileann chaol of granaries built for a lean year wanting a second storey, and Tormod Pinn struck through his own note of a hungry year to come. Known for the Crown's grain-store.

**Cathair gheal** (Muileann àrsaidh). Founded 5 am Màrt, GE 1,378. A walled town of the north-west coast, its harbour a shallow bay below the town wall. In the second year its people loosed the humans' locked loft of nets to every boat in the harbour on a single tide. From the twelfth year ships flying no flag worked its waters; a fishing house was burned below the town and two boats taken, and the council's minute asked that the matter be watched. In the twentieth year Nell Barrow, a skipper's widow, wrote twice to the council for a boat or leave to arm its own and was answered by neither letter. On the night of 8 an Giblean three flagless hulls stood into the bay; the largest ran onto a shifted bar and was boarded and burned by seven town boats before dawn, at a cost of two dead and four hurt. The council fined the town four purses of the realm-coin for bearing arms without leave, and Walter Hale carried the Moot's share of it north; the fine was counted out at the maor's door. Known for the bay cleared, and the fine paid.

**Cathair mhòr** (Cathair mhòr). Founded 9 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,847. The mountain town of the house of Mac Ùisdein, whose family had held an overseer's post under the humans at the Sloc Mòr. Uisdean mac Ùisdein came from it to the capital in the eleventh year to take the Sloc Mòr concession, and in the twentieth year the house raised a market cross at its own cost, cut on all four faces with its name, and moved the wool and coal markets to its foot. The Mine Board moved its clerks here in the twenty-seventh year, into rooms above the wool market, and set down that its surveys should be kept in its own presses and not sent to the Library. The house built its stone hall of spoil-stone in the thirtieth year and feasted the Guild of Hewers in it. After the search for a second vein the house let the hall to the Board in the fifty-second year, and Catrìona nic Neacail hung her one sheet of the vein on its chamber wall in the fifty-sixth. Known for the house of Mac Ùisdein, and the Board's presses.

**Cathair naomh** (Seann Toll). Founded 22 an Dùbhlachd, GE 3,162. A town of the north whose chronicle has been kept by one family through four generations without a council's asking, begun by a great-grandmother on the back of an unused rent-roll. When Mòrag nic Coinnich called in the shire chests in the sixty-sixth year, the family's eldest daughter packed the town's rolls and chronicle into two carts herself and rode them south rather than trust a hired carter, and unpacked them at Mòrag's own table. Mòrag entered it as the best-kept shire record the Library received. Known for the family chronicle of four generations.

**Ceann àrsaidh** (Ceann àrsaidh). Founded 17 an t-Sultain, GE 4,328. A town on the Abhainn fhionn east of the capital, seat of custodian houses of the east. Its ship-chandlers took a guild charter in the fourteenth year and with it the sole right to fit out the Crown's patrol boats, and the yearly fitting-out became the guild's show of its charter before the shire's maor. Seumas mac Coinnich Ghlais, who sat for the eastern custodian houses at the council's table, was a man of the town, and it was he who brought a map to the council in the tenth year and proposed the border wall, and saw it die without a vote. Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill's mother lived in a village by it, and the two parted here on the eastern road after the walk to Allt an Àigh. A room over a chandler's shop here was the last of the eleven northern schools the Moot counted in the twenty-ninth year. Known for the chandlers and the patrol boats.

**Ceann leathan** (Seann Chwen). Founded 19 an t-Samhain, GE 2,061. A town of the south where the droves from Muileann fhionn came down to market and where the fair-wardens grazed the fair's horses on rising ground outside the walls. In the twenty-third year the wardens called an old custom of arms the Còmhrag, the melee, and fought it on that field, drawing men from every vein-town within two days' walk; Calum Ruadh of Muileann chrom won it, took a year's wages and the right to bear arms, and four inn-keepers who had built new houses for the crowd kept his table free. Two men died in the first and six in the thirty-sixth year, and the wardens refused the custodians' petition to end it within the hour; the circus pitched on the trampled ground a week after the six burials. The coal line reached the town the same season and its quays spread half a mile past the old gate. Ealasaid nic Coinnich of Àth ghlas won it in the forty-fifth year and did not fight again; edged iron was banned from the ring in the fifty-fourth. By the fifty-seventh year its coal quays stood half idle and the wardens raised the gate-price. Known for the Còmhrag.

**Ceann mhin** (Ceann mhin). Founded 18 an Lùnastal, FE 745. The great port south-east of the capital. In the ninth year its shire closed the old burial ground at Cnoc dhìreach to new graves, the vines having split so many stones that no clear plot could be found without turning up someone else's dead. In the fifty-fourth year it opened a covered market over its old strand for the fish that came up from Seann Bhral in the south and from the eastern grounds, the first roof the port had raised over that trade, so that the buyers of the capital could stand dry-shod while they haggled; the strand's old traders grumbled at first and less once a wet winter let them keep a fire by the scales. Known for the covered fish-market.

**Ceann mhòr** (Ceann mhòr). Founded 6 an Cèitean, FE 163. The harbour of the north-west where a fisherman with a hammer and a bad temper broke the lock of the humans' harbour store in the second year, and the town, not the man, shared out rope, canvas and salt by the same rough justice that had shared a thin catch at Caol mhòr. Its fishermen traded in the broken store for two years on their own custom, and in the third year the council granted them a market right for the north-west coast, the smallest clause on Ailean's map of the shires and the one thing on it the town had already made true. Its first maor took the old human magistrate's house, which the town went on calling by its old name. In the fifteenth year Eilidh nic Leòid held her assize here in the heat of an t-Iuchar, heard nineteen causes to their ends and found fifteen for the Crown; the Coombes and the Pettifers kept their ground on a custodian's countersign. Its timber yard took the order for Àth leathan's props in the thirty-ninth year. Known for the broken lock, and the seventeen suits.

**Cnoc bheag** (Cnoc bheag). Founded 5 an t-Sultain, GE 3,908. A river town of the north-central country, heart of the Hawk's houses, whose altars answered to no custodian above them. In the sixth year the houses round it wrote to Seann Skell that the Rite's written order was handsome and not needed. The shire's arms carried a plain white billet from the fourth year for no reason any clerk could give, until the thirty-sixth, when a delegation of the Hawk houses asked for a hawk, and the maor broke the old die and pressed a white hawk among twelve crescents. An obelisk of unread script stands near it, which Una copied stroke by stroke in the thirty-second year and the council fenced against the cattle; its marks were laid beside those of the pillar at Cnoc chiar and the column at Cnoc ghorm by the students of Caol shean. By the forty-sixth year its river quays took in more grain in a season than the granaries of Cathair mhòr showed for a year. Known for the Hawk's country, the hawk on the seal, and the obelisk.

**Cnoc chaol** (Seann Vell). Founded 23 am Faoilleach, LE 167. A small town low on its shingle on the south coast, which gave its name to the Great Wave of the fourth year, Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol. The water broke it in a single night before running on to Cuan dhearg and Achadh mhin. It was built again the following spring on the slope behind its old ground, high enough that the sea would have to climb a hill to trouble it a second time, and the old site was left as the water left it; the townsfolk call it an Tràigh Bhàthte, the drowned strand, and do not build there. Its shepherds and those of Ros gharbh had summered their flocks time out of mind on the low island of Eilean mhin offshore, over which the wave also passed. Its houses were raised again faster than Ros gharbh's boats, a house wanting only hands and a boat wanting a builder. Known for the wave's name, and the drowned strand.

**Cnoc fhiadhaich** (Muileann chrom). Founded 17 am Màrt, LE 488. A town below the spoil-heaps of old coal galleries, never levelled, on the mountain where the council would not end the working of the vein by day and night. When coal-fuel doubled in price at the fair in the seventieth year, households of the town took to picking coal off the heaps to burn in their own grates, and in the seventy-first year the Board posted watchmen over the heaps. The watchmen were men of the town, and every night of the posting they saw nothing, though the heaps grew lower and the poorer grates burned warmer than the fair's price could have bought. Known for the watchmen who saw nothing.

**Cnoc ghorm** (Cnoc ghorm). Founded 15 an Dàmhair, GE 1,362. A market town of the northern coast, nearer the shire's seat than Baile chrom and twelve miles from it. In the ninth year the north raised here the largest church it had built since the crossing closed, its stone hauled from a quarry two shires south on carts the Moot paid for by subscription, and in its tower hung the bell of the old chapel at Ros bheag, crated in a barn since the first spring; it rang first on a market morning and carried to the shore road. The next year the church opened a school for its priests, with a master from Seann Skell. A thin blessing of the boats was kept here each spring, and after Seann Bhral refused the north in the twenty-fifth year Mary Coyle made it the full Fleadh na Mara: more than fifty boats came on the second Sunday of an Gearran in the twenty-sixth year, blessed with heather dipped in harbour water, and David Hale counted them. The Carters' Road runs through it south to Àth fhada. Known for the church of the Ros bheag bell, and Fleadh na Mara.

**Cnoc leathan** (Cnoc leathan). Founded 11 am Màrt, FE 172. A shire of the east. On the twenty-first day of an Giblean in the fiftieth year it opened a school in every one of its six parishes, the first shire on the island to do so entire and out of its own dues rather than the Moot's purse or a guild's charity. The last and smallest opened with eleven children and a teacher hired from Baile chiar, who had never taught so few; within two years the benches held twenty and she stayed past her term. The council sent a clerk to ask how a shire so far from its notice had found the coin, and was shown plain accounts in a plain hand, the dues that would have gone to a road never built turned to six rooms and six teachers, and asked nothing further. Known for the six parish schools.

**Cnoc thais** (Cnoc thais). Founded 19 an t-Sultain, GE 4,328. A pit town of the western hills, where Tuathaich hewers worked under the Board's overseers and scales. When the overseers left in the sixty-eighth year with the closing of the Àth leathan branch, the pits passed to the hewers, and they chose to keep the accounts Sam Varley, four-and-fifty, who had kept a private tally beside the Board's scale for eleven years. He opened a book of the pit's own accounts headed only with the day and the pit's name, the earliest page of the town's register of its pits, and his small son Tom carried the figures between the scale-house and his table. The carters who took Àth leathan's first coal to Seann Bhral by road passed through it. Known for the register of the pits.

**Cuan bheag** (Caol mhòr). Founded 10 am Màrt, SE 17. A Tuathaich fishing harbour of the north coast. On the second night of an t-Sultain in the nineteenth year a westerly drowned eleven men of seven of its boats, Thomas Coyle of Caol mhòr among them; the sea gave back two broken hulls and a stranger's oar. The town had no lifeboat. Mary Coyle wrote the eleven names on one sheet for the mason in the order the boats went out, and the Moot opened a subscription the same week; the lifeboat, white-painted with cork along her gunwales, came up the coast from Cuan shean in an Cèitean of the twentieth year and was put into the water off the town's jetty by that autumn's five widows. Its boats sailed with Mary Coyle to Seann Bhral in the twenty-fifth year, and its fishermen walked to Walter Hale's burial. Known for the eleven drowned, and the lifeboat.

**Cuan dhearg** (Seann Vell). Founded 31 am Faoilleach, FE 1,384. The larger harbour of the south coast struck by Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol in the fourth year. The wave broke its mole and carried its boats inland, so that when Ailean mac Iain came with the relief party the boats of the town lay among the barley and the harbour was gone. Its dead were carried up onto the rise behind the town, above the old harbour line, and buried through that first fortnight in ground the sea had not reached. The Crown paid a third of the relief, the first time it had paid for anyone's loss. The town righted what boats it could and went back to fishing before the winter closed in. A generation later, in the twenty-seventh year, the harbour was opened again behind a new mole of dressed stone, and of the hulls the wave had cast into the fields one was found sound, caulked, and warped into the new harbour ahead of every boat built for it; the harbour-master keeps it moored at the quay-head as a relic. Known for the boats in the barley, and the boat kept for a relic.

**Cuan ruadh** (Cuan ruadh). Founded 1 an t-Sultain, GE 2,387. A town far up the eastern coast, past even Seann Dunn, which had none of the five lighthouses the humans left the kingdom to keep. It had a mole built in the humans' time for a fleet larger than the one that used it. After two boats were lost on the harbour rocks in a winter fog, its council voted in the twenty-third year to burn a light on the end of the mole with coal bought out of the town's own purse. It asked the Lighthouse Board to take the light on, and the Board wrote back that its charter named five lights and no more, and that the town's light, being no charge on the Crown, might continue as it was; the chronicler entered the refusal in four lines. The light burned on the town's coal. When the coal line shut in the thirty-fourth year the town lived on its stored coal. Known for the light on the mole.

**Cuan shean** (Cuan shean). Founded 18 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,755. The harbour of the west coast where the first humans came ashore generations before; a stone laid into the quay near the harbour-master's steps, worn nearly smooth, is still touched by children for luck. Households were walked north out of it under guard in the first year. An Sireadh sailed from it on the eleventh of an t-Ògmhios in the third year under Aonghas mac Mhurchaidh, a Cuan shean man, to seek the crossing north-about. Seumas Crùbach kept his shipwright's yard here, building frame first, and took Harry Marlow of Doire mhin on as a bound apprentice; when the guild charter reached the coast in the fourteenth year he tore the boy's indenture and kept him as a free hand at half wage, and other yards took up the rate. Harry measured a derelict human hull on the hard in his own book. The Cuan bheag lifeboat was built in its yard. Known for the first landing-stone, and Harry Marlow's torn indenture.

#### D

**Doire ghlas** (Doire ghlas). Founded 26 an Giblean, GE 2,470. An inland town of the northern moss, on rush pasture the settled households were given because the better land nearer the coast was claimed. It buried more of its own in the first hungry winter than any town of the north, and its dead were named on a sheet in the church porch before the Moot had a book to name them in. Meal was carried to it from Caol mhòr on carts that sank to the hubs. In the fifteenth year Agnes Pike opened her school in a widow's byre here, with eleven scholars and no primer but the psalms and the Moot's minutes, and moved it to the church porch each summer; Daniel Frayne walked in to it daily from Muileann leathan. Its weavers wove An Snàthainn Geal, the white thread, into their cloth, and sold under their own mark from the fifty-fifth year. The wool mills raised here with the Moot's coin turned their first bolt in the fifty-ninth year, and the Rail Board's refusal to carry it brought the suit at Seann Bhral. Known for Agnes Pike's byre school and the white thread.

**Doire mhin** (Caol mhòr). Founded 3 an Giblean, FE 2,743. A small inland town of the north, where the Pike family had ground grain since before the Severance and the smith Joseph Marlow kept his forge. When the humans' coin was cried down in the fifth year, half the town brought its dead coin to Marlow, and he melted it and cast it into ploughshares and sold them back at the cost of the charcoal; the first furrow of that spring was cut with one of them by the last day of am Màrt. Walter Hale walked ten miles through snow to see it. The Tuathaich sang of Marlow after, that he turned the king's silence into iron and the iron into bread. The Moot took seed oats from the town's mill on credit in the first hungry year. Marlow's son Harry went from the forge to a shipwright's yard at Cuan shean, and sent his wage home each year; Agnes Pike, who opened the byre school at Doire ghlas, was a miller's daughter of the town. Known for Joseph Marlow's ploughshares.

**Doire shean** (Doire shean). Founded 14 an Lùnastal, GE 695. A harbour town of the south-west on the road between Cathair dhomhain and Seann Bhral, where Eilidh nic Leòid's circuit passed. A grave-list from the town was among the first papers the chronicler copied fair, and a wedding there went into the chronicle beside Brìghde's death. In the thirtieth year it built its own harbour, the first raised anywhere in the kingdom since the Severance without a coin of the Crown's in it, the house of the Stone lending against the town's dues and the masons building the mole to the Stone's measure; the house took its first quarter's dues off the quay before the last course was dry. A fishing boat of the town struck the reef below Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg in the fifty-fourth year, and the keeper Artair mac Mhurchaidh drowned bringing in her crew; the town's fishing families paid half the reef bell that followed. Known for the harbour built on the Stone's loan.

**Dùn chrom** (Dùn chrom). Founded 7 am Faoilleach, GE 2,801. A walled town of some size on the road east out of Cathair dhearg, its citadel old and its market square older. Oighrig nic Mhathain kept the weighing-scales of its market nine years and caught short weight better-paid men missed, until in the twenty-first year the council's eastern factor made her toll-mistress of the new fair at Muileann òg; she left her scales to a niece she had trained two summers. The carpenters of the town roofed the fair's court, a plain frame open on three sides, a fortnight before the first fair. In am Faoilleach of the twenty-second year the last stretch of the fair's road was metalled past the town, and the toll taken at its gate built a new wall along its southern side by an Lùnastal, which the townsfolk called the fair's wall and the carters called by their own name for the gate. Known for Oighrig's scales, and the fair's wall.

**Dùn dhearg** (Dùn dhearg). Founded 9 an Gearran, GE 4,274. A town of the hill and moor country where the search for a second vein began. In the fifty-first year the first of Alasdair mac Ùisdein's shafts went down on the rise above it in stone that gave every hopeful sign, and was judged barren within the fortnight; a dozen of the forty-one dry shafts were sunk on its hills. An old digger of the town, who had cut peat there as a boy, told Catrìona nic Neacail that the shepherds called the ground am Fearann Falamh, the empty ground. In the fifty-second year the town brought its claim for spoiled grazing to the circuit court, two shepherds swearing that the search cost them more lambs in two years than wolves had in ten, and the court found for the town; the house of Mac Ùisdein let its stone hall to meet the damages. A Holy Age survey in the Library had named the same hills searched and barren long before. Known for the first of the forty-one shafts.

**Dùn thais** (Dùn thais). Founded 28 am Màrt, GE 2,473. The Dùn thais of the east, seat of its own shire and its own dues; the other town of the name lies on the west coast. In the thirty-eighth year it raised at the shire's own charge a long timbered covered market for the hill farms that had traded in its square uncovered since the town was walled, and its first trading was held under a roof that smelled more of new-cut wood than of the grain it sheltered. A clerk at Cathair dhearg filed its petition and the western town's against the one name, and the royal record confused the two for ten years until Tormod Pinn ruled a line through the record marking them west and east. Known for the covered market.

**Dùn thais** (Ros bheag). Founded 23 an Gearran, FE 2,142. The Dùn thais of the west coast, within a morning's ride of Ros bheag; there are two towns of the name, and the record keeps them apart as west and east. Its fishermen settled salvage among themselves by custom until a wrecked raider's hulk driven ashore proved too rich a prize for custom to divide, and in the thirty-seventh year the town was granted a court of the sea of its own to judge salvage and wreck along its shore. At its first sitting, held on the strand, the court awarded the hulk whole to the crews who drove it aground. For ten years the royal record confused its court with the eastern town's market, until Tormod Pinn marked the two west and east in the forty-eighth year. Known for the court of the sea.

#### I

**Inis àrsaidh** (Cnoc ghorm). Founded 28 an t-Sultain, FE 242. A town of the north-western coast whose harbour officers sailed with the last ships and took their keys with them. In the second year its people opened the locked harbour store after Ceann mhòr and Cathair gheal did, and it is told that three women of the town drew up a reckoning of what was taken and by whom, so that the sharing could be answered for if anyone ever came to ask; no maor came. The old Carters' Road runs down to it from Cnoc ghorm and Àth fhada, and the wool trains of the forty-first year crossed the flooded low ground short of it in a cold rain, the carts finding their own way round the water. A household at a crossing near it kept one of the three lamps that lit the road by night. In the fifty-third year An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn pitched on the common near the town, and its magistrate licensed the acts as various, the fee paid. Known for the three women's reckoning, and the circus licensed as various.

**Inis bhàn** (Inis bhàn). Founded 16 an Giblean, GE 3,916. A town on the Abhainn ìseal in the north-central country, a river port of storehouses. In the twenty-ninth year fire took its warehouse quarter, three storehouses and a dozen dwellings above them, and burned two days before the town beat it back street by street with buckets and wet sacking and a chain of hands to the river; no one died. The town's Hawk house, which had never taken in households outside those sworn to it, sheltered every family the fire put out of a roof, sworn or not, through the spring cold. The council bought the town a bell from the founders' yard at Cathair dhearg to stand where the old warehouse bell burned, and rang it once on the quay before it was hung; by the town's own telling it is heard further up and down the river than any bell in the kingdom. Known for the fire and the loudest bell.

**Inis bheag** (Inis bheag). Founded 25 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,435. A parish of the island's north-east, whose Seann Spioradan house keeps a parish roll that names its households back before the coming of the humans, older than any book the south's forty chests gave up to the first chronicle circuit. In the nineteenth year the old keeper heard the circuit clerks' warrant once, without asking it twice, and let the roll be copied at his own table under his own eye, but would not let the book travel so much as to the harbour, telling them a book kept that many generations belonged to the house and not to any seal. The copy went to Muileann chaol; the book stayed. Known for the parish roll copied and not carried.

**Inis chrom** (Inis chrom). Founded 25 an Giblean, FE 1,601. A harbour town of the south-west coast. On the twenty-third day of am Màrt in the fiftieth year a storm tide came into its lower town and drowned the net-lofts and the rope-walk. The town did not ask the Crown for the rebuilding: its own carpenters raised both a second time on driven piles a fathom above the old floor, with timber floated down the Abhainn ghorm from the woods above Àth gharbh, and the work was finished before the autumn herring. The lofts stand so now, and the town's own telling of it is that the sea taught it once what it would not trouble to teach twice. Known for the lofts on piles.

**Inis ìseal** (Cnoc bheag). Founded 9 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,060. A town of the Hawk country in Siorrachd Cnoc bheag, whose altar Raonaid nic Iain's mother's mother kept before her. In an Cèitean of the thirty-fifth year the Hawk houses met in its hall and named Raonaid custodian of their own by standing up house by house, and Murchadh Ruadh gave her a white feather kept three generations in his house. The letter from Seann Skell refusing to own her was read once in the hall and put away, not burned. Here she wrote the Hawk's spoken order into a farm account-book, read it aloud once at the full moon of an t-Samhain, and locked it in the iron box that had held the altar's lamp-oil, wearing the key on a cord under her shawl. The shire's new seal of a white hawk was brought to it in the thirty-sixth year. Known for the Hawk's own custodian.

**Inis mhin** (Inis mhin). Founded 5 an Lùnastal, FE 2,644. A Tuathaich fishing harbour of the far north coast; boats were promised from its country to the second Fleadh na Mara at Cnoc ghorm. In the seventieth year, when the east-coast boats came north to the grounds the licence law kept for them and crowded the Tuathaich boats off the grounds nearest home, its boats took to the deep water beyond the northern isles, which no boat of that coast had fished in living memory for its roughness and the distance a crew had to keep from land. Two were lost the first year and none after, and before the next season was out its catch had passed Caol mhòr's. Known for the deep water beyond the northern isles.

**Inis thais** (Inis thais). Founded 21 an Lùnastal, GE 2,408. A harbour town of the south-west coast, where the new coin was slower to come than almost anywhere in the kingdom. Its merchants did not wait on the mint: through the sixth year they traded in chits written on the paper of the house of the Stone, whose name was old enough and trusted enough to stand in for coin, and when the coin came the chits were redeemed at the house's door, the house keeping back a tenth. A Ros bheag trader told Walter Hale that a tenth kept back by a name a man trusted was cheaper than a savings box kept by a name he did not. A Stone priest of the town heard the first reading of the Rite's written order. Its harbour court was well enough kept that the circuit justice's sitting there in the eighth year was brief. Known for the Stone's chits.

#### M

**Muileann chaol** (Cnoc bhàn). Founded 18 an t-Ògmhios, GE 3,218. A town east of the mountain, where the town's own custodians had kept rolls and bound books since before the Severance on planks above standing water in a cellar under the old grain-store. In the sixteenth year the council founded the Library here and named Ailean mac Iain, Ailean Leabhar, its first keeper; the council's minute-books and the humans' tithe ledgers came east to it, the copyists turned its dates into the civil calendar, and its keepers opened Leabhar nan Sloinnidhean, Leabhar nan Aithrisean and the table of the ages, counting the Age of Ailean apart. The royal chronicler kept her seat here from the eighteenth year rather than at the capital. The town was given a market charter in the seventeenth year, its first fair held in the Library's yard. Ailean was buried in a small ground behind the Library in the fortieth year, and Mòrag nic Coinnich kept it thirty years after, calling in the shire chests and building the new wing with its empty fourth floor. A chur san Leabharlann, to put it in the Library, was first said here. Known for the Library.

**Muileann chrom** (Muileann chrom). Founded 11 an Gearran, FE 1,556. The shunting town where the line from the Sloc Mòr meets the older line down to the ports. The council mended the coal line as far as it in the eighth year and no further, and the humans' own timetable, copied fair, was hung on a board at its terminus. The Rail Board laid new sidings here in the thirteenth year, and the shunting families, who had worked the humans' small engines, were counted apart on a roll of their own and housed in the rows nearest the lines; in the twenty-fourth year the rows had more children born than they had cradles for, among them Seachran and Brean. Calum mac Aonghais, called Calum Ruadh, a hewer of the town, won the first Còmhrag. When the Abhainn ìseal took the embankment in the thirty-fourth year the Moot sent it coal from the north. In the sixty-third year its yard families stopped the coal trains three days over a cut wage, with Dòmhnall Ruadh mac Ailein as their spokesman; the wage was restored and eleven men dismissed. Known for the shunting rows and the stopped trains.

**Muileann dhearg** (Muileann dhearg). Founded 30 an t-Sultain, LE 2. A town of narrow streets and spoil-stone chapels five miles from the great shaft, grown fat on the Sloc Mòr's overflow and working its own pits to keep the greater mine's yield steady. It took the most of the hungry families who came to the vein in the twelfth year, and its old druid hall was cut into lodgings over ground the Board had to mark as sound or not. The Rite's house here sent the old custodian who blessed the first train. It sent the largest company to the first Còmhrag. The Cill ghlas district under it, shut since the Rending of the humans' time, was reopened by the Board; on the first day of an t-Iuchar in the thirty-ninth year its galleries fell and thirty-one men died, and they were buried in a single ground at the edge of the town's yard, the custodian reading over each grave. By the fifty-seventh year its maor counted above sixty houses empty; its Fèidh hall, given back to the druid school, was locked by its last teacher, and its bell sold to Caol shean. Known for the fall of the thirty-one.

**Muileann dhomhain** (Muileann dhomhain). Founded 8 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,747. A mill town south-east of the capital, where the grain of three shires had gone to be ground since before the humans came, its miller-families' mark cut into a millstone before any shire kept a chest for a charter. In the fifty-third year, with the vein-towns' grain orders thinned by scarce coin, the mills began for the first time in any keeper's memory to grind bark for the tanners of the coast instead of grain, and the families kept their mark and changed the trade under it without asking the Board's leave. The eldest miller, a woman near seventy, told a passing clerk that a wheel does not know what is under it, and that the grain would come back once the vein-towns had coin to buy it. Known for the mills that turned to bark.

**Muileann fhionn** (Caol mhòr). Founded 12 an t-Iuchar, AE 23. The mill-town the humans built to watch the northern landing and left to whoever wanted the keeping of it. In the ninth year it was granted a market right for the inland country of the north-west, the second such right any northern town had been given, and the carpenters spent most of a month laying hurdles on the old common green, where mill hands had played ball, to pen the first market's beasts. The Tuathaich drovers of the hill farms, who had walked their stock the long way south, brought them here on set days instead, and from here the droves went on south by the old tracks to Ceann leathan; by midsummer the green stood full every market day and the innkeepers let every room. The vigil-keepers of the Grey Night answered to nobody south of it, and carters driving in from it heard the Cnoc ghorm bell before they saw the tower. Known for the cattle-market on the green.

**Muileann leathan** (Muileann leathan). Founded 24 an Giblean, GE 1,610. A weaving town of the northern moss, close enough across the moor from Doire ghlas that a boy could walk it before the school bell finished. Its householders came to the first sitting of the Moot. Daniel Frayne was a fisherman's son of the town and walked from it daily to Agnes Pike's byre in the fifteenth year; he kept a bindery here from the forty-eighth year on a mended cider-press, teaching young Tuathaich hands a craft the southern guilds would not, and bound the Moot's registers and Muileann shean's primers at his bench. The wool trains of the forty-first year set out from it for Muileann òg by the Carters' Road. The register of the hurt was bound here, and its second copy kept at a house in the town that no southern search ever troubled. The Rail Board's factors here refused the Doire ghlas mill's wagon in the fifty-ninth year and weighed its first bale onto the line in the sixtieth. Known for Daniel Frayne's bindery.

**Muileann mhin** (Muileann mhin). Founded 20 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,458. The lamp-making town of the vein country, whose forges turned out the greater part of every shaft-lamp the pits burned. Its lamp-makers were chartered as a guild in the fourteenth year, and set their mark, a flame struck over a hammer, on every lamp that left their sheds, so that the lamp carried the record of where it was made and under what oath; of all the guild marks the humans' traders had copied this one only. The carters of the coal line complained at every siding between it and Muileann chaol when, in the sixty-second year, the lamp-makers halved their making for want of coal to fire their forges, the coal reaching the town thinner and dearer each season. Shaft-lamps were lent from pit to pit after that, and the Guild of Hewers kept a minute-book of who lent to whom. Known for the flame over the hammer.

**Muileann naomh** (Muileann naomh). Founded 24 am Faoilleach, GE 2,986. The southernmost of the Hawk's houses, close by the coast and far south of Cnoc bheag. It did not wait on the reading: in the sixth year it sent word to Seann Skell that it would take the Rite's written order entire, whatever it proved to be, and hung in its doorway a bell cast new for the purpose, the first bell any hawk-house had hung, to ring at the Rite's measured burnings. It rang it that summer at the burning of the year before a small crowd in the lane. Dòmhnall mac Thormoid wrote to it in his own hand, the first letter of thanks he composed in his office, and sent it a last copy of the order made with more care than any other. It became a house of Òrd Bhrìde, the one hawk-house of its kind. Known for the first bell hung in a hawk-house.

**Muileann shean** (Muileann shean). Founded 1 an t-Samhain, FE 1,093. A town of the northern pits. In the fifty-ninth year, when the Guild of Hewers had bound no apprentices for two years, its maor opened a school for the sons and daughters of hewers the guild would not bind, to teach them to read, to reckon and to survey, reasoning that a hewer's child shut out of the pit might follow his father's trade from the surface with a chain in place of a pick. He wrote for primers to Daniel Frayne, who bound forty copies at his own bench and sent them north on the first cart. The benches passed thirty within the year, though several of the first pupils had already gone south to the ports to hire as chain-hands. Known for the school of hewers' children.

#### R

**Ros bheag** (Ros bheag). Founded 2 an Dàmhair, GE 1,274. A harbour of the west coast where Walter Hale clerked the humans' harbour office twenty years before the crossing closed. In the first year the council shut the humans' chapel here for good and carted its bell north, and households were walked north out of the town under guard; the bell hung at last in Cnoc ghorm's tower. Agnes Pike copied herring and salt tallies in its harbour agent's office for a dozen years. Its harbour would not give Mary Coyle's eleven boats its quay in the twenty-fifth year and sent them to a mooring buoy off the point. In the thirty-sixth year a coal-ship yard was opened here, and the eldest masters of Ros dhomhain lost their protest against it before the guild court. Known for Walter Hale's harbour, and the chapel bell.

**Ros dhomhain** (Ros dhomhain). Founded 19 an t-Iuchar, GE 1,694. The harbour below the capital on the lake shore, whose counting-house had come through the war with its shelves whole and whose garrison marched out under terms. In the third year Dùghall mac Iain took the humans' harbour-houses into the kingdom's keeping, and Ailean mac Iain spent eight months copying the humans' tariff out of eleven bound ledgers into Dia-thìris, saying exactly the old thing in the new tongue; the old tariff stood until the mint gave the council coin to take dues in. Its shipwrights took a guild charter in the fourteenth year and its guild court refused a Tuathaich rope-maker's plea in a single sitting. A shipwright of the town was the first name in the Library's reading-book. Its harbour clerk's corrected copy of Brìghde's crowning proclamation, Niall's name scored through, hangs under glass at the gate. In the thirty-sixth year its eldest masters lost their protest against Ros bheag's coal-ship yard before the guild court. Known for the tariff copied fair, and the proclamation under glass.

**Ros gheal** (Ros gheal). Founded 29 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,009. A fishing town of the north-central coast. In the twenty-fourth year it gave over its whole spring to a dock long enough to take three grain-ships abreast, for the Hawk country had begun to send its barley and oats down by water rather than by cart. The Hawk houses blessed the dock and asked a tithe of its dues; the shire's factor haggled them down to a twentieth and paid it, and has paid it every quarter since, so that the clerks of the town call the due simply the Hawk's and few of them can say why a fishing town owes a grain due to a bird that flies inland. Northern boats that landed fish at the new dock paid the same twentieth out of the Moot's harbour purse, which Mary Coyle raised in the Moot the first night she stood up to speak. Known for the grain dock and the Hawk's twentieth.

**Ros mhòr** (Caol mhòr). Founded 15 an t-Ògmhios, LE 432. A harbour of the northern coast, deep enough for a hull of any size the north was likely to want and far enough from the southern yards that no guild master troubled to ride up and ask under what charter it worked. Its boats sailed with Mary Coyle to Seann Bhral in the twenty-fifth year, and its fishermen walked to Walter Hale's burial. In am Faoilleach of the forty-first year the Tuathaich shipwrights turned out of the southern guild yards came together here to lay a keel on the open strand, Harry Marlow cutting it to the humans' old lines, low and full in the bow; the hull went up on evenings and Sabbaths, and by an Cèitean of the forty-second year there was a shed over the slip and the place was called a yard. Its first hull took the water clean, swifter than anything the south had launched in a long season. Known for the northern boatyard.

#### S

**Seann Bhral** (Seann Bhral). Founded 30 an Lùnastal, VE 1,005. The Seann Bhral of the southern coast, not the older town of the name in the west, which is a different town and always has been. In the twenty-fourth year it passed Ros dhomhain in the weight of fish landed and became the greatest fishing port of the kingdom; its curing-sheds, which had been four, became eleven and ran the whole length of the harbour, so that a stranger walking it after dark could follow the smell of the smoke from end to end. Fish from it went up to the capital through Ceann mhin's covered market. In the sixty-first and sixty-second years the three great pumps of the Sloc Mòr came to it by rail from above Achadh dhomhain to drain its new dry dock. Known for the curing-sheds, and the Sloc Mòr's pumps.

**Seann Bhral** (Baile àrsaidh). Founded 5 an Dàmhair, VE 196. The Seann Bhral of the west, on its harbour with the mud flats grey below the town wall and a scorpion carved over the old counting-house door that no one living can account for. Here on the ninth of an t-Sultain in the eighth year Eilidh nic Leòid gave the Leòid ruling, that land held under human title passes to the Crown and the working of it stays with the holders; it was cited in nearly every land case after. The western branch of the coal line was carried to it in the thirteenth year. Its house of Manannan, reckoned the oldest on the coast, turned away Mary Coyle's eleven boats in the twenty-fifth year: the sea was the same, the house was not. Ruairidh mac Phàdraig ruled here in the fifty-ninth year that the Rail Board is a carrier of the Crown and must carry for any who pay, the first ruling the Moot won. Àth leathan's hewers sent their coal to its factors by cart from the sixty-ninth year. Known for the Leòid ruling, and the ruling on the Rail Board.

**Seann Dunn** (Cnoc dhubh). Founded 5 an Cèitean, VE 642. A town of the east coast, past the last of the shires the Crown garrisoned closely, below which the Abhainn chaol meets the sea. The houses of the Seann Spioradan there had never had a hall of their own, only the hearth of whichever family kept the year's rite. In the twenty-second year forty households raised a common hall in a single season, working the stone by day, and roofed it before the first frost; it holds no image or carving, only two hearths. At its first naming forty heads of houses spoke the names of their dead, one old woman of the town reciting nine generations before her son finished the tenth, and the chronicler Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill rode east to watch. From the next year the hall sent the Library a copy of its naming every year, a little longer each time. In the sixty-eighth and sixty-ninth years the herring did not come to the grounds off the river mouth, and the town's boats went north. Known for the ancestors' hall.

**Seann Skell** (Seann Skell). Founded 29 am Faoilleach, GE 2,664. The Seann Skell of the southern coast, not the harbour of the west, where the Rite's greatest house stands in a hall with blackened beams. In the sixth year Dòmhnall mac Thormoid was seated here as the first high custodian of Òrd Bhrìde, and here he wrote the Rite's first order of worship, read aloud near the end of am Faoilleach to eleven custodians and a scattering of hearth-keepers and a Stone priest; he kept every letter the Rite sent or received in a plain ledger. From here went the copies of the order, and the refusals came back to it: the Hawk houses' letter of the sixth year and, in the thirty-fifth, the three-line letter refusing to own Raonaid nic Iain. In the forty-seventh year its council read the Hawk houses of Cnoc bheag their terms a seventh time, and they stood. Known for the high custodian's house and the order of worship.

**Seann Skell** (Seann Skell). Founded 6 an Gearran, VE 173. The humans' great harbour of the west, on the coast below the capes, where the fishing fleets still came in under a flag they had never learned to read and the old harbour bell rang the hours by a humans' clock. In the second year Ailean mac Iain found in its counting-house eleven district surveys behind a locked grating, every field about the town walked and numbered, and boxed them apart for the council; from them the shires were drawn. An Sireadh came home to its quay in the third year after sixteen days north-about and no land, and the priests of Manannan said over her return the prayer they had said over her going, that the sea be kept shut. Its innkeeper told Ailean of Niall's crowning. The ship lay careened here that winter. It is not the Seann Skell of the southern coast, where the Rite's high custodian sits, and the record keeps the two apart as west and south. Known for the district surveys, and An Sireadh's berth.

**Seann Tarr** (Muileann bheag). Founded 30 an Cèitean, VE 884. A town of the northern coast where the coal line does not run, whose rope-walks take their hemp from the fields about Doire uaine and Achadh naomh by cart roads older than the survey lines. In the fifty-third year the restored custom chartered its rope-makers as a guild, the last trade the humans never touched to be given a charter of its own. Asked to send the charter south to be filed, the shire keeper answered that it would stay in the shire's own chest, as every paper of the shire had stayed since the chest was locked, and sent south a list of what the chest held and no more. When the Library called in the shire chests in the sixty-sixth year the old keeper, who had held the key since before Mòrag nic Coinnich was born, burned the chest rather than send it, met the clerks at the gate the next morning with the smoke still on his coat, and paid the council's fine without argument or apology. It is the one shire record of the calling-in the Library never read. Known for the chest that was burned.

**Seann Toll** (Seann Toll). Founded 8 an t-Samhain, VE 1,033. A town of the north that sent its chest to the Library willingly in the sixty-seventh year and asked, as no shire before it had, for a copy of everything the chest held to be returned. Mòrag nic Coinnich's clerks made the copy, a full transcription bound in the same hand and set beside the original before either left the shire's hall, and the shire's copy became the pattern every later copy the Library made was cut to. Known for the pattern copy.

**Seann Vell** (Ros dhomhain). Founded 29 an Lùnastal, GE 3,560. A town of the capital shore. In the twenty-seventh year its glass-houses, which had lately begun blowing small flasks, found a trade no one had planned for them: the women of the town filled the flasks with waters they distilled themselves from bog-myrtle and meadowsweet and heather honey and sold them by the dozen, and within a few years scent was sold in every market town. A cloth trader out of the town, putting in at Cuan shean, offered Harry Marlow a northern passage in the fourteenth year, which Harry refused. Two of its masons drove and cemented the iron reef post at Tobar dhearg for Ciorstaidh nic Artair in the fifty-fifth year, working only the hour either side of the ebb. The glass-houses still stand, and the scent trade still runs from them. Known for the scent-makers' flasks.

#### T

**Tobar dhìreach** (Cnoc bhàn). Founded 25 an t-Iuchar, VE 42. A village a few miles from the Library, on the stream below it. In the eighteenth year a family of millers who had not grain enough to keep three wheels busy built a paper-mill here instead, and the Library's copyists spoke of its first sheets before they had them in hand. Forty quires of its paper went up to Muileann chaol on a borrowed cart, better and cheaper, the copyists judged, than anything the council's stationers had sent, and within the year near enough every sheet the Library used came from the one stream; nearly every page of the royal chronicle in this age is written on its paper. The road east past it smells of wet paper before the mill comes in sight. Known for the paper-mill.
